title: Are splay trees dynamically optimal?
importance_reason: Dynamic optimality is a central benchmark for adaptive data structures: one simple online BST would compete with every offline BST on every access sequence.
focus_reason: Dynamic optimality is a central benchmark for adaptive data structures: one simple online BST would compete with every offline BST on every access sequence.
formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let OPT(X) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree T₀ and every X, $\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)$? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.
definitions: Keys are [n]={1,…,n}, n≥1, ordered by their integer values. A binary search tree has one node per key, every key in a left subtree smaller than its root and every key in a right subtree larger. A rotation on a parent-child edge exchanges those two nodes while reattaching the intermediate subtree so that the order is preserved. To splay a requested key x, repeatedly apply the following bottom-up rule until x is root. If its parent is root, rotate the edge from x to its parent (zig). Otherwise let p be its parent and g its grandparent. If x and p are both left children or both right children, first rotate p above g and then x above p (zig-zig). Otherwise rotate x above p and then x above g (zig-zag). Each access costs one plus its number of rotations. The tree after the access is the initial tree for the next access. For a finite sequence X∈[n]*, cost_splay(X;T₀) is the sum of these costs starting from T₀. A comparator execution may start with any tree, knows X in full, and serves each request by any finite sequence of parent-child rotations anywhere in the current tree whose final root is the requested key. Its cost is the same one-plus-rotations sum. OPT(X) is the minimum cost over all such initial trees and executions; it is zero for the empty sequence. There are no insertions, deletions or additional node operations. This root-BST cost convention is the one used in the saved source, with the additive n term accounting for the initial tree.
answer_criterion: Prove that one finite constant C bounds cost_splay(X;T₀)/(OPT(X)+n) for all n, all initial trees T₀ and all finite access sequences X, or prove that this ratio is unbounded over those inputs. A counterexample to a particular proposed value of C alone does not refute the universal-constant claim.
context:
A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost Θ(n), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by O((OPT(X)+n) log log n · log² log log n). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.
why: It asks whether a simple local adjustment rule can match every legal strategy with complete knowledge of the future. The issue is fundamental to instance-sensitive data structures: success would replace a growing competitive penalty by a constant for all access patterns. A counterexample would identify a limitation of splaying that its many separate locality guarantees fail to reveal.
status_note: The July 2026 primary preprint gives a growing competitive factor and still distinguishes its theorem from constant dynamic optimality. The primary text and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026; no complete resolution was found in that check. This review does not independently verify the new proof.
progress: 1985 / background: Splaying has logarithmic amortized access cost and stronger guarantees for useful special patterns. These do not establish competitiveness against an arbitrary changing offline tree. | 2007: Tango trees give an online BST with an $O(\log\log n)$ competitive ratio. This result is for a different data structure and does not settle splaying. | 2026-07-20: The preprint proves $O((\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\log\log n\,\log^2\log\log n)$ total splay cost. Theorem 1 includes the initialization term explicitly. Constant competitiveness remains the target.
working_summary: Splay trees reorganize a binary search tree after each access using local rotations. The question asks whether this simple rule is always within a constant factor of the best tree strategy that knows the entire request sequence. An additive linear allowance pays for the initial tree. Frequency and locality guarantees cover useful patterns but do not establish this universal comparison. Understanding this gap would show whether local adaptation can exploit every advantage available to an offline search tree.

title: Expected linear-time integer sorting for every word length
importance_reason: A foundational algorithmic primitive whose optimal complexity tests the computational power of the word RAM and would affect many tasks built on ordering integer keys.
focus_reason: A foundational algorithmic primitive whose optimal complexity tests the computational power of the word RAM and would affect many tasks built on ordering integer keys.
formal: Does there exist a uniform Las Vegas word-RAM algorithm and a constant C such that, for every n≥2, every integer word length w≥⌈log₂(n+1)⌉, and every list x₁,…,xₙ∈{0,…,2ʷ−1}, the algorithm outputs the list in nondecreasing order with expected running time at most Cn?
definitions: The input occupies n words, with one unsigned w-bit key per word; repeated keys are allowed. The output must contain exactly the input multiset in nondecreasing numerical order, with no stability requirement. The machine is sequential and has w-bit data registers and random-access memory. Unit-cost operations are reads and writes, comparisons, branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication of two words with the product returned in two words, quotient and remainder of two words with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and left or right shifts by a word-specified amount. Shifted-out bits are discarded, and shifts by at least w return zero. Addresses may use a constant number of words to index polynomially many memory cells; all address computation is charged. An operation can generate one fresh independent uniform w-bit random word. These are the only primitive operations; arbitrary-length arithmetic, a built-in sorting operation and free tables are unavailable. All preprocessing, memory initialization performed by the algorithm, and output writes count. A fixed finite program receives n and w; it may select methods according to their values but has no advice depending on them. Las Vegas means every terminating computation is correct and the algorithm terminates with probability one. Expectation is over the internal random choices for each fixed input. C must be independent of both n and w, including when w grows with n.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a single uniform, always-correct Las Vegas program whose expected running time is at most Cn on every admissible (n,w,input), for one C independent of n and w. A negative answer must show that every such sorting program has unbounded expected-time/n ratio over these inputs. A lower bound only for comparison sorting, deterministic programs, or a different word instruction set does not establish that negation.
context:
Integer sorting asks how much of the cost of comparison sorting comes from treating keys as indivisible objects. If only comparisons are allowed, identifying one of n! possible orders needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Word operations can inspect several bits at once, compute bucket addresses and manipulate packed fields. The comparison decision-tree lower bound therefore does not rule out a linear number of word operations.

The relevant input size is n words, not nw individual bits. Reading one entire word is a unit operation regardless of w, but reading a whole list is still n operations. Conversely, the machine cannot concatenate all n keys into an nw-bit integer and then treat that enormous object as one register. Fixing the register width and the permitted instructions is essential; unrestricted unit-cost arithmetic would answer a different question.

Simple radix sorting already handles w=O(log n). Divide each key into digits of about log₂n bits, and sort stably by one digit at a time using counting arrays of size O(n). There are O(1+w/log n) passes, giving O(n(1+w/log n)) time. For any fixed polynomial-size universe this is linear. If w=(log n)^{3/2}, however, that same argument takes about √log n passes and does not prove the desired bound.

Surprisingly, very large words also admit linear expected time. Belazzougui, Brodal and Nielsen achieve this for w=Ω((log n)² log log n), improving an earlier sufficiently-large-word regime. Their construction replaces full keys by shorter signatures and processes many packed fields with a single word operation. Larger keys bring more possible values, but the larger machine words simultaneously provide more internal parallelism. The difficult range sits between the easy radix regime and the proven large-word regime.

The best general expected upper bound retained in the sources is Han and Thorup’s O(n√log log n), independent of word length. It is substantially below n log n, but the square-root iterated-log factor still grows without bound. The problem asks whether this remaining overhead can be removed completely. An upper bound with any unbounded overhead factor does not imply the stated linear bound.

Han also gives deterministic O(n log log n) sorting with linear space. This is a different guarantee: it bounds every computation without random choices. The present question allows randomization and asks only for an expected linear bound on every input. A deterministic linear-time algorithm would answer it affirmatively, while a lower bound confined to deterministic algorithms would not answer it negatively.

Zero error is explicit because sorting has a convenient final check but not every failure mode is detected by checking adjacent comparisons alone. A proposed randomized procedure must preserve the input multiset as well as produce a sorted sequence. The large-word construction uses a verifiable randomized sorting procedure and repeats when needed to obtain a Las Vegas guarantee. This is different from relying on a typical distribution of input keys: adversarially selected keys are permitted here.

Uniformity also prevents the missing work from being hidden in preprocessing. An enormous lookup table listing answers for all possible word patterns cannot be supplied for free. Any table needed for a particular n and w must be constructed within the expected time budget. Likewise, treating a concrete machine’s 64-bit width as an immutable constant does not address the asymptotic problem, where n and w vary together.

The question is fundamental because sorting supplies order to many other algorithmic tasks: grouping equal identifiers, scanning consecutive values, merging collections and organizing events. An affirmative answer would give a clean linear-time primitive across the whole word-RAM range. A negative answer would explain a basic limitation of word arithmetic that is invisible to ordinary comparison-counting arguments. The 2025 teaching source still explicitly presents the unrestricted linear-time target as open.
why: A basic limit on what word-level arithmetic can accomplish beyond comparisons. The challenge is a uniform bound across all word lengths, rather than the already solved polynomial-universe or sufficiently-large-word cases.
status_note: The checked primary bounds and the CMU Spring 2025 source leave expected linear-time sorting across all word lengths open. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no result settling this full target. Recent parallel sorting results for keys in [n] concern a restricted universe and a different performance model.
progress: 2002: Han–Thorup achieve O(n√log log n) expected time and linear space for arbitrary word-sized integer keys. | 2004: Han’s journal paper gives deterministic O(n log log n) time and linear space, following STOC 2002. | 2014: Belazzougui–Brodal–Nielsen extend expected linear time to w=Ω((log n)² log log n). | 2025: The CMU integer-sorting lecture retains linear sorting for arbitrary word lengths as an open question and distinguishes polynomial-size universes.
working_summary: Integer sorting can inspect the bits of keys instead of treating them only as objects to compare. The question asks for one always-correct randomized word-RAM algorithm taking expected linear time for every permitted word length. The constant must remain uniform when keys occupy much more than logarithmically many bits. Ordinary radix sorting handles smaller universes but its number of passes can grow. This tests whether powerful word operations can completely remove the asymptotic overhead of ordering an arbitrary list of machine words.

title: An explicit static problem requiring superlogarithmically many cell probes
importance_reason: A model-wide challenge connecting algorithms, communication complexity, pseudorandomness and circuit lower bounds, with implications beyond any single geometric or graph problem.
focus_reason: A model-wide challenge connecting algorithms, communication complexity, pseudorandomness and circuit lower bounds, with implications beyond any single geometric or graph problem.
formal: Does there exist a fixed integer k≥2 and a uniformly polynomial-time computable family of Boolean functions F_n on an n-word database and a k⌈log₂ n⌉-bit query such that its optimal deterministic static cell-probe query complexity t*F(n), with word size ⌈4log₂ n⌉ bits and n⌈log₂ n⌉² memory cells, satisfies t*F(n)/log₂ n→∞ as n→∞?
definitions: For each integer n≥2 put w=⌈4log₂ n⌉ and s=n⌈log₂ n⌉². A database is D∈({0,1}^w)^n, a query is q∈{0,1}^{k⌈log₂ n⌉}, and F_n(D,q)∈{0,1}. Explicit means that a single deterministic Turing machine computes F_n(D,q), given (1^n,D,q), in time polynomial in n; no advice is allowed in this definition. A data structure may preprocess D by any map E_n into s cells of w bits each. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and this encoding may be nonlinear and nonuniform. For each query, a deterministic adaptive decision tree reads cells, choosing the next address from the query and previously read contents, and must output F_n(D,q) exactly for every database. Computation between probes is free. The trees may depend on n, F and the query, but their only access to D is through E_n(D). Each query starts without free database-dependent private information; memory is static and read-only. Define t*F(n) as the minimum, over all such encodings and trees, of the maximum number of probes over all D and q. All memory cells count toward s. This card fixes a near-linear-space, short-query, one-bit-answer specialization of the broader static lower-bound challenge; it does not assert equivalence to every space or word-size variant.
answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed k and admissible uniform family F satisfy: for every real B>0 there is N such that t*F(n)>B log₂ n for every n≥N. Alternatively, prove the exact negation: for every fixed k and every admissible family F, there is a finite B>0 such that t*F(n)≤B log₂ n for arbitrarily large n. In particular, the negative answer need not establish an O(log n) bound for all sufficiently large n.
context:
A static data structure pays an initial cost to organize a database and then answers queries against that fixed information. In the cell-probe model, only the number of memory cells read during a query matters. The query algorithm has unlimited computational power between reads. Consequently, a lower bound must identify information that cannot be made locally accessible even by an ingenious encoding; showing that a particular search procedure or arithmetic computation is slow is insufficient.

The space allowance is central. With enough space, preprocessing could store every answer in a table, giving constant-probe queries. Here there are at least n² possible queries, while the stored representation has only O(n log³ n) bits. Conversely, the database itself fits in n cells, so reading all n cells always suffices. The target therefore lies strictly between two elementary strategies: an unrestricted table with one entry for every possible query exceeds the budget, but the problem is always solvable without a computational-time obstruction.

The one-bit answer avoids obtaining a large probe bound merely because the output contains many independent bits. The query length is O(log n), with a fixed constant k. Increasing the query length to n bits can create communication lower bounds of an entirely different magnitude. Likewise, allowing only linear combinations in preprocessing or forbidding adaptive reads changes the collection of encodings and algorithms that a lower bound must defeat.

Koucký, Loff, Molli and Saks formulate the broad static challenge explicitly as Open Problem 1.1. Away from storage that is extremely close to the information-theoretic minimum, familiar general lower-bound approaches have not exceeded the logarithm of the number of queries. The present card turns this challenge into one yes/no proposition by fixing the word size, storage overhead, output alphabet and uniform meaning of an explicit problem. Its stricter conventions should be kept in mind when transferring results from a survey.

Korten, Pitassi and Impagliazzo obtain stronger tradeoffs through local pseudorandom generators. Their improvements are especially informative when the number of probes is small and the cells contain few bits. Their general bound includes an explicit dependence on word size. A gain proved for one-bit cells therefore cannot simply be carried over unchanged to Θ(log n)-bit words. These results advance the tradeoff frontier without proving the superlogarithmic lower bound at the parameters fixed here.

Ko’s 2025 result illustrates another important parameter distinction. For random linear operators with m possible row queries, the lower bound is Ω(min{log(m/s), n/log s}) in a bit-cell formulation. It can exceed log n when the number m of queries grows sufficiently rapidly. With only polynomially many queries, the first term is at most O(log n). The random choice of an operator also does not by itself supply the uniformly polynomial-time explicit family required in this card.

The STOC 2026 natural-proofs paper supplies conditional obstacles to a broad class of proof methods. Such a proof recognizes a sufficiently large, efficiently testable property of function tables that implies data-structure hardness; conjectured local pseudorandom functions would obstruct that recognition. This is not an unconditional impossibility theorem for stronger lower bounds. The authors’ errata also flag a new sampling method whose coverage had not been checked and explain why a previously cited rigidity consequence no longer constitutes an unachieved barrier.

Static and dynamic memory have different sources of hardness. Larsen, Weinstein and Yu crossed the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean problems, where updates limit how information can be reorganized. Ko’s March 2026 preprint claims a further Ω((log n/log log n)²) bound for a dynamic multiphase problem. Those update constraints are absent here: the whole database may be preprocessed without a time bound before any query arrives. Neither dynamic result automatically gives the requested static lower bound.

A positive solution would identify a uniformly computable query whose information cannot be recovered with only logarithmically many reads, even after unrestricted preprocessing. This separates a memory-access bottleneck from the running time of known implementations. The limit in the statement is stronger than an arbitrarily large ratio on an infinite subsequence: the ratio must eventually exceed each fixed constant and remain above it. That distinction also affects the exact negative answer.
why: A central unconditional lower-bound bottleneck for data structures: establish that a short, explicitly defined static query fundamentally needs more than logarithmically many memory accesses despite unrestricted preprocessing.
status_note: Primary sources and later-result searches checked on 11 September 2026 did not supply a resolution of the stated static specialization. The STOC 2026 paper retains the broader static barrier as Open Problem 1.1. The fixed near-linear space, short-query Boolean output and uniform polynomial-time family are an expressly recorded specialization; conditional proof barriers and bounds for dynamic memory or superpolynomial query sets do not resolve it.
progress: 2018: Larsen–Weinstein–Yu cross the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean data structures; the journal version appeared in 2020. This does not settle the static question. | 2025-05-28: Revision 1 of Korten–Pitassi–Impagliazzo improves cell-probe space/time tradeoffs using local PRGs and studies conditional barriers. | 2025-10-22: Ko proves stronger bit-cell bounds for random linear operators, including regimes with superpolynomially many queries. | 2026-03-26: Ko’s preprint claims a nearly log-squared lower bound for dynamic Boolean multiphase problems. No independent proof audit of that claim is supplied here. | 2026-06: Koucký–Loff–Molli–Saks appears at STOC 2026, with conditional natural-proofs barriers and an explicit statement of the static challenge.
working_summary: A static data structure preprocesses a database and later answers queries by reading stored memory cells. This question seeks an explicitly computable Boolean query problem forcing more than logarithmically many reads despite unrestricted preprocessing. The saved formulation fixes short queries, logarithmic word size, near-linear space, and deterministic adaptive access. Free computation between reads makes this an information-access lower bound. Such an example would expose a fundamental limit on making useful information locally accessible through clever storage alone.

title: Can a static dictionary be built deterministically in linear time?
importance_reason: A foundational derandomization question for exact lookup: linear construction, linear storage and constant worst-case queries would give many algorithms an optimal deterministic dictionary primitive. The 2024 and 2026 string-indexing applications show concrete dependencies on dictionary construction costs.
focus_reason: Optimal deterministic construction of a basic dictionary tests whether randomness is necessary for linear preprocessing with constant-time queries.
formal: Is the following proposition true? For every fixed integer d≥1 there are uniform deterministic construction and query programs A_d,Q_d and a constant C_d≥1 such that, for every n≥2, every word length ⌈log₂(n+1)⌉≤w≤d⌈log₂(n+1)⌉, and every n-record input with distinct w-bit integer keys and w-bit values, A_d builds a static dictionary in at most C_d n operations and C_d n words of total space, and Q_d answers every membership-and-value query in at most C_d operations.
definitions: The universe is U_w={0,…,2ʷ−1}. An input is a list of n pairs (x_i,v_i)∈U_w×U_w with pairwise distinct x_i and arbitrary v_i; the input order is unrestricted. On query q∈U_w the output is (1,v_i) if q=x_i and (0,0) if q is absent. The stored set and values do not change after construction. The machine is a sequential word RAM with w-bit registers and cells. The primitive unit-cost instructions are memory reads and writes, copies, comparisons, conditional branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication returning the full product in two words, integer quotient and remainder of two words with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts. A shift by at least w returns zero; otherwise shifted-out bits are discarded. Addresses may occupy a fixed number of words, and all operations computing them are charged. Programs have finitely many instructions and constants, may receive n and w, and contain no input-size or word-size advice, random instruction, free table or special hashing primitive. Every table, parameter computation, memory initialization and output write performed by construction counts toward its time; input storage, the resulting dictionary and temporary storage count toward its space. Query reads the constructed representation and may use temporary workspace, with every operation charged; all retained information about the input is in the counted representation. The query must be correct on every q, including absent keys. Programs and constants may depend on d but not on n, w, the input or query. This spells out the saved w=Θ(log n) convention as a claim for every fixed polynomial-size universe; Pagh’s broader arbitrary-word-length formulation is not asserted equivalent here.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition with deterministic algorithms meeting all three bounds for every fixed d, or disprove it for at least one fixed d. The negation says that no pair of admissible correct programs has simultaneously linear worst-case construction time, linear total space and constant worst-case query time for all inputs in that word-length range. Failure of a particular hash family, an average-input lower bound, or a lower bound in a comparison-only model is not that negation.
context:
A dictionary is an exact lookup table for a sparse set of keys. For example, records (12,5), (47,9) and (103,2) require the answers 9 on key 47 and absent on key 48. The values need not be unique. The problem is to prepare a representation in time proportional to the number of records and then answer every lookup in a bounded number of machine steps, regardless of whether the key is present.

Direct addressing uses the key itself as an array index. This achieves constant lookup time, but an array for a universe of n² possible keys occupies n² cells even if only n keys are present. Such space is outside the target. At the opposite extreme, keeping the keys in sorted order uses linear space but ordinary binary search needs logarithmically many comparisons. These examples show why construction, storage and query time must be required simultaneously.

Randomized perfect hashing already gives linear expected construction time, linear storage and constant worst-case lookup time. The randomness concerns finding a suitable representation during construction; once a valid dictionary has been built, lookup can be exact and have a worst-case bound. Thus the open issue is not whether every query can avoid probabilistic errors, but whether the construction time can be bounded linearly without any random choices.

Pagh obtained deterministic O(n log n) construction for logarithmic-size words. Ružić subsequently related construction cost to integer sorting with only a log log n overhead. The latter is a much smaller overhead, but it still grows with n. The source question asks for its complete removal while retaining the other two guarantees. A representation whose existence is known but whose parameters take longer to find does not meet the construction requirement.

The dependence on word length matters even when keys occupy one machine word. Here a fixed polynomial-size universe is intended: the constant relating w to log n is fixed before the inputs vary. Constants in the guarantees may depend on that fixed bound. This is the logarithmic-word version already selected for this card; it does not silently claim a solution for word lengths growing faster than log n.

Uniformity also matters. Earlier dictionary results sometimes supplied word-size-dependent constants at no construction cost. The present formulation charges for computing every table and parameter that is not part of a fixed program. A one-time computation on a particular physical machine cannot disappear from an asymptotic bound that covers arbitrarily large inputs.

The dependency remains visible in modern applications. The 2024 internal-pattern-matching paper uses constant-time deterministic dictionaries with a general O(m(log log m)²) construction bound for a dictionary of size m, and treats very small dictionaries separately. The surrounding text length can be much larger than m, so that application must not be read as fixing word length to Θ(log m). Kosolobov’s 2026 compressed index likewise records a slowdown when dictionary randomness is removed.

These applications explain the scientific stakes: a basic lookup operation can determine whether a larger construction remains deterministic within its intended time bound. The 2026 index is evidence that the issue remains useful, rather than a theorem resolving this static linear-construction question.
why: Exact constant-time lookup is a basic component of many larger data structures. The unresolved cost is obtaining the representation deterministically in optimal time, so a resolution would settle whether randomness is essential to this combination of construction, storage and lookup guarantees.
status_note: The primary dictionary results, later applications and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No complete resolution of the specified logarithmic-word deterministic construction target was found. The accessible 2025 draft Slightly more practical deterministic static dictionaries was also inspected; it contains unfinished statements and does not claim the required linear construction, so it is not used to certify a new bound.
progress: 1999-12: Pagh gives deterministic O(n log n) construction with linear space and constant lookup for w=O(log n); the paper contrasts this with randomized expected linear construction. | 2008: Ružić brings deterministic construction within a log log n factor of sorting time while retaining linear space and constant lookup. | 2024-10-14: The internal-pattern-matching journal paper uses general deterministic dictionaries with O(m(log log m)²) construction and distinguishes restricted small instances. | 2026: Kosolobov’s CPM paper records a construction slowdown when replacing randomized dictionaries in a compressed index. This is an application, not a solution of the present static target.
working_summary: A static dictionary stores distinct integer keys together with associated values and supports exact membership queries. The question asks for deterministic linear-time construction, linear space, and constant worst-case query time on the stated word RAM. All preprocessing work must be included in the construction bound. Random hashing motivates the desired efficiency but does not itself provide a deterministic construction. A solution would give other algorithms a dependable dictionary primitive without making their preprocessing randomized or increasing their asymptotic running time.

title: Can all pairwise sums X+Y be sorted in quadratic time?
importance_reason: A long-standing structured sorting question: only 2n real parameters generate n² values, yet converting known comparison savings into optimal total time remains unresolved. Documented geometric reductions and connections to convolution give the question significance beyond one sorting routine.
focus_reason: Sorting all pairwise sums is a classical structured comparison problem: the output is quadratic, but exploiting the inherited order with equally efficient total computation remains the target. It adds real-key comparison algorithms alongside word-RAM integer sorting and data structures.
formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic real-RAM algorithm A and a constant C such that, for every integer n≥2 and every X=(x₁,…,xₙ), Y=(y₁,…,yₙ)∈ℝⁿ, A outputs a permutation ((i₁,j₁),…,(i_{n²},j_{n²})) of [n]×[n] satisfying x_{i_r}+y_{j_r}≤x_{i_{r+1}}+y_{j_{r+1}} for 1≤r<n², in at most Cn² unit-cost operations?
definitions: The input consists of n and the 2n exact real numbers in random-access arrays; no sortedness, distinctness, integrality or magnitude bound is promised. All n² index pairs must occur once in the output, including pairs with equal sums. Ties may appear in any order. A real RAM has exact real registers and cells, supporting copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero reals and comparisons at unit cost. A fixed finite program may use rational constants, with no advice depending on n. It also has integer registers and cells of b=d⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits for some fixed integer d≥3 chosen with the algorithm. Integer instructions are copy, comparison, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2ᵇ, quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts; shifts by at least b return zero. Integer addresses access individual real or integer cells, and each read or write costs one operation. Integer-to-real conversion is permitted, but real-to-integer conversion, floor on reals, extraction of their bits and arbitrary-precision integer operations are not primitives. Memory starts empty apart from the input and fixed program constants; all preprocessing, table construction, address computation and output writes are charged. The algorithm must halt correctly on every input and uses no randomness. Constants C and d are independent of n and of the real values. This is the quadratic-time real-RAM version explicitly asked in the cited necklace paper and identified as the main target in TOPP. Indexed multiset output resolves possible equal sums; allowing repeated input entries does not change the target, since repetitions can be grouped by O(n log n) comparison sorting and expanded within the output budget.
answer_criterion: Give one uniform deterministic program with a proof of exact output correctness and the O(n²) worst-case total-time bound for every real input, or prove that no such program exists in the specified model. Equivalently, a negative answer shows that every correct program has unbounded worst-case running-time/n² ratio. Neither a bound only on the number of comparisons nor an algorithm restricted to bounded integers resolves this claim.
context:
The input is small compared with the output. For X=(0,3) and Y=(1,4), the four indexed sums are 1,4,4,7. Both occurrences of 4 remain in the sorted output because they come from different pairs. In general there are n² output entries, but only 2n independent input numbers. This strong dependence is the reason ordinary sorting bounds for n² unrelated numbers may be wasteful.

If the two input lists are already sorted, the matrix M_ij=x_i+y_j increases along every row and every column. That information alone does not determine the relative order of every two cells: a later row may contain an entry smaller than an entry in an earlier row. Moreover, sum matrices satisfy additional equalities such as M_ij+M_kl=M_il+M_kj. The question concerns the full algebraic structure, not just arbitrary matrices with sorted rows and columns.

Explicitly generating and comparison-sorting all n² sums takes O(n² log n) time. Writing the required output already takes Ω(n²) operations, so quadratic time would match the output-size lower bound. TOPP identifies removal of the logarithmic factor as the main question. The real-valued input convention avoids assuming a small integer universe, where different operations can change the complexity.

Fredman proved that O(n²) comparisons suffice. A decision tree specifies the next comparison after every possible history of answers and places the sorted order at its leaves. Its depth counts comparisons, but it does not charge for constructing the tree or determining the next comparison from a succinct program. Consequently, a short decision tree does not automatically become an equally fast uniform algorithm.

Lambert and Steiger–Streinu made the comparison savings algorithmic while retaining O(n² log n) total running time. This is a concrete separation between counting tests and charging the bookkeeping that organizes them. The target includes both costs, as well as all preprocessing and output writes.

Kane, Lovett and Moran later obtained O(n log² n) decision-tree depth by allowing tests involving differences of sums; each such linear test uses at most eight input coordinates. Those tests are more expressive than simply comparing two entries of X+Y. The subquadratic depth does not conflict with the quadratic output-size lower bound, because decision-tree depth does not charge for writing the output.

Related convolution problems ask only for a minimum, maximum or median on each antidiagonal of the sum matrix. These requests can have subquadratic algorithms without supplying a complete sorted list of all entries. The necklace-alignment paper explicitly records this distinction and the unresolved quadratic-time real-RAM question.

The importance of the question extends beyond sorting. Pairwise sums describe many ordered geometric events, and TOPP records reductions from this sorting task to polygon-containment and arrangement-ordering problems. A resolution would clarify how much algorithmic work can be saved when a large output is generated from a much smaller collection of numerical parameters.
why: This is a basic test of whether algebraic dependence among many sortable objects can be exploited with no overhead beyond writing them down. It also makes the distinction between short comparison decision trees and fast uniform algorithms unusually concrete.
status_note: TOPP Problem 41, primary comparison and real-RAM sources, and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No uniform quadratic-time algorithm or matching impossibility result for the stated real-valued problem was found. The 2017/2018 decision-tree result does not settle total time. This is a source review, not an independent proof audit.
progress: 1976: Fredman proves an O(n²) comparison bound for sorting X+Y; this does not provide quadratic total running time. | 1992–1995: Lambert and Steiger–Streinu give algorithms combining O(n²) comparisons with O(n² log n) total time. | 2014: The necklace/convolution paper explicitly retains quadratic-time sorting on the real RAM as open while proving faster algorithms for more limited convolution outputs. | 2017 / STOC 2018: Kane–Lovett–Moran obtain O(n log² n) depth using 8-sparse linear tests. The bound concerns decision-tree queries and excludes output and general computational costs.
working_summary: Given two lists of n numbers, form every sum consisting of one number from each list. The task is to sort these quadratically many sums as quickly as possible. They have substantial inherited order, so they are not an arbitrary collection of unrelated values. The source distinguishes having few comparisons from implementing those comparisons with equally small total running time. Removing avoidable overhead would improve both structured sorting and geometric problems whose events are ordered by pairwise sums.

title: Do splay trees support deque operations in constant amortized time?
importance_reason: A longstanding concrete stress test for splay-tree adaptivity, already on the elementary deque interface; less sweeping than dynamic optimality.
formal: Start from an arbitrary binary search tree containing $n$ ordered keys, and perform $m$ legal double-ended queue operations. Insert-min creates a new minimum as the root with the old tree as its right child; insert-max is symmetric. Delete-min splays the minimum to the root, removes it, and keeps its right subtree; delete-max is symmetric. Is the total number of primitive pointer operations and rotations always $O(n+m)$, with a universal constant? This is Tarjan’s deque conjecture for the specified splay implementation.
definitions: Splaying uses the standard zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rules. Deletions are allowed only on a nonempty tree, and an inserted key must be outside the current key range at the specified end. Amortized cost is a bound on the total sequence, not a worst-case guarantee for each deletion. The initial tree may have any shape.
answer_criterion: Prove a universal O(n+m) total bound for the specified splay implementation, or prove that the ratio between total cost and n+m is unbounded over legal initial trees and operation sequences.
context:
A deque allows insertion and deletion at either end of a sequence. A linked representation can implement this abstract interface in constant time per operation. The conjecture concerns what happens when the same interface is implemented by a self-adjusting search tree: it asks whether the tree automatically achieves the linear total cost available for this restricted workload.

Deleting the minimum of a long left spine can require many rotations in a single operation. That does not disprove the conjecture, because the initial tree contributes an additive budget proportional to its size. The real difficulty is to understand whether alternating insertions and deletions at opposite ends can repeatedly rebuild expensive configurations.

For a concrete contrast, deleting keys in increasing order is a sequential-access pattern. A deque workload can switch ends after every operation and introduce new extreme keys between deletions. A bound for one monotone scan therefore does not immediately control this more flexible sequence.

The known total bound has an iterated inverse-Ackermann factor, which grows extraordinarily slowly but is asymptotically unbounded. Removing it would answer a structural question about how rotations reuse earlier work. This is a focused subproblem of the broader study of splaying, with updates included explicitly rather than only searches.
why: I include this because it tests whether one general-purpose adaptive representation can recognize a workload whose optimal cost is linear. The remaining gap is tiny numerically but significant mathematically: a proof would explain why expensive local restructuring cannot accumulate across arbitrary alternations of the two ends.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the July 2026 splay result. The conjecture asks for linear total cost under insertions and deletions at either end.
progress: 2007 / 2008: Pettie proves $O((n+m)\alpha^*(n+m))$ total cost, where $\alpha^*$ counts how many iterations of the inverse-Ackermann function reduce the argument to a constant. | 2019: Levy and Tarjan connect the deque conjecture to a subsequence property sufficient for dynamic optimality. This provides a structural route to a proof, not the required linear bound itself. | 2026-07: The new analysis of splay competitiveness still describes the deque guarantee as nearly constant per operation. Its general search bound does not supply constant amortized deque cost.
working_summary: A deque permits insertions and deletions at either end of an ordered collection. This question studies the implementation that inserts extreme keys and splays an extreme key before deleting it. It asks whether every operation sequence costs linear total time, including an allowance for the initial tree. Alternating ends and inserting new keys creates behavior beyond a single sorted scan. The conjecture would show that self-adjusting search trees automatically attain the efficiency expected from this restricted interface.

title: Does splaying every BST preorder take linear total time?
importance_reason: A sharply stated linear-cost conjecture for structured access sequences, probing whether splaying exploits an unknown traversal tree.
formal: Is there an absolute constant C such that, for every n and every two binary search trees A and B on the same n distinct ordered keys, searching for the keys of preorder(B), in order, using bottom-up splaying starting from A costs at most Cn? Define preorder recursively as root, then left-subtree preorder, then right-subtree preorder. Every key is searched once. Charge one unit per visited search-path node and one per single rotation; perform no insertions or deletions.
definitions: A binary search tree stores one key per node, all left descendants smaller and all right descendants larger. On a search for x, first follow comparisons from the root to x. Then repeatedly splay x: if its parent is the root, rotate x over its parent (zig); if x and its parent are both left children or both right children, rotate the parent over the grandparent and then x over the parent (zig-zig); otherwise rotate x over its parent and then over its former grandparent (zig-zag). The same node x remains the splayed node until it becomes root. The arbitrary starting tree A and the tree B defining the permutation are separate inputs to the mathematical claim; splay receives only the search requests.
answer_criterion: Prove a universal linear bound for all pairs (A,B), or show that the ratio of this cost to n is unbounded over a family of such pairs. A bound requiring the traversal tree B to be balanced does not settle the proposition.
context:
This asks about a particularly structured access sequence, rather than every possible sequence in the dynamic-optimality conjecture. A traversal visits each key exactly once, but its order reflects a second tree that may be quite different from the tree currently being searched. The proposed linear total bound says that this hidden structure is enough for splaying to adapt efficiently.

For example, the preorder of a balanced tree on seven keys can be 4, 2, 1, 3, 6, 5, 7. This is not a sorted scan: after finishing one subtree, the sequence can jump to a distant part of the key order. If the starting tree is a long chain, even the first requested key can be far from the root. The question concerns the total cost, so a single expensive access is harmless if later savings pay for it.

The distinction between access and insertion matters. Building a tree by inserting the preorder keys into an empty splay tree is a different operation sequence, and that version is known to be linear. Linear access bounds are also known when the tree defining the preorder is weight-balanced. Neither restriction covers all traversal trees.

This is a useful intermediate target because the input family is precise and recognizable. A proof can exploit the recursive order of the permutation; a counterexample would have to show that this order still permits repeated expensive restructuring.
why: I include this as a concrete test of whether a local restructuring rule detects global order in requests without being told that order. It isolates a major obstacle in understanding adaptive search trees while avoiding the full freedom of arbitrary repeated-access sequences.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The July 2026 paper still distinguishes special traversal cases from unrestricted optimality. This card asks specifically about preorder access from an arbitrary initial tree.
progress: 1985: The traversal conjecture originates in the introduction of splay trees, as recorded in the later primary studies. | 2019: Levy and Tarjan prove linear-time preorder and postorder insertion into an empty tree, and linear access when the traversal tree is weight-balanced. | 2026-07: The new splay competitive analysis still records traversal optimality only in special settings. Its competitive factor is not constant.
working_summary: Take the preorder traversal of one binary search tree and access its keys in another tree using splaying. Each key appears once, but the resulting order can jump between distant parts of the key range. The conjecture asks whether the total search and rotation cost is always linear, regardless of either tree's shape. Building a tree by inserting the same sequence is a different task. This structured workload offers a focused test of how well splaying discovers organization hidden in an access sequence.

title: Cut-Sparsification of Hypergraphs
importance_reason: The question concerns the general power of sparsification, linear sketches, or adversary-robust summaries, which are widely reused algorithmic tools.
formal: Cut-Sparsification of Hypergraphs
context: Computation with limited memory or compressed summaries. Passes, adaptivity, and update models affect the attainable bounds.
why: The significance of this particular question has not yet been individually assessed. The question concerns algorithmic solvability in a specified model. Its structural value is to locate the boundary between an effective procedure and a computational or logical obstruction.
status_note: Imported from the previous catalogue. Current open status has not been established by a new review.
working_summary: A hypergraph cut counts the total weight of hyperedges meeting both sides of a vertex partition. A cut sparsifier replaces the hypergraph by a smaller weighted hypergraph that approximately preserves every cut at once. The question asks whether O(n/epsilon squared) hyperedges always suffice for multiplicative error epsilon. This matches the natural target from ordinary graphs, while a hyperedge can involve arbitrarily many vertices. The size measure counts hyperedges rather than their total incidence size, making the project specifically about how many distinct multiway interactions must be retained.

title: Does recursively splitting a splay tree always take linear total time?
importance_reason: A precise decomposition property of splaying that could illuminate the structural arguments needed for broader adaptive-search conjectures.
formal: Start with an arbitrary n-node binary search tree. A split operation receives a current component tree and a key x in it, searches for x, splays x to that component’s root, and deletes x, leaving its left and right subtrees as separate components. Is the total cost of every legal sequence of n splits O(n)? Count all searches, rotations, and constant-time component bookkeeping. The input to each operation supplies the component’s root handle; identifying which component contains x is not a separate search problem.
definitions: Keys have a fixed total order and are compared rather than arithmetically manipulated. Splaying uses zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations. Each key is removed exactly once; no insertions occur. The sequence can choose any currently nonempty component. The bound is a worst-case bound on total cost over complete sequences, not a per-split worst-case bound.
answer_criterion: Prove one universal linear bound for every initial tree and legal split order, or prove that total cost divided by n is unbounded over such inputs. A bound with any unbounded multiplicative factor is partial progress.
context:
Ordinary search adjusts one tree and keeps all its keys available. A split removes its accessed key and permanently separates the keys on its two sides. Subsequent operations happen independently in the resulting components. Every original key is accessed as a pivot exactly once, but it can participate in rotations caused by earlier pivots.

For example, splitting at the median key first separates the two halves of the key order. Continuing recursively with medians gives a balanced pattern of subproblems. Another legal sequence repeatedly chooses an extreme key and leaves almost the entire tree in one component. The conjecture must cover both, including mixtures chosen from different components.

There are only n requested pivots, which explains the linear target, but not a linear upper bound for the actual implementation. A key may lie deep in the current tree. The proof must show that restructuring work can be charged globally without repeatedly charging the same surviving material too much.

This differs from the deque conjecture: a deque deletes only an extreme, whereas a split may select any internal rank and produce two nonempty trees. The July 2026 analysis gives a new nearly linear bound for this splitting process, making the remaining multiplicative gap explicit.
why: I include this because recursive partitioning is a basic way to organize ordered data. The conjecture asks whether splaying pays only for the number of objects eventually removed, regardless of the partition order. It is a sharply delimited test of the amortization techniques used for adaptive search trees.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The July 2026 preprint supplies the displayed nearly linear upper bound, not a linear one.
progress: 2007: Pettie records Lucas’s split conjecture and distinguishes it from traversal and deque workloads. Even the deletion-only extreme-key case captures a restricted form of the deque question. | 2026-07: Chmel and coauthors prove total split cost $O(n\log\log n\,\log^2\log\log n)$ in Appendix D. The O(n) bound remains the target.
working_summary: A splay-tree split brings a chosen key to the root, removes it, and leaves two separate component trees. Repeating this process eventually deletes every original key exactly once. The question asks whether every such sequence has linear total search, rotation, and bookkeeping cost. Pivots may be internal keys, so the workload includes recursive separations unavailable to ordinary end deletions. A proof must account globally for repeated restructuring of surviving keys, rather than merely count the number of requested splits.

title: Can reachability diameter be approximated within a constant in near-linear time?
importance_reason: Relates directed reachability structure to near-linear algorithms and isolates a basic obstruction behind shortcutting and parallel graph computation.
formal: For an unweighted directed graph $G=(V,E)$, define $D(G)=\max\{d_G(u,v):d_G(u,v)<\infty\}$. Is there an absolute constant $C\ge1$ and one randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every input, returns an estimate $D(G)/C\le\widehat D\le D(G)$ with probability at least 2/3 in $\widetilde O(n+m)$ worst-case time? Here $n=|V|$, $m=|E|$, words have $\Theta(\log n)$ bits, and self-distances are included, giving D(G)=0 on an edgeless graph. The constant and the hidden logarithmic exponent are independent of G.
definitions: Distances count edges on a shortest directed path. The maximum concerns finite distances only; it is neither the longest simple path nor the maximum of the smaller of the two directional distances. $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. This card focuses the broader approximation–time tradeoff on near-linear running time.
answer_criterion: Give a randomized algorithm and one absolute constant C meeting the displayed guarantee in near-linear time on every directed graph, or prove that no constant approximation is possible with that time bound.
context:
A directed graph need not be strongly connected. Taking the maximum over all ordered pairs then produces infinity as soon as one pair is unreachable, concealing the lengths of the routes that do exist. Reachability diameter discards unreachable pairs. On a one-way path of five vertices it is four, even though most ordered pairs have no directed route.

A familiar undirected idea is to search from an arbitrary vertex and use a farthest vertex as a witness. Directionality breaks its guarantee. Consider a long one-way path and an extra sink reached by an edge from the first path vertex. Searching from that sink sees no other vertex; searching toward it sees only the first path vertex. Both searches reveal a distance of one while the reachability diameter can be arbitrarily large. This is an illustrative counterexample to that particular pivot choice, not a lower bound against every sampling algorithm.

There is also a distinction between additive and multiplicative error. An estimate within $k$ of the truth is useful when $D(G)$ is much larger than $k$, but gives little information when the diameter is small. The question requires a useful relative guarantee on every input, including graphs whose longest finite shortest path has only a few edges.

The 2026 paper makes this a fine-grained algorithmic question and leaves a substantial gap for unweighted graphs. Its strong hardness results for weighted graphs do not settle the unit-weight case.
why: This asks how quickly an algorithm can summarize the routes that actually exist in a directed network. I include it because it exposes a basic weakness of transferring undirected diameter intuition to directed graphs and provides a concrete benchmark for algorithms based on reachability, sampling, and shortcuts.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. Open Problem 1 at ESA 2026; the near-linear constant-factor target is a focused part of that broader question.
progress: 2026: Theorem 9 gives an $n^{1/2+o(1)}$-approximation in near-linear time. Theorem 7 gives additive error $k$ in $O(nm/k)$ time; these guarantees leave the constant-factor near-linear target unresolved. | 2026: Corollary 5 conditionally excludes better-than-two approximation below the Boolean-matrix-multiplication exponent; its combinatorial version excludes truly subcubic combinatorial algorithms under combinatorial BMM. These results do not exclude every constant approximation.
working_summary: Reachability diameter measures the largest finite shortest-path distance in a directed graph. Unreachable ordered pairs are omitted so that disconnected directions do not make the answer automatically infinite. The question asks for a constant-factor estimate in near-linear time on every unweighted directed graph. Simple searches from arbitrary pivots can miss a long directed route. A successful method would summarize the extent of reachable routes without computing distances from every vertex or imposing strong connectivity.

title: Can the final survivors of an offline heap sequence be found with linear comparisons?
importance_reason: A clean offline-versus-online information question for the priority-queue primitive. It could reveal a general way to avoid reconstructing unneeded intermediate outputs, while remaining narrower than model-wide dynamic lower bounds.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic comparison algorithm and an absolute constant C that, for every legal sequence of N insert and delete-min operations starting from an empty priority queue, determines exactly which inserted items remain after the entire sequence using at most CN key comparisons? The complete operation sequence and all inserted keys are available before computation begins. Only the final membership vector is required; the algorithm need not output the items removed at intermediate delete-min operations or their removal order.
definitions: Each insert introduces a distinct item with a key in an opaque totally ordered universe; all inserted keys are pairwise distinct. A delete-min removes the currently present item of smallest key. Legality means that in every prefix the number of delete-min operations is at most the number of inserts. If I is the total number of inserts, the output is an I-bit vector in insertion order, marking exactly the items still present after all N operations. The algorithm may examine any part of the input sequence at any time. Its only access to key values is by pairwise order comparisons; operation positions and item identities carry no information about key order. Count every key comparison, including preprocessing comparisons. Ordinary computation on indices and comparison outcomes is not the cost measure, but the algorithm must terminate and be correct on every input.
answer_criterion: Give a uniform deterministic algorithm meeting the CN comparison bound for every legal sequence, or prove that every such algorithm requires a superlinear number of comparisons on a family of inputs. Sorting all removed items or simulating the queue online would solve stronger tasks; a lower bound for those stronger tasks is not a negative answer here.
context:
A usual priority queue must identify each minimum when the corresponding request arrives. The offline task can postpone every decision and return only a final set. For example, after insert(8), insert(2), delete-min, insert(1), the survivors are 8 and 1. This is not simply the set of the two largest inserted keys: 2 disappeared before 1 became available. The interleaving still matters even though the intermediate outputs are discarded.

One upper bound is to simulate a comparison heap and mark its remaining elements, using O(N log(N+2)) comparisons. At the other extreme, when all insertions precede all deletions, one linear-time selection suffices to find the surviving upper part of the key order. The question asks whether arbitrary temporal interleaving can be handled without losing that linear comparison bound.

The ordinary heap sorting lower bound depends on recovering the entire order of the extracted keys. Here, if I items were inserted, there are at most 2^I possible membership vectors. Counting outputs therefore does not give the usual factorial number of leaves needed for sorting. This observation only removes one lower-bound argument: a small output space by itself is not a construction of a shallow comparison decision tree.

A successful approach can exploit future deletions and later insertions, because the complete schedule is known. It need not maintain any particular heap representation. That freedom makes the problem a useful test of how much information an algorithm really needs when only a summary of a dynamic process is requested. The formulation deliberately asks about comparisons, leaving a linear total running time as a stronger goal.
why: This isolates a basic gap between maintaining a dynamic process and computing its final outcome. It connects offline data structures with selection and comparison lower bounds, in a small enough model that both algorithms and adversaries can be stated precisely.
status_note: Open in the 2021 primary source. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate a published resolution for this final-survivor comparison problem. Other problems called offline heaps may require every intermediate answer and should not be conflated with it.
progress: 2021: Kozma explicitly asks whether final heap survivors can be computed in o(N log N), or even O(N), comparisons. The source identifies the all-insertions-first case as solvable by linear-time selection and notes that the usual sorting argument does not apply.
working_summary: An offline heap sequence specifies all insertions and delete-min requests before computation starts. Only the identities of items surviving at the end must be returned. The question asks whether linear many key comparisons always suffice, even when operations are arbitrarily interleaved. The surviving set need not be the largest inserted keys because some items arrive after earlier deletions. This separates the information needed for final membership from the much richer task of reporting the entire extraction order.

status_note: Imported from the previous catalogue. Current open status has not been established by a new review.

The modified graph must stay within a prescribed number of edge edits. The project asks how much freedom is needed before this task becomes polynomial-time solvable. title: Does ordinary median-of-medians selection with groups of three run in linear time?
importance_reason: A basic unresolved analysis of a canonical selection rule, valuable for understanding dependent recursion. Its algorithm-specific scope places it below general adaptive-data-structure and compressed-access barriers.
formal: Is there an absolute constant C such that the fixed deterministic comparison algorithm Select3 below uses at most Cn key comparisons on every sequence A of n distinct ordered keys and every requested rank $1\le k\le n$? Its output must be the k-th smallest key. The question concerns the one-grouping-pass algorithm exactly as specified; all recursive pivot-selection comparisons count toward the same cost.
definitions: Define Select3(A,k) as follows. If |A| <= 3, sort a copy by insertion sort and return its k-th element. Otherwise put the first $3q$ elements, where $q=\lfloor |A|/3\rfloor$, into consecutive disjoint triples. Obtain each triple's median by sorting a copy using compare-exchanges (1,2), (2,3), (1,2); this leaves A unchanged. Let B be these q medians in group order. Set $p=\mathrm{Select3}(B,\lceil q/2\rceil)$. Scan all of A, including its at most two ungrouped final elements, comparing each key with p and forming L of keys below p and R of keys above p, preserving their original order. If k=|L|+1 return p; if k<=|L| return Select3(L,k); otherwise return Select3(R,k-|L|-1). One comparison returns the relative order of two keys at unit cost. The algorithm stores subsequences explicitly and uses no randomization, arithmetic on keys, or reuse of comparison outcomes beyond this description. These rounding and base-case conventions make the source's algorithm fully specified.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated comparison bound for every input sequence and every requested rank, or give a family of inputs and ranks for which comparisons divided by n are unbounded. An O(n log n) upper bound alone is not a refutation of linear time. A different small-group selection algorithm is not a positive answer for Select3.
context:
Selection asks for one position in sorted order without requiring the whole sorted sequence. The pivot controls how much work can be discarded: after finding it, only the side containing the requested rank is relevant. Here the pivot itself must be selected recursively from the medians of small groups. Its quality and the cost of obtaining it therefore have to be analyzed together.

The familiar three-group analysis bounds two recursive subproblems by roughly n/3 and 2n/3, plus a linear scan. This gives an O(n log n) upper bound. It does not exhibit an input on which both recursive calls repeatedly realize their separate worst cases. They are linked: the median list is made of elements from the very array that is partitioned. An adversarial construction cannot freely choose the two subproblems independently.

A useful distinction is between the grouping size and the number of grouping passes. The repeated-step method groups the medians into triples again before selecting a pivot recursively. That modified algorithm has a linear-time analysis, but it makes a different recursive call from Select3. The present question preserves the simpler, single-pass rule.

For a proof attempt, the stable ordering in L and R matters because it determines the triples at the next call. Fixing these details turns an informal discussion of small groups into one mathematical proposition. A positive answer would establish that the standard recurrence loses an asymptotic factor; a negative answer must capture actual coupled executions, rather than just solve the upper-bound recurrence.
why: This is a compact fundamental algorithm-analysis problem: even for a textbook primitive, independently worst-case recursive bounds may not be simultaneously attainable. It provides a concrete place to develop sharper tools for dependent subproblems or an explicit adversary.
status_note: The 2025 primary seminar source states this as open. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate a later resolution. The explicit rounding conventions are editorial; the ordinary algorithm and stable partition rule follow the cited author manuscript.
progress: 2019: Chen and Dumitrescu give linear-time modified small-group algorithms and leave ordinary three-group selection unresolved. Their Conjecture 1 asks for o(n log n), which is weaker than the linear bound asked here. | 2025: Kozma restates the three-group question as open at the Adaptive and Scalable Data Structures seminar.
working_summary: Median-of-medians selection chooses a pivot recursively from medians of small groups and discards an irrelevant partition. This project fixes the ordinary version using one grouping pass with groups of three. The question is whether its worst-case number of comparisons is linear. The familiar recurrence allows a logarithmic overhead, but its recursive worst cases need not occur simultaneously on one input. Resolving their dependence would distinguish a loose analysis from a real limitation of this particularly simple deterministic selection rule.

title: Do pure pairing heaps support O(log log n) amortized decrease-key?
importance_reason: Tests optimality of one particularly simple self-adjusting heap against an established model barrier; a focused algorithm-analysis question.
formal: For the pure pairing heap defined below, is there a universal constant C such that every legal sequence of M operations starting with empty heaps costs at most $C[M+D(1+\log N)+K(1+\log\log(N+2))]$? Here D counts delete-min operations, K counts decrease-key operations, and $N\ge2$ is the maximum of 2 and the total number of live items across all heaps at any moment. The allowed operations are make-heap, insert, find-min, meld, decrease-key, and delete-min. Count comparisons and pointer-machine steps; keys are distinct opaque values in a totally ordered set, compared at unit cost. Handles to the affected items and heaps are supplied.
definitions: A heap is one rooted heap-ordered tree whose child lists are ordered from left to right. Linking two roots compares their keys and makes the larger root the leftmost child of the smaller; cut removes a node with its subtree from its parent in constant time. Store O(1) pointers per item, with doubly linked child lists. Make-heap creates an empty tree; find-min returns its root; insert links a singleton to the root; meld links the roots and destroys the old heap handles. Decrease-key changes the supplied key and, if its node is not the root, cuts that node and links its subtree with the remaining root. Delete-min removes the root and scans its children left to right, linking disjoint adjacent pairs; an unpaired last child remains. Winners keep their positions in the root list. Identify its minimum-key remaining root v, remove v from that list, and prepend all other remaining roots in their existing order to the child list of v. The resulting tree is the heap. Use the ordinary constant-time list splice, rather than doing an additional recursive linking pass. All loops, comparisons, pointer accesses, and writes are charged. Logarithms have base two.
answer_criterion: Prove this total-cost bound for the specified algorithm, or construct legal operation sequences for which its ratio to the displayed budget is unbounded. A decrease-key call changes an item that is already present. It may execute only a few pointer operations immediately, yet the structural disorder it creates can make later deletions more expensive. The pure pairing heap simplifies deletion by pairing neighboring roots once and then attaching all survivors beneath the smallest survivor. It does not maintain a rank or balance invariant. The desired estimate asks whether this sparse restructuring still prevents expensive configurations from being recreated too often.

The operation budgets must be considered together. A sorting sequence already forces substantial comparison work when many minima are deleted, so the logarithmic delete-min allowance is intentional. title: Can lazy B-tree priority queues keep their I/O bounds with stable handles?
importance_reason: Isolates the cost of stable item handles in an external-memory priority queue; a useful model distinction with more limited scope than general I/O lower bounds.
formal: Is there a deterministic comparison-based external-memory priority queue with a universal constant c of internal storage at most cB words that satisfies the following bounds for every capacity $N\ge B\ge2$? Starting empty and never holding more than N elements, it uses $O(1+N/B)$ external blocks, supports insertion and handle-based decrease-key in $O(1+\log_B\log_B N)$ worst-case I/Os, and supports extract-min in $O(1+B^{-1}\log_2 N+\log_B\log_B N)$ amortized I/Os. Every handle remains valid until its element is removed. All handle maintenance and lookup costs count. Each logarithm is truncated below at one.
definitions: One I/O transfers B consecutive words between internal and external memory. N is an announced upper bound on the number of live elements, fixed for the operation sequence. Words contain O(log N) bits; keys and handles occupy a constant number of words, and key values are accessed by comparisons. A returned handle must continue identifying the same object after internal relocation. Decrease-key receives a handle and a no-larger priority; extract-min returns and removes an element with minimum priority. All auxiliary tables count toward the space bound. Amortized extract-min cost means that total cost of any legal sequence is bounded by the sum of its stated operation budgets.
answer_criterion: Construct a deterministic priority queue satisfying every stated operation and space bound with all stable-handle costs charged, or prove that no such structure exists in the fixed external-memory model.
context:
A handle lets an algorithm change a particular queued object after that object has moved. For example, a graph algorithm may keep a reference to a vertex’s queue entry and lower its priority when a better route is discovered. The reference must still identify that entry after other insertions, extractions, and internal rearrangements.

Block transfers make this subtle. Moving $B$ consecutive records between a few blocks can cost only a constant number of I/Os. If each record has a reference stored in a different disk block, repairing those references can cost $\Theta(B)$ I/Os. An analysis of the records alone can therefore miss the operation that dominates the running time.

Adding an indirection table is a possible design choice, not a complete solution. It can keep the caller’s handle stable, but the structure must update the table when entries move and look up the correct location on later decreases. Those accesses can again be scattered. The question requires charging these costs to the same operation bounds.

The December 2025 revision explicitly corrects the conference claim about priority-queue performance. It identifies the cost of external references as unaccounted for and reports logarithmic extract-min cost for the straightforward implementation when every element has a reference.
why: I include this because stable object identity is part of a data structure’s interface, and its cost can conflict with the locality that makes external-memory algorithms fast. The target is specific enough to attack with a representation or a lower bound, while the obstruction also matters for other structures that move records in blocks.
