title: Is weighted falsifiability of unambiguous DNFs in polynomial time?
importance_reason: A focused but structural tractability question connecting unambiguous representations, binary-weight optimization, and complementation. It has a clear gap between polynomial unweighted methods and an unresolved weighted case.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the total binary input length, that solves the following problem? The input consists of an unambiguous DNF $F=\bigvee_{j=1}^{m}T_j$ over n Boolean variables, nonnegative integer weights w_1,...,w_n encoded in binary, and an integer threshold t encoded in binary. Decide whether there exists $a\in\{0,1\}^n$ such that $F(a)=0$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i a_i\ge t$. Each T_j is an explicitly listed conjunction of literals. Unambiguous means that no assignment satisfies two distinct terms simultaneously.
definitions: A literal is either x_i or its negation. A term is true exactly when all its literals are true; the DNF is true when at least one term is true. Contradictory terms can be discarded. For the remaining terms, unambiguity is equivalent to every pair containing opposite literals on some variable, so this promise is itself checkable in polynomial time. Weights are exact integers, with no rounding. The running time must depend polynomially on their bit lengths rather than on their numerical sum. The threshold uses at least, not exactly; a strict-threshold formulation is equivalent by shifting the integer threshold by one. The output is a yes/no answer. A tautology has no falsifying assignment and always gives no, regardless of the threshold.
answer_criterion: Give a polynomial-time decision algorithm for all such inputs, or prove that the decision problem is not in P. An NP-hardness proof would provide a negative answer conditional on P differing from NP; its assumption must be stated. A pseudopolynomial algorithm, a method only for unweighted assignments, or hardness after changing the comparison to exact equality does not settle the specified question.
context:
Unambiguity makes the satisfying regions disjoint. This is useful for counting: after fixing the literals of one consistent term, every remaining variable is free, and the term’s satisfying assignments can be counted directly. Summing across terms gives the total without any inclusion-exclusion correction. Subtracting that count from 2^n decides whether a falsifying assignment exists at all.

The weighted version asks where the complement lies relative to an additive score. Knowing how many points lie outside the DNF does not reveal whether even one of them has a large score. For example, take F=(x AND y) OR ((NOT x) AND z), whose two terms are incompatible. With weights 8, 3, and 5, the assignment (1,0,1) falsifies F and has score 13. The all-ones assignment has larger score 16 but satisfies F, so unconstrained maximization does not answer the question.

There is an important asymmetry between maximizing over satisfying and falsifying assignments. To maximize over satisfying assignments, optimize each term separately by setting every unrestricted positive-weight variable to one, then take the best result. To falsify the DNF, every term must fail at once, and choices made to destroy one term can interact with all the others.

Dynamic programming over achievable scores gives a pseudopolynomial algorithm; it becomes polynomial when weights are unary. The missing guarantee is polynomial dependence on binary descriptions of potentially large weights. Amarilli also explains a connection to complementing compiled Boolean representations: efficient complementation into a representation supporting weighted maximization would give an algorithm, while suitable hardness would obstruct that route.
why: The problem separates easy counting from optimization on the complement of a simple disjoint representation. It tests whether unambiguity retains its algorithmic value when a compactly encoded additive objective is introduced, and it bears on the power of knowledge-compilation representations under negation.
status_note: Open in the original 2024 question and the maintained list accessed 10 September 2026. Searches did not locate a polynomial algorithm or hardness resolution. TCS-0485 is a duplicate seminar pointer to the same formulation, not a separate open question.

working_summary: P versus NP asks whether every efficiently verifiable decision problem can also be solved efficiently. The independence question concerns the possibility that a chosen mathematical axiom system proves neither equality nor inequality. title: Černý conjecture: a reset word of length at most (n−1)²
importance_reason: The flagship quantitative question about synchronizing automata, connecting finite-state control, extremal combinatorics, and linear-algebraic methods.
focus_reason: The flagship quantitative question about synchronizing automata, connecting finite-state control, extremal combinatorics, and linear-algebraic methods.
formal: Does every synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with n≥1 states have a reset word of length at most (n−1)²?
definitions: An automaton here is a finite transition system A=(Q,Σ,δ), with |Q|=n, a finite nonempty alphabet Σ, and a total function δ:Q×Σ→Q. Extend δ to words by δ(q,ε)=q and δ(q,wa)=δ(δ(q,w),a). A word w is a reset word when |{δ(q,w):q∈Q}|=1. The automaton is synchronizing if at least one such word exists; its reset threshold rt(A) is the minimum number of letters in a reset word. The quantification ranges over every n and every finite alphabet and total transition function satisfying this promise. The common final state need not be specified beforehand. Initial states and accepting states play no role. The empty word handles n=1. No strong-connectivity, binary-alphabet, permutation-letter, or other structural restriction is imposed. Partial automata, nondeterministic transitions, and synchronizing only a prescribed proper subset of Q are different models.
answer_criterion: Prove that rt(A)≤(n−1)² for every synchronizing complete deterministic n-state automaton, or exhibit such an automaton with rt(A)>(n−1)² and prove that strict inequality. Alphabets and state counts are unrestricted as specified above.
context:
Synchronization asks how to restore a finite system to a known state when its current state is unknown. A fixed input sequence must work simultaneously from every possible starting state; it cannot observe the intermediate state and adapt its next letter. The length bound therefore measures the cost of an open-loop reset, rather than ordinary shortest-path navigation from a known vertex.

The proposed constant is forced by a concrete family. On states 0,…,n−1, let a cyclically increment the state and let b send n−1 to 0 while fixing the other states. For n≥2, the word b(a^{n−1}b)^{n−2} has length (n−1)² and resets this automaton. Černý’s construction also proves that no shorter reset word works. A proof of the conjecture must match this obstruction exactly.

Knowing that a reset exists is much easier than establishing its sharp maximum length. Pairwise merging gives polynomial criteria for synchronizability, and successive compression of subsets gives general polynomial length bounds. The bottleneck is how much progress one can force as the current set of possible states shrinks. Adding separate worst-case bounds for these stages gives a cubic estimate and can lose information about how the stages interact.

The August 2026 open-problems survey records a general upper bound of approximately 0.1654n³+o(n³), due to Shitov’s refinement of Szykuła’s result. The gap is therefore in the exponent as well as the leading constant: the conjecture asks for the exact quadratic bound (n−1)². Results for restricted transition systems do not establish that bound for all synchronizing automata.

A July 2026 preprint reports the conjectured bound for one-cluster automata: systems having a letter whose functional graph has exactly one directed cycle. Its sharper positive-level estimate uses the cycle length and the distance of off-cycle states from that cycle. This is a claim for a restricted class, and the later general survey still states the unrestricted conjecture as open.
why: A central extremal problem in automata theory, with a simple finite-state formulation and a sharp explicit candidate bound. It tests whether local compression and algebraic structure can force globally short control sequences in every synchronizing system.
status_note: Szykuła’s survey posted 25 August 2026 explicitly states the unrestricted conjecture as open and records the cubic upper bound. Sources and later work were checked on 11 September 2026. The July one-cluster preprint is a restricted-class claim whose proof was not independently verified.

The project asks whether every synchronizing complete deterministic automaton with n states has such a word of length at most (n−1)². title: Can every two-way NFA be determinized with polynomially many states?
importance_reason: The flagship state-complexity problem for two-way finite automata, open since 1978, with unusually direct connections between finite-state descriptions and logarithmic-space complexity.
focus_reason: The flagship state-complexity problem for two-way finite automata, open since 1978, with unusually direct connections between finite-state descriptions and logarithmic-space complexity.
formal: Do universal constants C,k≥1 exist such that, for every n≥1, every finite nonempty input alphabet Σ and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over Σ with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most C(n+1)^k states satisfying L(D)=L(A)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
definitions: The read-only input tape contains a left endmarker, a word w∈Σ*, and a right endmarker. Each automaton has one head, initially on the left endmarker, a finite set Q of states with a designated initial state and designated halting accepting states. In each nonhalting configuration it uses its current state and the scanned symbol to choose a new state and a head displacement in {−1,0,+1}; moves outside the endmarkers are forbidden. A missing transition rejects that branch. A word is accepted if some finite computation reaches an accepting state. Infinite nonaccepting branches do not count as acceptance. For a deterministic automaton there is at most one available transition in each state-symbol pair, and its unique infinite run, if any, rejects. There is no work tape, rewritable input, second head, stack, counter, randomness or advice. State count includes all control and halting states, but the bound is independent of word length and alphabet size. The target is existence of D for each A; computing D from A is not required to take polynomial time. Standard endmarker and stay-put conventions change these state bounds only by polynomial factors.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of universal constants C,k giving an equivalent 2DFA with at most C(n+1)^k states for every n-state 2NFA, or prove that no such constants exist. In the negative direction, every proposed polynomial bound must fail on some source automaton; all language comparisons concern words of every length.
context:
All four basic finite-automaton models—one-way or two-way, deterministic or nondeterministic—recognize exactly the regular languages. Their descriptions can nevertheless have very different sizes. The familiar subset construction gives an exponential conversion from a one-way NFA to a one-way DFA. The open issue is whether the deterministic machine can avoid that cost by repeatedly revisiting the original input instead of remembering all possible nondeterministic states at once.

A simple example shows why a one-way lower bound is insufficient. Over {0,1}, consider words whose r-th symbol from the right is 1. A one-way deterministic automaton must distinguish all binary suffixes of length r and therefore needs at least 2^r states. A two-way deterministic automaton can scan to the right endmarker, walk left r positions while counting in its finite control, and inspect the symbol. It uses O(r) states. Rereading changes the representation cost even though the accepted language is unchanged.

Known unrestricted upper bounds still pass through a one-way representation and are exponential in a polynomial of the number of states. At the opposite end, exponential separations are known if the deterministic target has restricted head motion, such as reversing only at endmarkers. Those restrictions can themselves make deterministic automata exponentially larger. A lower bound using them therefore cannot be transferred to an unrestricted 2DFA without another argument.

The unary case remains meaningful: the input then consists of repetitions of one letter, and only its length can carry information. Unary two-way NFAs can be simulated by two-way DFAs with n^{O(log n)} states. This is far smaller than an exponential bound but still exceeds every fixed polynomial. It demonstrates that even removing almost all input syntax does not make the remaining determinization question routine.

Connections to logarithmic-space computation require careful quantifiers. Kapoutsis proves that polynomial-state deterministic simulation on inputs of length at most the source state count is equivalent to NL⊆L/poly. Here L/poly allows a deterministic logarithmic-space machine polynomially long advice depending only on input length. That theorem concerns bounded-length agreement, whereas this card requires agreement on every word. It should not be restated as an unconditional equivalence of the full Sakoda–Sipser question with L=NL.

Clerici Lorenzini, Pighizzini, and Prigioniero study letter-bounded languages in 2025: languages contained in a_1*⋯a_t* for fixed letters. They obtain a polynomial-cost normal form in which nondeterministic choices and head reversals occur at endmarkers. The source language restriction is crucial; the theorem does not put every two-way NFA into that normal form.

Guillon, Prigioniero, and Taheri’s STACS 2026 theorem complements arbitrary two-way NFAs with a polynomial-size self-verifying 1-limited automaton. Such a machine can annotate input cells on their first visit; the construction uses a shared guessed annotation that subsequent traversals can inspect. It remains a recognizer of regular languages, but its ability to retain those annotations is absent from a 2DFA. Their introduction explicitly leaves ordinary determinization and ordinary two-way-NFA complementation open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision proves a quadratic state lower bound for deterministic two-way automata solving one-way liveness. The problem encodes paths through successive layers of a graph; a small nondeterministic automaton can guess a path, whereas a deterministic one must use more control states. The lower bound also applies to conversion from one-way NFAs. Quadratic growth is compatible with the polynomial simulation asked here, so this strengthens the documented lower-bound picture without resolving the conjecture.
why: A principal unresolved measure of the succinctness provided by nondeterminism. It isolates the issue in finite-state machines, connects to nonuniform space complexity, and asks whether revisiting read-only data can replace a large internal record of possible computations.
status_note: Checked on 11 September 2026. The STACS 2026 paper explicitly retains ordinary two-way determinization as open. Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision supplies a quadratic lower bound, still compatible with polynomial determinization. Writable-annotation complementation and bounded-input-length simulations are separate results.

working_summary: Two-way finite automata can reread their input by moving their head in either direction. This project asks whether every n-state nondeterministic machine has an equivalent deterministic two-way machine with polynomially many states. Both machines must agree on all finite words, with no restriction on input length. Rereading sometimes replaces exponentially much one-way memory, but that observation does not supply a general simulation. Resolving the question would quantify how much finite-state succinctness comes from nondeterministic choice once unrestricted revisiting of the input is available.

title: Does any regular language require generalized star height greater than one?
importance_reason: A longstanding foundational problem connecting regular expressions, finite automata, algebraic language theory and logical descriptions.
focus_reason: A longstanding foundational problem connecting regular expressions, finite automata, algebraic language theory and logical descriptions.
formal: Does there exist a finite nonempty alphabet Σ and a regular language L⊆Σ* such that every generalized regular expression denoting L has Kleene-star nesting depth at least two, when complement is allowed without increasing that depth?
definitions: Σ* is the set of all finite words over Σ, including the empty word ε. A regular language is one accepted by a finite deterministic automaton. Generalized expressions are finite expressions built from ∅, ε, and the letters a∈Σ using binary union E∪F, concatenation EF, complement E^c, and Kleene star E*. Their meanings are respectively the empty language, {ε}, {a}, language union, all concatenations uv with u∈L(E) and v∈L(F), Σ*∖L(E), and the union of all finite concatenation powers of L(E), including power zero {ε}. Set h(∅)=h(ε)=h(a)=0, h(E∪F)=h(EF)=max{h(E),h(F)}, h(E^c)=h(E), and h(E*)=h(E)+1. Define h_g(L)=min{h(E):L(E)=L}, which exists because every regular language has an ordinary regular expression. The question is whether h_g(L)>1 for at least one such L. There is no bound on expression size, number of complements, union or concatenation depth, automaton size, or alphabet size. Intersection is permitted as the abbreviation (E^c∪F^c)^c and does not add star depth. Backreferences, infinite words, additional predicates and auxiliary alphabets in the final expression are not part of the syntax.
answer_criterion: Prove that some regular language has generalized star height at least two, including a lower bound over all generalized expressions for that language, or prove that every regular language over every finite nonempty alphabet has a generalized expression of star height at most one. Expression size is unrestricted in both alternatives.
context:
Kleene star represents arbitrary finite repetition. Nested stars arise naturally when repetitions occur inside other repeated blocks. The question is whether such nesting expresses a real hierarchy once a language can also be complemented at no cost to the height measure. Complement preserves regularity, so it does not enlarge the class recognized by finite automata. It may nevertheless radically change the shape of the shortest-depth expression for the same language.

Even elementary examples demonstrate that syntax and language height must be separated. Over Σ={a,b}, the language of all words has the ordinary expression (a∪b)*, with a star. With complement, it is simply ∅^c and has height zero. The language avoiding the factor ab is (Σ*abΣ*)^c; replacing each displayed Σ* by ∅^c makes this a star-free expression. Infinitely many words can therefore belong to a language of generalized height zero.

Height zero does not capture all regular languages. Over the unary alphabet {a}, the even-length language (aa)* has generalized height exactly one. Its two-state automaton remembers length modulo two. Schützenberger’s theorem characterizes height zero through an aperiodic syntactic monoid, and this parity language has a nontrivial two-element group. Thus the first separation, between zero and one, is known; the question asks for the next separation.

The syntactic monoid packages how words behave inside arbitrary contexts: u and v are equivalent when puq belongs to L exactly when pvq does, for every pair of words p,q. Concatenation induces multiplication on the finitely many equivalence classes. A finite monoid is aperiodic when some exponent N makes x^N=x^{N+1} for every element x. Schützenberger’s characterization gives an effective algebraic test for star-freeness, but no corresponding complete height-one criterion is known.

The ordinary, or restricted, star-height problem disallows complement. In that setting, arbitrarily high heights exist and the minimum height is computable. These facts cannot be transferred to generalized height by reusing an ordinary expression or an automaton cycle measure: allowing complement introduces additional descriptions that the old lower-bound argument may not exclude. Pin’s problem page explicitly distinguishes these two versions and separately lists the existence of height two and the algorithmic computation of height.

Pin, Straubing and Thérien prove height at most one for several algebraic classes, including languages recognized by finite nilpotent groups of class at most two, and eliminate a proposed height-two example. They also show that every regular language is the inverse image of an ordinary height-one language under a suitable word morphism. That representation does not bound generalized height without an additional closure statement: inverse morphisms preserve regularity, but their preservation of generalized height one is part of the unresolved issue.

Bourne and Ruškuc extend the height-one territory using factor-counting arguments. Their results cover specified counting cases and languages recognized by Rees zero-matrix semigroups over abelian groups. A factor here is a contiguous occurrence of a word, which differs from counting scattered subsequences. The theorem handles a substantial recognizing-semigroup class, while leaving the existence of a language above height one unresolved.

Daviaud and Paperman study languages generated from sets u* with a single word u, under Boolean or lattice operations and, in some cases, quotients. They give effective equational characterizations of those particular classes. These are deliberately restricted families inside the broader problem: a full height-one expression may take the star of an arbitrary star-free language and combine the resulting languages by concatenation and Boolean operations. Their paper describes its result as a step toward that larger structural challenge.

Cotumaccio’s 2025 account of connections between compressed indexing and automata again identifies generalized star height as an open structural question. It does not supply a new separation or universal flattening theorem. The relevance extends beyond a formal-expression puzzle: a solution would clarify how finite-state iteration, modular behaviour and Boolean operations interact, while allowing descriptions to grow arbitrarily large.
why: A basic unresolved expressive-depth question for regular languages: determine whether Boolean operations eliminate every need for nested iteration, or whether a genuine second level exists.
status_note: The checked author sources distinguish the open generalized question from the solved ordinary star-height problem. A later-work search on 11 September 2026 found no verified height-two example or universal height-one theorem. The inspected factor-counting results establish additional height-one subclasses only.
progress: 1965: Schützenberger characterizes generalized height zero by aperiodic syntactic monoids; height one is already necessary for simple parity languages. | 1992: Pin–Straubing–Thérien prove additional height-one classes and remove a proposed height-two candidate. | 2016-09-27: Bourne–Ruškuc’s revised manuscript establishes height-one bounds for specified factor-counting languages and Rees zero-matrix semigroups over abelian groups. | 2018: Daviaud–Paperman give effective characterizations of restricted classes generated by stars of individual words. | 2025: Cotumaccio’s automata/compression survey still identifies generalized star height among the open structural questions.
working_summary: Generalized regular expressions describe regular languages using concatenation, Boolean operations and arbitrary finite repetition. Their star height counts nested repetitions while allowing complementation without an additional height charge. The question asks for a language whose every such description needs at least two nested stars. Ordinary examples with complicated repetitions may simplify drastically when complements are allowed, so inspecting one expression proves little. Establishing a separation beyond height one would reveal a further intrinsic layer of repetition complexity within regular languages.

title: Decidability of every level of the dot-depth hierarchy
importance_reason: A longstanding structural decision problem linking finite automata, logical definability and finite monoids; a full solution would explain much more than the known low-level algorithms.
focus_reason: A longstanding structural decision problem linking finite automata, logical definability and finite monoids; a full solution would explain much more than the known low-level algorithms.
formal: For every fixed integer k≥0, is there an algorithm that, given a deterministic finite automaton over a finite alphabet A, always halts and decides whether its language belongs to DD_k(A), the k-th dot-depth level defined below?
definitions: For each finite nonempty alphabet A, let A* be its finite words, ε the empty word, and A+=A*∖{ε}. Set DD₀(A)={∅,{ε},A+,A*}. For a class C of languages over A, Pol(C) consists of all finite unions of marked products L₀a₁L₁⋯a_rL_r, where r≥0, each a_i∈A, and every L_i∈C; r=0 gives L₀. Let Bool(C) be closure under finite union, finite intersection and complement relative to A*. Define DD_{k+1}(A)=Bool(Pol(DD_k(A))). The input automaton is given by finite explicit tables, including its alphabet, initial state and accepting states; its accepted language is L(M). The question quantifies ∀k∃a total Turing algorithm A_k∀M, with A_k(M)=yes exactly when L(M)∈DD_k(A). Each A_k must handle arbitrary finite input alphabets. No polynomial-time or elementary-time bound is requested. This fixes the full integer levels and the four-language level-zero convention; it does not merge distinct concatenation hierarchies or leave the logical signature implicit. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove that membership in DD_k is decidable for every fixed integer k≥0, with each decider handling all finite alphabets, or prove that membership is undecidable for at least one fixed level k. The positive statement does not require an effective procedure that takes k as an additional input.
context:
Finite automata provide a complete and effective representation of regular languages, but the number of states is only one measure of a language’s complexity. Another asks how complicated a logical description must be. Two automata with similar state counts can recognize languages requiring very different combinations of order, concatenation and negation. The dot-depth hierarchy measures that descriptive structure.

A marked product picks a sequence of distinguished letters and constrains the substrings around them. Over an alphabet containing a and b, A*aA*bA* says that some a occurs before some later b. Replacing the middle A* by {ε} requires the two distinguished letters to be adjacent. Boolean combinations can require several such patterns or forbid them. Iterating these operations permits the pieces between distinguished letters to satisfy properties that were already built at earlier levels.

The level is a minimum over all descriptions of the same language. Seeing four layers in a supplied expression does not prove the language needs four: another expression may be simpler. The input is therefore an automaton, rather than a proposed optimal expression. The algorithm must discover whether some description at the requested level exists, regardless of how the language was initially presented.

The union of the levels is the star-free class, whose membership is decidable through the aperiodicity of the syntactic monoid. This answers whether any finite level suffices, while the present question asks about a prescribed bound. Place and Zeitoun’s account of the dot-depth problem emphasizes this distinction between the classical star-free theorem and the finer unresolved classification.

There is a useful logical interpretation: full levels correspond to Boolean combinations of first-order formulas with bounded quantifier alternation, with the appropriate word predicates. The closely related Straubing–Thérien hierarchy starts from just the empty and universal languages and uses the order-only signature. Dot-depth also captures successor information. The card defines the language operations directly so that changing the basis or adding predicates cannot silently change its target.

Positive instances are effectively enumerable. Enumerate expressions at level k, convert each to a finite automaton, and check language equality with the input. If a suitable expression exists this eventually finds it. The obstruction is recognizing negative instances: continuing to search without success is not a certificate that every candidate fails. A decision theorem needs an effective stopping criterion or an equivalent finite characterization.

Separation asks whether a language from a prescribed class can contain one given regular language while avoiding another. Covering asks whether a given language can be covered by finitely many languages from the class such that each covering language is disjoint from at least one member of a given finite list of forbidden regular languages. These are stronger classification tasks than membership. Place and Zeitoun’s 2021 result decides separation and covering for dot-depth two.

Their 2024 result uses a generic algebraic characterization of Boolean polynomial closure. For levels at least two, it reduces membership at the next full level to covering at the preceding level. Together with the known covering result, this decides dot-depth three. The reduction does not by itself decide covering at every new level, so it cannot simply be iterated to settle the entire hierarchy.

A January 2025 preprint by Barloy, Cadilhac, Paperman and Straubing announced decidability of the first-order alternation hierarchy and related half-level results. It was withdrawn on January 31: the authors identify a fatal flaw in the proof of Lemma 19. The unchanged title and abstract still appear in search results, so they cannot be treated as an established resolution. No corrected replacement resolving this card was found in the present review.

MeSCaL implements established membership tests, including computations for level two and intermediate levels, while its 2025 account explicitly retains the general hierarchy problem. Such tools make existing decision theorems usable without implying that every level is decidable.

Lambert’s July 2026 paper develops effective methods that turn automata into logical descriptions for dot-depth one and specified extensions. Its target classes are fixed; it does not claim a procedure for every level of this hierarchy.

Settling the question would determine whether a major logical complexity measure for regular languages can always be recognized effectively at any prescribed finite level. It would also clarify which finite algebraic information is sufficient to describe bounded alternation. An undecidable level would be equally revealing: even these finite-state languages would resist a complete algorithmic classification by that natural form of descriptive simplicity.
why: Determine whether bounded logical alternation can be recognized effectively throughout a fundamental hierarchy of regular languages.
status_note: Checked on 11 September 2026. Place–Zeitoun’s full-level-three decidability theorem remains distinct from the all-level target. The January 2025 alternation-hierarchy announcement is still explicitly withdrawn because of a fatal flaw in Lemma 19. No corrected result settling every fixed full dot-depth level was located.

working_summary: The dot-depth hierarchy sorts star-free regular languages by how repeatedly concatenation and Boolean operations must be combined. Given a finite automaton and a fixed level, the project asks whether membership in that level can always be decided. The relevant level concerns the simplest possible description of the language, rather than the syntax initially supplied. Deciding star-freeness only establishes membership somewhere in the hierarchy and does not identify a prescribed level. An effective test for every level would connect automaton behavior to precise bounds on logical descriptive complexity.

title: Equivalence of deterministic macro tree transducers
importance_reason: A central longstanding transducer-equivalence problem, connecting functional program verification with finite-state methods, algebraic invariants and structural recursion.
focus_reason: A central longstanding transducer-equivalence problem, connecting functional program verification with finite-state methods, algebraic invariants and structural recursion.
formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given two deterministic macro tree transducers with the same finite ranked input and output alphabets, decides whether they define exactly the same partial function from finite ordered input trees to finite ordered output trees?
definitions: Fix the ordinary inside-out, or call-by-value, semantics. A ranked alphabet assigns a nonnegative arity to each symbol; a tree node has exactly that many ordered children. A transducer has finitely many states q, each with one input-tree argument and m(q) output-tree parameters, and an initial state q₀ with m(q₀)=0. For each state q and input symbol σ of arity k there is at most one rule q(σ(x₁,…,x_k),y₁,…,y_m)→r. The finite right-hand side follows the grammar r ::= y_j | δ(r₁,…,r_l) | q′(x_i,r₁,…,r_{m(q′)}), with δ an output symbol of arity l and 1≤i≤k. Subtrees and parameters may be copied or deleted, and calls may be nested inside parameter arguments without a fixed nesting bound across instances. On input σ(t₁,…,t_k), evaluate parameter arguments to output trees, then evaluate a call q′ on the indicated child t_i with those parameter values. A missing rule makes the corresponding evaluation undefined, and under call-by-value an undefined argument makes its enclosing evaluation undefined. There is no inspection or pattern matching on parameter trees. Every recursive call processes a proper input child, so evaluation terminates on each finite input, with either a finite tree or undefined. A transducer with a rule for every state/symbol pair is total. There is no regular look-ahead oracle in this chosen syntax. Equality requires identical domains and, on that domain, identical labelled ordered output trees, without identifying different trees by their leaf strings, shapes or origin annotations. Input alphabets, state sets, arities and rules are all part of the finite input to the desired decision algorithm.
answer_criterion: Prove that equivalence of the specified partial deterministic macro tree transducers is decidable by a total algorithm, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. Equivalence requires equality of domains and of the labelled ordered output trees on every input in the common domain.
context:
A macro tree transducer is a small recursive program for transforming structured data. Its input could be a syntax tree, and its output another syntax tree. A state examines the current input symbol and recursively processes child subtrees. Output parameters act as accumulated pieces of the result that can be inserted, duplicated or passed onward. This makes the model more expressive than a finite-state traversal that simply emits output around its recursive calls.

The restriction to proper input children guarantees termination. It does not bound output size by a polynomial, because a rule may copy a parameter or call a state repeatedly. For example, repeatedly replacing an accumulated tree y by b(y,y) along a unary input chain produces an exponentially large output from a small input. The equivalence question must account for that output implicitly if it hopes to avoid constructing every possible result.

The question asks about all finite inputs. Different rule tables can compute the same transformation through different intermediate structures, so syntactic comparison is too restrictive. Testing every tree up to a chosen height can discover a counterexample, but success on that finite collection proves nothing without a theorem giving an adequate height bound. There is no such bound built into the problem statement.

Non-equivalence is semidecidable: enumerate finite input trees, evaluate both programs, and stop when their definedness or outputs differ. Every individual evaluation terminates even if it takes a long time. The missing counterpart is a complete way to confirm equivalence. No terminating equivalence decider is supplied by this semidecision observation.

Maneth’s survey describes three substantial decidable subclasses: ordinary top-down tree transducers without output parameters, macro transducers of linear size increase, and macro transducers with both input and output alphabets monadic. Linear size increase connects to deterministic MSO-definable tree translations. These restrictions remove different difficulties and do not collectively cover all macro transducers. In particular, restricting the input to unary trees alone is not the same as restricting both alphabets.

The survey also records that inverse images of regular tree languages are effectively regular. Taking the inverse image of all output trees gives an effective description of the domain, so domain equality is already decidable. That useful fact does not decide whether two different output functions agree everywhere on their common domain. The hard part is comparing the unbounded structured outputs rather than merely determining where a computation is defined.

Seidl, Maneth and Kemper settle equivalence of deterministic top-down tree-to-string transducers using inductive invariants expressed through polynomial ideals. Their result combines a search for an equivalence proof with a search for a counterexample. That theorem concerns a particular tree-to-string formalism; the present target is the parameterized tree-to-tree model.

The inherited Maneth–Seidl paper studies origin equivalence: each output node also records which input node caused its creation. It decides this stronger equality test for weakly self-nesting transducers. An origin mismatch can occur even when the ordinary output trees are identical, so a negative answer to origin equivalence is not a negative answer to the present question. The paper further shows that for unrestricted unary-input macro transducers, origin equivalence is as difficult as ordinary equivalence.

Gallot and Maneth’s June 2025 paper decides shape preservation for compositions of total deterministic macro tree transducers. Shape preservation means that the output has the input’s ordered tree shape, although labels may change. This property concerns a transformation’s relation to its own input and does not decide equality of two arbitrary transformations.

Gallot, Lhote and Nguyên’s January 2026 revision decides polynomial size-to-height growth and computes its degree. Such a bound compares the height of the output tree with the number of input nodes. Two transformations can satisfy the same growth bound while differing in their output labels or branching, so growth classification is distinct from functional equivalence.

Dartois, Nguyên and Peyrat’s May 2026 paper characterizes a class of functions of linear size-to-height increase using tree-to-tree Hennie machines and a typed lambda calculus. Its equivalence proof concerns the expressive power of two models. It is not an algorithm for deciding whether two arbitrary macro tree transducers produce identical outputs. Keeping these senses of equivalence separate prevents a misleading reading of the recent abstract.

A resolution would locate an important boundary of automatic program comparison. These programs already terminate and have a disciplined recursive structure, but still support nested parameter passing and copying. Decidability would provide a foundation for validating transformations and optimizations in that model; undecidability would demonstrate that structural recursion alone does not make full semantic equality effectively recognizable.
why: Locate the decidability boundary for equivalence of terminating recursive tree programs with copying and nested output parameters.
status_note: Primary-source review and a later-work search on 11 September 2026 found no decider or undecidability theorem for the unrestricted model stated here. The inspected 2025–2026 papers classify shape, growth or expressive power. Their claims do not decide ordinary functional equivalence of arbitrary pairs.

working_summary: Deterministic macro tree transducers are recursive programs that turn finite ordered trees into other trees. Parameters carry intermediate output pieces, which rules may pass onward or duplicate during processing. The project asks whether two such programs define exactly the same partial transformation on every finite input tree. Testing examples can reveal a disagreement but cannot certify universal agreement without a completeness argument. A general decision procedure would provide an exact equivalence test for an expressive model of structured-data transformation, including cases with very large outputs.

title: Equivalence of deterministic higher-order recursion schemes
importance_reason: A central equivalence problem joining higher-order functional computation, infinite-tree semantics, and deterministic collapsible pushdown automata.
formal: Is there a Turing algorithm that, on every pair of finite deterministic higher-order recursion schemes G,H over the same finite ranked alphabet, halts and decides whether their possibly infinite value trees are exactly equal, including divergence leaves?
definitions: Types are generated by o and τ→σ. A terminal a of rank r has type o→⋯→o with r arguments. A scheme has finitely many typed nonterminals, a start S:o, and exactly one rule F x₁⋯x_k→t for each F:τ₁→⋯→τ_k→o. The distinct parameters x_i have the indicated types; t:o is a well-typed applicative term made from terminals, nonterminals and those parameters. There is no pattern matching, test on constructor values, nondeterministic choice, or restriction called safety. To obtain the value at a node, unfold the head nonterminal with substitution until a terminal a is exposed, then repeat for its r ordered arguments. If no terminal is ever exposed, that node is a nullary ⊥ leaf. This defines a tree over the alphabet extended with ⊥. Equality means identical node domains and labels at every finite address in the ordered tree; evaluation-step counts are ignored. The order of o is 0 and ord(τ→σ)=max(ord(τ)+1,ord(σ)); the maximum nonterminal order is finite but part of the input. Inputs may have different orders. No time bound is imposed beyond halting on every valid pair.
answer_criterion: An affirmative answer is a single effective decision procedure for all finite input orders, with a proof of termination and correctness on equal as well as unequal trees. A negative answer proves this decision problem undecidable. Decidable model checking of one generated tree, a bounded-order subclass, or a conditional reduction to another open problem is not a full resolution.
context:
A finite recursive program can describe an infinite object without listing its nodes. The rule S→a S, for unary a, describes an endless chain of a labels. The two-rule system S→a T and T→a S describes exactly the same chain even though its internal call structure differs. This card asks whether such equality of the entire observable unfolding can always be decided when functions may also be passed as arguments.

The output is an uninterpreted constructor tree. A binary constructor named plus is merely a label with two ordered children; the model does not add the arithmetic equation plus(0,x)=x. Likewise, it does not include a program context allowed to inspect generated values. This narrow semantics matters because equivalence questions for richer programming languages can be undecidable for reasons absent from recursion schemes.

Divergence is also observable in a precise way. The rule S→S generates ⊥, while S→a S generates an infinite productive chain. A scheme S→b S c, with binary b and nullary c, can expose infinitely many labels despite never completing its left subtree. Head unfolding therefore differs from an evaluation convention that insists on fully evaluating every argument before producing a constructor.

At order zero, the generated trees are regular and equality can be checked by comparing finite state descriptions. At order one, the problem connects to deterministic pushdown-language equivalence, whose decidability follows from Sénizergues’s theorem. Allowing higher-order parameters makes the finite description much more expressive. The inherited Hague–Murawski–Ong–Serre paper identifies equivalence as a central remaining question.

That paper’s positive equivalence theorem concerns two kinds of representation: higher-order recursion schemes and collapsible pushdown automata generate the same tree class, with effective translations. It transfers the problem to language equivalence for deterministic collapsible pushdown automata. It does not give an algorithm that compares arbitrary trees represented in either formalism. The difference between representation equivalence and instance equivalence is essential here.

Powerful properties of a single tree are nevertheless decidable. Broadbent–Carayol–Ong–Serre provide effective model checking, logical reflection and selection for monadic second-order logic and the modal μ-calculus. Reflection can enrich node labels with the truth of a chosen logical property. Having this machinery does not automatically turn two unrelated infinite descriptions into one object in the same decidable class on which all corresponding nodes can be compared.

Jochems supplies a route through coinductive higher-order constrained Horn clauses. The translation represents the generated tree using predicates interpreted through a greatest model and creates separate positive and negative instances. A suitable semidecision procedure for the resulting coinductive problems would yield a decision procedure by interleaving the two searches. The needed semidecidability is left open, so this is a reduction rather than a completed decision algorithm.

The same work handles divergence constructively: it transforms a scheme so that each ⊥ leaf is replaced by an infinite chain over a fresh unary symbol. Equality is preserved and reflected. Thus treating divergence carefully need not restrict the question to an informal assumption that every program is productive. The present formulation keeps divergence explicit so readers can compare two given schemes without an unstated promise.

Recent results with similar terminology concern other targets. Bojańczyk–Fabiański–Stefański’s April 2026 undecidability theorem compares functions at higher-order types in the polyregular λ-calculus, a language with list-processing operations and extensional input/output semantics. Its theorem is not a stated undecidability result for the closed constructor-tree generators defined above. No reduction identifying the two decision problems is assumed here.

Dal Lago–Fiorillo–Pistone’s LICS 2026 work instead decides almost-sure termination for a typed subclass of probabilistic recursion schemes, using algebraic generating functions. That achievement concerns termination probabilities under additional type restrictions. The inherited question asks exact equality of deterministic value trees at unrestricted finite orders, and remains separate.
why: A fundamental decidability boundary for comparing higher-order recursive computations: expressive tree generators admit strong verification procedures, while exact equality of two generated behaviors remains unresolved.
status_note: Open for unrestricted finite-order deterministic schemes with the exact tree semantics stated here, following the inspected primary sources and a later-result search through 11 September 2026. Conditional Horn reductions, model checking, probabilistic termination and higher-order polyregular functional equivalence do not by themselves settle it.
progress: 1997–2002: Sénizergues establishes deterministic pushdown equivalence, giving the order-one recursion-scheme boundary described in the inherited survey. | 2008–2017: Hague–Murawski–Ong–Serre give effective translations between recursion schemes and collapsible pushdown automata; the journal article explicitly retains instance equivalence as open. | 2021-03-02: Broadbent–Carayol–Ong–Serre’s revision develops effective logical reflection, selection and model checking. | 2021: Jochems reduces scheme equivalence to an open coinductive-Horn semidecidability problem and gives an equality-preserving removal of divergence leaves. | 2026-04-13: Higher-order polyregular functional equivalence is proved undecidable in a different model and semantics. | 2026: LICS work gives almost-sure termination decidability for a typed probabilistic subclass, not unrestricted deterministic tree equivalence.
working_summary: A higher-order recursion scheme is a finite system of typed recursive rules that unfolds into a possibly infinite labeled tree. The project asks whether two deterministic schemes always admit an effective test for equality of their complete value trees. Equality includes divergence leaves and compares labels at every finite address, irrespective of internal evaluation steps. Functions passed as arguments make the generators much richer than finite-state descriptions. Solving this comparison problem would extend our ability to verify higher-order recursive behavior beyond properties of one generated tree at a time.

title: First-order definability of regular tree languages
importance_reason: The tree analogue of effective first-order definability for regular word languages.

title: Does the specified weighted temporal logic express every weighted FO sentence over natural numbers?
importance_reason: A quantitative analogue of a central expressiveness theorem, connecting finite-word logic with aperiodic weighted automata. The fixed natural-number setting makes the question concrete while retaining the difficulty of counting multiple witnesses.
formal: For every finite alphabet Sigma and every closed weighted first-order expression E in the fragment defined below, with weights in the semiring (N,+,times,0,1), does there exist a weighted temporal expression H in the specified grammar such that E(w)=H(w,1) for every nonempty finite word w over Sigma? The weighted temporal grammar is $H ::= 0\mid Ls\mid\langle s\rangle H\mid s\,U_w\,H\mid H+H\mid\operatorname{if}(\varphi,H,H)$, where s is a finite conditional expression returning a natural-number constant and phi is an ordinary Boolean LTL formula with both future and past. Its exact semantics and the source weighted-FO grammar are given in Model & notation. No additional weighted operator may be introduced. This fixes the natural-number instance of the weighted Kamp question discussed in Gastin’s December 2025 slides.
definitions:
Words w have positions 1,...,N, with N=|w|>=1. Boolean FO formulas theta use letter predicates a(x), equality, order, Boolean connectives, and quantification over positions. A step-FO expression s_F is a natural constant r or if(theta,s_F,s_F). Weighted FO expressions have grammar E ::= 0 | product_x s_F | sum_x E | E+E | if(theta,E,E). A sum or product ranges over every word position and binds x; conditionals select the indicated branch according to ordinary Boolean truth. Products are permitted only over step expressions, not arbitrary weighted expressions. E is closed when all position variables are bound.

Boolean LTL guards phi use true, letter tests, negation, disjunction, strong next X, strong previous Y, until U, and since S. X phi is false at the last position and Y phi false at the first. At i, phi U psi holds if some k>=i satisfies psi and every j with i<=j<k satisfies phi; since is the reverse-time counterpart. Guards are evaluated on the entire word, at the indicated position. A step-temporal expression s is a natural constant or if(phi,s,s).

Write s(w,i) for its value. The weighted semantics is: 0 has value zero; addition is pointwise ordinary addition; conditionals select one branch. (Ls)(w,i)=s(w,i) if i=N and zero otherwise. (<s>H)(w,i)=s(w,i) H(w,i+1) if i<N and zero otherwise. Finally, $(s\,U_w\,H)(w,i)=\sum_{k=i}^{N}(\prod_{j=i}^{k-1}s(w,j))H(w,k)$, with empty product one. This U_w is a numerical summation operator, distinct from Boolean until inside a guard. A temporal expression denotes the function w -> H(w,1). Arbitrary multiplication of weighted expressions and weighted past operators are absent from the grammar. All expressions are finite, with any fixed natural constants allowed; equality is exact on every word, not approximation or equality only of nonzero supports.
answer_criterion: Translate every closed expression of the specified weighted FO fragment into the specified weighted temporal grammar, or give an expression E and prove that no temporal expression in that grammar agrees with it on all nonempty finite words. It is enough for a negative answer to use one finite alphabet. Changing the semiring or adding a new weighted operator does not answer this fixed question. Agreement only on the underlying Boolean language is insufficient.
context:
Classical first-order logic and temporal logic can describe the same finite-word languages despite using different means of referring to positions. Weighted expressions ask for an exact number associated with a word. A position quantifier can now add contributions from many witnesses, rather than merely asserting that a witness exists. The question is whether a temporal expression can reproduce those totals without explicit position variables.

The source FO fragment deliberately restricts products to step expressions. Permitting products of arbitrary weighted sums would define a stronger language and change the question. Similarly, weighted until has a step expression on the left: it accumulates products along an interval and adds the possible endpoint contributions. These restrictions are part of the mathematical target, not choices left to a proposed translation.

For intuition, a weighted FO sentence can count occurrences of factors belonging to a chosen FO-definable language L. It sums one over pairs x<=y whenever the substring between those positions belongs to L. A temporal formulation must reproduce the same multiplicity, including overlapping occurrences. Ordinary Boolean temporal tests can decide many properties of prefixes and suffixes, but that alone does not give a way to sum over two independently chosen endpoints.

The February 2025 seminar leaves the appropriate weighted LTL formulation unspecified. Gastin’s later slides give an explicit grammar and semantics, establish equivalences in unambiguous and finite-ambiguity fragments, and mark the full weighted-FO/weighted-LTL equivalence with a question mark. This card uses that later formulation and fixes the natural-number semiring. Thus an answer concerns a particular expressive-power claim, rather than whether some future language definition would be considered adequate.
why: This asks whether the classical equivalence between variable-based and temporal descriptions survives exact quantitative aggregation. It could identify a basic limit of temporal specification languages and clarify which operations are needed to describe the counts and weights recognized by aperiodic automata.
status_note: The unrestricted correspondence is marked open in the December 2025 primary slides. This card fixes their temporal syntax and restricts to the natural-number semiring; it does not claim all alternative weighted LTL definitions are equivalent. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate a resolution of this exact instance.
progress: 2019: Droste and Gastin characterize the relevant weighted FO fragment using aperiodic polynomially ambiguous weighted automata, with finer correspondences when first-order and binary sums are removed. | 2025-02: The Dagstuhl problem discusses extending the classical star-free, aperiodic, FO, and LTL equivalences to weighted languages; the temporal-language definition is still part of its research direction. | 2025-12-16: Gastin gives explicit weighted LTL syntax and semantics. Slides 25–28 establish restricted-fragment equivalences and leave the full weighted FO versus weighted LTL correspondence open; slide 30 highlights counting factors as a test example.
working_summary: Weighted first-order expressions assign natural-number values to words by combining contributions from positions and witnesses. The project asks whether every expression in the specified fragment has an exactly equivalent weighted temporal expression. The temporal grammar is fixed, including its restricted weighted-until operator and Boolean tests with past and future. Matching Boolean acceptance is insufficient because different witnesses, including overlapping occurrences, contribute separately to numerical totals. A positive translation would extend the classical first-order and temporal correspondence to this precise quantitative setting without introducing stronger weighted operators.

title: Is positivity of integer linear recurrences decidable?
importance_reason: A longstanding foundational decision problem with an elementary input model, strong links to verification, and consequences for the separate Skolem problem; unrestricted decidability is unknown before any efficiency requirement is imposed.
focus_reason: A longstanding foundational decision problem with an elementary input model, strong links to verification, and consequences for the separate Skolem problem; unrestricted decidability is unknown before any efficiency requirement is imposed.
formal: Does there exist a Turing machine that, on every input consisting of an integer d≥1, integer initial values u_0,…,u_{d−1}, and integer coefficients a_0,…,a_{d−1}, halts and decides whether u_n≥0 for every n≥0, where u_{n+d}=sum_{i=0}^{d−1}a_i u_{n+i}? The order d is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound.
definitions: All integers are given exactly in signed binary, and the coefficient and initial-value lists are explicit. The recurrence is homogeneous and its coefficients are constant in n. The requested property includes every term from u_0 onward and allows zero terms. Coefficients may be zero, including a_0; the decision procedure must accept these inputs as well. No promise of distinct characteristic roots, reversibility, eventual nonnegativity, or bounded order is imposed. The recurrence supplied need not be of minimal order. Computation uses the ordinary Turing model, with no real-number or number-theoretic oracle. No polynomial-time or other specified running-time bound is required, but the machine must halt for both possible answers. A simple sequence has a minimal characteristic polynomial with no repeated complex roots. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove that nonnegativity of every term is decidable for integer linear recurrences of arbitrary input order, by a machine halting on both positive and negative instances, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. The property is u_n≥0 for all n≥0, including the initial values.
context:
A recurrence is a finite description of an infinite trajectory. One can compute any requested term exactly, but checking every term asks for a finite justification covering unbounded time. This makes positivity a basic test case for the limits of algorithmic verification. The July 2026 survey still lists its general decidability among the central unresolved problems. The word positivity is conventional here: the inequality is non-strict.

The connection to linear dynamics is direct. Store d consecutive values in a vector x_n. A fixed integer companion matrix M then gives x_{n+1}=Mx_n, and the first coordinate of M^n x_0 is u_n. The question is whether that coordinate ever enters the negative half-line. Even though the transition is linear and deterministic, the trajectory can combine growth, decay and oscillation through its characteristic roots.

No universal finite amount of simulation certifies the desired answer. For any chosen integer N, the sequence u_n=N−n satisfies u_{n+2}=2u_{n+1}−u_n, is nonnegative through index N, and becomes negative afterward. Of course this particular family is easy to analyze. Its role is to distinguish sampling a long prefix from proving a bound that is computed from an arbitrary input and is sufficient for that input.

Ouaknine and Worrell decide positivity for all sequences of order at most five. Their analysis combines effective estimates from Diophantine approximation with decision procedures for real algebraic conditions. At order six, decidability would already imply that certain approximation constants associated with transcendental numbers are computable. This is a precise mathematical consequence, rather than a proof that no algorithm can exist.

Removing repeated characteristic roots improves the known frontier: positivity is decidable for simple sequences through order nine.

A separate theorem decides ultimate positivity for simple sequences of every order, in polynomial space. Ultimate positivity asks whether some finite prefix contains all negative terms. The algorithm need not provide an effective cutoff beyond which the terms are nonnegative. Without such a cutoff, the theorem cannot be turned into a positivity decider by checking the remaining prefix.

There are larger decidable orders under a different structural promise. An integer recurrence is reversible when its extension to all negative indices also has integer values. Kenison and coauthors decide positivity through order eleven for reversible sequences, and through order seventeen when they are also simple. The extra integrality in backward time matters; these bounds do not apply to arbitrary integer recurrences of those orders.

A general solution would also decide the Skolem problem, which asks whether an integer recurrence ever equals zero. Integer recurrence sequences are effectively closed under termwise products and subtraction of a constant. Thus w_n=u_n²−1 is another such sequence, and it is nonnegative at every index exactly when u has no zero. Negating the answer to a positivity decider would decide Skolem. This reduction explains why positivity has consequences beyond sign analysis itself.
why: A basic infinite-time safety question for finite linear descriptions. Its resolution would establish a major decidability boundary connecting verification, discrete dynamical systems and effective number theory, and would also settle general Skolem decidability.
