title: Can simple stochastic games be solved in polynomial time?
importance_reason: An elementary game model with broad consequences for synthesis and stochastic verification; short optimal strategies and efficiently checkable certificates coexist with an unresolved polynomial-time search problem.
focus_reason: An elementary game model with broad consequences for synthesis and stochastic verification; short optimal strategies and efficiently checkable certificates coexist with an unresolved polynomial-time search problem.
formal: Is the following decision problem in deterministic polynomial time? Given an explicitly represented finite simple stochastic game G, a start vertex s, and a binary rational threshold r∈[0,1], decide whether v_G(s)>r, where v_G(s)=sup_σ inf_τ Pr_s^{σ,τ}[eventually reach the target sink 1]. The game and threshold follow the exact conventions below, and time is polynomial in their total bit length.
definitions: The vertices are partitioned into Max, Min, random, and two distinct terminal sinks 0 and 1. Every nonterminal vertex has two listed successor slots; slots may have the same successor. At a Max or Min vertex its owner chooses a slot. At a random vertex each slot is chosen with probability 1/2, independently at each visit. Both players observe the complete finite history and the current vertex. Strategies may use history and private randomness; there is no bound on play length. Reaching 1 gives Max payoff one; reaching 0, or playing forever without reaching 1, gives payoff zero. Min minimizes the same expected payoff that Max maximizes. No promise of almost-sure termination is imposed. All vertices, ownership labels and successor indices are explicit; r=a/b is exact with binary integers 0≤a≤b and b>0. Equality v_G(s)=r is a NO instance. The algorithm is an ordinary uniform deterministic Turing algorithm; its polynomial bound has universal constants independent of the game and threshold. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove that the exact threshold language {(G,s,r):v_G(s)>r} belongs to P, or prove that it does not. The polynomial-time algorithm must handle arbitrary finite games, including nonterminating plays, and reject equality to the threshold.
context:
This game combines three elementary kinds of branching: a controller chooses, an adversary chooses, or a fair coin chooses. Removing one player gives a Markov decision process; fixing both players’ strategies leaves a Markov chain. The hard case is their interaction across cycles. Condon established that the threshold problem has polynomially checkable certificates on both sides, placing it in NP∩coNP. That classification has not yielded a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm.

Both players have optimal deterministic positional strategies: one successor choice per owned vertex suffices, even though the definition permits history and randomization. A candidate strategy is therefore short. Fixing one player leaves a one-player optimization problem that can be solved in polynomial time, which explains the certificates. The difficulty is finding a suitable strategy among the exponentially many combinations, rather than needing to represent an optimal strategy of enormous length.

The local equations look deceptively simple: a Max vertex takes the maximum successor value, a Min vertex the minimum, and a random vertex their average. In a nonterminating component these equations alone can have multiple solutions. For example, a random vertex whose two slots both lead back to itself satisfies x=(x+x)/2 for every x, but its actual target-reaching probability is zero. A solver must identify the reachability values rather than accept an arbitrary fixed point.

Exact thresholds matter. A chain of k independent fair choices can reach the target with probability 2^(−k), with any failed choice leading to 0. Its graph has only O(k) vertices. Thus an additive error suitable for many numerical applications may be too large to distinguish a positive value from zero or to decide a nearby rational threshold. Polynomially many bits of precision can still require very many iterations if convergence is slow.

Ludwig’s classical randomized algorithm uses an expected 2^{O(√n)} operations on n-vertex games. It demonstrates that straightforward enumeration is not the only way to search the strategy space. It still gives a subexponential bound rather than the polynomial deterministic bound requested here.

Recent progress develops both practical solvers and structural cases. Azeem, Kretinsky and Weininger extend sound value iteration to games with end components, maintaining lower and upper bounds while addressing probabilistic cycles.

Gärtner, Haslebacher and Hoang’s FUN 2026 paper solves stopping binary games on ladders: distance layers toward the sinks contain two vertices, except possibly the last layer. Their algorithm recovers an ordering of optimal values from this special geometry. This restricted-class theorem does not supply a polynomial-time solver for unrestricted games.

The consequences extend to more expressive objectives. Berthon, Katoen and Zhou give a direct polynomial reduction from quantitative stochastic parity games to simple stochastic games, using binary representations of transition probabilities. This strengthens the explanatory connection between recurring long-run conditions and a single reachability target. Their paper invokes the known polynomial equivalence of the usual probability encodings; the reduction does not itself remove the open algorithmic bottleneck.

Baldan, Gurke, König and Wittbold’s 2026 work extends convergent fixed-point iteration to simple stochastic games. Convergence of numerical approximations is a different guarantee from deciding every exact rational threshold using polynomially many bit operations. The iteration theorem does not establish the polynomial-time classification asked here.
why: A central test of efficient decision-making under both adversarial control and randomness. A polynomial algorithm would solve a canonical NP∩coNP problem and carry through reductions to quantitative verification tasks with more expressive objectives.
status_note: Rechecked on 11 September 2026. The inspected 2026 work on iteration and stopping ladder games does not give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for all exact threshold instances. No resolution was located in the later-work search.
progress: 1992: Condon establishes NP∩coNP membership for the stochastic-game decision problem and the foundational positional-strategy framework. | 1995: Ludwig gives a randomized subexponential algorithm requiring an expected 2^{O(√n)} operations. | 2025-08-18: Berthon, Katoen and Zhou publish a direct polynomial reduction from quantitative stochastic parity games to simple stochastic games with binary probability encodings. | 2025-09-17: Azeem, Kretinsky and Weininger present sound value iteration for stochastic games, including end components, with certified approximation bounds. | 2026-01-22: Baldan and coauthors extend fixed-point iteration to simple stochastic games. This convergence result does not give a general exact polynomial-time threshold decider. | 2026-05-15: Gärtner, Haslebacher and Hoang solve stopping binary SSGs on ladders in polynomial time; their introduction explicitly retains the general P question as open.
working_summary: A simple stochastic game combines choices of a maximizing player, choices of a minimizing player and fair random branching. The project asks for a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm deciding whether the optimal probability of reaching a target exceeds a given rational threshold. Optimal positional strategies provide short certificates, but finding them may require navigating exponentially many combinations. Cycles also mean that solving local value equations without the correct reachability interpretation can give misleading answers. Progress would clarify the computational cost of exact planning against both adversarial and random uncertainty.

title: An internal tower of semisimplicial types in ordinary HoTT
importance_reason: A central expressiveness problem for homotopy type theory; precise internal construction would remove a major obstacle to formalizing higher structures without enriching the theory.
focus_reason: A central expressiveness problem for homotopy type theory; precise internal construction would remove a major obstacle to formalizing higher structures without enriching the theory.
formal: In the fixed ordinary HoTT theory T below, can one define a single internal family S:ℕ→U₁ and restriction maps r_n:S(n+1)→S(n) whose finite stages are equivalent, compatibly with restriction, to the canonical finite semisimplicial telescopes D_n?
definitions: Fix T to be intensional Martin–Löf type theory with dependent function and pair types Π,Σ, identity types with their J eliminator, empty and unit types, finite coproducts, natural numbers and W-types, a cumulative predicative sequence U₀:U₁:⋯ closed under these constructors, and univalence for these universes. Also allow propositional truncation and homotopy pushouts with their ordinary dependent eliminators and propositional computation rules for path constructors, as in the HoTT book. There is no equality reflection, axiom K/UIP, resizing, choice, excluded middle, second equality type, display modality, or additional primitive for semisimplicial types. The question concerns definability in this specified theory; a negative result would apply to this theory, not automatically to every possible extension called HoTT. Define an external, finite family of syntactic telescopes as follows. D₀ is U₀, with element A₀. Given data d=(A₀,…,A_{j−1}) in D_{j−1}, form B_j(d), the dependent type of labelled boundaries of a j-simplex: for every nonempty proper subset F of {0,…,j}, in increasing cardinality and then lexicographic order, choose a label x_F in A_{|F|−1} evaluated on the labels of all nonempty proper subfaces of F. Identify F with {0,…,|F|−1} by its increasing enumeration when supplying these arguments. For singleton F this means x_F:A₀. Set D_j=Σ(d:D_{j−1})(B_j(d)→U₀), whose last field is A_j, and let p_j:D_{j+1}→D_j forget the last field. This describes an ordinary finite T-expression for each external integer j; it does not postulate an internal function j↦D_j. The required output is finite closed T-terms S:ℕ→U₁ and r:Π(n:ℕ)(S(n+1)→S(n)), together with a metatheoretic proof that for every external j there are T-terms e_j:S(j)≃D_j and homotopies e_j∘r_j ~ p_j∘e_{j+1}. Here j inside T denotes its numeral, ≃ is the usual type equivalence, and ~ is pointwise identity. No judgmental equality between S(j) and D_j is required. The equivalences classify the full type-valued telescopes, with arbitrary U₀-small simplex types and no fixed truncation bound.
answer_criterion: Prove that the specified theory T admits finite closed terms S and r together with the external stagewise equivalences and compatibility homotopies required above, or prove that no such terms and witnesses exist in T. The positive conclusion must hold at every external finite stage and allow arbitrary U₀-small simplex types.
context:
Homotopy type theory treats identity as mathematical data that can itself have nontrivial identities. This makes it a natural setting for spaces and higher structures, but it changes what it means to give a diagram. In set-level mathematics, equations between composites can be recorded once and used without further information. For general types, chosen identifications can have multiple distinct witnesses, and comparisons between those witnesses may matter in the next dimension.

A semisimplicial type begins with a type A₀ of vertices. For every ordered pair of vertices, A₁ gives a type of edges. For every triangle boundary—three vertices and three specified edges—A₂ gives a type of fillers. At dimension three, a filler is indexed by four vertices, six edges and four triangular fillers sharing their appropriate faces. Nothing forces a filler to exist, and the type of fillers may itself have arbitrarily rich homotopy.

The finite telescope description records shared boundaries through dependent types. A triangle’s three edges are already assigned the required endpoints; one does not choose unrelated edges and then append a collection of endpoint equations. The same idea works at each externally fixed dimension. The difficulty is making the whole construction into one function that accepts an internal natural number, rather than a growing list of separately written definitions.

This is why the card distinguishes its externally specified D_j from the sought internal S. A script can generate the expression for D_100 and a type checker can check it. That does not supply a HoTT term whose argument is an arbitrary n:ℕ. The compatibility requirement also matters: a collection of unrelated types with the right apparent sizes would not tell us how to forget the highest-dimensional data.

The statement deliberately allows equivalence at each stage instead of demanding a particular syntactic normal form. Thus a clever alternative encoding can solve the problem if it represents all the prescribed data and respects truncation. Once the internal tower exists, dependent sums, products and identity types already express a compatible infinite sequence. The missing step is constructing the tower itself, not adding a primitive that merely asserts an infinite sequence exists.

Kraus’s TYPES 2018 discussion identifies uniform finite-dimensional semisimplicial types as a major open problem and explains their role in higher category theory. Adding suitable Segal and completeness conditions to such data provides a route toward internal higher categories. Those conditions are additional structure: this card asks first for unrestricted semisimplicial data, with no composition, identity or horn-filling axioms imposed.

Two-level type theory introduces an outer equality satisfying uniqueness of identity proofs, alongside the homotopical inner theory. It can formalize constructions indexed by outer natural numbers. Annenkov, Capriotti, Kraus and Sattler distinguish this from constructing an inner universe of infinite semisimplicial types; additional hypotheses relating the two natural-number objects support the latter. The May 2026 revision is labelled a typo and reference update, not a new solution in ordinary HoTT.

Displayed Type Theory takes another route. Kolomatskaia and Shulman introduce discrete and simplicial modes together with a primitive display operation, then use it for a coinductive construction of semisimplicial types. This is a substantive solution in their enriched system, with a detailed semantic correctness argument. It does not give a definition from the constructors of T alone, because those additional primitives are precisely what enable the construction.

Chen’s 2025 thesis studies internal models and Reedy-fibrant inverse diagrams directly. It explicitly retains the ordinary-HoTT semisimplicial problem as open. Section 6.1 labels its proposed classifier construction a sketch whose Agda formalization has unresolved termination and definitional-equality issues, and states that it is not intended to solve the unrestricted problem. This is useful progress toward articulating the required coherence, rather than a completed internal classifier.

A set-valued construction also does not suffice. If every simplex type is a set, identities between elements have no higher ambiguity, and ordinary categorical equations behave much more rigidly. The requirement that the simplex types range over U₀ preserves the higher-dimensional content that motivates the problem. Likewise, having a satisfactory semantic construction in a model does not automatically produce a finite term definable in the specified syntax.

A positive answer would show that ordinary dependent types can organize this fundamental form of unbounded coherence without additional structure in the language. A negative answer would identify a precise expressive limitation and help explain why successful alternative foundations introduce new primitives. Either outcome would guide the design of proof assistants intended to support higher category theory and internal constructions of type-theoretic models.
why: Determine whether ordinary HoTT can express a fundamental unbounded coherent structure internally, a basic issue for higher categories and foundational proof languages.
status_note: The original question and the May 2026 two-level revision were rechecked on 11 September 2026. No construction in the specified theory T, or nondefinability theorem for T, was located. Results with outer strict equality or display primitives use additional structure and are recorded separately.
progress: 2013: The HoTT book supplies the ordinary dependent-type, univalence and higher-inductive framework fixed for this card. | 2018: Kraus states the uniform finite-level semisimplicial family problem and explains its connection to higher categories and internal metatheory. | 2023: Annenkov and coauthors develop the two-level framework and distinguish outer-indexed constructions from inner semisimplicial universes. | 2025: Chen’s thesis develops internal-model methods but explicitly marks the classifier construction incomplete and the unrestricted ordinary-HoTT problem open. | 2025-12-17: The journal version of Displayed Type Theory gives semisimplicial types using additional modal/display primitives; the preprint dates from 2023–2024. | 2026-05-26: Two-Level Type Theory v5 updates typos and references while retaining the distinction between ordinary HoTT and enriched constructions.
working_summary: Semisimplicial types organize vertices, edges, triangles and higher-dimensional fillers with compatible shared boundaries. Ordinary homotopy type theory can describe any fixed finite collection of these stages externally. The project asks for one internal family indexed by natural numbers, together with compatible maps forgetting the highest stage. Higher identities carry data, so specifying all coherence requirements uniformly is harder than listing equations in ordinary set-based mathematics. Such a construction would provide an internal foundation for important higher-dimensional structures without extending the stated type theory.

title: Can a Scott-continuous lambda model validate exactly beta-conversion?
importance_reason: The classical completeness question of whether denotational semantics can capture exactly the syntactic equality of a basic programming model.
focus_reason: The classical completeness question of whether denotational semantics can capture exactly the syntactic equality of a basic programming model.
formal: Does there exist a pointed directed-complete partial order D and Scott-continuous maps F:D→[D→D] and L:[D→D]→D with F∘L=id such that, for every pair of finite untyped lambda terms M,N, equality of their interpretations for every environment in D holds if and only if M and N are beta-convertible?
definitions: Terms are generated by variables from a countably infinite set, application MN and abstraction λx.M, modulo renaming bound variables. Beta-convertibility is the least equivalence relation closed under application and abstraction containing (λx.M)N=M[N/x], with capture-avoiding substitution. A directed set is nonempty and every two of its elements have an upper bound in the set. D is a set with a partial order, a least element, and a supremum for every directed subset. Scott-continuous means monotone and preserving directed suprema. [D→D] consists of all Scott-continuous functions, ordered pointwise. An environment ρ assigns an element of D to each variable. Interpret x as ρ(x), MN as F(⟦M⟧ρ)(⟦N⟧ρ), and λx.M as L(d↦⟦M⟧(ρ[x:=d])). The desired condition is ∀M,N: (∀ρ, ⟦M⟧ρ=⟦N⟧ρ) ⇔ M=βN. Models need not be countable, algebraic, effectively presented or extensional; in particular L∘F=id is not required. These are set-based directed-complete orders and all their continuous maps, without a restriction to graph models.
answer_criterion: Prove that a pointed dcpo and continuous retraction F,L satisfying the stated exact-theory condition exist, or prove that none exist. A negative answer must cover all such dcpos, without assuming an effective presentation, algebraicity or extensionality.
context:
The untyped lambda calculus describes functions using variables, application and abstraction. Beta-reduction substitutes an argument into a function body. A denotational model assigns mathematical meanings to terms and makes every beta-conversion valid. The question asks whether continuity can coexist with complete precision: no two terms should become equal in the model unless beta-conversion already equates them.

In domain semantics, an order represents increasing information and a directed supremum combines compatible approximations. Scott continuity requires functions to preserve these suprema. The map L represents each continuous self-map by an element of D, and F turns an element back into its associated self-map. The equation F∘L=id ensures that interpreting function application recovers the represented function. This makes beta-reduction sound.

Representability is a semantic condition. The element representing a continuous function need not be denoted by any finite lambda term. Requiring every continuous function to have a finite program would change the question. The model need not have computable elements, a computable ordering or a computable interpretation algorithm.

Extensional equality makes an additional identification. If x is not free in f, eta-conversion equates λx.f x with f, although these terms need not be beta-convertible. Imposing L∘F=id would validate this extra equality. This card therefore requires only the retraction in the other direction and keeps the beta-eta version as a separate target.

Quotienting syntax by beta-conversion gives a term model with exactly the desired equality. It does not automatically provide a pointed dcpo representing all continuous self-maps. The issue is whether the exact syntactic theory can be realized in this particular semantic setting.

Berline, Manzonetto and Salibra prove that the effective models defined in their paper cannot have theory exactly λβ or λβη. They also prove non-enumerability of the order theory, which records inequalities between denotations. Equational theory records equalities instead. A theorem restricted to effective models, or to order rather than equality, cannot be generalized silently to arbitrary dcpos.

Divergent terms reveal another source of extra equations. A term is unsolvable when no finite reduction exposes a head normal form: an outer variable applied to arguments after any leading abstractions. A sensible model equates all unsolvable closed terms. This is stronger than beta-conversion, which distinguishes some of them. The 2025 filter-model paper studies when unsolvables receive nontrivial interpretations and which type-theoretic conditions govern that behavior.

Lambda Galore, published in 2026, constructs sensible filter models representing all continuous functions whose theories do not contain the full Böhm-tree theory. It separates two semantic properties and resolves a different question about models. Sensibility still identifies unsolvables, so these constructions do not realize exactly λβ. Continuous representability alone does not make their equational theory the one requested here.
why: A foundational completeness question for denotational semantics: does the mathematical structure used to describe approximation and recursion inevitably identify programs beyond beta-conversion, or can it preserve every distinction made by that computation rule?
status_note: The exact question is explicit in Honsell’s primary statement. A search through 11 September 2026 found no resolution of its λβ alternative. The inspected 2025–2026 filter-model papers study unsolvables and other equational theories. Proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2007: Honsell records the exact λβ and λβη continuous-model questions, tracing discussion to the 1980s. This card asks the λβ alternative. | 2007: Berline, Manzonetto and Salibra rule out exact λβ and λβη theories for their class of effective models. | 2025: Dezani-Ciancaglini, Giannini and Honsell analyze nontrivial interpretations of unsolvable terms in filter models. | 2026-04-15: Lambda Galore constructs sensible continuously complete filter models not extending Böhm-tree theory; sensibility prevents these constructions from realizing exactly λβ.
working_summary: Scott's continuous semantics interprets untyped lambda terms using mathematical domains and continuous functions. The project asks whether some model identifies exactly the pairs of terms related by beta-conversion. Beta-conversion expresses equality generated by applying functions to arguments and substituting those arguments into their bodies. Many semantic constructions validate additional equations, so soundness for beta-reduction alone does not answer the question. An exact model would show whether this influential notion of continuous meaning can distinguish every pair of terms that the basic operational equations keep separate.

title: Does weak normalization imply strong normalization for every pure type system?
importance_reason: Asks whether the existence of a terminating reduction for every typable term forces every reduction of every such term to terminate.
focus_reason: Asks whether the existence of a terminating reduction for every typable term forces every reduction of every such term to terminate.
formal: For every pure type system (S,A,R) defined below, does weak normalization of every typable term imply strong normalization of every typable term?
definitions: S is a set of sorts, A⊆S×S is a set of axioms, and R⊆S×S×S is a set of product rules. Terms are finite expressions t ::= x | s | t u | λx:B.t | Πx:B.C, with s∈S and variables from a countably infinite set, modulo renaming bound variables. A context is a finite sequence of declarations of distinct variables. Typing is the least relation Γ⊢t:B generated by the following rules. Axiom: ∅⊢s:t when (s,t)∈A. Start: Γ,x:B⊢x:B when Γ⊢B:s and x is fresh. Weakening: Γ,x:C⊢t:B when Γ⊢t:B, Γ⊢C:s and x is fresh. Product: Γ⊢Πx:B.C:s₃ when Γ⊢B:s₁, Γ,x:B⊢C:s₂ and (s₁,s₂,s₃)∈R. Abstraction: Γ⊢λx:B.t:Πx:B.C when Γ,x:B⊢t:C and Γ⊢Πx:B.C:s for a sort s. Application: Γ⊢t u:C[u/x] when Γ⊢t:Πx:B.C and Γ⊢u:B. Conversion: Γ⊢t:C when Γ⊢t:B, Γ⊢C:s and B=βC. All substitutions avoid capture. A beta step contracts (λx:B.t)u to t[u/x] at any subterm, including inside annotations and product types. =β is the reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure of those steps. A term is typable if Γ⊢t:B for some finite Γ,B. Weak normalization means that each typable term has some finite beta-reduction sequence ending in a term with no beta redex. Strong normalization means that no typable term starts an infinite beta-reduction sequence. Both predicates quantify over open as well as closed terms and over all their reduction choices. The sets S,A,R need not be finite, decidable or functional.
answer_criterion: Prove that every pure type system in which all typable terms are weakly beta-normalizing is strongly beta-normalizing, or exhibit a pure type system that is weakly normalizing for every typable term but has a typable term admitting an infinite beta-reduction sequence.
context:
A term can contain several reducible applications, so computation involves choices. Weak normalization says that some sequence reaches a normal form. Strong normalization says that every sequence of beta-reductions terminates. The conjecture asks whether these two system-wide properties coincide for all pure type systems, a common framework for typed lambda calculi.

The distinction is real for untyped terms. Let Ω=(λz.zz)(λz.zz). The term (λx.y)Ω reduces to y in one step if the outer application is chosen, but it can also reduce Ω forever. Thus it is weakly but not strongly normalizing. This only illustrates the distinction: a counterexample to the conjecture needs a pure type system whose entire collection of typable terms is weakly normalizing.

A pure type system specifies which sorts classify other sorts and which dependent function types may be formed, through its sets A and R. The common typing rules generate the resulting calculus. Familiar simply typed, polymorphic and dependent systems fit the framework, but the conjecture also covers unusual specifications, beyond established proof languages.

The global hypothesis concerns every typable term. Confluence cannot replace it: confluence says that two finite reductions can be joined, making normal forms unique when they exist. It does not prevent an infinite path from coexisting with a terminating path. The untyped example already separates these ideas.

Reduction here includes type annotations and components of dependent products. Termination of an implementation’s selected evaluation strategy therefore differs from strong normalization of the calculus. Results after erasing annotations, or for closed programs only, have a different scope from the property of every annotated typable term in every context.

Sørensen’s 1997 work proves the implication for specified classes of typed calculi. Barthe, Hatcliff and Sørensen extend it to a class of non-dependent pure type systems in 2001. Their structural hypotheses are substantive: the theorem does not claim to cover every non-dependent specification, let alone every dependent one. The TLCA list records these as partial results.

Mull’s TYPES 2022 paper, published in 2023, enlarges the known class using a translation preserving typability and infinite reduction paths while removing certain sorts and rules. The theorem includes some systems with dependent rules that earlier results did not cover. The author explicitly retains the unrestricted conjecture; the translation’s structural hypotheses cannot be omitted.

A universal implication would connect the existence of normal forms with complete freedom of reduction order throughout this family of type theories. A counterexample would identify a system in which every term can finish, yet some legal choices continue forever. Either outcome would sharpen normalization arguments in proof checking and the metatheory of dependent types.
why: Normalization connects computation with the metatheory of typed proofs. This conjecture asks whether the pure-type-system rules turn the existence of a terminating computation for every typable term into termination under every reduction order.
status_note: The primary statement and Mull’s 2023 paper leave the unrestricted conjecture open. A later-result and author-publication search on 11 September 2026 found no general proof or counterexample. The positive theorems impose additional PTS structure.
progress: 1993–1995: The conjecture appears in Geuvers’ thesis and is circulated by Barendregt; the TLCA list records it as Problem 9. | 1997: Sørensen proves the implication for specified typed calculi and generalized non-dependent systems under additional hypotheses. | 2001: Barthe, Hatcliff and Sørensen extend the known non-dependent class, recorded as a partial result in the problem statement. | 2023-07-28: Mull’s TYPES 2022 proceedings paper extends the known class to some systems with dependent rules, retaining the general conjecture.
working_summary: A pure type system specifies a typed lambda calculus through a uniform collection of formation rules. Weak normalization means that every well-typed term has some terminating reduction path. The conjecture asks whether that global property forces every reduction path of every well-typed term to terminate. A term may have both a normalizing route and a divergent route in less constrained rewriting settings, so the type-system hypothesis is essential. A proof would connect existence of normal forms with unrestricted evaluation termination across a broad family of typed calculi.

title: Can parity games be solved in deterministic polynomial time?
importance_reason: A defining algorithmic question of verification and infinite-duration games, with direct modal-logic and synthesis connections and a major quasipolynomial breakthrough. Its former rank came from a provisional unassessed score, not a low-significance assessment. The score does not certify the correctness or failure of the located solution claim.
formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants K,c>0 such that, on every finite parity game G and designated vertex s, A decides whether Even has a winning strategy from s in at most K(L+1)^c steps, where L is the explicit binary encoding length of (G,s)?
definitions: G consists of a nonempty vertex set V={1,…,n}, a directed edge set E⊆V×V with at least one outgoing edge at every vertex, a partition V=V_Even⊔V_Odd, and a priority function p:V→N. Self-loops are allowed. The input explicitly lists all vertices, edges, owner bits and priorities, with integers in binary and delimiters; s∈V is included. A play is an infinite sequence v_0v_1… with v_0=s and (v_i,v_(i+1))∈E. At a vertex owned by a player that player chooses the next vertex. A strategy maps every finite valid play ending at a vertex owned by that player to a legal successor. Even wins a play if the minimum priority occurring infinitely often is even; Odd wins otherwise. A winning strategy for Even makes every play consistent with it winning for Even, irrespective of Odd’s choices. The algorithm must answer YES exactly when such a strategy exists. Strategies are not part of the input. The number and magnitude of priorities are unrestricted input data; the running-time exponent may not depend on them. The task has perfect information, alternating vertex ownership and no probabilistic transitions.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.
context:
Parity games describe infinite behavior using a finite graph and a priority condition. The question is not how to simulate an infinite play; it is how to decide whether one player can force the eventual recurrence pattern of priorities to favor it. This decision problem underlies central constructions in logical verification and synthesis.

Positional determinacy says that a winning player can choose moves using only the current vertex. Thus finite strategies suffice even though the winning condition concerns an infinite play. Their existence does not by itself give a polynomial-time algorithm for finding or choosing the winning strategy. The problem lies in both NP and coNP, and more precisely in UP and coUP.

Calude and coauthors established a quasipolynomial-time algorithm in 2017. Czerwiński and coauthors proved quasipolynomial lower bounds for separating automata used by a broad collection of such algorithms. That lower bound concerns the specified approach, not arbitrary algorithms for parity games.

A November 2025 preprint by Rick van der Heijden claims a polynomial-time algorithm for the full problem. This review located and inspected the claim but did not independently verify its proof or find an authoritative resolution of its correctness. It must be visible on the card rather than omitted from a statement that the problem is confirmed open.

Suilen and Pérez’s April 2026 paper still describes polynomial-time parity-game solving as a longstanding open question while reducing parity games to a robust-MDP threshold problem. This later usage is evidence about the literature, not a proof that the earlier claim is false. The card therefore carries an explicitly unverified current status while completing the mathematical formulation and preserving its historical identifier.
why: Determine the exact polynomial-time boundary for a central finite representation of infinite game behavior.
status_note: Current status unverified as of 11 September 2026: arXiv:2511.03752v1 claims a full polynomial-time solution, while arXiv:2604.26748 (April 2026) still treats the question as open. This review did not establish the claim’s correctness or locate an authoritative rejection. The record is neither certified open nor marked resolved.
progress: 2017: Calude and coauthors give a quasipolynomial-time decision algorithm. | 2018: Separating automata require quasipolynomial size; this is a restricted-method lower bound. | 2025-11-04: Van der Heijden posts a claimed polynomial-time solution. Its correctness is not independently established by this review. | 2026-04-29: Suilen–Pérez still treat the general polynomial-time question as open. This is not a refutation of the 2025 claim.
working_summary: Parity games ask which player can force an infinite play whose minimum infinitely recurring priority has the desired parity. The target is a uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm for arbitrary finite arenas and binary-encoded priorities. Quasipolynomial algorithms and lower bounds for separating-automaton methods are known. A November 2025 preprint claims a polynomial-time solution, but this review did not establish its correctness. A separate April 2026 paper still treats the question as open, so the completed card explicitly records an unverified current status.

title: Is the Skolem problem for integer linear recurrences decidable?
importance_reason: A longstanding central decidability problem with an elementary finite input, substantial arithmetic content, and direct links to verification and automata. The 2026 work confirms current specialist attention; the importance is independent of the record’s previous incomplete wording.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that halts on every input k≥1, c_0,…,c_(k−1)∈Z and u_0,…,u_(k−1)∈Z, and correctly decides whether the sequence defined by u_(t+k)=∑_(j=0)^(k−1)c_j u_(t+j) for all t≥0 has u_t=0 for some integer t≥0?
question_excerpt: Although the Skolem-Mahler-Lech Theorem is almost 90 years old, decidability of the Skolem Problem remains open.
definitions: All integers, including k, are given in binary with signs and delimiters; the input explicitly lists exactly k coefficients and k initial values. These data uniquely define the infinite integer sequence. The order k is unrestricted and is part of the input, not a fixed parameter. Coefficients may vanish, the supplied recurrence need not be of minimal order, and no simplicity, non-degeneracy or nonzero-leading-product promise is imposed. The search includes the given initial terms and all subsequent nonnegative indices. There is no supplied upper bound on t. The required output is YES exactly when a zero occurs and NO otherwise; only termination and correctness are demanded, without a time or space bound. This is the discrete recurrence problem over integers, not the continuous-time Skolem problem or the question whether every term is nonnegative.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.
context:
A short recurrence determines infinitely many exact integer values. Testing any particular term is effective, but deciding that no term will ever be zero requires a terminating procedure for a global property. Even this elementary linear evolution leaves an unresolved boundary between arithmetic structure and algorithmic decision.

The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem constrains zero sets to a finite union of arithmetic progressions together with a finite exceptional set. That qualitative description is not, by itself, an algorithm that determines all exceptional zeros from the input. The distinction explains why a structural theorem about the sequence does not automatically settle the decision question.

Bilu and coauthors study simple recurrences and relate termination of their proposed procedure to transcendence conjectures. The arbitrary integer recurrence in this card also allows repeated characteristic roots and other cases outside the simple setting. Conditional termination for a subclass therefore has a different scope from an unconditional decision algorithm for the full input domain.

Bacik, Ouaknine and Worrell improve the complexity of low-order and bounded-index versions. Their July 2026 revision places the unrestricted order-at-most-four problem in coRP. A bounded index range is additional input, and an order bound of four excludes general recurrences; neither restriction answers the unrestricted decision problem.

Luca, Ouaknine and Worrell’s July 2026 paper obtains general decidability conditionally on a strengthened Cramér-type conjecture. Its unconditional density results for possible large zeros do not guarantee a decision for each individual recurrence. The new review preserves TCS-5773 and its original 2022 source rather than creating a second general Skolem entry.
why: Locate the decidability boundary for exact zero reachability in discrete linear dynamics.

title: Can mean-payoff games be solved in polynomial time?
importance_reason: A canonical NP∩coNP problem central to quantitative synthesis and long-run control; resolving the binary-weight complexity gap would have consequences across several equivalent algebraic and game formulations.
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm, running in time polynomial in the total input bit length, that decides the following problem? Given a finite directed graph G=(V,E), a partition V=V_Max⊔V_Min, integer edge weights w:E→Z, and a start vertex s, determine whether Max has a strategy σ such that every strategy τ of Min produces a play s=v_0,v_1,… satisfying liminf_{T→∞}(1/T) sum_{t=0}^{T−1} w(v_t,v_{t+1})≥0.
definitions: The graph, its ownership partition, its start vertex and all weights are represented explicitly; weights use signed binary. Each vertex has at least one outgoing edge, so plays are infinite. The owner of the current vertex chooses the next edge with full knowledge of the finite history. Strategies are arbitrary deterministic functions of this history. There are no chance vertices, simultaneous moves, hidden observations or multiple payoff coordinates. Max seeks a nonnegative lower limit of average accumulated weight; equality zero is winning. No bound is imposed on intermediate losses or on the size W=max(1,max_e |w(e)|). The running-time requirement concerns ordinary bit operations, so a polynomial dependence on W is not sufficient. Zero threshold loses no generality: a binary rational threshold a/b with b>0 can be absorbed by replacing w(e) with b w(e)−a, with polynomial growth of the encoding.
answer_criterion: Prove that this exact winner-decision language is in P, or prove that it is outside P. A pseudopolynomial algorithm, a smoothed or average-case guarantee, or a lower bound for one strategy-improvement rule does not settle the unrestricted worst-case question. Strongly polynomial time would suffice but is a stronger requirement than this card asks for.
context:
Mean payoff measures sustainable long-run performance. Edge weights can represent net resource gains, rewards or the negative of costs; an adversary controls some of the transitions. A finite initial loss disappears from the limiting average, while a repeatedly traversed cycle continues to matter. For example, eventually repeating weights −5 and +7 has mean payoff one, regardless of any fixed initial prefix. This distinguishes the objective from requiring the accumulated sum to remain nonnegative at every step.

Optimal positional strategies exist for both players, so a player can make the same choice whenever a vertex is revisited. With both choices fixed, the resulting path eventually repeats a cycle, and its value is the cycle’s average weight. This yields compact certificates and NP∩coNP membership. It does not make the search easy: the number of positional strategy combinations can be exponential. Zwick and Paterson gave the classical complexity analysis and a polynomial reduction to simple stochastic games.

The size of a weight and the size of its representation differ sharply. A weight 2^b takes only b+1 binary digits. An algorithm using O(nmW) arithmetic operations, where n is the number of vertices and m the number of edges, can therefore take exponential time in the input length. Brim and coauthors obtain such a pseudopolynomial bound for the threshold problem through energy-game progress measures. The result is powerful for small weights, but it leaves the dependence needed for this question unresolved.

Universal graphs provide a way to organize and compare value-iteration algorithms. Fijalkow, Gawrychowski and Ohlmann establish tight bounds within that framework, including improved dependence on the largest weight for a fixed number of vertices. Such a matching lower bound identifies a limitation of the framework being analyzed; it does not rule out an unrelated polynomial-time algorithm for mean-payoff games.

Smoothed analysis gives a different kind of progress. Loff and Skomra’s ICALP 2024 theorem obtains polynomial running time with high probability after sufficiently random independent perturbations of rewards, on ergodic game graphs. Here ergodicity is stronger than ordinary strong connectivity: for every reward assignment, the game value is independent of the start vertex. The theorem helps explain efficiency on perturbed inputs while retaining both a graph restriction and distributional assumptions. It does not decide the present worst-case complexity question.

There are also increasingly direct links to linear optimization. Maat’s September 2025 preprint identifies many strategy-improvement variants with instances of the simplex algorithm under nondegeneracy assumptions. This gives a structural bridge between algorithms and their lower-bound constructions. A correspondence between local improvement methods, however, is not a proof that their number of iterations is polynomial.

A July 2026 preprint by Adenwalla and coauthors connects tropical inequality systems and mean-payoff games with deciding chromatic boundedness for certain classes of graphs defined by equality patterns. Its reverse encoding uses a specified succinct representation. This creates another setting in which a solver would be useful. The paper explicitly leaves polynomial-time mean-payoff solving open, and its graph-class reduction should not be mistaken for a polynomial algorithm for games.
why: A foundational complexity question for long-run adversarial optimization. It connects finite graph games, quantitative verification, resource reasoning and tropical algebra, with short optimal strategies but no known polynomial-time method to find the winner on arbitrary binary-weighted inputs.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The July 2026 primary source explicitly states that polynomial-time solution with binary weights remains open. The card fixes a single deterministic mean-payoff objective with a nonnegative liminf threshold. Pseudopolynomial, ergodic smoothed-analysis and framework-specific results do not resolve arbitrary worst-case inputs.

The maximizing player wants the limiting lower average weight to be nonnegative against every opposing strategy. title: Is the first-order theory of the real exponential field decidable?
importance_reason: A longstanding central question of real model theory with direct relevance to symbolic reasoning about exponential expressions. The explicit 2026 conditional result confirms continuing specialist interest without settling the unconditional target.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine which, on every first-order sentence φ in the language {0,1,+,−,×,<,exp}, halts and correctly decides whether φ is true in (R,0,1,+,−,×,<,x↦e^x)?
definitions: Sentences have finite syntax and no free variables. Terms are formed from variables, 0,1, the unary symbols − and exp, and binary + and ×; atomic formulas are equalities or strict inequalities of terms. Formulas use Boolean connectives and first-order quantifiers, all ranging over R. Equality has its usual logical interpretation. Inputs are finite parenthesized strings over a fixed finite alphabet, with variable indices written in binary; any fixed effectively interconvertible syntax encoding gives the same decidability question. No arbitrary real constants or oracles for real numbers are allowed. The symbol exp denotes the standard real exponential function on all of R, not a restricted function or an unspecified solution in another structure. There is no time or space bound beyond termination. A positive resolution must be unconditional, rather than assuming an unresolved transcendence conjecture.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
context:
First-order arithmetic over the real numbers can describe polynomial equalities, inequalities and quantifier alternation. Adding the exponential function permits expressions involving growth and decay that are unavailable in the polynomial language. The target is exact truth of every sentence, including cases in which a numerical approximation alone cannot distinguish equality from a very small nonzero quantity.

The syntax is finite even though the quantified domain is infinite. An algorithm receives a formula such as an existential statement about real solutions; it does not receive an arbitrary real constant as an infinitely long input. Fixing the standard exponential function and excluding such parameters prevents representation choices from changing the decision problem.

Macintyre and Wilkie proved decidability under Schanuel’s conjecture. Berarducci and Gallinaro’s 2026 paper obtains an axiomatization under the same assumption and recovers that conditional decidability result. Its unconditional result for a related restricted exponential setting does not settle the unrestricted theory on this card.

This question is not the task of efficiently evaluating e^x to a specified error. Exact logical decision also includes formulas with arbitrary quantifier patterns and exact equalities. Conversely, the card imposes no polynomial running-time demand. An unconditional terminating algorithm of any complexity would answer it affirmatively.

The catalogue already contains individual questions about linear recurrences and linear dynamical systems. TCS-6265 concerns safety exactly at a specific robustness threshold, not the full elementary theory of the real exponential field. The new card supplies a broader, distinct boundary for algorithmic reasoning with real analytic operations.
why: Locate a fundamental decidability boundary beyond polynomial real arithmetic, where exact reasoning interacts with transcendence.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. The June 2026 revision remains conditional for the full theory, and no unconditional decision procedure or undecidability result was found.

title: Decidability of unbounded Continuous Skolem
importance_reason: A fundamental boundary for verification of linear differential systems, with a precisely finite rational input and an unrestricted exact reachability target.
formal: Is there a Turing algorithm that, given any dimension d≥1, rational matrix A∈Q^{d×d}, and rational column vectors b,c∈Q^d, always halts and correctly decides whether cᵀexp(tA)b=0 for some real t≥0?
definitions: Every input rational is represented exactly by a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. The dimension is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound. The matrix exponential is exp(tA)=Σ_{j=0}^∞ t^j A^j/j!, and x(t)=exp(tA)b is the unique real solution of x′(t)=Ax(t), x(0)=b. The target is the hyperplane {x:cᵀx=0}; c=0 is allowed and gives an immediate yes instance. Time ranges over all finite nonnegative real numbers, not just rational or integer times. Equality is exact. A zero at t=0 counts, as does a trajectory that is identically in the hyperplane. If the scalar function approaches zero only in the limit t→∞, the answer is no unless it also has a finite zero. No promise of diagonalizability, simple eigenvalues, bounded dimension, stability, spectral separation, transverse intersection, or robust distance from the hyperplane is supplied. The requested algorithm is an ordinary finite-input decision procedure without real-number or number-theoretic oracles; no complexity upper bound is prescribed. This card retains the rational-data version; some cited work treats the more general real-algebraic-data version.
answer_criterion: Give an unconditional always-halting decision algorithm for every rational input, or prove that no such Turing algorithm exists. A conditional procedure assuming Schanuel’s conjecture, a solver for a fixed low dimension, a procedure that may run forever on some inputs, or a certified answer only under a nonzero distance promise is partial progress. An undecidability theorem allowing more general coefficients or nonlinear differential equations must be reduced to this rational linear model to refute the proposition.
context:
Linear differential equations have explicit matrix-exponential solutions, yet an explicit formula does not automatically decide whether a trajectory hits an exact target. The scalar output cᵀx(t) may combine growth, decay, polynomial factors and oscillations. The matrix and vectors are finite rational data, while the possible hitting time is an unrestricted real number. This makes the question a basic test of what exact verification can decide even for linear continuous dynamics.

Numerical proximity is insufficient. The one-dimensional system x′=−x, x(0)=1 has output e^{−t}, which becomes arbitrarily small but never reaches zero. Conversely, a zero need not be accompanied by a sign change: the polynomial (t−1)² touches zero and returns to positive values. Such a polynomial is itself an output of a rational nilpotent linear system. A grid search or a sign-change detector can therefore miss the distinction required by the card.

Simple degenerate cases can be removed exactly. The initial-time condition is cᵀb=0. By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, the scalar function is identically zero precisely when cᵀA^j b=0 for j=0,…,d−1. These are finite rational calculations. Outside that case, analyticity ensures only finitely many zeros in each bounded interval, but neither a uniform numerical precision nor a final time beyond all zeros follows from that finiteness statement.

Spectral decomposition writes the output as a sum of polynomial multiples of exponentials, with conjugate terms combining into real sine and cosine expressions. The imaginary parts of eigenvalues give oscillation frequencies. Repeated eigenvalues can introduce polynomial factors. Competing terms can nearly cancel at very large times, so a proof that the long-term behaviour is simple enough to inspect is a substantive part of an unbounded decision procedure.

Chonev, Ouaknine and Worrell prove decidability of the bounded Continuous Skolem problem assuming Schanuel’s conjecture. That conjecture gives a transcendence-degree lower bound for complex numbers linearly independent over the rationals together with their exponentials. Their algorithm uses it to handle possible tangential zeros. The result does not supply an unconditional bounded-time procedure, and a bounded-time procedure alone does not supply a stopping criterion for checking all t≥0.

The same paper reduces certain unbounded spectral cases to the bounded problem, including the case with at most one rationally independent frequency. A separate recurrent-reachability result decides whether a solution of differential order at most seven has infinitely many zeros and gives an effective last-zero bound when it has only finitely many. Combined with the conditional bounded solver, this yields conditional decisions in that low-order regime. Infinite recurrence and existence of even one zero are nevertheless different questions.

The broader algebraic-coefficient formulations reveal a connection with effective Diophantine approximation: handling multiple independent oscillations can entail computing quantities measuring unusually good rational approximations to algebraic numbers. Those implications are evidence of the mathematical obstacles, not undecidability proofs. Their precise dimension thresholds belong to the coefficient model of the cited theorem; this card does not automatically transfer them to the rational-matrix representation fixed above.

Platzer and Qian’s 2025 completeness theorem for compact initial-value problems concerns specified open safety and liveness properties. Its discussion explicitly identifies exact hyperplane reachability as an obstacle to replacing those topological conditions by arbitrary closed targets. A proof system that certifies entry into an open neighbourhood need not decide whether the trajectory touches its central hyperplane. This distinction matters when interpreting advances in numerical verification as progress on exact decision questions.

The July 2026 survey by Bacik and coauthors places the continuous problem alongside discrete recurrence questions, while emphasizing differences in technique. Sampling only integer times gives a sequence but changes the question: for example, a rational rotation system can have output cos t and reach zero at π/2. The card asks whether any real hitting time exists, so discrete-time zero testing cannot simply replace the continuous analysis.
why: A minimal exact reachability question for continuous linear systems whose decidability remains unresolved, linking algorithmic verification to real analysis, transcendence and effective number theory.
status_note: No unconditional decision procedure or undecidability proof for this rational linear model was found through 11 September 2026. Bounded conditional results, low-order recurrence algorithms, approximate/robust verification and nonlinear-system hardness do not settle the unbounded exact question.

working_summary: A rational linear differential system evolves as a matrix exponential applied to its initial state. Continuous Skolem asks whether a specified linear observation of that trajectory is exactly zero at some nonnegative real time. The dimension is unrestricted, and the project seeks decidability without a time horizon. Approaching zero or changing sign are inadequate substitutes because trajectories may approach without hitting or touch zero without crossing it. A resolution would establish the limits of exact reachability verification even for continuous systems with linear, fully specified dynamics.
