title: Can every polynomial-time decision problem be efficiently parallelized?
importance_reason: The foundational tractability question for parallel computation: whether every polynomial-time task admits polylogarithmic dependency depth with polynomial work.
focus_reason: The foundational tractability question for parallel computation: whether every polynomial-time task admits polylogarithmic dependency depth with polynomial work.
formal: Is P=NC, where NC consists of decision languages recognized by logspace-uniform Boolean circuit families of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have such a circuit family?
definitions: P is deterministic polynomial time on ordinary Turing machines. For L∈NC there must be fixed constants c,k,C and a family (Cₙ)ₙ≥0 such that Cₙ decides membership in L correctly on every n-bit input, has at most C(n+2)ᶜ gates, and has depth at most C(log₂(n+2))ᵏ. Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; fan-out is unrestricted and one output bit is designated. Depth is the longest input-to-output gate path. A deterministic O(log(n+2))-space transducer given 1ⁿ must output the description of Cₙ; its polynomial output bound is part of the size requirement. Constants and the generator may depend on L but not on n. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered Boolean gate DAG, its input-bit values, and an output-gate index; it asks whether that gate evaluates to 1. Its input length n is the entire binary encoding length, and malformed encodings are rejected. No randomization, advice, oracle, or restriction to monotone gates is permitted. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Circuit evaluation makes the apparent obstacle concrete. A sequential algorithm processes the gates in their supplied topological order and computes every value in polynomial time. A circuit can contain a long chain of dependent gates, but that chain only limits the obvious evaluation procedure. A faster algorithm may reorganize the computation, exploit algebraic identities, or avoid evaluating intermediate gates. Proving that every possible efficient parallel computation must retain substantial sequential dependence is the unresolved step.

Ladner proved Circuit Value complete for P under logarithmic-space reductions. These reductions themselves admit NC computation, and NC is closed under their composition. An NC algorithm for this one problem would therefore parallelize every problem in P. P-completeness supplies this conditional consequence; it does not already prove the absence of a parallel algorithm.

The resource tradeoff is polynomial total circuit size against polylogarithmic dependency depth. The exponent of the polynomial work budget may be large, so a positive answer would not automatically provide nearly linear work or useful speedups on a small machine. Logspace uniformity prevents the circuit descriptions from supplying arbitrary nonuniform information. The union over all fixed depth exponents also makes this broader than asking whether P equals NC¹.

Restricted circuit models reveal real obstructions. Raz and McKenzie separate monotone NC from monotone P, and separate consecutive levels of the monotone NC hierarchy. Their lower bounds restrict the computing circuit to AND and OR. A monotone function can still have a substantially more powerful circuit when NOT gates are allowed, so the restriction cannot be removed from the conclusion.

Recent matching lower bounds sharpen this caution. Cavalar and coauthors prove a stretched-exponential monotone circuit-size lower bound for perfect matching, a problem with polynomial-time general algorithms. The separation measures the cost of forbidding negation. It supplies progress in circuit lower bounds while leaving the general uniform parallel-computation question untouched.
why: This asks whether a feasible computation can require intrinsically many sequential stages even when polynomially many processors are available. It is the central unresolved premise behind P-completeness as an explanation for resistance to parallelization, spanning graph algorithms, simulation, optimization, and language processing.
status_note: P versus NC is explicitly open in the primary P-completeness monograph. The literature check through 10 September 2026 located no unrestricted resolution. Monotone-circuit separations do not settle the stated Boolean circuit model.
progress: 1975: Ladner establishes that Circuit Value is logspace complete for P, giving a concrete universal target for efficient parallelization. | 1995: Greenlaw, Hoover, and Ruzzo organize the theory of P-completeness and its open P-versus-NC question, including uniform circuit and parallel-machine formulations. | 1999: Raz and McKenzie prove monotone NC≠monotone P and a strict monotone NC hierarchy. These results restrict the gates used by the computing circuits. | 2025–2026: Cavalar and coauthors prove perfect matching requires monotone circuit size 2^{n^{Ω(1)}}, improving Razborov’s quasipolynomial lower bound. The November 2025 revision appears in STOC 2026; general Boolean circuits are not covered.
working_summary: NC describes computations with polynomial total circuit size and only polylogarithmic dependency depth, under a uniformity requirement. The question asks whether every problem solvable in polynomial sequential time belongs to this parallel class. Circuit Value is a concrete complete problem: given a circuit and its input, compute the designated output. An NC algorithm for circuit evaluation would therefore parallelize every problem in P. The challenge is to distinguish a long chain in the supplied circuit from an unavoidable chain in every possible algorithm for evaluating its behavior.

title: Directed reachability with nearly linear memory and polylogarithmic passes
importance_reason: A basic directed-graph primitive with a polynomial-versus-polylogarithmic pass gap, connections to communication lower bounds and consequences for other streaming tasks.
focus_reason: A basic directed-graph primitive with a polynomial-versus-polylogarithmic pass gap, connections to communication lower bounds and consequences for other streaming tasks.
formal: Do there exist constants a,b,C and a uniform randomized streaming algorithm that decides directed s–t reachability on every n-vertex graph using at most Cn(log(n+2))^a bits of memory and C(log(n+2))^b passes, with success probability at least 2/3 for every adversarially ordered edge stream?
definitions: The input is a finite simple directed graph on the labelled vertex set [n], n≥2, with distinct designated vertices s,t. The algorithm knows n,s,t before reading the edges. Each directed edge occurs once in an insertion-only stream, in an arbitrary order fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits. Each pass scans this same stream in the same forward order. The input is read-only: there are no adjacency queries, random-access reads, sorting operations on external storage, or writable auxiliary streams. All mutable working storage counts toward the bit bound; fresh independent random bits may be read from a one-way random source. The memory and pass bounds hold on every execution. Computation between successive input items is unrestricted but must terminate; no running-time bound beyond termination is imposed. A yes answer means that there is a directed path from s to t in the input graph. The constants and algorithm are independent of n, the graph, and the edge order.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Directed reachability asks an elementary question: can one vertex eventually lead to another by following arrows? With the whole graph in memory, a search answers it in linear time. In a graph stream, the difficulty is that the next useful edge may already have gone past before the algorithm learns that its tail is reachable. Repeated scans provide another opportunity to use the edge, but every scan revisits the entire input.

Nearly linear memory means linear in the number of vertices, up to powers of a logarithm. It can store labels, several values per vertex and a sparse auxiliary graph, but a dense input may have quadratically many edges. The card allows every fixed polylogarithmic memory overhead: it does not ask for an especially restrictive exact n-bit implementation. Conversely, allowing storage proportional to all the edges would erase the intended obstacle.

A simple baseline maintains the set of vertices already reached from s. Whenever an edge leaves this set, its head is marked reachable. After at most n−1 scans every reachable vertex has been found, using a bit per vertex and counters. A path whose edges appear in reverse path order makes this particular algorithm advance slowly. That example is not a lower bound for all algorithms: a path has only linearly many edges and fits entirely in the permitted memory.

The undirected analogue has a much stronger one-pass solution: maintain connected components with union–find. Direction removes the equivalence-relation structure that makes this summary sufficient. Strongly connected components can still be contracted in a digraph, but their directed reachability relation is another graph rather than just a partition. A small summary must somehow preserve the information needed for the specified source and target.

Jambulapati, Liu and Sidford give a randomized parallel reachability algorithm using nearly linear work and n^{1/2+o(1)} depth. Their shortcut construction can also be implemented in the streaming model. Assadi and coauthors explicitly state the resulting n^{1/2+o(1)}-pass semi-streaming path-finding algorithm as Proposition 4. This supplies the relevant upper bound through a concrete simulation, rather than through an assumption that every shallow parallel computation automatically yields a streaming algorithm.

The shortcuts preserve which pairs are reachable while reducing how many edges a useful path needs. They can be stored because there are only nearly linearly many of them. This explains why the upper bound is much better than repeated ordinary reachability propagation. It also exposes a possible source of new ideas: construct better shortcuts within the streaming resources, or find a method that does not depend on such a shortcut set.

On the lower-bound side, Guruswami and Onak extend earlier path-output barriers to the decision problem itself. Their multipass space bound implies that semi-streaming reachability requires Ω(log n/log log n) passes. The exact theorem includes polynomial factors in the pass count and logarithmic factors in n; these should not be dropped when comparing parameters. The conclusion rules out constant passes but leaves the polylogarithmic target available.

Chen, Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, Song and Yu prove that o(√log n) passes require n^{2−o(1)} space. This is a striking strengthening of how much memory is necessary when the pass budget is very small. It is not a larger asymptotic lower bound on the number of passes with nearly linear memory than the Ω(log n/log log n) statement above. The two results describe different parts of the tradeoff.

Azarmehr and coauthors’ September 9, 2026 revision still identifies n^{1/2+o(1)} as the fastest known semi-streaming reachability pass bound. Their Theorem 9 links an improved streaming approximation for distance to monotonicity to an improved reachability algorithm. This is evidence that the question controls progress beyond reachability itself, and gives a recent explicit check of the benchmark used on this card.

A positive answer would show that repeated sequential access with a compact memory can recover global directed information surprisingly quickly. A negative answer would establish a fundamental barrier to that access pattern, even without restricting local computation time. Either result would help explain the difference between graph problems admitting compact summaries and those that require many rounds of discovering dependencies.
why: Determine whether global directed reachability can be recovered from repeated sequential scans with only nearly linear memory, a central unresolved graph-streaming tradeoff.
status_note: No polylogarithmic-pass semi-streaming algorithm or superpolylogarithmic lower bound settling the stated question was found through 11 September 2026. A 9 September 2026 primary source explicitly retains the n^{1/2+o(1)} upper bound. The card fixes randomized decision, adversarial fixed edge order, bit space and unrestricted terminating local computation.
progress: 2013–2016: Guruswami–Onak establish multipass superlinear space lower bounds for directed reachability decision; these imply Ω(log n/log log n) passes in semi-streaming space. | 2019: Jambulapati–Liu–Sidford develop nearly linear-work, approximately square-root-depth parallel reachability and its sparse shortcut construction. | 2021: Chen and coauthors prove almost-quadratic space is necessary for o(√log n) passes, strengthening the few-pass space tradeoff. | 2022: Assadi and coauthors state and explain the n^{1/2+o(1)}-pass semi-streaming implementation, including path recovery, in Proposition 4. | 2023-09: Assadi’s survey records the gap and explains the transition from search lower bounds to reachability-decision lower bounds. | 2026-09-09: The revised streaming-monotonicity paper retains the square-root reachability benchmark and reduces faster approximation to faster reachability.
working_summary: Directed reachability in a stream asks whether one vertex can reach another when graph edges arrive in an adversarial order. Nearly linear memory in the vertex count cannot store every edge of a dense graph. The question asks for a randomized algorithm using only polylogarithmically many passes and n times a polylogarithmic number of memory bits. Simple repeated scans can propagate reachability one step at a time, taking many passes on badly ordered paths. The project is to combine a small memory footprint with far fewer scans without relying on favorable edge order.

title: Is perfect matching in general graphs in deterministic NC?
importance_reason: A canonical deterministic parallel-algorithm and derandomization question for a basic graph optimization problem.
focus_reason: A canonical deterministic parallel-algorithm and derandomization question for a basic graph optimization problem.
formal: Do there exist constants C,a,b>0 and a logspace-uniform family of Boolean circuits which, on the adjacency matrix of every n-vertex simple undirected graph, output a perfect matching or correctly report that none exists, with at most C(n+2)^a gates and depth at most C(log₂(n+2))^b?
definitions: The input is the n×n binary adjacency matrix of a graph on [n], with symmetry and zero diagonal promised. A perfect matching is a set of edges with exactly one edge incident to each vertex. Output is a flag and an n×n binary incidence matrix for the chosen matching; when the flag reports nonexistence the remaining output bits are ignored. The empty graph has the empty perfect matching. Circuits use fan-in-two AND/OR, fan-in-one NOT, constants 0,1 and unrestricted fan-out. Depth counts gates on the longest input-output path and size counts gates; the n² output positions are specified as part of the description. A deterministic Turing transducer on unary input 1^n writes the description using O(log₂(n+2)) work bits, with read-only input and write-only output. Constants and generator are fixed across n; every valid input must receive an exact answer. No randomness, oracle, advice, bipartiteness or other structural graph promise is supplied.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A polynomial-time sequential algorithm is known, so the open issue is the length of the dependency chain after work is spread across many processors. Following one augmenting path after another does not automatically give a polylogarithmic number of parallel steps. The processor bound matters too: solving many possibilities simultaneously is useful only if the total work remains polynomial.

Choosing matching edges independently is dangerous. On a four-cycle, every edge can be excluded while preserving some perfect matching. Removing all four edges at once nevertheless destroys every solution. A parallel construction must coordinate its choices around one compatible matching rather than around separate existence certificates.

General graphs also need more structure than the bipartite case. Two disjoint triangles have an even total number of vertices and admit a fractional assignment of one half to every edge, giving total incident weight one at each vertex. They have no perfect matching. This example shows why degree constraints alone do not describe the general matching polytope; odd vertex sets impose additional conditions.

The June 2026 bipartite result is a major nearby advance. Its theorem covers bipartite graphs, including polynomially bounded weights. The present card deliberately asks for arbitrary graphs, where the deterministic polynomial-processor target remains unresolved in the checked literature.
why: I include this because perfect matching is a basic polynomial-time graph problem for which randomization and parallelism interact in a particularly sharp way. The question asks whether randomness is needed to find globally compatible choices quickly, and whether the structural tools for odd cycles can be made as parallel as the algebraic ones.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The 2026 bipartite advance is included; arbitrary graphs are the remaining target. New preprint proofs have not been independently audited.
progress: 1987 / background: The randomized parallel approach of Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani uses isolation to single out a matching. Svensson and Tarnawski review this starting point and the need to derandomize it. | 2017: Svensson and Tarnawski give a deterministic general-graph algorithm in $O(\log^3 n)$ parallel time with $n^{O(\log^2 n)}$ processors. It achieves quasi-NC, leaving a quasipolynomial-versus-polynomial resource gap. | 2026-06: Chatterjee, Ghosh, Gurjar, Raj, and Thierauf prove an NC result for bipartite matching. This new preprint does not state the general-graph theorem sought here.
working_summary: Perfect matching seeks pairwise disjoint edges that cover every vertex of a graph. The question asks for a deterministic parallel algorithm on general graphs with polynomially many processors and polylogarithmic running time. Sequential polynomial-time algorithms do not supply this bound because their matching updates may depend on earlier choices. General graphs also contain odd cycles, which require coordination beyond the constraints that suffice in bipartite graphs. The saved card distinguishes this target from the nearby bipartite advance and asks whether compatible matching decisions can be organized efficiently in parallel without randomness.

title: Distributed Lovász Local Lemma in O(log log n) rounds
importance_reason: A canonical obstacle to resolving local conflicts rapidly, with consequences for many distributed graph algorithms.
focus_reason: A canonical obstacle to resolving local conflicts rapidly, with consequences for many distributed graph algorithms.
formal: Does there exist an integer c≥2 such that, for every fixed integer d≥2, a uniform randomized LOCAL algorithm A_d and a constant K_d solve every n-event variable Lovász Local Lemma instance of dependency degree at most d and maximum bad-event probability p with p·d^c<1/2, within K_d(1+log₂log₂(n+2)) rounds, with probability at least 1−n^(−3) of avoiding all bad events simultaneously?
definitions: There are n≥2 bad events, each a predicate on a specified finite subset of finitely many mutually independent variables. Each variable has a finite nonempty alphabet and a rational probability distribution; event predicates and distributions are given by finite tables. Variables occurring in no event can be omitted. Two distinct event nodes are adjacent exactly when their variable sets intersect; this graph is the communication network. Its maximum degree is at most d. The number p is the largest probability of an event under the product of the specified distributions. Each node initially knows n,d, its own event table, its variables and their distributions, its neighbours and their identifiers. Node identifiers are distinct integers in [n²]; shared variables have consistent names. LOCAL means synchronous rounds with arbitrarily long finite messages in each direction on each edge, and unrestricted terminating local computation. Nodes have private independent fair random bits. A single finite program is used at all nodes, independently of n and the instance. Each node outputs one value for each of its variables. Success requires agreement on shared variables and falsity of every event. The round bound holds on every random tape; the success probability is over all node coins for each fixed instance and identifier assignment. title: Optimal exact single-source shortest paths in CONGEST
importance_reason: A basic distributed graph primitive with an unresolved gap between algorithms and communication lower bounds.
focus_reason: A basic distributed graph primitive with an unresolved gap between algorithms and communication lower bounds.
formal: For every fixed integer b≥1, do there exist constants K,c>0 and a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm which, on every connected simple undirected graph with n≥2 vertices, integer edge weights in [0,n^b] and a designated source s, makes every vertex output its exact weighted distance from s in at most K(√n+D)(log₂(n+2))^c rounds on every execution, with simultaneous correctness probability at least 1−n^(−3)? definitions: A path length is the sum of its edge weights; the distance is the minimum path length, and the source distance is zero. D is the maximum over vertex pairs of the minimum number of edges on a path between them. The graph itself is the network. In each synchronous round, each endpoint of each edge can send at most B⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits to the other endpoint, for a constant B depending only on b. Nodes initially know n,b, the source identifier, their own identifiers, and the identifiers and weights of incident neighbours. Identifiers are distinct integers in [n²]. Local computation and memory are unrestricted, but each local computation between rounds terminates. Nodes use independent private fair random bits. One finite program, allowed to depend on b, runs at all nodes; no global graph description, advice, routing tables or preprocessing is supplied. The graph, weights, source and identifiers are fixed before randomness is drawn. Output at v is an ordinary binary integer for dist(s,v), stored locally. The guarantee concerns all vertices together, over all coins. All communication, including finding termination and any preprocessing, counts in the round bound. context: This short research proposal states the target identified in the September 2026 fundamental-problem search. The references give the source models and related results. A full self-contained formulation and detailed progress review remain to be written.

title: Can directed reachability have near-linear work and polylogarithmic depth?
importance_reason: Combining near-linear work with polylogarithmic depth for directed reachability would resolve a major barrier in efficient parallel graph algorithms.
formal: Given an $n$-vertex, $m$-edge directed graph and a source $s$, is there a randomized shared-memory parallel algorithm that outputs every vertex reachable from $s$ using $\widetilde O(n+m)$ total work and $(\log n)^{O(1)}$ depth, with high probability? Both bounds must hold on arbitrary inputs, including sparse graphs with long directed paths. Work counts all primitive operations across processors; depth is the longest chain of dependent operations.
definitions:
The model is a standard word-based PRAM/shared-memory parallel model, with $O(\log n)$-bit words and concurrent access handled by standard PRAM conventions. Local primitive operations, auxiliary data construction, and shortcut generation count toward work. $\widetilde O$ hides polylogarithmic factors. High probability means $1-n^{-c}$ for a requested fixed $c>0$. The output is reachability, not shortest-path distances.

For definiteness fix a CREW PRAM: concurrent reads are allowed, and concurrent writes to one cell are prohibited. Word operations are arithmetic, multiplication, bitwise operations, shifts, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of logarithmic-size words. The target permits the polylogarithmic overhead of simulating common alternative PRAM conventions.
answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm meeting the work, depth, and error guarantees simultaneously on all directed inputs, or prove that no such algorithm exists in the specified PRAM model. Work measured by transitive-closure size is insufficient.
context:
A breadth-first search does little total work but exposes only the next frontier after processing the current one. On a directed path, that dependency chain is long. Matrix-based transitive closure can instead exploit massive parallelism, but it computes reachability for every pair and may do far more work than one-source search needs. The target asks for the useful properties of both approaches in one algorithm.

The size of the input and the size of its transitive closure are very different parameters. A one-way path has only $n-1$ edges but $\Theta(n^2)$ reachable ordered pairs. Thus an algorithm whose work is nearly linear in the closure size can still be quadratic in the input size. This remains true even though the requested one-source answer has only $n$ bits.

Shortcuts are a natural way to shorten dependencies: add an edge only when its endpoints were already connected by a directed path, then search the augmented graph. Constructing and storing these edges costs work too. Bounds on what a particular shortcut representation can achieve should not be mistaken for lower bounds on every parallel reachability algorithm.

The August 2026 result improves the polylogarithmic-depth side of the tradeoff using the size of the transitive closure as a parameter. It is relevant progress, but does not supply near-linear input work on all graphs. This distinction is essential when reading the phrase “faster than transitive closure.”
why: I include this because reachability is one of the simplest linear-time sequential graph tasks, yet obtaining fast parallel time without wasting substantial work remains difficult. The two-resource formulation makes the goal precise: a faster wall-clock computation should not require polynomially more total computation.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the August 2026 closure-sensitive algorithm. Near-linear input work with polylogarithmic depth remains the target.
progress: 2019: Jambulapati, Liu, and Sidford obtain almost-linear work with $n^{1/2+o(1)}$ depth for directed reachability. | 2026-05: Ashvinkumar, Bernstein, Probst Gutenberg, and Saranurak improve the near-linear-work depth bound as graph density increases; their dense-graph reachability bound is $n^{0.136}$. The theorem does not give polylogarithmic depth for every density. | 2026-08: Kogan and Parter give polylogarithmic depth with $\widetilde O(T^{\omega/2})$ work, where $T=|TC(G)|$ and $\omega$ is the matrix-multiplication exponent. Even the hypothetical $\omega=2$ gives work in terms of $T$, which may be quadratic for a linear-size input.
working_summary: A parallel reachability algorithm must identify every vertex reachable from a source in a directed graph. The target combines nearly linear total work in the input size with polylogarithmic depth, using randomization and high-probability correctness. Ordinary graph search does little work but can expose a long sequence of dependent frontiers. Highly parallel transitive-closure methods may perform far more work than this one-source task requires. The question is whether shortcuts or another representation can remove long dependencies while accounting for the cost of constructing all auxiliary information.

title: Quantum 3-coloring of cycles in o(log* n) rounds
importance_reason: A central concrete benchmark for quantum distributed computation, with an elementary output condition and a sharp classical threshold. The recent zero-error breakthrough leaves the practically standard high-probability regime unresolved.
formal: Is there a uniform quantum-LOCAL algorithm that, for every n≥3 and every identifier assignment to an n-cycle, outputs a proper 3-coloring with global probability at least 1−1/n in $T(n)=o(1+\log^* n)$ communication rounds? Every node is given n, its own identifier from [n²], and a consistent clockwise/counterclockwise orientation. Initial quantum registers are unentangled across nodes.
definitions: The network is a simple cycle; the orientation only identifies predecessor and successor, and communication is allowed in both directions. Nodes do not receive their numerical position in the cycle, a leader, or the list of other identifiers. They run one finite classical control program which may perform arbitrary finite local quantum computations, then exchange finite but unbounded numbers of qubits with each neighbor in each synchronous round. For a concrete uniform model, local quantum operations are finite circuits over H, T, and CNOT, fresh |0⟩ ancillas, and computational-basis measurements with adaptive classical control. Register size, message size, and local computation time are not charged, but are finite on every branch. Initially the joint quantum state is a product of local |0⟩ registers; the given classical local input may affect subsequent operations. No shared randomness, initial entanglement, or graph-dependent advice is supplied. The protocol may generate entanglement by sending qubits during its counted rounds. Every node eventually outputs one color in {1,2,3}. Success means that every cycle edge has differently colored endpoints, simultaneously. T(n) bounds all branches of the protocol, not its expected time. The little-o condition is T(n)/(1+log* n)→0 as n→∞; log* counts iterated base-2 logarithms down to at most 1. This card fixes the standard directed-cycle input variant, while allowing communication in either direction.
answer_criterion: Construct such a protocol with a proof of its worst-case round bound and global success probability, or prove that no such protocol exists. A constant-round protocol would answer yes. An anonymous zero-error lower bound, a two-color lower bound, or a lower bound using unbounded-degree trees does not by itself answer this high-probability three-color cycle question.
context:
A cycle is the simplest network in which many nearby choices must be coordinated. Two colors encode a global parity constraint, but three colors allow a much more local solution. In classical distributed computing, the exact deterministic cost of this symmetry breaking is Θ(log* n).

Naor’s lower bound shows that classical randomization with high-probability correctness still needs Ω(log* n) rounds. Quantum messages can create correlations unavailable to classical messages, but a coloring algorithm still has to return ordinary classical colors. The question is whether those correlations allow neighboring processors to agree on a valid local pattern faster than the classical symmetry-breaking threshold. The orientation and identifiers are explicit inputs, so no lower bound may rely on their absence.

There is a fundamental obstacle to arguments based only on causality. Finitely dependent proper colorings exist: far-separated sets of outputs can be independent while all adjacent colors differ. Consequently, the output distribution of a hypothetical constant-round quantum coloring algorithm need not violate a general no-signaling or finite-dependence constraint. Existence of such a distribution does not provide a quantum protocol that samples it.

The August 2026 result attacks the quantum implementation itself using matrix-product-state structure and a teleportation-based reduction. It proves a linear lower bound for anonymous finite-qubit protocols that must always succeed. Its Section 1.4 explicitly identifies the extension to high-probability correctness as the remaining problem. That is precisely the error regime retained on this card.

A separate July 2026 paper proves a log-star lower bound for 3-coloring rooted trees through growing-degree instances, and a linear lower bound for 2-coloring even cycles. Neither theorem handles the combination here: degree exactly two, three available colors, and small nonzero failure probability.
why: This is a canonical test of quantum advantage for a natural distributed symmetry-breaking task. A faster protocol would improve one of the basic local coordination primitives; a lower bound would have to explain a limitation of quantum realizability that mere causal consistency does not capture.
status_note: The August 2026 primary paper explicitly leaves high-probability cycle 3-coloring open. Its new theorem is for anonymous nodes and success probability exactly 1, so it is not recorded as resolving this identified, bounded-error protocol question. No later resolution located through 10 September 2026.
progress: 1980s–1990s: Cole–Vishkin and subsequent algorithms give O(log* n) classical coloring. Linial proves a matching deterministic lower bound. These classical bounds also give a quantum upper bound by running a classical protocol. | 1991: Naor proves the classical randomized ring-coloring lower bound, preserving the log-star obstruction when small failure probability is allowed. | 2016: Holroyd and Liggett construct finitely dependent colorings. These establish the barrier to deriving the desired quantum lower bound solely from finite dependence or causality. | 2026-07: Fraigniaud, Magniez, and Ziccardi give quantum lower bounds for rooted-tree 3-coloring and even-cycle 2-coloring. Their rooted-tree lower bound uses degree as a growing parameter. | 2026-08: Coiteux-Roy and coauthors prove that for any fixed c≥3, anonymous quantum-PN c-coloring of an even directed n-cycle with probability 1 needs more than floor(n/2)−2 rounds. They explicitly leave high-probability correctness open.
working_summary: Processors arranged on an oriented cycle must choose three classical colors so that adjacent processors receive different colors. The question allows quantum communication and asks for a round bound asymptotically smaller than log-star n. Nodes have distinct identifiers and know the cycle size, while their initial quantum registers are unentangled. The complete coloring must be valid with probability at least one minus one over n. A successful algorithm would beat the classical symmetry-breaking threshold, whereas a lower bound must handle quantum correlations without relying only on coarse causality constraints.

title: Can distributed MIS be solved in sublogarithmic time on every graph?
importance_reason: A basic randomized symmetry-breaking question on arbitrary graphs whose resolution would sharpen the global locality frontier.
formal:
In the randomized LOCAL model, does there exist an algorithm that finds a maximal independent set in $o(\log n)$ rounds on every $n$-vertex simple graph? Its output $I\subseteq V$ must satisfy $(u,v)\in E\Rightarrow\{u,v\}
subseteq I$ and $v
otin I\Rightarrow N(v)\cap I
e\varnothing$. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each fixed constant $c>0$, allowing the constant in the running time to depend on $c$. The bound must hold uniformly over all maximum degrees $\Delta\le n-1$.
definitions:
The network is the input graph. Rounds are synchronous; each edge can carry an arbitrarily large message in each direction. Vertices may have distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifiers and private random bits. Every vertex outputs its own membership bit. The measured time is the number of elapsed rounds until all outputs are available, not the number of rounds in which an individual processor stays awake.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree. Both the algorithm and the asymptotic time bound are uniform over input graphs and valid identifier assignments.
answer_criterion: Give one randomized LOCAL algorithm with a uniform o(log n) round bound and the stated success probability on all graphs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A degree restriction does not settle the proposition.
context:
A sequential greedy algorithm can scan vertices and select each vertex whose neighbors have not been selected. The difficulty here is distributing those decisions: a processor sits at each vertex and initially sees only local information. After r communication rounds, it cannot have learned anything beyond distance r. Message size and local computation are free in LOCAL, so a lower bound measures the reach of coordination itself.

Maximal means that no further vertex can be added. It does not require the largest possible independent set. For example, on a star, either the center alone or all leaves is a valid answer. The challenge is to choose consistently across a general network, rather than to optimize the number of selected vertices.

Degree-sensitive algorithms achieve $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds. This is already sublogarithmic when the degree is sufficiently small; the unresolved target includes polynomial-degree graphs. Repeatedly making only constant-factor progress leaves a logarithmic running time.

Recent work breaks that pattern on graphs with no cycles of length at most six. It does not extend to arbitrary graphs. Together with stronger lower bounds, this leaves a concrete question: can local choices still make sufficiently rapid progress when short cycles create dependencies between nearby decisions?
why: This isolates the communication needed for a basic symmetry-breaking task whose feasibility is easy to check locally. I include it because either outcome would change the benchmark for distributed graph algorithms: a faster algorithm would supply a stronger primitive, while a logarithmic lower bound would expose a substantial limitation of local coordination.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. General-graph sublogarithmic elapsed-round complexity remains open in the checked literature; awake-time and high-girth results have different guarantees.
progress: 2016: Ghaffari gives the degree-sensitive MIS algorithm. With subsequent deterministic finishing routines, the standard bound is $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$. | 2025: Khoury and Schild give a randomized lower bound $\Omega(\min\{\log\Delta,\sqrt{\log n}\})$ for maximal matching and, by reduction, MIS on general graphs. This implies an $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ worst-case barrier, not an $\Omega(\log n)$ barrier. | 2025: Their separate degree-reduction paper obtains $O(\log\Delta/\log(\log^{*}\Delta)+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds for girth at least seven. Its Open Question 1 asks for the general-graph improvement.
working_summary: A maximal independent set contains no adjacent vertices and leaves every unselected vertex next to a selected one. The question asks for a randomized LOCAL algorithm that finds such a set in o(log n) rounds on every graph with high probability. Message sizes and local computation are unrestricted, so the resource measures the distance over which decisions must be coordinated. The running-time improvement must hold uniformly even for graphs of very large degree. Degree-sensitive algorithms already improve some cases, but the target requires a mechanism that also avoids logarithmically many phases on unrestricted graphs.

title: One cycle versus two: is logarithmic time necessary in low-memory MPC?
importance_reason: A small connectivity promise problem serves as a basic round-complexity benchmark for low-memory massively parallel computation.
formal: For every fixed $0<\delta<1$, must every randomized MPC algorithm distinguishing one n-cycle from two vertex-disjoint (n/2)-cycles use $\Omega(\log n)$ rounds in the worst case over even n and input placement? Each machine has $O(n^\delta)$ words and total memory is O(n) words. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each requested fixed $c>0$. An $o(\log n)$-round algorithm for one fixed $\delta<1$ would refute this lower-bound conjecture.
definitions: Words have $O(\log n)$ bits. The input edge list is distributed across machines without exceeding their local memory. Each synchronous round allows arbitrary local computation followed by sending and receiving at most $O(n^{\delta})$ words per machine. The desired success probability is $1-n^{-c}$ for fixed $c>0$. This card fixes linear total memory; variants allowing more total space must be stated separately.
answer_criterion: Prove the logarithmic lower bound for every fixed sublinear-memory exponent and every admissible randomized algorithm, or refute that universal lower bound. An o(log n)-round algorithm for one fixed exponent would suffice for a refutation.
context:
Both promised inputs have exactly n vertices and n edges, and every vertex has degree two. Counting vertices, counting edges, and checking degrees therefore gives the same answer. The difference is how those edges join into components. Vertex identifiers are arbitrary, so the labels do not reveal where a cycle begins or whether two pieces belong together.

A sequential scan with graph traversal solves the problem in linear time. With the edge list spread across machines, no one machine can store the whole instance. Repeatedly joining path fragments or doubling the length represented by a pointer gives a natural logarithmic-round approach. The conjecture says that general distributed computation cannot compress this process into asymptotically fewer communication rounds under the stated memory limits.

It is tempting to justify the conjecture by saying that information travels only one graph edge per round. That would be incorrect here. Any machine may send to any other machine, and local computation between exchanges is unrestricted. The restriction is how much information a machine can store, send, and receive at once. A valid lower bound must cope with arbitrary encodings and nonlocal communication.

Extra geometric structure can change the answer. The 2025 grid-connectivity algorithm uses an embedding with bounded edge lengths to obtain constant rounds in its parameter regime. An arbitrarily labelled cycle does not provide that embedding, so the geometric result does not refute this promise-problem conjecture.
why: I include this because the input removes most graph-theoretic complications and leaves the cost of assembling global connectivity information. It is a standard conditional-hardness benchmark for massively parallel algorithms, and a resolution would clarify whether limited memory creates an inherent logarithmic coordination cost even on degree-two graphs.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The lower bound is conjectural. Constant-round results for geometric graphs or larger local memory do not establish this variant.
progress: 2022: Nanongkai and Scquizzato develop equivalence classes and conditional-hardness connections around this cycle problem and logarithmic-space computation. Their reductions have explicit global-memory requirements; those should be checked before transferring them to the linear-total-memory variant here. | 2025: Gan, Wirth, and Zhang explicitly state the linear-total-memory 2-CYCLE conjecture while giving a constant-round algorithm for embedded grid graphs. The promised arbitrary-cycle problem is left unresolved.
working_summary: The one-cycle-versus-two problem distinguishes a single n-vertex cycle from two disjoint cycles of half that size. In the low-memory MPC model, edges are spread across machines with sublinear local memory and linear total memory. The conjecture says randomized algorithms require Ω(log n) communication rounds under these resource bounds. Both input types have identical vertex counts, edge counts, and degrees, so only their global connectivity distinguishes them. A lower bound must handle arbitrary communication between machines and arbitrary encodings, rather than assuming information can travel only along graph edges.

title: Constant non-signaling locality beyond deterministic log-star LOCAL
importance_reason: A foundational boundary question between local computation and causal output distributions. The fixed degree and constant locality requirements isolate an unresolved structural issue beyond the already known logarithmic quantum separations.
formal: Does there exist a fixed locally checkable labeling problem Π on all finite graphs of some fixed maximum degree Δ, with finite input and output alphabets, that admits a zero-error non-signaling outcome of constant locality, but has no deterministic LOCAL algorithm using $O(1+\log^* n)$ rounds? The degree bound, checking radius, alphabets, and non-signaling locality must all be independent of n.
definitions: An LCL is specified by an integer Δ≥2, a fixed radius r≥1, finite input/output alphabets, and a finite list of permitted rooted radius-r neighborhoods with input/output labels, degrees, and ports. A labeling is valid when every vertex sees a permitted pattern. Legality does not depend on identifiers or n. Inputs range over all simple undirected n-vertex graphs of maximum degree at most Δ, all finite-alphabet input assignments, all port numberings, and all injective identifiers from [n²]; disconnected graphs are included. For one constant integer R, a non-signaling outcome assigns each input a joint probability distribution on all vertex outputs, supported entirely on valid labelings. For every vertex subset S and any two inputs of the same size, an identifier-, input-, and port-preserving isomorphism of their radius-R neighborhoods of S must carry one marginal output distribution on S to the other. This condition applies to every subset, not only to individual vertices. Arbitrary real probabilities and correlations are allowed; there is no requirement that the outcome be sampled by a classical or quantum protocol. Exact n may be used. In deterministic LOCAL every node initially knows n, its identifier, its input, degree, and ports, follows one finite computable program, and exchanges arbitrarily long messages with neighbors in synchronous rounds. Local computation is unrestricted but must terminate. The negative classical condition is: for every correct algorithm A and constant C, arbitrarily large inputs require more than C(1+log* n) rounds. Here log* counts base-2 logarithms needed to reduce n to at most 1.
answer_criterion: Exhibit one finite LCL specification and a constant-locality family of non-signaling distributions, and prove that no deterministic O(log* n)-round solver exists; or prove that every LCL with such a distribution has a deterministic O(log* n)-round solver. This card fixes the all-bounded-degree-graphs, zero-error formulation of the saved question. A family whose degree grows with n, or an outcome of logarithmic locality, does not establish the required separation.
context:
A distributed algorithm can only react to information that has reached it. Non-signaling keeps this causality requirement but removes the demand for a physically implementable algorithm. It asks whether the joint output probabilities could exist without letting a distant input change the observations of any group of nearby or far-apart observers. This makes it a useful setting for proving strong communication lower bounds.

Requiring consistency only for one vertex would be much too weak. For example, choosing the two colors of a connected bipartite graph with a random global flip makes each vertex individually uniform. The correlation between two vertices can nevertheless reveal whether their distance has even or odd parity. The marginal condition for every subset is what detects such hidden signaling.

The iterated logarithm marks an established symmetry-breaking regime. Every LCL solvable there by a deterministic LOCAL algorithm has a constant-locality, finitely dependent solution distribution, and therefore a constant-locality non-signaling distribution. The question asks whether constant non-signaling locality reaches further than this classical regime.

The rooted-tree case is constrained by a simulation theorem: sufficiently small non-signaling locality leads back to a deterministic O(log* n)-round algorithm there. That theorem cannot simply be extended to unrooted trees or arbitrary graphs. The corrected February 2026 manuscript explicitly withdraws an earlier claim about unrooted trees.

Recent quantum separations show that the models can differ for a fixed LCL, but at a larger time scale. The August 2026 revision gives a quantum O(log n) upper bound and a classical randomized lower bound of Ω(log n·(log log n)^0.99). These rates leave the constant-locality threshold on this card unresolved.
why: A resolution would locate the boundary of what causality alone permits for locally verifiable tasks. It would either extend a fundamental symmetry-breaking classification to arbitrary non-signaling correlations, or provide a concrete obstruction to such a classification and a benchmark for quantum lower bounds.
status_note: The February 2026 author-maintained list explicitly poses the constant non-signaling versus deterministic log-star question. The checked August 2026 quantum separation does not supply the constant-locality witness required here. No resolution of this fixed zero-error formulation was located through 10 September 2026.
progress: 2024–2026: Akbari and coauthors prove that deterministic O(log* n) LCLs admit constant-locality finitely dependent distributions. They also show that o(log log log n) randomized online locality in rooted trees implies deterministic O(log* n), which covers non-signaling outcomes through their simulation. | 2026-02: Suomela’s updated problem list still asks for an LCL with constant non-signaling locality and classical deterministic complexity beyond the log-star regime. This card fixes zero error and a finite specification on all bounded-degree graphs. | 2026-08: Balliu and coauthors strengthen the established quantum separation to O(log n) versus Ω(log n·(log log n)^0.99). Their general simulation also bounds the power of finitely dependent distributions; finite dependence imposes an extra independence condition absent from general non-signaling outcomes.
working_summary: A locally checkable labeling problem specifies valid distributed outputs through finite constraints on bounded-radius neighborhoods. Non-signaling solutions satisfy consistent locality conditions on joint output distributions without necessarily corresponding to an implementable algorithm. The question seeks a bounded-degree problem with a constant-locality non-signaling solution but no deterministic O(log-star n)-round LOCAL algorithm. The alphabets, checking radius, and locality must all remain fixed as the graph grows. Such a separation would show that causally consistent correlations solve some local coordination tasks beyond the established deterministic symmetry-breaking regime.

title: Can deterministic LOCAL algorithms find an MIS in O(log n) rounds?
importance_reason: Matching a logarithmic deterministic bound for MIS would settle a central gap in local symmetry breaking.
formal: Is there a deterministic LOCAL algorithm that outputs a maximal independent set on every $n$-vertex simple graph in $O(\log n)$ synchronous communication rounds? Each vertex has a distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifier, and the guarantee must hold for every valid identifier assignment and every maximum degree. The output must be independent, and every vertex outside it must have a neighbor inside it. No random bits are available.
definitions:
LOCAL allows unbounded messages along input edges and unrestricted local computation. A vertex’s r-round view contains only its radius-r neighborhood and the identifiers and input data revealed there. The complexity is elapsed communication rounds until all vertices output. The target is uniform over arbitrary graphs, not restricted to bounded degree, planar graphs, or trees.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree; the time guarantee must still be O(log n) uniformly over degrees.
answer_criterion: Give one deterministic LOCAL algorithm with a uniform O(log n) bound over all graphs and valid identifiers, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Constants must not depend on maximum degree.
context:
Identifiers make deterministic symmetry breaking possible, but they do not automatically make it fast. Consider the rule that selects every vertex whose identifier is smaller than those of all its remaining neighbors, then removes the selected vertices and their neighbors. On a path with identifiers increasing from one endpoint to the other, each phase selects just the smallest remaining endpoint. This rule takes linearly many phases, even though much faster algorithms exist for paths.

Randomized MIS algorithms avoid adversarial identifier patterns by making new random choices. A deterministic algorithm has to arrange useful progress from the graph and identifiers alone. The existence of a good assignment of random choices is insufficient: processors must find suitable choices while paying for the communication that coordinates them.

Network decomposition supplied a general way to organize that work into small-diameter clusters that can be processed in groups. It settled the old question of whether polylogarithmic deterministic MIS is possible. The present target concerns the finer exponent and cannot be recorded as the already-solved polylogarithmic-time question.

The 2024 improvement reaches approximately $\log^{5/3}n$ rounds and avoids the log-squared cost of the standard decomposition-based route. Closing the remaining gap requires more than optimizing the constants of that route. The 2026 coloring reduction still uses this improved MIS bound as its benchmark.
why: This measures the quantitative cost of removing randomness from a basic distributed task. I include it separately from randomized sublogarithmic MIS because the algorithm must work against every identifier assignment with no failure probability. An O(log n) result would match the familiar randomized worst-case benchmark and propagate through reductions to other symmetry-breaking problems.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. Polylogarithmic deterministic MIS is solved; the O(log n) target remains open in the checked literature.

The output must be independent and dominate all unselected vertices, without requiring maximum cardinality. Reaching the logarithmic bound would require organizing deterministic progress efficiently even when identifier patterns defeat simple greedy local rules.

title: Can constant-time LOCAL solvability on unrooted trees be decided?
importance_reason: A core decidability boundary for local distributed computation, linking finite specifications, algorithm synthesis, and lower-bound certificates on trees. It isolates a fundamental unresolved stage of full complexity classification.
formal: Is there a Turing algorithm D that, given a finite description of a locally checkable labeling problem Π on trees of maximum degree Δ, always halts and decides whether Π has a deterministic LOCAL algorithm that solves every allowed input instance in at most t communication rounds, for some constant t depending only on Π? Trees are unrooted, arbitrary finite input labels are allowed, and each node knows the exact number n of nodes.
definitions: The input description is (Δ,r,Σ_in,Σ_out,C), with integers Δ≥2,r≥1, finite nonempty input and output alphabets, and a finite list C of permitted rooted radius-r neighborhood types. Neighborhoods record input/output labels, degrees and incident port numbers, but not processor IDs or n. Ports at a degree-d node are numbered 1,…,d; the two port numbers of an edge need not agree. A labeling is valid precisely when every node’s radius-r neighborhood is isomorphic, preserving this data and its center, to a type in C. Instances range over every finite nonempty simple undirected tree of degree at most Δ, every input labeling, and every port numbering. Processors additionally have distinct IDs in {1,…,n²}. Initially a node knows its own input, ID, degree, ports, n, and Π. In each synchronous round it can send arbitrary finite messages to its neighbors; local computation is unrestricted in cost but must be computable and terminate. The same finite program runs at every node and works for all n and all ID assignments. No distinguished global root, parent pointers, randomness, or additional advice is supplied. D itself is centralized, with no running-time bound. Descriptions with an unsolvable instance are no instances of the decision problem.
answer_criterion: Give an always-terminating decider for exactly the described constant-round solvability property, or prove that no such decider exists. A procedure that eventually recognizes every positive instance but may run forever on negative instances is insufficient. This is an explicitly chosen binary subproblem of the saved broader question about deciding the entire asymptotic complexity.
context:
An LCL is specified by local rules rather than a global objective. Proper coloring and maximal independent set illustrate the distinction: a completed labeling can be checked from small neighborhoods, yet finding a valid labeling may require substantially more communication. Here the input to the decision procedure is the rulebook itself, not one network to label.

The question asks whether a finite rulebook reveals that a bounded communication radius will always suffice. The radius may be enormous and may depend on the rulebook, but it cannot grow with the network. Testing small trees alone cannot certify this property; a procedure must account for every larger tree, every input labeling, and every assignment of identifiers.

The possible round complexities and the ability to recognize them are separate issues. Grunau, Rozhoň, and Brandt prove that an LCL on bounded-degree trees with o(log* n) complexity actually has constant complexity. Their paper nevertheless explicitly leaves constant-time decidability open. A gap theorem supplies a separation between cases without automatically providing a test for which case applies.

Positive instances can be recognized by searching the finite local-rule candidates associated with each fixed radius. If a suitable radius exists, this search eventually finds it. The missing part is a terminating certificate or other method for the negative answer. The full complexity-classification question would also need to distinguish further classes, so an affirmative answer here is only one stage of that larger goal.

Rooted-tree classification results use the supplied parent-child direction to organize their certificates. An arbitrary port numbering on an unrooted tree provides no such globally consistent direction. Recent results also show that knowledge of network size and the computability of local state transitions can matter. This card fixes both assumptions rather than silently moving between models.
why: This asks whether one can automatically recognize when local verification can be converted into truly local construction on the simplest branching networks. A decider would be a basic ingredient of distributed algorithm synthesis; undecidability would expose a limit that persists even on trees.
status_note: The 2022 primary paper poses this exact constant-time subproblem. The February–June 2026 sources retain the unrooted-tree decidability gap; recent model and rooted-tree results do not settle it. Search checked through 10 September 2026.
progress: 2022: Grunau, Rozhoň, and Brandt close the o(log* n)-to-O(1) gap on bounded-degree trees. Their Section 1.4, Question 1.7, explicitly asks whether constant-time solvability is decidable and explains why recognizing positive instances is not the missing direction. | 2022: Balliu, Brandt, Chang, Olivetti, Studený, and Suomela classify the O(log n)-versus-polynomial region efficiently for their regular-tree formalism. Their abstract explicitly leaves finer classification in the O(log n) region open for unrooted trees. | 2026-02: Cruciani and coauthors show that computable and arbitrary local transition functions give the same round complexity for LCLs when a bound on n is supplied. Without such knowledge they can differ. The exact-n convention of this card avoids that ambiguity. | 2026-05: Balliu and coauthors show that weakening exact network-size knowledge changes the tree complexity landscape. Their result motivates keeping that assumption fixed; it does not decide constant-round solvability from an arbitrary LCL description. | 2026-06: Piombi extends decidable polynomial complexity gaps to a more general logical formalism on unbounded-degree rooted trees. The paper still identifies the lower-complexity classification of unrooted LCLs as an unresolved boundary.

It asks for an algorithm deciding whether some constant number of deterministic LOCAL rounds suffices on every permitted input tree. The constant may depend on the rulebook, but must be independent of tree size and input labels. Known gaps in the possible round complexities do not themselves decide which side contains a given specification. title: Can randomized O(log log n) LOCAL solvability on trees be decided?
importance_reason: A basic recognition problem at the boundary where randomization yields exponential speedups on trees. It connects local specifications, algorithm synthesis, and effective lower-bound theory.
formal: Does there exist an always-terminating Turing algorithm that, given a finite locally checkable labeling specification Π on unrooted bounded-degree trees, decides whether Π admits a randomized LOCAL algorithm using O(1 + log log(n+2)) rounds and producing a globally valid labeling with probability at least 1 − 1/(n+1) on every n-node input? Nodes know the exact n. The implicit constant may depend on Π, but not on n or the input instance.
definitions: A specification consists of integers Δ≥2 and r≥1, finite nonempty input/output alphabets, and a finite list of permitted rooted radius-r neighborhood types. Types record input/output labels, degrees and incident port numbers, but do not mention identifiers or n. All finite nonempty simple unrooted trees of maximum degree Δ, all input labelings, and all port numberings are allowed; a degree-d vertex has ports 1,…,d, independently of ports at the other endpoint. Every node must output one symbol, and the labeling is valid when every node sees a permitted neighborhood. Nodes have distinct identifiers in {1,…,n²}, initially know their own input, ID, ports, degree, Π and n, and use independent private fair random bits. A single finite computable program operates at every node. Communication is synchronous with arbitrary finite messages and unrestricted terminating local computation. The round bound holds for every random tape; the success requirement is joint over the entire labeling, for each fixed input and ID assignment. There is no supplied root, shared random advice, or graph-dependent preprocessing. A specification with an unsolvable instance is a negative instance of the decision problem. Logs have base 2.
answer_criterion: Construct a total decider for this exact property, or prove its undecidability. A classification for one fixed specification, a promise of solvability, or only a test for O(log n) algorithms does not answer the question. This card explicitly specializes the saved full-classification question to one binary threshold; it does not claim this threshold alone decides every complexity class.
context:
A local rulebook describes what a solution should look like near each node. Here a centralized program receives that rulebook and must decide whether random local decisions can coordinate a valid solution within a doubly logarithmic number of communication rounds. It is a question about automatically understanding algorithms, rather than running a particular algorithm on one tree.

On trees under the usual network-size convention, randomness can produce an exponential improvement: sinkless orientation has logarithmic deterministic complexity and doubly logarithmic randomized complexity. Other locally checkable problems remain logarithmic with randomness. Thus the threshold in this card distinguishes real algorithmic behaviors; it is not simply asking whether random bits can be removed.

The known landscape has substantial empty intervals. A gap theorem can tell us that no problem occupies an interval without giving an effective way to determine which side a supplied rulebook occupies. The regular-tree classification paper explicitly marks the gap between randomized doubly logarithmic and logarithmic complexity as having unknown decidability.

The answer required from the decider is only yes or no. On a negative input it need not compute the exact larger complexity, and on a positive input it need not distinguish constant, iterated-logarithmic, and doubly logarithmic algorithms. This avoids hiding an undefined symbolic representation of an arbitrary asymptotic function inside the output requirement.

A small failure probability at one vertex is not the same as a small chance of any error in the network. The statement fixes the latter, and also fixes exact knowledge of n. The 2026 network-size results show that changing this knowledge can change the relationship between randomized and deterministic complexities.
why: Recognizing this threshold would give a general test for fast randomized coordination on branching networks. Undecidability would instead establish a limit on automated classification despite the remarkably sparse list of possible round complexities.
status_note: The 2022 classification figure explicitly leaves this threshold undecided, and 2026 primary sources retain the lower-complexity decidability gap on unrooted trees. No resolution located through 10 September 2026.
progress: 2022: Grunau, Rozhoň, and Brandt establish the complete standard tree complexity landscape, including the randomized doubly logarithmic class; knowing the possible classes does not decide membership. | 2022: Balliu and coauthors give polynomial-time classification of the logarithmic-versus-polynomial region in their regular-tree formalism. Figure 1(c) leaves recognition of the randomized O(log log n) threshold open. | 2026-02: Suomela’s updated primary problem list continues to ask for randomized complexity decidability for LCLs with inputs on unrooted trees. This card selects a concrete threshold within that broader request. | 2026-05: Balliu and coauthors show that weakening exact knowledge of n changes the tree landscape and the circumstances in which randomness helps. Those variants are not silently substituted for this card’s model. | 2026-06: Piombi’s discussion still identifies only the polynomial gaps as known decidable for unrooted trees. The new main results concern a logical generalization on rooted trees, rather than the randomized threshold here.
working_summary: The input is a locally checkable labeling specification on unrooted trees of bounded degree. The question asks whether one can decide if randomized LOCAL algorithms solve it in O(log log n) rounds with globally high probability. Nodes know the exact network size, and the guarantee must hold over all input labelings and identifier assignments. Some tree problems benefit exponentially from randomness, while others still require logarithmic rounds. An effective classification at this threshold would determine from the local rules whether a task permits the stronger randomized speedup.

title: Sketching vs. Streaming
importance_reason: Separating sketching from general streaming would identify the power and limitations of a widely used algorithmic abstraction.
formal: Sketching vs. Streaming

status_note: Imported from the previous catalogue. Current open status has not been established by a new review.

title: Does sublinear deterministic volume always collapse to O(log* n)?
importance_reason: A proposed collapse of an entire deterministic complexity interval, rather than a bound for one task. It clarifies the power of adaptive exploration and the role of randomness in local computation.
formal: For every locally checkable labeling problem Π on all finite graphs of some fixed maximum degree Δ, does the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm A with V_A(n)=o(n) imply the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm B with V_B(n)=O(1+log* n)? Algorithms know the exact size of their input graph, and node identifiers are distinct integers in {1,…,|V(G)|²}. Here V_A(n) is the maximum number of distinct vertices visited to determine one vertex’s output, over all allowed instances with at most n vertices and all requested vertices.
definitions: An LCL is specified by fixed Δ≥2, a fixed verification radius r≥1, finite nonempty input/output alphabets, and a finite set of permitted rooted radius-r labeled neighborhoods. Rules may inspect degrees and local ports, but not n or IDs. Instances include every finite nonempty simple undirected graph of maximum degree Δ, possibly disconnected, every input labeling and every port numbering. A labeling is valid exactly when all neighborhoods satisfy the rules. A deterministic VOLUME computation for a requested vertex v starts with v’s ID, degree, input, ports, Π and the exact |V(G)|, and visited set {v}. It may adaptively choose a visited vertex w and one of its incident ports, learning the neighbor u, its ID, degree, input and incident port names, then add u to the visited set. Arbitrary jumps to unseen IDs are forbidden. Only the number of distinct visited vertices, including v, is charged; local computation must terminate but its time and temporary space are unrestricted. Queries at different vertices run independently with no preprocessing or shared mutable state. Their outputs must jointly form a valid labeling for every input and ID assignment. Each algorithm is one finite computable program for all graph sizes. log* n is the number of iterated base-2 logarithms needed to reach at most 1; the added 1 handles small n.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal implication, or specify one fixed LCL with a sublinear-volume deterministic algorithm and prove it has no O(log* n)-volume deterministic algorithm. Precisely, the latter lower bound means that for every correct B, every C>0 and every n₀, some n≥n₀ satisfies V_B(n)>C(1+log* n). This gap formulation fixes the asymptotic quantifiers without assuming an optimal algorithm or an arbitrary symbolic complexity function exists.
context:
A processor that sees far through a narrow part of a graph can inspect much less information than one that explores an entire ball of the same radius. The VOLUME model measures that inspected information. Its adaptive exploration captures a central feature of answering a query about a huge graph without first constructing an entire solution.

Correctness still couples the answers. Independently determining the color or matching status of one vertex must agree with the answers obtained for every other vertex. The algorithm cannot save previous answers and use their accumulated state as a growing global solution. This makes a low-volume construction substantially stronger than an arbitrary sequential greedy algorithm.

Rosenbaum and Suomela ask whether there is any deterministic volume complexity strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear, and conjecture there is none. Their model supplies exact graph size and polynomially bounded identifiers. Removing these conventions changes the indistinguishability arguments, so the card keeps them explicit.

The known small-complexity gaps leave the central interval unresolved. Randomized examples inhabit many intermediate scales, but an algorithm that follows a favorable random exploration does not automatically give a deterministic procedure that succeeds on every labeled graph. A deterministic counterexample to the proposed collapse would establish a new basic behavior.

July 2026 work constructs additional randomized polylogarithmic and polynomial volume complexities. Its introduction explicitly separates those results from the still-open deterministic question. The increased richness on the randomized side makes the contrast sharper while supplying no deterministic intermediate example.
why: This tests whether deterministic access to local solutions has only a tiny-information regime and an essentially global regime. Either outcome would substantially constrain the design and possible complexity classes of deterministic local computation algorithms.
status_note: The July 2026 primary paper explicitly retains the deterministic gap as open. The new constructions are randomized; no deterministic resolution located through 10 September 2026.
