Their results also give linear deterministic volume lower bounds for fixed-color tree-coloring tasks in the relevant bounded-degree setting. These do not cover every LCL. | 2022: Grunau, Rozhoň, and Brandt close the gap between constant and iterated-logarithmic VOLUME complexity. The much larger interval above log* n remains the issue here. | 2026-02: Suomela’s updated problem list retains the question of deterministic volume strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear. | 2026-07: Peng gives randomized VOLUME and LCA constructions of complexity Θ(log^k n) for positive integers k and polynomial scales up to logarithmic factors. Section 1.1 explicitly leaves the deterministic gap unresolved.
working_summary: The VOLUME model measures how many graph vertices an adaptive local algorithm inspects to determine one requested output. Outputs from separate queries must still fit together into a single valid labeling. The conjecture says every deterministic locally checkable problem with sublinear worst-case volume actually has O(log-star n) volume. It concerns fixed bounded-degree graph families with exact size information and polynomially bounded identifiers. Proving the collapse would eliminate an entire intermediate range of deterministic local information complexity, despite the richer range available to randomized algorithms.

title: Does sublogarithmic randomized volume collapse to deterministic log-star?
importance_reason: An unresolved universal speedup threshold for randomized local computation. It isolates the remaining gap between a proven square-root-logarithmic threshold and the first established logarithmic examples.
formal: For every fixed locally checkable labeling problem Π on all bounded-degree graphs, does a randomized VOLUME algorithm with worst-case volume $o(\log(n+2))$ and global success probability at least 1−1/(n+1) imply a deterministic VOLUME algorithm with volume $O(1+\log^* n)$? The degree bound, checking radius, and finite input/output alphabets are fixed independently of n.
definitions: An LCL is a finite list of permitted rooted radius-r neighborhoods with input/output labels, degrees, and local ports, for fixed integers Δ≥2 and r≥1. All finite nonempty simple undirected graphs of maximum degree at most Δ, all input labels, all port orders, and all distinct identifiers from [|V(G)|²] are allowed; disconnected graphs are included. Legality depends on the finite neighborhoods, not on IDs or n. The query algorithm knows exact |V(G)| and starts at the requested vertex with its ID, degree, ports and input. It may follow any port of any visited vertex, revealing the next vertex and its local data; the visited set remains connected. Volume counts distinct visited vertices, including the queried one. Each graph vertex has its own independent infinite sequence of fair random bits, sampled once and used consistently by every query that visits it. A query may read finitely many bits from visited vertices, but has no access to a separate shared random tape. There is no preprocessing or mutable memory shared between queries. With probability at least 1−1/(|V(G)|+1), the answers to all vertex queries together must be a valid labeling. For a fixed algorithm A, V_A(n) is the maximum number of visited vertices over graphs of at most n vertices, all queries and all random tapes. Every computation must terminate; temporary space and local computation time are unrestricted. Both algorithms are uniform finite programs. log* is the number of iterated base-2 logarithms needed to reach at most 1.
answer_criterion: Prove the implication for every fixed LCL, or give one finite LCL specification with a sublogarithmic-volume randomized solver and prove that every deterministic solver fails every O(log* n) volume bound on arbitrarily large inputs. The known speedup below √log n makes deterministic and randomized O(log* n) equivalent for this purpose, so a counterexample would supply the missing intermediate randomized regime.
context:
A randomized local oracle can decide which parts of a graph to inspect using random choices. Its separate answers still need to fit together into one valid solution. The card samples one random tape per graph vertex and reuses it across queries, so an answer cannot evade an inconsistency by drawing fresh, unrelated randomness each time.

The cost is a worst-case information budget, with failure probability assigned to correctness. Bounding only the expected exploration size would be a different question. Likewise, success at one requested vertex is weaker than saying that all answers are simultaneously correct. These distinctions are significant when small failure probabilities are amplified across an entire graph.

There is already a strong speedup theorem: below √log n, randomized local computation can be replaced by deterministic O(log* n) computation. The conjectured threshold is log n. A candidate at, for example, (log n)^(3/4) would escape the existing theorem while remaining strictly below the proposed threshold.

Logarithmic randomized volume really occurs. The Lovász local lemma and sinkless orientation provide benchmark behavior at that scale in the cited work. The question is whether the whole interval immediately below log n is empty, beyond the familiar tiny-information symmetry-breaking regime.

Peng’s July 2026 constructions provide Θ((log n)^k) for positive integers k and polynomial scales up to polylogarithmic factors. Since the smallest exponent k is one, these do not insert a problem into the sublogarithmic interval. Figure 2 of that paper continues to mark the interval from √log n to log n as unknown.
why: A gap theorem would classify every sufficiently small randomized local computation as ordinary deterministic symmetry breaking. A counterexample would reveal a new scale of useful random exploration. This is a general complexity-landscape question, with consequences extending beyond any one coloring or matching algorithm.
status_note: The July 2026 primary paper still marks the remaining sublogarithmic randomized VOLUME interval as unknown. Its new polylogarithmic constructions have integer exponent at least one. No resolution located through 10 September 2026.
progress: 2020: Rosenbaum and Suomela formalize randomized VOLUME with connected exploration and per-vertex random strings, and construct logarithmic and larger intermediate randomized complexities. | 2021: Brandt, Grunau, and Rozhoň prove the o(√log n) → deterministic O(log* n) speedup in Theorem 1.2. Their Conjecture 1.3 proposes the stronger o(log n) threshold for LCA; the VOLUME question considered here is explicitly tracked by later sources. | 2026-02: Suomela’s list asks whether an LCL can have randomized volume strictly between the log-star and logarithmic regimes. | 2026-07: Peng’s Theorem 1 fills the positive-integer polylogarithmic scales, and Theorem 2 gives rational polynomial exponents. Section 1.1 and Figure 2 retain the unknown interval from √log n to log n.
working_summary: A randomized VOLUME algorithm adaptively inspects a small part of a bounded-degree graph to answer a local output query. Its random choices must support a globally consistent solution across all queries, with high probability. The question asks whether worst-case volume o(log n) always implies a deterministic algorithm using O(log-star n) volume. A known speedup covers a smaller sublogarithmic range, leaving the proposed logarithmic threshold as the target. The result would identify a sharp boundary below which randomness cannot buy additional power for locally checkable graph tasks.

title: What is the deterministic round complexity of maximum independent set in the congested clique?
importance_reason: A canonical exact optimization task testing the communication power of the congested clique. Its relevance extends beyond symmetry breaking, although the chosen deterministic model is one specific frontier.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors as n grows, the optimal worst-case number $T_{\mathrm{MIS}}(n)$ of synchronous communication rounds needed to output an exact maximum independent set of an arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex graph in the deterministic unicast congested-clique model below. For every vertex v, its processor must output one bit indicating whether v belongs to the chosen set. Local computation and local storage are unrestricted; only communication rounds are charged. Here maximum means largest cardinality, not merely inclusion-wise maximal.
definitions: There is one processor for each vertex in {1,...,n}. Initially every processor knows n, all processor identifiers, its own identifier, and exactly the edges incident to its vertex. The communication network is the complete graph regardless of which input edges exist. In each synchronous round, each processor may send a different message of at most $b=\max\{1,\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\}$ bits to each other processor; messages sent in a round become available at its end. Protocols are deterministic and must terminate correctly on every input. An independent set S contains no edge with both endpoints in S; maximum requires |S| >= |I| for every independent set I of the input graph. Define T_MIS(n) as the minimum round bound among protocols for n processors in this model. No polynomial bound is imposed on the computation between rounds. The deterministic and fixed-bandwidth conventions specialize the broader seminar question.
answer_criterion: Give asymptotically matching upper and lower bounds: identify an explicit asymptotic function f(n), construct protocols taking O(f(n)) rounds on every graph, and prove that every correct deterministic protocol requires Omega(f(n)) rounds on some n-vertex graph for all sufficiently large n. Bounds separated by a logarithmic factor or a result only for maximal independent sets do not settle this target.
context:
The graph being optimized and the network carrying messages are different objects. Two vertices that are not adjacent in the input can still communicate directly. This removes distance as an obstacle while retaining a limit on how much information a processor can receive in one round. The task asks how much this distributed information limits exact optimization.

A simple baseline is to collect the entire graph at processor 1. Each other processor sends its n-bit adjacency row along its direct link, in blocks of b bits. These transmissions happen simultaneously and take O(n / log n) rounds for n >= 2. Processor 1 then enumerates subsets locally, chooses a largest independent set, and sends each processor its membership bit. This is an elementary upper bound for the stated model, rather than a claim that centralizing the graph is optimal.

The unlimited local computation is essential to interpreting this baseline. The exponential subset enumeration has no communication cost. Conversely, a faster centralized algorithm does not by itself reduce the number of rounds needed to assemble the input. The question isolates information movement from the ordinary running-time difficulty of exact independent set.

Lower bounds are especially delicate in the unicast clique. Drucker, Kuhn, and Oshman relate this model to powerful circuit computations, explaining why familiar sparse-network bottleneck arguments do not transfer directly. Chechik nevertheless identifies exact maximum independent set as a concrete round-complexity question. The catalogue has a separate constant-round question for a maximal independent set; that weaker output requirement must not be substituted here.
why: This places a canonical exact graph optimization problem in a model where computation is free but communication is limited. Understanding its round complexity would help distinguish the benefit of distributing information from merely gathering the graph at one processor.

Randomness and bandwidth are fixed explicitly here; results for maximal MIS, broadcast cliques, or edge-restricted CONGEST do not resolve this formulation.

Their work supplies model context, not a tight bound for the present task. | 2025: Chechik explicitly asks for the communication rounds necessary to compute a maximum independent set in the congested clique.
working_summary: Maximum independent set asks for a largest collection of pairwise nonadjacent vertices. Here each vertex is a processor in a congested clique, whose communication links exist even between nonadjacent input vertices. The question asks for the optimal deterministic number of rounds, with unlimited local computation and storage. Collecting the full graph at one processor gives an elementary upper bound, after which even exhaustive local optimization costs no communication rounds. The challenge is to determine how much information must move to identify an exact optimum, independently of the usual centralized NP-hardness barrier.

title: Bipartite maximal matching with polynomial-in-degree volume
importance_reason: A fundamental maximal-matching oracle question that isolates degree dependence and the difference between distance and volume. It asks for a qualitative polynomial-versus-superpolynomial classification with no network-size term.
formal: Do there exist constants C>0 and k≥1 and one deterministic VOLUME algorithm that computes a maximal matching on every bipartite graph of maximum degree at most Δ, inspecting at most C(Δ+1)^k distinct vertices per queried vertex, independently of the number n of graph vertices? A proper input two-coloring specifying the bipartition is supplied. Answers to all vertex queries must describe the same matching.
definitions: The input is a finite simple undirected graph, arbitrary local port orders, a supplied proper two-coloring, distinct identifiers in [n²], and known integers n and Δ≥1 bounding its size and degrees as stated. A query at v must output either ⊥ for unmatched or the local port of its matching edge. If v names u then u must name v. Every edge must have at least one matched endpoint, which is equivalent to maximality by inclusion. Initially the algorithm sees only v’s identifier, degree, color, ports, n, and Δ. It may adaptively follow a port at any already visited vertex; doing so reveals the neighbor’s identifier, degree, color, and reciprocal port. Count all distinct visited vertices, including v. The explored set is connected: arbitrary jumps to identifiers are forbidden. Each query starts afresh, with no preprocessing or memory retained between queries. Repeating a query must give the same answer regardless of other queries or their order. Local computation and temporary memory are unrestricted but finite, and only the number of distinct visited vertices is charged. One finite deterministic program must work for all n, Δ, graphs, identifiers, and port orders; the constants C,k are universal. There is no additional log n or log* n term in the allowed volume.
answer_criterion: Construct the uniform polynomial-in-Δ algorithm with globally consistent matching answers, or prove that every correct deterministic algorithm violates every such polynomial bound on some valid input and query. A randomized bound, expected volume, an approximation to maximum matching that need not be maximal, or a polynomial bound containing a factor depending on n does not settle this formulation.
context:
A matching is maximal when there is no edge that can be added while keeping its endpoints disjoint from the current matching. It can be much smaller than a maximum matching. The local output is only one port or an unmatched symbol, so the difficulty is the information needed to make this small answer consistent with answers elsewhere.

The supplied bipartition lets the two sides play different roles. A simple distributed procedure has unmatched vertices on one side propose along a new incident edge, while vertices on the other side accept at most one proposal and remain matched thereafter. After O(Δ) rounds this yields a maximal matching. Gathering a whole neighborhood to simulate those rounds can inspect Δ raised to a linear-in-Δ power many vertices.

Volume asks whether that exploration can be made much narrower. A vertex may follow a few carefully chosen dependencies far into the graph, instead of collecting every branch of a large ball. But it cannot simply choose a convenient partner in isolation: when that partner is queried separately, the answers must agree. The lack of shared mutable query state makes this coordination part of the algorithm itself.

The independence from n is essential. For each fixed Δ, even an enormous function such as Δ^(2Δ) is constant as n grows. This question compares those constants uniformly as Δ grows, asking for a single polynomial. It is therefore different from obtaining logarithmic dependence on n for fixed degree or from studying only a single fixed-degree LCL.

Known round lower bounds force at least linear dependence on Δ when n is sufficiently large. They leave a large interval between that obstruction and full-neighborhood simulation. Suomela conjectures an exponential degree dependence for volume, so even deciding whether a polynomial is possible would determine which side of that major gap is achievable.
why: This is a basic test of whether a fast distributed symmetry-breaking algorithm can be evaluated locally without exploring an exponentially branching dependency structure. A polynomial bound would give a small deterministic oracle for a fundamental graph primitive; a superpolynomial lower bound would expose an information cost that round complexity alone does not capture.

title: Can bipartite 3-coloring be maintained with logarithmic recoloring radius?
importance_reason: A canonical coloring task that tests the power of maintaining solutions under local changes. The logarithmic target matches a known lower bound, and its resolution would clarify the relationship between two general locality models.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm and a universal constant C such that, for every n and every adversarial sequence of edge insertions into an initially edgeless graph on [n], with every intermediate graph bipartite, the algorithm maintains a proper coloring with colors {1,2,3} while changing colors only within distance C log₂(n+2) of an endpoint of the newly inserted edge? Distance is measured in the graph immediately after that insertion. The algorithm sees the entire current graph and may retain arbitrary state, but has no knowledge of future insertions.
definitions: The vertex set [n] and n are supplied initially. The graphs are finite, simple and undirected, and maximum degree is unrestricted. An insertion adds one previously absent edge {u,v}; no edge deletions or supplied bipartition are included. The adversary may select its next insertion after inspecting the algorithm’s previous colors. Before any insertion the algorithm chooses a color for each isolated vertex. After update i it must output c_i:[n]→{1,2,3} with c_i(x)≠c_i(y) for every edge {x,y} of G_i. If min(dist_G_i(w,u),dist_G_i(w,v))>⌈C log₂(n+2)⌉, then c_i(w)=c_{i−1}(w); vertices in other components have infinite distance. All colors must be valid after every update. One computable program works for all n and terminates on every update. Global reading, computation time, memory and the number of recolorings inside the permitted neighborhood are unrestricted. The resource being bounded is the worst-case spatial radius of changed output, not amortized update time or communication rounds. This fixes the incremental edge-update convention of dynamic-LOCAL.
answer_criterion: Give such an algorithm with a proof valid for every bipartite insertion sequence, or prove that no deterministic algorithm has an O(log n) worst-case recoloring radius. A bound only for trees, only on the number of recolored vertices, or for a model with advance access to future edges does not settle this formulation.
context:
Every intermediate graph has a two-coloring, but a maintained coloring commits to choices before future edges are known. Two separately colored components may later be joined with incompatible parities. With only two colors, repairing that conflict can force a change across a large component. A third color offers additional ways to create a local transition between regions.

The question measures where a repair spreads. It does not limit how much of the graph the algorithm may inspect to decide on that repair. In particular, an algorithm could perform expensive global computation and still have small dynamic locality if only nearby output labels change. Conversely, a fast data structure could recolor a distant vertex and violate the radius bound.

The online-LOCAL model has a different source of power: when a vertex must be colored, a neighborhood in the eventual input graph is revealed. The ICALP 2023 algorithm uses logarithmic visibility to 3-color bipartite graphs. That result is a useful benchmark, but does not provide a logarithmic repair radius when edges themselves arrive without such advance visibility.

The later logarithmic lower bound for online-LOCAL already holds on grids and transfers to the weaker dynamic-LOCAL setting. Therefore an affirmative answer here would attain the correct asymptotic order. It remains possible that repairing a sequence of past commitments requires a substantially larger radius than choosing a color with a view into the eventual graph.

The corrected February 2026 comparison paper still lists a logarithmic lower bound and a roughly square-root upper bound for dynamic-LOCAL bipartite 3-coloring. It also withdraws an earlier general claim about derandomizing LOCAL in dynamic-LOCAL. The card uses the corrected version when describing the relationship between the models.
why: Bipartite 3-coloring is a simple test of whether global information and local repairs can match the power of online lookaround. A tight answer would clarify a basic separation between dynamic and online computation without hiding the issue in expensive local processing.

The online algorithm is not a dynamic repair algorithm. | 2024: Chang, Mishra, Nguyen, Yang, and Yeh establish an Ω(log n) deterministic online-LOCAL lower bound even for grids. Its corrections section withdraws a claimed general dynamic derandomization theorem from earlier versions. | 2026-02-23: Suomela’s updated open-problem page explicitly asks whether dynamic-LOCAL can 3-color bipartite graphs with O(log n) locality.

The algorithm must maintain a proper three-coloring and repair each insertion by changing colors only within logarithmic distance of its endpoints. A third color may help reconcile components whose earlier colorings have incompatible parity. The question is whether that flexibility always permits local repairs despite adversarial insertions and no knowledge of future edges.

title: How many rounds does triangle detection require in CONGEST?
importance_reason: Triangle detection is a basic distributed subgraph task. Its exact round complexity calibrates techniques used for many larger patterns.
formal: For arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex networks, determine the optimal worst-case randomized round complexity of triangle detection in CONGEST, up to constant factors. Each vertex initially knows its distinct O(log n)-bit identifier and its neighbors, and may send a separate O(log n)-bit message in each direction of every incident edge per synchronous round. On a triangle-free graph all vertices must output NO; otherwise at least one must output YES. The joint answer must be correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input and identifier assignment. The algorithm is uniform, has private random bits, and may know n. The currently established bounds are $\Omega(\log\log n)$ and $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$.
definitions: $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. Local computation is unrestricted, vertex identifiers have $O(\log n)$ bits, and the communication graph is exactly $G$, not an all-to-all overlay. Nodes may know $n$. The output convention avoids charging the graph diameter merely to inform every vertex of a remote triangle. The triangle is a subgraph on three distinct mutually adjacent vertices.
answer_criterion: Determine a function f(n) with an O(f(n))-round randomized algorithm and an Omega(f(n)) worst-case lower bound for every randomized algorithm in the stated model, up to constant factors. Either a faster algorithm or a stronger lower bound alone is partial progress.
context:
Every vertex knows two of the three edges of a triangle containing it. The missing information is whether two of its neighbors are adjacent. If messages had unlimited length, neighbors could exchange their complete adjacency lists in one round. The difficulty comes from fitting the relevant information through bounded-capacity edges.

For example, a vertex with many neighbors cannot simply send its entire neighborhood to every neighbor in one short message. On the other hand, most pairs of its neighbors may be irrelevant, so transmitting every adjacency list can be wasteful. An algorithm must exploit the topology to decide which information needs to move and where it can be combined.

Detection asks for one bit of global evidence, whereas listing requires the network collectively to output every triangle. A graph can contain a cubic number of triangles. Consequently, a lower bound driven by the volume of listed output does not automatically apply to detection. The near-optimal listing algorithm supplies a detection upper bound, but leaves this distinction unresolved.

The 2025 lower bound rules out every fixed number of rounds, including randomized protocols. It changes the old question of whether even two rounds are necessary into a quantitative gap. Conventional two-party communication reductions encounter barriers here, making stronger lower bounds a problem about proof techniques as well as about graph algorithms.
why: I include this because it isolates the cost of learning one local pattern under network bandwidth constraints. A sharp answer would distinguish the communication needed for deciding existence from the communication needed for distributing all witnesses, and would test how far current lower-bound methods reach.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The 2025 multi-round lower bound is included; the detection/listing distinction is essential.

The challenge is to exploit that smaller output requirement while still communicating enough information to discover an edge between two neighbors.

title: Can a congested clique find a maximal independent set in constant rounds?
importance_reason: Asks whether all-to-all communication suffices for constant-round symmetry breaking, sharply testing the congested-clique model.
formal: Is there a randomized algorithm that, on every n-vertex simple input graph, finds a maximal independent set in O(1) rounds in the Congested Clique model, with success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for every requested fixed $c>0$? Processor v initially knows its identifier and incident input edges. Every ordered pair of processors may exchange an O(log n)-bit message per synchronous round, whether or not the input edge exists. Each processor outputs whether it belongs to an independent set that dominates every vertex outside it. The algorithm must be uniform across inputs; it cannot be chosen after seeing the graph.
definitions: Here $\Delta$ is the maximum degree of the input graph, not of the communication network. Messages to different recipients may differ. Local computation is unrestricted. $O(1)$ means independent of both $n$ and $\Delta$, with constants allowed to depend on the requested failure exponent. This is the unicast Congested Clique, rather than the weaker broadcast variant.
answer_criterion: Construct one randomized algorithm whose round bound is constant on every input graph, with the stated high-probability guarantee, or prove that constant rounds cannot suffice for all graphs in this model.
context:
This changes the communication network while leaving the graph problem unchanged. A vertex can contact a distant processor immediately, so graph distance no longer limits the spread of information. Bandwidth still matters: one processor can receive only $O(n\log n)$ bits per round, whereas a general graph can contain $\Theta(n^2)$ independently specified edges. Sending the entire input to one leader is therefore not a constant-round solution.

That bottleneck is not itself a lower bound for MIS. A complete graph has many edges but is easy: a designated vertex can join the independent set and all others can stay out. The sought algorithm only needs enough information to coordinate a valid answer; it need not reconstruct every edge in one place.

Known algorithms exploit this by solving suitably sparse sampled subgraphs and reducing the remaining degrees. The general upper bound is $O(\log\log\Delta)$ rounds. The central question is whether a bounded number of communication phases can remove the need for repeated sparsification.

A closely related relaxation is already possible in constant rounds: a 2-ruling set remains independent but only has to put every vertex within distance two of a selected vertex. MIS requires distance one. This supplies a precise nearby success case against which to assess the unresolved target.
why: I include this beside the LOCAL MIS problem because it tests a different limitation of distributed computation: restricted bandwidth despite universal communication. A constant-round algorithm would show that exact local domination needs only a bounded number of global exchanges. A lower bound would have to explain why distributed processing cannot avoid the bottleneck.

They also identify graph families on which existing sparsification methods require $\Omega(\log\log n)$ iterations. That restriction applies to those methods, not to all Congested Clique algorithms.

The target is to replace repeated sparsification and degree-reduction phases with a bounded amount of globally coordinated communication.

title: Can deterministic (Delta+1)-coloring beat square-root dependence on degree?
importance_reason: Breaking the square-root degree barrier for the canonical coloring task would improve a broadly reused distributed primitive.
formal: Is there one deterministic LOCAL algorithm that properly colors every simple n-vertex graph of maximum degree $\Delta\ge2$ with colors in $\{1,\ldots,\Delta+1\}$ in $O(\Delta^{0.499}+\log^* n)$ synchronous rounds? Vertices have arbitrary distinct O(log n)-bit identifiers and know n and Delta. Messages along input edges and local computation are unbounded. The constant in the round bound must be independent of both n and Delta.
definitions: Proper coloring means adjacent vertices receive different output colors. Delta denotes a supplied upper bound on degree, and the guarantee holds for every such valid bound. The algorithm is uniform over n, Delta, and identifier assignments. Log-star n is the number of repeated base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. Elapsed synchronous rounds are measured; this is not a sequential running-time or message-count target.
answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm with the specified uniform round bound, or prove that no deterministic LOCAL algorithm attains it. Improving a logarithmic factor while retaining degree exponent one-half does not meet the target.
context:
A sequential greedy algorithm needs only one more color than the maximum degree: when processing a vertex, at most Delta colors have already been used by its neighbors. In a distributed algorithm many adjacent vertices act simultaneously, so they can choose conflicting colors unless their decisions are coordinated.

Unique identifiers break perfect symmetry, but treating every identifier as a color starts with far too many colors. Color reduction has to compress this large palette while preserving a distinction across every edge. The degree controls how many simultaneous conflicts a vertex may need to avoid.

The two parameters in the target play different roles. Even when degree is fixed, the network can have arbitrarily many vertices, and iterated logarithmic time captures the unavoidable symmetry-breaking dependence on that size. An algorithm taking a power of log n cannot simply replace this term: for sufficiently large n, it exceeds every bound depending only on Delta plus log-star n.

The target chooses a specific exponent strictly below one-half, as in Suomela’s list. The numerical improvement is small; its purpose is to cross the apparent degree barrier while keeping the optimal-size palette. Allowing more colors, randomness, or a larger n-dependent term gives separate questions.
why: I include this because the familiar greedy palette bound hides a distinct distributed coordination problem. A fixed improvement in the degree exponent would reveal new ways to resolve local conflicts, while an impossibility result would explain why the square-root dependence persists across different coloring methods.

title: Can bipartite maximal fractional matching be found in sublinear-in-degree rounds?
importance_reason: Tests whether fractional matching permits sublinear degree dependence under bipartiteness; a focused separation inside local symmetry breaking.
formal:
Is there a deterministic LOCAL algorithm and a function $f(\Delta)=o(\Delta)$ that, on every simple bipartite graph of maximum degree at most Delta, outputs a maximal fractional matching within f(Delta) rounds, independently of n? Each edge e receives a nonnegative rational weight x_e, agreed upon by its endpoints. Require $\sum_{e
i v}x_e\le1$ for every vertex v, and for every edge uv require $\sum_{e
i u}x_e=1$ or $\sum_{e
i v}x_e=1$. The bipartition is supplied as an input two-coloring, nodes know n and Delta, and identifiers are distinct O(log n)-bit integers.
definitions: LOCAL uses synchronous rounds with unbounded messages along input edges and unrestricted local computation. Rational weights have finite encodings; there is no imposed output-bit bound. The algorithm must work for every identifier assignment and every valid supplied degree bound. The little-o statement concerns Delta tending to infinity and must hold uniformly over all graph sizes. Vertices output weights for all incident edges, with exact endpoint agreement.
answer_criterion: Construct a uniform algorithm with a degree-only bound whose ratio to Delta tends to zero, or prove that no such deterministic algorithm exists. An additive log-star n term, an almost-maximal solution, or a lower bound only for nonbipartite graphs does not settle this target.
context:
A fractional matching divides one unit of capacity at each vertex among its incident edges. Maximality means that no single edge can have its weight increased without exceeding an endpoint’s capacity. It does not mean that the total edge weight is as large as possible.

For example, on a star one can place the entire unit on a single leaf edge or divide it equally among all leaf edges. Both assignments saturate the center and are maximal, even though many leaves are unsaturated. Allowing fractions gives the algorithm ways to share capacity that do not exist for ordinary integral matching.

Bipartiteness supplies a globally consistent division into two sides, and the card gives that division to the algorithm. This can remove symmetry obstacles that occur when a vertex does not know which role it should play. Nevertheless, neighboring choices still have to agree on edge weights and achieve exact saturation somewhere along every edge.

Approximate saturation is a different requirement: leaving a small amount of unused capacity at both endpoints violates the condition on that edge. The known linear-degree lower bound on general graphs therefore cannot simply be combined with an approximation algorithm or transferred to the supplied-bipartition setting. The source specifically leaves this bipartite case open.
why: I include this because it asks whether relaxing discrete choices to fractional ones changes the intrinsic time needed for local coordination, once a bipartition is available. The constraints are simple, but exact maximality makes the question stronger than approximately solving a packing problem.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The question fixes a supplied bipartition, exact rational output, and no additive dependence on network size.

This does not resolve the bipartite question as stated. | 2026-02: Suomela’s open-problem list explicitly asks for o(Delta) rounds on bipartite graphs and conjectures that the answer is negative.

title: Linear LOCAL versus constant dynamic locality for a promise-free LCL
importance_reason: A broad model-separation benchmark resolved through general simulation machinery. Retained for its structural meaning and traceability, with resolved status rather than counted as a remaining open problem.
formal: Does there exist one promise-free LCL on bounded-degree graphs that has a deterministic incremental dynamic-LOCAL algorithm with O(1) repair radius, but requires Ω(n) rounds in deterministic LOCAL? Under the models below, the answer is no: combining the cited simulations gives a deterministic O(√n·polylog n)-round LOCAL algorithm whenever constant dynamic locality is possible.
definitions: A promise-free LCL Π has one fixed degree bound Δ≥2, one fixed checking radius r≥1, finite vertex input/output alphabets, and a finite list of permitted rooted radius-r input/output neighborhoods. A labeling is legal exactly when all vertices pass this check. The problem must admit a legal output for every finite simple undirected graph of degree at most Δ and every input assignment, including disconnected graphs. Legality is invariant under isomorphism and does not depend on identifiers, port orders, or graph size. No assumption of bipartiteness, planarity, a rooted structure, or a special global input encoding is made. In deterministic LOCAL, vertices initially know n, their own input, degree, ports, and a distinct identifier in [n²]. They exchange unbounded messages with neighbors in synchronous rounds. One finite computable program must work on every input, with unrestricted terminating local computation. Round complexity is the worst case over input graphs, labels, ports, and identifiers. In incremental dynamic-LOCAL, a central deterministic algorithm starts with the empty graph and a known upper bound N on the eventual number of vertices. An adversary inserts isolated vertices with immutable input labels and identifiers, or inserts edges between existing vertices, always respecting Δ and the size bound. After every event the algorithm must maintain a legal output on the entire current graph. Existing outputs may change only within distance R(N) of an endpoint of the inserted edge, or of the inserted vertex, measured after the event. The algorithm may inspect the entire revealed graph and retain arbitrary state, but future vertices, inputs, and edges are unknown. The locality is the largest radius of any output change, not the number of changes or the update time. All algorithms are uniform finite programs, all local computation must terminate, and all guarantees are deterministic and worst case. A constant locality bound is independent of size and may depend only on the fixed problem. A linear lower bound means that for every correct algorithm A there are a constant c_A>0 and arbitrarily large size bounds with an input or update sequence forcing locality at least c_A times that bound. This infinitely-often formulation is already ruled out by a uniform sublinear upper bound.
answer_criterion: A positive answer would require one finite total LCL specification, a constant-radius dynamic algorithm, and a linear deterministic LOCAL lower bound. A negative answer rules out this combination for every such LCL. The latter follows from the sublinear simulation described below; this is a derived corollary, not a claim that either cited paper states this exact saved question verbatim.
context:
Dynamic computation retains the history of how a graph was built. This history can provide choices that a fresh synchronous computation has to establish through communication. The saved question asks whether local repairs could exploit that advantage so strongly that a constant repair radius replaces a linear number of communication rounds.

The requirement to work on every bounded-degree graph and every input matters. Special graph families may have global promises that affect what an algorithm can infer from a partial view. Here all intermediate graphs are valid inputs to the same total problem, so the simulations can build disjoint copies, delete edges, and introduce isolated vertices without leaving the problem’s domain.

A constant-radius dynamic algorithm yields a constant-locality online algorithm. On each online request, reveal a slightly larger constant-radius neighborhood and simulate its vertex and edge insertions. Once a requested vertex is labeled, later revelations are too far away to change it. This uses the incremental model beginning with an empty graph; unseen input labels are not supplied in advance.

The first step removes dependence on unrelated revealed components. Lemma 7.5 turns an online algorithm of locality T(n) into one whose decision depends only on its current revealed component, with locality T(2^O(n³)). If T is a constant, this enormous change of the size argument leaves locality constant. The family of all bounded-degree graphs satisfies the lemma’s closure assumptions.

The second step simulates that component-wise algorithm in sublinear deterministic LOCAL time. The clustering framework separates small-diameter regions with only O(√n) leftover vertices. Grouping nearby leftovers gives components of diameter O(√n) whose constant-radius views are mutually separate. Each such component can simulate the deterministic online rule on its leftovers independently; these simulations form one valid online prefix. Each remaining region can then choose a compatible completion by finite exhaustive search. Local checkability makes the separate completions compatible. The total communication radius is O(√n·polylog n). This explains the deterministic specialization of the component-wise simulation.

Combining these steps gives dynamic O(1) → online O(1) → deterministic LOCAL O(√n·polylog n). Since √n times any fixed polylogarithm is o(n), a linear LOCAL lower bound is impossible. Smaller separations can still exist; the result only rules out the specified linear-versus-constant target.
why: The question probes the limits of using construction history to replace communication for locally verifiable tasks. Its negative resolution places a general upper bound on that advantage and demonstrates why exact size regimes and the absence of promises matter when comparing locality models.

The chain of implications is spelled out in context. The original open statement is retained for history; the result does not classify all smaller dynamic/LOCAL separations.

formal: Does there exist one promise-free LCL on bounded-degree graphs with deterministic online-LOCAL complexity O(1), but deterministic incremental dynamic-LOCAL complexity Ω(n)? A negative answer excludes every such witness. The cited simulations imply the negative answer; the conclusion is an editorial composition of the results, with its reasoning given below.
context:
Online lookaround reveals nearby parts of the eventual graph before a vertex commits to its output. Incremental dynamic computation instead sees the graph as it is built and repairs earlier outputs. The question asks whether even constant lookaround can prevent changes that would otherwise have to spread linearly far.

These are spatial resource bounds. A dynamic algorithm may examine the whole current graph and perform very expensive computation, yet its output changes must remain close to the update. An online algorithm may use all previously revealed information but cannot revise a requested vertex. Neither definition bounds ordinary centralized running time.

The first step removes dependence on unrelated revealed components. Lemma 7.5 turns an online algorithm of locality T(n) into one whose decision depends only on its current revealed component, with locality T(2^O(n³)). If T is a constant, this enormous change of the size argument leaves locality constant. The family of all bounded-degree graphs satisfies the lemma’s closure assumptions.

The second step simulates that component-wise algorithm in sublinear deterministic LOCAL time. The clustering framework separates small-diameter regions with only O(√n) leftover vertices. Grouping nearby leftovers gives components of diameter O(√n) whose constant-radius views are mutually separate. Each such component can simulate the deterministic online rule on its leftovers independently; these simulations form one valid online prefix. Each remaining region can then choose a compatible completion by finite exhaustive search. Local checkability makes the separate completions compatible. The total communication radius is O(√n·polylog n). This explains the deterministic specialization of the component-wise simulation.

A deterministic T(n)-round LOCAL algorithm also supplies a dynamic algorithm with repair radius at most T(n)+O(1). Recompute its prescribed outputs after each insertion. Farther vertices have unchanged input neighborhoods and therefore unchanged outputs. For growing graphs, use the fixed size bound N and pad unseen vertices as isolated vertices with fixed dummy inputs; the problem is total and its legality is independent of N, so outputs on the real components remain valid.

The complete implication is online O(1) → component-wise online O(1) → deterministic LOCAL O(√n·polylog n) → dynamic O(√n·polylog n). This excludes the requested linear dynamic lower bound. It does not prove that online and dynamic locality always agree, nor give a constant-radius dynamic simulation.
