working_summary: Robust low-rank approximation measures reconstruction error by the sum of absolute entrywise differences. The source asks for a polynomial-time algorithm returning a rank-k factorization within a factor one plus epsilon of the best such approximation. This changes the geometry from the squared-error setting where singular values and standard sketching methods are especially effective. Approximating a sum of row norms is also a different guarantee and does not settle the entrywise objective. An algorithm or hardness classification would clarify whether near-optimal robust matrix compression admits the same broad computational tractability as classical low-rank approximation.

title: Crouzeix’s sharp numerical-range inequality
importance_reason: Historically central in numerical linear algebra and operator theory, with direct relevance to matrix approximation; resolved scalar status keeps it after remaining open questions in category ordering.
formal: For every integer n≥1, every complex matrix A∈C^{n×n}, and every scalar polynomial p∈C[z], does ‖p(A)‖₂≤2 max_{z∈W(A)}|p(z)| hold?
definitions: The numerical range is W(A)={x*Ax:x∈C^n,‖x‖₂=1}, where x* denotes conjugate transpose and ‖x‖₂ is the Euclidean norm. The matrix norm is its induced spectral norm, ‖B‖₂=max_{‖x‖₂=1}‖Bx‖₂. For p(z)=Σ_{j=0}^m c_j z^j, define p(A)=Σ_{j=0}^m c_j A^j with A⁰=I. There is no restriction on degree, coefficients, normality, diagonalizability or dimension, and no coordinate-encoding assumption. W(A) is compact, so the scalar maximum exists. The coefficient 2 must work universally. This is the scalar-polynomial conjecture. It does not assert the stronger complete inequality for matrices of polynomials [p_ij], where one compares the norm of the block matrix [p_ij(A)] with max_{z∈W(A)}‖[p_ij(z)]‖₂ for all block sizes.
answer_criterion: The requested universal inequality is affirmative in the July–August 2026 proofs described below. A negative answer would require a finite complex matrix and scalar polynomial violating it. The constant cannot be reduced: for J=[[0,1],[0,0]] and p(z)=z, ‖J‖₂=1 and max_{W(J)}|z|=1/2. This historical problem is retained with resolved status; the stronger complete conjecture is not silently substituted for its original target.
context:
This saved open problem has been resolved in the scalar form stated here, according to two 2026 proof manuscripts and an explicit expert assessment. Jin’s first preprint was posted on July 27, and Lorist–Schwenninger’s independent proof on August 4. In an August 15 report, Townsend and Greenbaum state that they and Crouzeix checked Jin’s argument thoroughly and believe it correct. The catalogue therefore marks this entry resolved while recording that formal journal review was still pending in the inspected repository.

The underlying issue is the behavior of functions of a nonnormal matrix. For a normal matrix, a unitary diagonalization reduces the norm of p(A) to the largest |p(λ)| over eigenvalues λ. For a nonnormal matrix, eigenvalues alone can miss substantial amplification. The nilpotent matrix J in the answer criterion has only the eigenvalue zero, yet J itself has norm one. Taking p(z)=z shows why a bound based only on scalar values at the spectrum cannot work universally.

The numerical range incorporates all quadratic forms x*Ax on unit vectors, rather than only eigenvectors. For the same J, x*Jx=conjugate(x₁)x₂. Its maximum modulus is 1/2, attained when the two coordinates have equal modulus. Thus replacing the spectrum by the numerical range gives meaningful information, but still requires the factor two. This small example establishes sharpness independently of the general proof.

A numerical-range estimate transfers scalar approximation to matrix approximation. For example, if two scalar polynomials p and q differ by at most ε throughout W(A), the theorem gives ‖p(A)−q(A)‖₂≤2ε. That is useful when a matrix polynomial is applied to a vector: the same bound controls the resulting vector error relative to its norm. The role in matrix functions and polynomial or rational Krylov methods is discussed in the expert report.

The dimension-independent nature of the constant was already a major achievement before sharpness was settled. Crouzeix obtained the bound 11.08 in 2007, and Crouzeix–Palencia reduced it to 1+√2 in 2017. The inherited Ransford–Schwenninger paper clarifies the latter proof using the numerical-range functional calculus. The remaining gap from approximately 2.414 to 2 was small numerically but resisted the existing estimates.

Jin’s proof uses a positive-real completion theorem for a matrix-valued function. In the August 7 version, the key argument is organized around an auxiliary eigenbasis and a mass parameter; the numerical-range double-layer construction has mass two. The manuscript then uses approximation by matrices with simple spectrum and suitable convex outer domains to obtain the general statement. The theorem itself is stated for every finite complex matrix and scalar polynomial, exactly matching this card.

Lorist and Schwenninger use an operator-theoretic perturbation lemma. In their notation, T has a contraction dilation with error terms E_n=2V*Q^{*n}V−T^{*n}. Uniform boundedness of these errors and their commutation with T force ‖T‖≤2. Their proof exploits all powers n through a telescoping estimate, rather than only the first power. Applying this to T=f(A) and the double-layer representation proves the scalar spectral-set bound.

The two arguments are valuable for more than lowering a constant: they identify additional structure in the earlier functional-calculus estimates that had not been sufficient when used one power at a time. The Lorist–Schwenninger manuscript explicitly acknowledges Jin’s independent proof, and its August 17 revision adds exposition and remarks rather than a restriction to a special matrix class. The exact scalar theorem and main lemma were inspected for this catalogue; no local Lean verification was performed.

The complete version remains a separate question because it asks for a bound after replacing scalar polynomial values by matrices of polynomial values, uniformly in that additional matrix size. A proof for each scalar p does not automatically supply this stronger simultaneous norm estimate. Åhag, Czyż and Virtanen’s September 9, 2026 revision proves the complete conjecture for matrices A of order at most three and develops related square-function estimates. That result must not be presented as the all-dimensional complete theorem.

The original question is retained because it records a fundamental sharp relation between a scalar geometric set and nonnormal matrix computation, together with a very recent change in mathematical status. It also provides a useful test of catalogue freshness: an entry based only on the 2018 or 2024 references would incorrectly describe the scalar conjecture as still open. New work on complete bounds or related spectral sets should receive its own precise statement.
why: A sharp dimension-independent bridge from scalar approximation on the numerical range to norms of functions of nonnormal matrices; retained as a recently resolved foundational problem.
status_note: Resolved affirmatively in the scalar form by July–August 2026 preprints of Jin and independently Lorist–Schwenninger. The status is supported by the explicit August 15 expert assessment of Townsend–Greenbaum, including their report of Crouzeix’s checking. Formal journal peer review is still marked pending in Jin’s repository; no local formalization audit is claimed. Retained as a historical detailed card, not a remaining open problem. The all-dimensional complete conjecture is a different question.
progress: 2004–2007: Crouzeix formulates the conjecture and obtains the first dimension-independent constant 11.08; the inherited 2018 paper records the foundation. | 2017–2018: Crouzeix–Palencia prove the constant 1+√2; Ransford–Schwenninger clarify that argument. | 2024: O’Loughlin–Virtanen develop results for classes of matrices; this inherited reference predates the general resolution. | 2026-07-27: Jin posts The Numerical Range Is a 2-Spectral Set, proving the scalar constant two; the inspected latest version is August 7. | 2026-08-04: Lorist–Schwenninger post an independent scalar proof via a perturbation lemma for 2-dilations; inspected revision August 17. | 2026-08-15: Townsend–Greenbaum report that they and Crouzeix have checked Jin’s proof and believe it correct. | 2026-09-09: Åhag–Czyż–Virtanen’s revision addresses the stronger complete conjecture through dimension three; this is distinct from the now-resolved scalar question.
working_summary: Crouzeix's inequality controls the norm of a polynomial applied to a matrix through that polynomial's largest value on the matrix's numerical range. The sharp proposed constant is two, independent of matrix size or polynomial degree. The saved reviewed card marks this scalar formulation resolved following two 2026 proof manuscripts and a favorable explicit expert assessment. Its remaining qualification concerns formal publication review, rather than presenting the statement as currently open. The result connects scalar approximation with matrix-function error and controls amplification that eigenvalues alone may miss for nonnormal matrices.

title: Does every isotropic log-concave measure have a dimension-free Poincaré constant?
importance_reason: A foundational high-dimensional geometry conjecture with substantial consequences for sampling, integration, optimization, and concentration inequalities.
focus_reason: A foundational high-dimensional geometry conjecture with substantial consequences for sampling, integration, optimization, and concentration inequalities.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant C<∞ such that, for every dimension n≥1, every isotropic log-concave probability measure μ on ℝⁿ, and every locally Lipschitz f:ℝⁿ→ℝ with finite second moment and finite gradient energy, $\operatorname{Var}_\mu(f)\le C\int\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)$? This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
definitions: The measure has a Lebesgue density ρ=e^{−V}, where V:ℝⁿ→ℝ∪{+∞} is convex and ∫ρ=1; allowing V=+∞ includes uniform distributions on full-dimensional convex bodies. Isotropy means ∫x dμ(x)=0 and ∫xxᵀ dμ(x)=Iₙ. Variance is Varμ(f)=∫(f−∫f dμ)²dμ, and ∇f is the almost-everywhere Euclidean gradient. Let C_P(μ) be the infimum of constants that make the displayed inequality hold for all the stated f. The requested bound is supₙ supμ C_P(μ)<∞, with μ ranging over isotropic log-concave measures in ℝⁿ. There is no symmetry, product structure, smoothness, or positive lower curvature bound on V. The universal constant may depend on none of n, μ, or f. In the isoperimetric convention used by the recent papers, ψμ is the reciprocal Cheeger expansion constant; ψμ² is comparable to C_P(μ) up to universal factors. Thus a bound on ψμ must be squared when expressed as a bound on the Poincaré constant used here.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The inequality asks whether a function can vary substantially across a log-concave distribution while changing only slowly in the regions where that distribution places mass. Isotropy fixes the scale: each unit-direction linear function already has variance one and gradient energy one. The conjecture says that nonlinear functions cannot create an arbitrarily larger ratio as dimension grows.

The geometric version rules out a hidden bottleneck separating two substantial portions of the measure. For a log-concave density, the conjecture says that the best arbitrary separating set has boundary expansion comparable to an appropriate halfspace cut. Uniform distributions on convex bodies are included, so the question is not confined to smooth, strongly convex potentials where curvature can directly control a spectral gap.

The original algorithmic motivation was sampling by random walks. Poor expansion can trap a local walk in one part of a body for a long time; good expansion bounds its mixing. Sampling then supports volume estimation, integration, and convex optimization. A KLS theorem would improve the geometric ingredient in these analyses, though total algorithmic complexity would still account for access to the body, initialization, and the chosen walk.

Thin-shell concentration concerns the special observable ‖X‖₂. Klartag and Lehec’s 2025 result, revised in February 2026, bounds E(‖X‖₂−√n)² by a universal constant. This settles thin-shell concentration and also supports the resolved slicing question, but does not by itself control every test function in the Poincaré inequality. These neighboring geometric conjectures must therefore be tracked separately.

The remaining dimension dependence is small but substantive. Klartag’s 2023 theorem gives C_P(μ)=O(log n). Letwin’s July 2026 preprint reports a dimension-free inequality for quadratic forms and derives ψμ=O((log n)^{1/4}), hence C_P(μ)=O(√log n). The latter is a reported preprint improvement, and even that estimate still leaves a growing factor rather than the universal constant required here.
why: KLS links the geometry of high-dimensional convex sets to spectral gaps, concentration, and the efficiency of sampling. It asks whether covariance normalization alone removes every dimension-dependent bottleneck for log-concave measures, making it a central structural question behind continuous randomized algorithms.
status_note: The full KLS conjecture is explicitly open in the primary sources, including Letwin’s July 2026 preprint. Research through 10 September 2026 found no dimension-free general-function resolution. The recent quadratic-form and thin-shell results are not treated as proofs of the full conjecture; the July bound is labeled as a preprint result.
progress: 1995: Kannan, Lovász, and Simonovits formulate the isoperimetric conjecture in connection with localization and random-walk sampling in convex bodies. | 2022: Klartag and Lehec obtain the first polylogarithmic bounds for the KLS isoperimetric constant using stochastic-localization techniques. | 2023: Klartag proves ψμ=O(√log n), equivalently C_P(μ)=O(log n), through an improved log-concave Lichnerowicz inequality. | 2025–2026: Klartag and Lehec settle the thin-shell conjecture. The 23 February 2026 revision controls E(‖X‖₂−√n)² uniformly, a particular radial concentration target rather than the full Poincaré inequality. | 27 July 2026: Letwin’s preprint reports Var(XᵀMX)≤2E‖∇(XᵀMX)‖₂² for every symmetric M and isotropic log-concave X, and derives ψₙ=O((log n)^{1/4}). In this card’s normalization the resulting general-function bound is C_P=O(√log n), not O((log n)^{1/4}).
working_summary: The KLS conjecture concerns log-concave probability distributions normalized to have mean zero and identity covariance. It asks whether every sufficiently regular function has variance bounded by a universal constant times its average squared gradient. That constant must work in every dimension and for every such distribution. Geometrically, this would exclude narrow bottlenecks that covariance normalization fails to reveal. The question connects high-dimensional convex geometry with the mixing of sampling algorithms, and control of particular observables alone does not settle it.

title: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair conjecture
importance_reason: A central link between graph minor structure, metric embeddings and the quality of the basic sparsest-cut relaxation, already open in the planar case.
focus_reason: A central link between graph minor structure, metric embeddings and the quality of the basic sparsest-cut relaxation, already open in the planar case.
formal: For every fixed finite simple graph H, is there a finite constant C_H≥1 such that, for every finite connected simple undirected H-minor-free graph G with strictly positive real edge lengths, its shortest-path metric d_G admits a map f:V(G)→ℝᵐ into some finite-dimensional ℓ₁ space satisfying d_G(u,v)≤‖f(u)−f(v)‖₁≤C_H d_G(u,v) for all vertices u,v?
definitions: H-minor-free means that deleting vertices and edges and contracting edges of G cannot produce a graph isomorphic to H, after removing loops and duplicate edges. The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths, and d_G(u,v) is the minimum path length. In ℝᵐ, ‖x−y‖₁=Σⱼ₌₁ᵐ |xⱼ−yⱼ|. The displayed inequalities normalize the embedding to be noncontracting; permitting a common scaling factor gives the same distortion notion. The constant C_H may depend on the excluded graph H, but must be independent of |V(G)|, the edge lengths and their ratio. The target dimension m and the map f may depend on the entire weighted graph and have no computational or dimension bound. This is an existence question for all vertex pairs simultaneously. It concerns undirected shortest-path distances themselves, without a snowflake transformation, average-pair guarantee or restriction to selected terminals.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The conjecture asks whether excluding a fixed graph minor removes every large-scale obstruction to representing graph distances as sums of coordinate differences. The graph can have arbitrarily many vertices and very unequal edge lengths. Its topology supplies the restriction, while the conclusion concerns the metric generated by all those lengths. Gupta, Newman, Rabinovich and Sinclair formulate this connection in their work on cuts, trees and ℓ₁ embeddings.

The target ℓ₁ space is useful because its finite metrics are nonnegative combinations of cut metrics. A cut metric assigns distance one to pairs separated by a chosen vertex subset and zero to other pairs. Coordinates can be decomposed by thresholding their values, producing precisely such cuts. Thus an ℓ₁ embedding replaces a complicated distance function by weighted separation tests that are closely connected to graph partitioning.

Trees give a concrete exact example. Root a weighted tree and assign one coordinate to each edge. For that coordinate, give a vertex the edge’s length if it lies below the edge and zero otherwise. Two vertices differ in exactly the coordinates corresponding to their unique connecting path. Their ℓ₁ distance therefore equals their original tree distance. Cycles allow competing shortest paths, which makes a common coordinate representation much harder.

The equivalent flow formulation compares two bounds on simultaneous routing. A concurrent flow routes the same fraction of every specified pair’s demand through a capacitated graph, splitting traffic among paths when useful. Every cut bounds that fraction by its available capacity divided by the demand it separates. GNRS predicts that, on any fixed-minor-free family, the best cut bound exceeds the achievable concurrent-flow value by at most a family-dependent constant, for arbitrary nonnegative demands.

Arbitrary demands are essential. Restricting to uniform demand between all vertex pairs gives an easier problem with stronger known results. Likewise, the capacity graph can be minor-free while demand pairs connect vertices in any pattern. Requiring the demands themselves to form a planar graph would change the target. The geometric formulation avoids these auxiliary conventions by requiring distance preservation for every vertex pair.

The planar case remains a central unresolved test. Rao’s general guarantee is O(√log n) distortion for n-vertex planar metrics, and Chekuri’s May 2026 lecture notes still list a constant bound as open. No growing lower bound for planar metrics is known in that account. Both a constant upper bound and a superconstant counterexample would therefore represent a substantial change in understanding.

Several restricted families do satisfy constant distortion bounds. The original work handles series-parallel graphs. Lee and Sidiropoulos prove a stronger random-tree embedding result for graphs of any fixed pathwidth k, with distortion depending only on k. Their theorem establishes GNRS for minor-closed families that exclude a tree. Fixed pathwidth is a substantial additional restriction and does not include all graphs of fixed treewidth.

This last distinction exposes a common pitfall in reading algorithmic progress. Chlamtac, Krauthgamer and Raghavendra obtain constant-factor sparsest-cut approximation on every fixed-treewidth class using the Sherali–Adams hierarchy. They explicitly explain that their stronger relaxation does not establish a constant gap for the ordinary concurrent-flow LP. Thus the inherited paper is important context and an algorithmic success, but it is not a proof of the bounded-treewidth case of GNRS.

Filtser improves a terminal-sensitive planar bound: when the terminals can be covered by γ faces of a planar drawing, their metric embeds with distortion O(√log(γ+1)). The added one simply handles the single-face case in asymptotic notation. This is constant for fixed γ and recovers the familiar n-dependent bound when all vertices require many faces. The 2024 journal-online publication refines which geometric parameter creates the loss.

There is also recent exact progress inside small planar families. Mori’s February 2026 preprint calculates the worst-over-edge-lengths distortion of K₂,ₙ as (3k−2)/(2k−1), where k=⌈n/2⌉. The values approach 3/2. This demonstrates a nontrivial bounded loss in an infinite family, rather than a counterexample with distortion growing without bound. Such examples help test the sharpness and limitations of proposed embedding mechanisms.

A solution would connect a qualitative structural restriction—excluding one fixed minor—to a uniform quantitative statement about all distances and all concurrent-routing instances. It would explain whether the logarithmic losses in current general embedding arguments are unavoidable on these graph families. The question remains meaningful independently of how efficiently the embedding can be constructed.
why: Determine whether excluded graph minors exactly prevent unbounded ℓ₁ distortion and multicommodity flow–cut gaps in proper minor-closed graph families.
status_note: The planar constant-distortion case remains explicitly open in the checked May 2026 notes. Restricted-family and face-cover results, including February 2026 exact values for K₂,ₙ, do not settle arbitrary fixed-minor-free metrics. The inherited fixed-treewidth approximation theorem uses a stronger relaxation and expressly does not prove a flow–cut-gap bound. No general settlement found through 11 September 2026.
progress: 1999–2004: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair formulate the conjecture and prove constant bounds for restricted families including series-parallel graphs; FOCS 1999 and Combinatorica 2004. | 2009–2012: Lee–Sidiropoulos prove bounded-distortion random-tree embeddings for fixed pathwidth, establishing GNRS for minor-closed families excluding a tree. | 2010: Chlamtac–Krauthgamer–Raghavendra give a constant-factor sparsest-cut approximation on fixed-treewidth graphs using a stronger LP; this does not bound the ordinary flow–cut gap. | 2019–2024: Filtser improves the planar terminal face-cover bound to O(√log(γ+1)); checked July 2024 revision and November 2024 online journal publication. | 2026-02-27: Mori determines the exact worst-weight distortion of each K₂,ₙ, approaching 3/2 with increasing n. | 2026-05-04: Chekuri’s updated approximation-algorithms notes still list the planar constant flow–cut-gap question as open, with O(√log n) upper bound and no superconstant lower bound.
working_summary: The GNRS conjecture asks how faithfully shortest-path distances in graphs excluding a fixed minor can be represented in ℓ₁. The graph may have arbitrary positive edge lengths, and every pair of vertices must be preserved within a constant factor. This constant may depend on the excluded minor but cannot grow with the graph. Because ℓ₁ metrics decompose into weighted cuts, the question also governs multicommodity flow–cut gaps. Even the planar case tests whether a strong topological restriction is enough to remove all growing distortion.

title: Unknot recognition in polynomial time
importance_reason: A central algorithmic topology problem in NP∩coNP; a fresh claimed polynomial-time solution makes precise formulation and validation especially valuable.
focus_reason: A central algorithmic topology problem in NP∩coNP; a fresh claimed polynomial-time solution makes precise formulation and validation especially valuable.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing algorithm and a constant c such that, on every explicit combinatorial knot diagram D of encoding length N, the algorithm decides in O((N+1)^c) bit operations whether the represented knot in the 3-sphere is ambient isotopic to the unknot?
definitions: A knot is a tame embedding of one circle into S³; the unknot is the isotopy class of a round circle. Ambient isotopy means a continuous family of homeomorphisms of S³ starting at the identity and carrying one embedded circle to the other at its endpoint. A diagram is a generic projection with transverse double crossings and specified over/under information. Encode it by an explicitly listed connected 4-regular planar multigraph, including loops when needed, its cyclic orders of half-edges at vertices, a distinguished outer face and the overpassing pair of opposite half-edges at each crossing. Tracing the opposite pairs must give one component. A separate constant-size encoding represents the crossing-free circle. The embedding is required to be a valid sphere embedding; malformed encodings may be rejected by polynomial-time combinatorial checks. If the diagram has n crossings, a standard such encoding has O(n log(n+1)) bits. The complexity parameter is the supplied encoding length N, not the minimum crossing number among equivalent diagrams. The input is explicit rather than a compressed description of an exponentially larger diagram. No disk, simplification sequence, knot invariant, auxiliary advice or promise of triviality is supplied. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Status requires special care: Chad Musick’s preprint of 6 September 2026 claims a positive answer in Corollary 1. Its route is a polynomial-time construction of a locally minimal bridge presentation using compressed descriptions, followed by an existing characterization of bridge presentations of the unknot. I checked the claim and its main proof dependencies, but have not independently verified the local-minimality argument or compressed-update complexity. The card is therefore marked uncertain pending validation of this fresh claimed resolution.

The underlying task is deceptively simple: determine whether a closed loop can be untangled without cutting it or passing one strand through another. A diagram can contain many crossings that are artifacts of its projection. Looking complicated does not prove knottedness, while repeatedly removing visible twists can get stuck on a diagram that still represents the unknot. The input can be deliberately chosen to frustrate familiar simplification strategies.

The chosen representation makes the computational question independent of numerical geometry. Coordinates, thickness, physical forces and drawing quality do not enter the running time. Cyclic orders record the planar embedding, and the crossing data tell us which strand passes over the other. The task concerns the topology represented by those finite combinatorial data, not the visual complexity of a particular rendering.

Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger prove that unknot recognition belongs to NP using normal-surface techniques. Informally, an unknot bounds an embedded disk, and a suitable disk can be encoded compactly through its intersections with tetrahedra in a triangulation. Large counts are stored in binary. The existence of a polynomial-size verifiable certificate gives an upper bound on nondeterministic complexity, while finding such a certificate may still require substantial search.

Lackenby proves that knottedness also belongs to NP, so unknot recognition lies in coNP as well. This is an unconditional theorem, unlike earlier approaches that required the generalized Riemann hypothesis. It places the problem in NP∩coNP and makes ordinary NP-completeness unlikely: an NP-hard language in coNP would imply NP=coNP. Membership in both classes does not itself give a polynomial-time decision algorithm.

There is another strong certificate theorem. Lackenby proves that any n-crossing unknot diagram can be reduced to a crossing-free circle using at most (236n)¹¹ Reidemeister moves. These are local diagram changes preserving the knot type. The result bounds the length of a successful route; it does not identify which route to choose efficiently. Enumerating a branching collection of polynomial-length routes can still take exponential time.

In 2021, Lackenby announced an algorithm with quasipolynomial running time. The SoCG 2025 source still describes this as an announcement, and the checked author webpage lists talks on it. I retain that attribution rather than presenting a fully checked published proof. Quasipolynomial time, of the form exp((log N)^{O(1)}), can be much smaller than exponential time while remaining above a fixed polynomial bound.

Practical algorithms illustrate a different kind of progress. He, Sedgwick and Spreer’s SoCG 2025 paper builds knot factorisation machinery around edge-ideal triangulations and normal-surface crushing. Their introduction notes that Regina’s unknot-recognition implementation behaves polynomially in experiments but has an exponential worst-case bound. Strong performance on a census or on difficult examples is useful evidence for implementation design, without controlling every possible input diagram.

Lackenby’s July 2026 preprint gives a new algorithm through incompressible surfaces and hierarchies. For a nontrivial knot, the boundary of its exterior is incompressible; for the unknot it is compressible. This turns knot recognition into a question about surfaces in a 3-manifold. The paper’s Section 9 explicitly leaves key hierarchy-length and surface-complexity parameters unbounded in terms of the input, so it does not establish polynomial running time.

The central challenge is algorithmic control over global topology. A small diagram may hide the disk or decomposition that makes its type evident. Good certificates show that concise explanations exist; an efficient recognizer would show how to decide without searching an uncontrolled space of explanations. Any verified polynomial-time solution, including the new claimed one, would resolve a basic benchmark of computational topology and change how we understand this gap.
why: Determine whether triviality of an explicitly given knot can be decided efficiently, a foundational test of the gap between topological certificates and algorithms.
status_note: Musick’s 6 September 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time solution. Its correctness has not been independently established in this review, so the card is not labelled either a settled theorem or an unqualified open problem. Established certificates and earlier algorithmic results are distinguished from this new claim. Checked through 11 September 2026.
progress: 1997–1999: Hass–Lagarias–Pippenger prove NP membership using normal surfaces, with deterministic exponential-time algorithms; FOCS 1997, JACM 1999. | 2013–2015: Lackenby proves a polynomial bound on the number of Reidemeister moves needed to simplify an unknot, without a polynomial algorithm to find the sequence. | 2016–2021: Lackenby establishes unconditional NP certificates for knottedness, placing unknot recognition in coNP; journal publication 2021. | 2021: Lackenby announces quasipolynomial-time unknot recognition; retained as an announced result. | 2025: He–Sedgwick–Spreer present practical factorisation algorithms and explicitly distinguish empirical performance from worst-case polynomial unknot recognition. | 2026-07-25: Lackenby gives a new hierarchy-based recognition algorithm; its Section 9 does not establish polynomial input-size complexity. | 2026-09-06: Musick’s preprint claims polynomial-time recognition via locally minimal bridge presentations. This review has not independently validated the proof.
working_summary: Unknot recognition asks whether a closed loop represented by a finite crossing diagram can be deformed into a circle without cutting. A complicated drawing may still represent an unknot, so simplifying visible crossings is not a complete decision method. The target here is a deterministic algorithm whose bit complexity is polynomial in the diagram encoding. The saved card records a September 2026 preprint claiming such an algorithm, with its proof not independently validated. This description therefore preserves the uncertainty around that claim while explaining the computational target.

title: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture for edge-path diameter
importance_reason: The surviving fundamental diameter question after the original Hirsch bound failed; it separates geometric existence of short routes from algorithmic navigation and the newly resolved circuit analogue.
focus_reason: The surviving fundamental diameter question after the original Hirsch bound failed; it separates geometric existence of short routes from algorithmic navigation and the newly resolved circuit analogue.
formal: Do universal constants C>0 and k≥1 exist such that every nonempty pointed d-dimensional convex polyhedron with n facets has vertex-edge graph diameter at most C(n+d)^k?
definitions: A polyhedron is an intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces over the real numbers. Work in its affine hull, identified with R^d, where d≥1, and require it to be pointed, meaning that it contains no affine line; this ensures that its vertices are present. Both bounded polyhedra, called polytopes, and unbounded pointed polyhedra are included. The number n counts distinct facets in an irredundant description, rather than repeated input inequalities. The graph G(P) has one vertex per geometric vertex of P and an undirected edge between u and v precisely when their segment is a bounded one-dimensional face of P. An unbounded ray is not an extra graph vertex or an edge to infinity. Graph distance counts edges, each at unit cost; diameter is the maximum distance between vertices and is zero for a one-vertex polyhedron. context:
The feasible region of a linear program is a polyhedron. Its vertices are candidate basic feasible solutions, and its edges describe elementary geometric moves between them. The diameter asks for the largest minimum number of such moves between any two vertices. It is therefore a question about the geometry of feasible solutions before one chooses a particular rule for navigating them.

The facet count is the relevant measure of description size here. A polyhedron described by a modest number of inequalities can have exponentially many vertices, so the trivial bound by the number of vertices is far too large. The d-dimensional cube illustrates the distinction: it has 2d facets and 2^d vertices, yet its diameter is only d because one can change differing coordinates one at a time.

Polynomial means a fixed exponent that works in every dimension. An n^d upper bound is polynomial in n when d is held fixed, but does not answer this question. Neither does a bound whose constant grows exponentially with d. The card includes pointed unbounded polyhedra, matching the saved formulation; pointedness removes polyhedra with no vertices, for which a vertex-graph diameter would not express the intended problem.

Hirsch originally proposed the much sharper n−d bound for bounded polytopes. Santos’s counterexample, announced in 2010 and published in 2012, has dimension 43 and 86 facets, with diameter exceeding 43. This refutes that linear expression, but it remains fully compatible with a bound such as Cn² or Cn¹⁰. The distinction between failure of one attractive formula and failure of every polynomial is the reason a major open question survived.

General upper bounds are quasipolynomial. Kalai and Kleitman’s 1992 argument gave n^{2+log₂d}; Todd improved it in 2014 to (n−d)^{log₂d}. For large d, Sukegawa’s later asymptotic refinement has the form (n−d)^{log₂d−log₂log d+O(1)}. The last exponent still grows with dimension. These are substantial structural bounds, but they do not reach one universal constant exponent.

The conjecture concerns shortest available paths, not the paths a chosen simplex pivot rule happens to take. A rule may visit exponentially many vertices even on a polytope whose graph has small diameter. Conversely, proving that short undirected paths exist would not tell a solver which edge to select efficiently, or ensure a short path that improves a specified linear objective at every step. Polynomial diameter is a geometric ingredient, not by itself a strongly polynomial linear-programming algorithm.

Recent complexity results make the distinction sharper. Wulf’s FOCS 2025 paper proves Π₂^p-hardness of computing the diameter of bipartite perfect-matching polytopes, and the corresponding decision problem is complete for that class. Such hardness is compatible with a polynomial upper bound on the value of the diameter. A small optimum can be difficult to compute exactly, just as short witnesses can be difficult to find.

Natura’s February 2026 paper proves a polynomial bound for a different geometric distance: circuit diameter. For a standard-form polyhedron {x∈R^N:Ax=b,x≥0}, with A having r rows, the stated bound is O(r²log r), and the construction also supplies monotone circuit walks. Circuit directions are support-minimal dependencies of A; a maximal feasible step in such a direction need not stay on an edge of the current polyhedron.

Every edge step is allowed among the circuit moves, but the converse fails. Consequently, a short circuit walk gives no automatic equally short edge walk: its intermediate points may lie inside higher-dimensional faces. The 2026 theorem settles the circuit analogue of the polynomial conjecture, while its introduction explicitly retains the ordinary combinatorial-diameter problem. The distinction is geometric, not a question of hiding logarithmic factors.

Other positive results exploit extra structure, such as totally unimodular constraint matrices or numerical bounds on subdeterminants. Those assumptions control features absent from the unrestricted statement. Random-polytope and smoothed analyses likewise describe particular distributions or perturbations; a worst-case theorem must include every allowed realization. This is why the model specifies arbitrary coefficients and requires constants independent of their encoding.

A positive resolution would reveal a universal short-route property of all polyhedral feasible regions, despite their potentially enormous vertex sets. A negative resolution would produce polyhedra on which every route between some vertices is intrinsically long. Both outcomes would identify a basic geometric limit underlying pivot-based optimization, independently of the performance of any individual implementation.

title: How many k-element subsets can a line separate from a planar point set?
importance_reason: A defining extremal-complexity question for geometric algorithms, already unresolved in the plane and connected to levels, geometric selection, and parametric optimization.
focus_reason: A defining extremal-complexity question for geometric algorithms, already unresolved in the plane and connected to levels, geometric selection, and parametric optimization.
formal: Let K₂(n,k) be the maximum, over sets P of n distinct points in $\mathbb R^2$ with no three collinear, of the number of distinct subsets S⊆P of size k strictly separable from P\S by a line. Determine K₂(n,k) up to universal constant factors, uniformly for all integers n≥2 and 1≤k≤⌊n/2⌋.
definitions: Strict separation means that there are real a,b,c with (a,b)≠(0,0), ax+by<c for every (x,y)∈S, and ax+by>c for every (x,y)∈P\S. The objects counted are subsets S, not their infinitely many possible separating lines. Coordinates have no bounded-precision, grid, or random-distribution promise. The target is worst-case combinatorial complexity, not the running time of an enumeration algorithm. A matching bound means an asymptotic expression F(n,k) and absolute constants 0<c₀≤C₀<∞ such that c₀F(n,k)≤K₂(n,k)≤C₀F(n,k) throughout the stated range, apart from finitely many n which can be absorbed into the constants. Bounds must cover k that grows with n. Complementation supplies the remaining values n/2<k<n; k=0,n each have one subset. This card specializes the original all-dimensions problem to the plane.

context:
A line can realize only a small fraction of all choices of k points. The question measures the combinatorial capacity of one linear cut at a fixed output size. For example, when k=1 the separable points are the convex-hull vertices, and their maximum number is n. The difficult regime lets k increase with the input size.

Point-line duality translates changes of a separating line into the structure of levels in a line arrangement. A level tracks positions having a specified number of lines below them. These level bounds recur in geometric selection and in analyses of parametric optimization. Dey’s method also yields bounds for related level structures, convex chains, and parametric spanning-tree problems.

For even n, the balanced case is closely tied to halving edges: segments joining two input points whose supporting line leaves (n−2)/2 of the other points on each side. A halving edge is not itself a separating line, since it passes through input points. The correspondence between k-sets and directed (k−1)-edges gives K₂(n,n/2) equal to twice the maximum number of undirected halving edges.

The known planar upper bound is O(n k^(1/3)), whereas constructions give n exp(Ω(√log k)) subsets. In the balanced regime the latter grows faster than n times any fixed power of log n, yet slower than n^(1+ε) for each fixed ε>0. Thus neither a linear bound nor an ordinary polylogarithmic correction to linear growth can describe the worst case.

Sharper finite-size constructions and improvements to the additive terms of halving-line bounds are useful progress. They do not close the gap in asymptotic growth. Keeping this distinction explicit matters here: an improved upper bound may retain the same 4/3 exponent in the balanced case.
why: A central unresolved counting problem in computational geometry, it controls the complexity of levels and line-separated ranges. Its persistent gap tests the strength of crossing-number methods and geometric constructions, with consequences for output-sensitive and parametric algorithms.
status_note: The June 2025 problem entry retains the gap. The 2024 halving-line improvement changes lower-order terms rather than the exponent. No matching asymptotic bound was located in the status search through 10 September 2026.
progress: 1997–1998: Dey proves K₂(n,k)=O(n k^(1/3)) for 1≤k≤n/2 through a crossing-number argument. The balanced specialization gives an O(n^(4/3)) upper bound. | 2000–2001: Tóth constructs planar point sets with n exp(Ω(√log k)) k-sets for n≥2k>0, improving the earlier n log k scale. This remains separated from the upper bound by an unbounded factor when k grows. | 2008: Nivasch gives a simpler halving-edge construction improving the constant in the square-root-log exponent. The asymptotic upper exponent remains 4/3. | 2025-06: The revised Open Problems Project entry still lists the planar asymptotic gap as unresolved. A search through September 2026 did not locate matching general upper and lower bounds.
working_summary: A k-set is a selection of k points that a line strictly separates from all remaining points of a planar configuration. The problem asks for the largest possible number of distinct k-sets among n points in general position. The desired estimate must remain sharp when k grows with n, including nearly balanced cuts. Duality turns this into a question about levels in arrangements of lines. Closing the gap between constructions and upper bounds would clarify the complexity of geometric selection and related optimization problems.

title: Hill’s conjecture for the crossing number of complete graphs
importance_reason: A foundational exact extremal problem for the most symmetric dense graph family. It tests the reach of general crossing-number lower bounds beyond drawing classes constrained by a particular geometry.
formal: For every integer n≥3, is the minimum number of edge crossings in a drawing of the complete graph K_n in the plane exactly $H(n)=\frac14\prod_{i=0}^{3}\left\lfloor\frac{n-i}{2}\right\rfloor$? Edges may be arbitrary simple curves. Drawings with H(n) crossings are known for every n; the unresolved assertion is that no drawing has fewer.
definitions: K_n has n vertices and one edge between each pair of distinct vertices. A drawing assigns distinct points of ℝ² to its vertices and represents each edge by a simple arc joining its endpoints, with no other vertex on the arc. Edge interiors intersect in finitely many points, all proper crossings; tangencies, shared subarcs and crossings of three or more edge interiors are excluded. Count intersection points of edge interiors, not shared graph endpoints. The crossing number cr(K_n) is the minimum over all these drawings and all vertex placements. Finite polygonal arcs suffice; restricting every edge to a single straight segment is a different problem. Allowing drawings on the sphere with arbitrary arcs gives the same minimum. H(n)=n⁴/64+O(n³), but the card asks for exact equality at every n, not just agreement of leading coefficients. For example H(5)=1, H(6)=3, H(12)=150 and H(13)=225.
answer_criterion: Prove cr(K_n)≥H(n) for every n, or exhibit one valid drawing of some K_n with strictly fewer than H(n) crossings. An asymptotic ratio of 1 would settle only the asymptotic version; a lower bound for straight-line, two-page, or shortest-geodesic drawings does not by itself settle arbitrary drawings.
context:
A complete graph asks every pair of vertices to communicate through a separate drawn edge. Planarity fails already at five vertices. The conjecture proposes an exact measure of the unavoidable interference as the number of vertices grows, independent of the choice of drawing coordinates or the shape of each edge.

The upper bound is constructive: there are systematic drawings with H(n) crossings. The challenge is universal. A lower bound must rule out every different way to route the edges, including configurations whose geometry bears little resemblance to the known constructions. Counting crossings in a visually natural drawing establishes only the upper bound.

The topological and geometric versions must be separated. Straight-line edges impose extra restrictions; shortest arcs on a sphere allow more freedom but still impose a geometric rule. Two-page drawings impose another rule: vertices lie on one spine and each edge stays on one of its two sides. Proving the formula for any of these families narrows the search for a counterexample without exhausting arbitrary curves.

General lower bounds are already close to the conjectured leading term. The flag-algebra approach derives inequalities from the frequencies and compatibility of small drawing configurations. Even a remaining gap of roughly one or two percent matters here: the goal is an exact extremal formula for all sizes, rather than a constant-factor estimate.

The April 2025 spherical-arc theorem is a substantial geometric advance: it establishes the conjectured lower bound for every shortest-geodesic drawing on the sphere. Its statement does not say that an optimal unrestricted drawing must be of this type. That missing reduction is why the original question remains open.
why: This is a basic benchmark for universal crossing lower bounds. Its study links topological graph drawing, geometric configurations, and extremal counting methods, and supplies a reference family against which crossing inequalities for more general graphs are compared.
status_note: The April 2025 primary paper explicitly leaves arbitrary drawings unresolved while proving the spherical-arc case. No general proof or counterexample located through 10 September 2026. Restricted drawing-class results are not treated as full resolutions.

The general assertion that these are optimal became the Hill or Harary–Hill conjecture, also known as Guy’s conjecture. | 2012: Ábrego, Aichholzer, Fernández-Merchant, Ramos, and Salazar prove that the two-page crossing number of K_n equals H(n). The unrestricted crossing number minimizes over a larger drawing class. | 2019: Balogh, Lidický, and Salazar use flag algebras to show an asymptotic general lower bound of at least 0.985H(n). This substantially improves the earlier general asymptotic ratio, while leaving a positive gap from the conjectured value. | 2025-01: The Gasarch–Hayes–Ostuni–Park column states the unrestricted formula as Conjecture 4.6. The linked manuscript is dated 4 January 2025, correcting the legacy record’s 2022 source year. | 2025-04: Streltsova and Wagner prove the lower bound H(n) for all spherical shortest-geodesic drawings, with equality for coneighborly configurations. Their introduction still lists the unrestricted conjecture as open and verified through n=12.

Vertices may be placed freely and edges may curve, so the task ranges over much more than straight-line drawings. The conjecture seeks an exact measure of unavoidable interference in the densest possible simple graph.

title: Can four-sided skyline reporting match ordinary range reporting?
importance_reason: Asks whether dominance among reported points imposes a genuine extra cost beyond orthogonal reporting; a clean geometric data-structure boundary.

A point is on the skyline if no other point in the query rectangle is at least as large in both coordinates and strictly larger in one.
definitions:
Coordinates are already in rank space; this avoids hiding a separate predecessor-search cost for a larger universe. The set is static. Space is measured in machine words, not bits. The factor $\log^{O(1)}N$ has a fixed exponent. The output parameter $k$ is query-dependent, and no scan of all of $P\cap Q$ is allowed unless its cost fits the stated bound.

The target is deterministic exact reporting with polynomial preprocessing time, using the usual word-RAM operations: arithmetic, multiplication, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of words.
answer_criterion: Construct a data structure meeting both the stated space bound and worst-case reporting bound for every point set and rectangle, or prove that these bounds cannot be achieved together in the specified model.
context:
Think of records scored on two attributes, with larger values preferred. A range filter first selects the eligible records; the skyline then removes options that are worse on both attributes. Therefore, storing only the global skyline loses information needed for later queries.

The output can be much smaller than the number of points inside the rectangle. If a rectangle contains thousands of points and one dominates all others, the requested bound permits only $O(\log\log N)$ time beyond outputting that one point. Reporting every point and filtering afterward cannot meet it. The data structure must skip large dominated regions without paying for their contents.

Counting and reporting have different targets. Four-sided skyline counting needs $\Omega(\log N/\log\log N)$ query time at near-linear space. The known reporting upper bound pays the same logarithmic overhead as counting, plus the output size.

working_summary: A unit-disk or unit-square intersection graph represents equal-size geometric objects, joining two vertices when their objects overlap. A maximum matching pairs as many objects as possible through intersections without using any object twice. The source asks whether such a matching can be computed in near-linear time from the geometric representation. The graph may have quadratically many edges, so explicitly listing all intersections would already defeat this target. The challenge is to exploit geometry while still finding an exact optimum, extending geometric speedups beyond merely detecting an intersecting pair or constructing a large approximate matching.

working_summary: A subspace embedding compresses a matrix while approximately preserving the Euclidean norm of every vector in its column space. The source conjectures an embedding dimension proportional to dimension plus logarithmic inverse failure probability, divided by accuracy squared. At the same time, multiplying by the embedding should take input-sparsity time with only the specified logarithmic and inverse-accuracy overhead. The two requirements must hold together, since a small sketch can still be expensive to construct. Such a construction would improve the foundational compression step used by fast regression and other numerical linear-algebra algorithms.

title: Does every VC class admit linear-size sample compression?
importance_reason: A longstanding general conjecture asking whether VC dimension controls sample representation up to a constant factor; it reaches far beyond any one learning algorithm or geometric example.
focus_reason: A longstanding general conjecture asking whether VC dimension controls sample representation up to a constant factor; it reaches far beyond any one learning algorithm or geometric example.
formal: Is there a universal constant C such that every nonempty binary concept class H⊆{0,1}^X of finite VC dimension d≥1 admits a labeled sample compression scheme with kernel bound k and side-information bound b satisfying k+b≤Cd, in the model below? The same compressor and reconstructor must work for every finite H-realizable sample, independently of its size.
definitions: The domain X is an arbitrary set, and a concept h∈H is a total function X→{0,1}. A finite set A⊆X is shattered if {h|_A:h∈H}={0,1}^A; d is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A realizable sample is a finite set S⊆X×{0,1} agreeing with some h∈H. A scheme consists of deterministic maps κ and ρ, which may depend on H, and nonnegative integers k,b. For every realizable S, κ(S)=(T,z), where T⊆S is an unordered labeled subset with |T|≤k and z∈{0,1}^b. The reconstructor receives only T and z and produces a total predictor ρ(T,z):X→{0,1} agreeing with every pair in S. It does not receive S, its size, the omitted points, or their indices. The side string has fixed length b; padding shorter strings changes only constant-factor size conventions. Reconstruction need not lie in H, be stable under deleting unused examples, or have any prescribed computational complexity. No probability distribution, efficiency, or measurability condition is part of this combinatorial existence question. Dimension zero is harmless: a nonempty such class has one labeling and needs no stored examples.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The stored object is a small selection of examples that lets a fixed decoding rule recover every training label. It need not identify the unknown target function on points never observed. For example, consider indicators of closed intervals on the real line. Retain the leftmost and rightmost positive examples, or the empty set if there are no positives. Decode to the interval between those retained points, or to the all-zero function in the empty case. Realizability ensures that no negative example lies between the extreme positives. Thus an arbitrarily large sample can be represented by at most two examples.

The distinction between examples and bits is essential. A real-valued example may itself require arbitrarily many bits to describe; sample compression charges one unit for retaining it. Conversely, permitting an arbitrary uncharged side message would trivialize the problem, because that message could encode the whole sample. The fixed reconstructor and the explicit bound b prevent this loophole. The question concerns the combinatorial information carried by selected observations, rather than ordinary lossless compression of their numerical representations.

Moran and Yehudayoff proved that every finite-VC binary class has a scheme of size 2^{O(d)}, settling the earlier existence question. Their argument combines learning with an approximate minimax principle. More precisely, their bound also involves the dual VC dimension: this reverses the roles of domain points and concepts, treating each point as its pattern of membership across the concepts. Since the dual dimension can be exponential in d, that result leaves a substantial quantitative gap. Their corrected 2015 version retains the binary theorem while withdrawing an erroneous multiclass extension.

A studied auxiliary question asks whether each class embeds in an extremal class of comparable VC dimension. Chase and coauthors show that such embeddings can require an exponential increase in dimension. Their COLT 2024 result rules out that general route to a linear bound; it does not show that the original class itself needs exponential compression. A failed intermediate representation is different from a lower bound against every compressor.

The problem also has concrete graph instances. Fix a graph and label sampled vertices according to membership in an unknown metric ball. Bourneuf and coauthors give proper schemes of size O(t log(t+1)) when the graph has treewidth at most t, and an analogous bound for cliquewidth. Proper means that decoding produces another ball, a stronger requirement than this card imposes. Their April 2026 work supplies structured examples and explicitly leaves the general linear-VC conjecture open.

Attias, Hanneke, and Ramaswami show how binary compression results transfer to multiclass, regression, and robust-learning settings, with additional factors or additional requirements on the binary scheme. Consequently, a solution could have consequences beyond binary prediction, but those transfers have hypotheses. In particular, their Open Problem 28 is about adversarially robust compression; the standard conjecture used here appears in their introduction.
why: A central question connecting the combinatorial complexity of prediction with how many observations suffice to represent all training decisions. Its universality across concept classes, and its links to learning, extremal set systems and graph geometry, make the linear-versus-exponential gap fundamental.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The general linear bound remains open in the primary sources checked. The 2026 graph-ball theorems concern structured classes. The claimed breakthrough at arXiv:2603.23561 is withdrawn and is included only to document its status. This card fixes labeled, possibly improper, unordered-subset compression with all side bits counted.

working_summary: Sample compression represents a labeled training set by retaining only a few examples and a bounded amount of extra information. A fixed reconstruction rule must recover a hypothesis agreeing with every original training label whenever the sample is realizable. This project asks whether every binary class of VC dimension d admits a scheme whose total charged size is proportional to d. The question concerns the number of retained examples and side-information bits, not the ordinary bit length of the examples themselves. A linear bound would connect the statistical capacity measured by VC dimension with a comparably small combinatorial explanation of every realizable sample.

title: Polynomial-time learning parity with constant random noise
importance_reason: A fundamental boundary between information-theoretic learnability and efficient learning, with broad consequences for noise-tolerant algorithms and cryptographic assumptions.
focus_reason: A fundamental boundary between information-theoretic learnability and efficient learning, with broad consequences for noise-tolerant algorithms and cryptographic assumptions.
formal: For every fixed rational noise rate η with 0<η<1/2, does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every n and every secret s∈{0,1}^n, recovers s with probability at least 2/3 from independent samples (a,⟨a,s⟩⊕e), where a is uniform in {0,1}^n and e is independently Bernoulli(η)?
definitions: The inner product ⟨a,s⟩ is Σ_i a_i s_i modulo two, and ⊕ is addition modulo two. The unknown s is fixed throughout an execution. Each requested sample uses a fresh independent uniform vector a and an independent error bit e, with Pr[e=1]=η. The learner knows n and the fixed rate η, and receives only classical samples. It cannot choose a, request a noiseless label, identify which labels were corrupted, or make coherent quantum queries. For each fixed η the algorithm and its polynomial bound pη may depend on η, but they must be uniform in n, without advice. Every execution uses at most pη(n) bit operations and requests at most pη(n) samples; reading and storing samples is charged. Polynomially many stored bits and repeated access to stored samples are allowed. The success probability is over the example generator and the learner’s random coins, for each fixed s. The desired output is the entire secret vector, not merely a predictor with unspecified advantage. No sparsity promise is imposed on s or on a. The quantifier over fixed rational η does not demand a running-time bound uniform as η approaches 1/2 with n.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A parity function is among the simplest algebraic classifiers: choose a hidden subset of coordinates and return their XOR. Without label noise, sufficiently many random examples give linear equations, and Gaussian elimination recovers the secret with high probability. Independent noise changes the task from solving a consistent system to identifying which apparent equations should be trusted. Ordinary elimination mixes error bits along with the equations, so its usual exactness argument no longer applies.

The difficulty is computational rather than a lack of information. For a fixed noise rate below one half, the true secret agrees with a fresh label with probability 1−η. Every other secret agrees with probability one half under the uniform distribution on inputs. With a sufficiently large constant multiple of n examples, concentration and a union bound over the 2^n candidates identify the true secret with high probability. Exhaustively testing those candidates takes exponential time, leaving open whether their search can be avoided.

At η=1/4, for example, the correct candidate has expected agreement 3/4, while every incorrect parity has expected agreement 1/2. A threshold strictly between these values separates them once enough independent samples have been collected. This simple gap explains why a polynomial sample bound alone is not the desired breakthrough. One must locate the exceptional candidate efficiently among exponentially many possibilities.

Writing the sample vectors as rows of a matrix A gives b=As+e over the binary field. The columns of A generate a random linear code, and the task becomes decoding a random noisy codeword. This connection explains the relevance to cryptography. It does not turn a worst-case NP-hardness theorem for decoding arbitrary codes into an average-case hardness theorem for the random distribution used here. Quantifiers over matrices, errors and sample counts have to survive the reduction.

Blum, Kalai and Wasserman give a 2^{O(n/log n)}-time algorithm using a comparable subexponential number of examples for constant noise. Combining examples cancels blocks of coordinates, while the analysis controls how the combined noise approaches a fair coin. Their work also separates noise-tolerant learning from the statistical-query framework in an appropriate restricted parity regime. Thus failure of statistical-query methods cannot simply be interpreted as failure of all algorithms with access to individual examples.

Lyubashevsky answers a different sample-efficiency question: subexponential computation is possible using only n^{1+ε} examples for each fixed ε>0. The resulting running time is 2^{O(n/log log n)}. This result is directly relevant to a learner that can collect only polynomially many samples, but its time bound is still superpolynomial. Keeping the two resources visible prevents the better exponent of the many-sample algorithm from being quoted as a polynomial-sample guarantee.

There are substantial unconditional lower bounds in restricted resource models. Garg, Kothari, Liu and Raz show that a streaming learner needs either Ω(n²/(1/2−η)) bits of memory or exponentially many samples, with a strong success-probability guarantee in their theorem. For fixed η, the memory alternative is quadratic, which is permitted by the polynomial-time question. This establishes a real storage cost without ruling out a general polynomial-time algorithm.

Aggarwal, Gupta and Zeyong’s May 2026 hardness amplification relates success on a small fraction of instances to success on almost all instances after changing the dimension and noise parameters. Aggarwal and coauthors’ September 8 revision gives low-noise LPN hardness under simultaneous worst-case assumptions concerning decoding a code and distinguishing noisy codewords of its dual. These strengthen the understanding of hardness assumptions; neither is an unconditional proof that this learner cannot exist.

The every-secret guarantee is not an artificial extra obstacle compared with a uniform random secret. A learner can choose a uniform mask r, replace each label b by b⊕⟨a,r⟩, learn the masked secret s⊕r and remove the mask. The transformed secret is uniform while the noise law is unchanged. The central uncertainty therefore persists even when randomness in the hidden parity itself is supplied for free.
why: A canonical computational learning problem where a tiny amount of independent label noise defeats the obvious algebraic method, connecting efficient learning, random-code decoding and cryptographic hardness.
status_note: The primary literature checked through 11 September 2026 leaves classical polynomial-time learning at fixed constant noise open. The card asks for all fixed rational rates separately, allowing rate-dependent polynomial bounds. The September 2026 reduction is conditional; sparse, quantum-example and limited-memory models do not replace the specified problem.

working_summary: A parity function returns the XOR of a hidden subset of input coordinates. Without label noise, random examples produce linear equations that reveal the hidden subset efficiently. This project asks whether a polynomial-time classical algorithm can still recover it when each label is independently flipped at a fixed rate below one half. Polynomially many samples contain enough information, but searching all candidate subsets takes exponential time. An efficient learner must avoid that search using only ordinary random examples, without chosen noiseless queries or restrictions that make the unknown subset sparse.

title: Learning Boolean juntas from uniform random examples
importance_reason: A central unresolved task in computational learning theory, isolating feature selection and serving as a prerequisite for efficient learning of general decision trees and DNF formulas.
focus_reason: A central unresolved task in computational learning theory, isolating feature selection and serving as a prerequisite for efficient learning of general decision trees and DNF formulas.
formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that learns every Boolean k-junta on n variables from independent uniform random labelled examples in time polynomial in n, 2^k and 1/ε, with uniform-distribution error at most ε and success probability at least 2/3?
definitions: For integers 0≤k≤n, a k-junta is a function f:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1} for which there is an unknown set S⊆{1,…,n}, |S|≤k, and an arbitrary Boolean function g on |S| bits such that f(x)=g(x restricted to S). The learner receives n,k and a positive integer t≥3, setting ε=1/t. Each requested example consists of an independently uniform x∈{0,1}ⁿ and its exact, noiseless label f(x). The learner may request further independent examples, but cannot choose inputs to be labelled or obtain correlated examples. The output is a finite Boolean circuit h on n input bits; it need not itself be a k-junta. With probability at least 2/3 over all examples and internal random bits, Pr over a fresh uniform x that h(x)≠f(x) is at most 1/t. One fixed classical probabilistic Turing machine must run, on every sample and random tape, for at most (n+2^k+t)^C steps, up to a fixed multiplicative constant, for a universal constant C independent of n,k,t,f. Reading examples, computation and writing the circuit count toward this bound. Restricting ε to reciprocal integers is equivalent, up to polynomial factors, to the usual arbitrary-accuracy requirement.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A junta is a model of prediction with many irrelevant features. The target may use only a small hidden subset of a very long input, but its behaviour on those relevant features is unrestricted. The goal is accurate prediction on a new uniform input. Identifying the support exactly is not required: variables that affect too little probability mass may be ignored at the requested accuracy.

The allowance of 2^k is deliberate. An arbitrary function on the relevant coordinates can have a truth table with 2^k entries, so a polynomial dependence on that quantity accommodates the complexity of the target itself. The desired improvement is in locating useful coordinates among n possibilities. For k proportional to log n, the proposed bound would give polynomial-time learning. Brute-force support enumeration has about n^k possibilities and becomes quasipolynomial in that regime.

The sample requirement already fits the target. There are at most (k+1)n^k·2^{2^k} juntas on n variables. A union bound shows that O((2^k+k log(n+1)+log(k+1)+1)/ε) independent examples suffice for every consistent hypothesis in this finite class to have error at most ε, with constant confidence. Such a hypothesis exists because the labels come from a junta. The difficulty is finding it efficiently; enumerating supports and filling their truth tables gives a direct but expensive method.

Mossel, O’Donnell and Servedio obtained the first constant-factor improvement in the exponent of this search. Their algorithm combines structural information about Boolean functions with algebraic computation and learns exactly in approximately n^{0.704k}·poly(n,2^k) time at the matrix-multiplication exponent used in the paper. This is an algorithm for arbitrary juntas from uniform random examples, so it addresses the same access model.

Gregory Valiant subsequently improved the exponent to below 0.6k, with polynomial factors in n and 2^k, through algorithms for finding correlations and learning sparse parities with noise. His argument combines a noise-robust parity learner with the junta structure used in earlier work. The approximately n^{0.6k} benchmark is still stated in Servedio’s November 2025 survey. It is a major improvement over exhaustive search, but the exponent on the ambient dimension still grows with k.

Simple correlation screening is insufficient. For example, f(x)=x₁ XOR x₂ XOR x₃ is independent of each individual input bit under the uniform distribution, although all three are relevant. This does not make noiseless parity computationally hard: one can learn an unknown parity by solving linear equations over the two-element field. It explains why a limitation of low-order correlations or statistical queries cannot automatically be converted into a lower bound for every algorithm using actual examples.

Membership queries change the task substantially. They allow the learner to choose an input and ask for its label, making it possible to isolate relevant variables by carefully comparing nearby points. Learning juntas in polynomial time in n and 2^k is known with this additional access. Servedio’s survey also notes that monotone juntas admit the desired bound from ordinary uniform examples; arbitrary juntas need not expose their variables through such first-order information.

The phrase “learning junta distributions” describes another problem: recovering a probability mass function that depends on a small coordinate set. Beretta’s RANDOM 2025 paper relates that distribution-learning task to learning sparse parities with noise. Its introduction explicitly distinguishes noiseless Boolean junta learning and reports the existing n^{0.6k} benchmark. An equivalence for distribution learning is not an unconditional lower bound for the noiseless prediction task here.

Cornacchia, Mikulincer and Mossel show in May 2026 that a suitable neural-network training procedure can learn juntas efficiently from a lazy random walk on the hypercube, with essentially linear sample complexity in ambient dimension for each fixed k. Their loss uses differences between consecutive samples. Even if each sample has a uniform marginal distribution, consecutive samples are correlated; an independent-example oracle does not provide those labelled neighbouring points. This result therefore leaves the present question intact.

The problem is a gateway to learning richer representations. A k-junta has both a decision tree and a DNF representation of size at most 2^k. Efficient uniform-example learners for those general classes would consequently learn juntas within the requested resource bound. A positive result here would solve a central obstacle, while a negative result for unrestricted learners would explain a computational limitation of feature selection even under a particularly simple input distribution.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 17.9, the source inherited as TCS-0023, concerns the class F_k of functions depending on at most k input bits. The old catalogue title incorrectly described it as growing-size DNF learning. Its challenge is to go beyond constant support size with polynomial-time learning, or justify a hardness assumption. This card retains the precise stronger target poly(n,2^k,1/ε) for every k. A positive answer supplies polynomial time when k=O(log n); a learner for only one slower-growing support regime need not meet the full target. Conditional hardness allowed as an outcome in the source is also weaker than an unconditional negative answer here. The source record is consolidated as a related milestone, not asserted to be an equivalent formulation; TCS-0023 preserves its own ID and bibliography as a retired pointer.
why: Determine whether arbitrary dependence on a small hidden set of variables can be learned efficiently from ordinary observations, separating computational search from sample sufficiency.
status_note: No general learner with the stated polynomial dependence, or impossibility theorem for unrestricted learners, was found through 11 September 2026. Current sources retain the uniform-example barrier. Efficient membership-query, monotone-junta and correlated-random-walk results do not meet this exact model.
