title: Do one-way functions imply classical key agreement?
importance_reason: A foundational boundary between symmetric cryptographic hardness and secret establishment through public interaction. Distinct from the existing stronger PKE-from-OWF target, and supported by a long research line on black-box barriers.
formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical two-party key-agreement protocol with negligible disagreement and computationally secret shared keys, against passive probabilistic polynomial-time eavesdroppers, in the plain public-channel model defined below?
definitions: All algorithms are uniform classical probabilistic Turing machines; security parameter λ is supplied in unary. A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that, for every probabilistic polynomial-time I, Pr[f(Y)=f(X) and |Y|=λ] is negligible in λ, where X is uniform in {0,1}^λ and Y is the single output of I(1^λ,f(X)); probability also includes I’s private coins. A function μ:N→[0,1] is negligible if for every integer d≥1 there is λ₀ such that μ(λ)≤λ^(−d) for all λ≥λ₀. The protocol consists of two interactive machines A,B with independent private fair coins and total worst-case computation and communication polynomial in λ. They exchange classical messages on a noiseless public channel, with no correlated initial secrets, trusted setup, random oracle or quantum communication. At termination each outputs a λ-bit string K_A,K_B. Correctness requires Pr[K_A≠K_B] to be negligible. Let T be the full public transcript, and let U_λ be an independent uniform λ-bit string. For every probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D, |Pr[D(1^λ,T,K_A)=1]−Pr[D(1^λ,T,U_λ)=1]| must be negligible, over the honest coins, D’s coins and U_λ. The eavesdropper observes T but does not alter the messages. The target is the unrelativized existence implication; neither the construction nor its proof is required to treat f as a black box. Both premise and conclusion use the same uniform adversary convention.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
context:
A one-way function supplies a computational asymmetry: evaluating it is easy, while recovering a preimage of a random image is hard. Key agreement asks for a different capability. Two parties begin without a common secret and exchange visible messages, yet their final common key must remain hidden from an observer. The question is whether the first kind of asymmetry always suffices for the second.

The security definition concerns the entire transcript. Merely showing that a transcript has many possible explanations is insufficient if an efficient observer can identify the common key. Likewise, keeping each party’s private randomness hidden is weaker than hiding the particular string on which both parties agree. Comparing the actual key with an independent uniform key makes the secrecy requirement explicit.

Impagliazzo and Rudich established a black-box barrier between one-way functions and key agreement. Couteau, Farshim and Mahmoody’s 2021 work studies stronger notions of black-box uselessness and proves results for specified restricted settings. Such results delimit families of constructions; they do not refute the unrestricted existence implication on this card.

The existing TCS-6545 asks for public-key encryption from one-way functions. Public-key encryption would yield a key-agreement protocol by sending a fresh random key under the published encryption key. General interactive key agreement is a separate, weaker desired primitive. A negative conclusion about a restricted encryption construction cannot by itself rule out all interactive protocols.

The classical and passive conventions matter. Quantum key distribution uses an additional communication resource, while protection against an active man-in-the-middle requires an authentication model. Neither is part of this target. The card isolates the foundational question of creating a secret by classical public interaction from the minimal generic computational assumption.
why: Determine whether generic one-wayness is enough to establish a shared classical secret without prior shared randomness or setup.
status_note: No unrestricted classical construction or refutation was found in the primary-source checks through 11 September 2026. Black-box impossibility is not treated as a resolution of the unrelativized target.
progress: 1989: Impagliazzo–Rudich initiate black-box separations of key agreement from one-way functions. | 2021: Black-box uselessness results address particular key-agreement settings and leave the unrestricted implication separate.

title: Does public-key encryption imply oblivious transfer?
importance_reason: A foundational comparison between ordinary public-key confidentiality and a primitive complete for secure computation; resolving it would change which assumptions suffice for a broad range of protocols.
formal: In the classical plain model, does the existence of an IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption scheme for bits imply the existence of a polynomial-time 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious-transfer protocol secure against static semi-honest corruption of either party? Both primitives have negligible error and computational security as defined below. The implication may use arbitrary non-black-box techniques and a polynomial number of communication rounds.
definitions: The security parameter is λ, supplied in unary. Honest algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines; adversarial distinguishers are polynomial-size classical circuit families. A function μ is negligible if for every c>0, μ(λ)<λ^(−c) for all sufficiently large λ. Public-key encryption consists of KeyGen(1^λ)=(pk,sk), Enc(pk,m;r), and Dec(sk,c), for m∈{0,1}; decryption fails with negligible probability over key generation and encryption coins, for each m. IND-CPA means that no such adversary given pk distinguishes Enc(pk,0) from Enc(pk,1) with nonnegligible advantage; public encryption is available to it. In OT, sender S has bits (m_0,m_1), receiver R has a choice bit c, and R must output m_c except with negligible probability for every input triple; S has no output. The parties follow their prescribed algorithms but keep their entire views, including inputs, random tapes, and messages. There must be uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulators Sim_S(1^λ,m_0,m_1) and Sim_R(1^λ,c,m_c) whose outputs are computationally indistinguishable from the corresponding real views for every sequence of input triples. Thus S learns nothing about c and R learns nothing beyond (c,m_c). The parties have independent private randomness and exchange classical messages directly. There is no trusted setup, common reference string, random oracle, pre-shared correlated randomness, trusted hardware, or quantum resource.
answer_criterion: Establish the stated existence implication without a second unproved hardness assumption, or refute that unrelativized implication. A construction may inspect and use the code of the encryption algorithms and use non-black-box security arguments. An oracle separation or a lower bound restricted to black-box reductions is a barrier, not a negative resolution of this question. A construction requiring an additional property of encryption must also derive that property from arbitrary IND-CPA encryption to settle the card.
context:
Ordinary encryption protects a message from someone who lacks the secret key. Oblivious transfer must arrange a more selective situation: the receiver can read one of two messages, cannot read the other, and does not disclose which one it selected. This combines privacy for both participants. Merely encrypting both messages under a key generated by the receiver fails, because that receiver can decrypt both ciphertexts. Asking the receiver to reveal which key it can decrypt would instead reveal its choice.

Some encryption schemes offer the missing structure. If a receiver can create two indistinguishable-looking public keys while knowing a decryption key for just one, it can place the decryptable key in position c. The sender encrypts the two messages under the corresponding keys. Such an argument needs a suitable oblivious-sampling property, including security even given the sampler’s retained randomness. Gertner and coauthors identify sufficient properties and also prove an oracle separation between general PKE and even semi-honest OT. Their historical separation uses uniform adversaries.

That result constrains a style of construction, rather than deciding the unrestricted implication. In an oracle argument all algorithms are given access to an additional idealized operation. A construction based on the actual implementation of an encryption scheme may use features that do not survive replacement by an arbitrary oracle. Consequently, the qualifier allowing non-black-box techniques is substantive; removing it would turn the card into a question already addressed by known barriers.

The semi-honest target is already powerful. Haitner, Ishai, Kushilevitz, Lindell, and Petrank show how to transform semi-honest OT into OT secure against malicious parties, and obtain general secure computation without an honest majority. Their result fixes static corruption and standalone security; it does not promise fairness or guaranteed output delivery against a party that aborts. This explains why the basic passive-security implication matters without building stronger composition or fairness requirements into the question.

Progress continues through additional algebraic or sampling structure. Li, Zhang, and Lin construct OT from rerandomizable PKE: anyone with the public key can turn a ciphertext into a fresh encryption of the same plaintext. This avoids their predecessors’ oblivious-sampling requirement but introduces a different hypothesis. Ordinary IND-CPA security alone does not include a public rerandomization algorithm.

A 2026 journal paper by Tanishita and coauthors studies updatable encryption, where update tokens let a third party transform ciphertexts across keys. With specified oblivious-sampling properties, it derives two- or three-round OT. Those theorems refine the boundary for a structured encryption primitive. They do not give a transformation starting with an arbitrary public-key encryption scheme.

A related barrier concerns fair coin tossing. Maji and Wang show limits for protocols using public-key encryption or key agreement as black boxes, whereas OT supports optimally fair constructions. This gives another operational way to see the distinction between ordinary encrypted communication and primitives complete for secure computation. The fairness result has its own model and does not constitute a proof against all non-black-box OT constructions.
why: Determines whether the ability to send secrets to a designated receiver already suffices for general private computation between mutually distrustful parties. It is a basic boundary in the hierarchy of cryptographic assumptions, with a longstanding black-box barrier and no known unrestricted implication.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No unrestricted classical implication from arbitrary IND-CPA public-key encryption to OT was identified. Known oracle/black-box separations and positive results for rerandomizable or suitably samplable encryption do not settle this formulation. The card fixes semi-honest standalone security with classical communication and no setup.
progress: 2000: Gertner and coauthors prove an oracle with PKE but no semi-honest OT, and give positive constructions when PKE has specified extra properties. Their oracle separations use uniform adversaries. | 2010–2011: Haitner and coauthors give a fully black-box compiler from semi-honest to malicious OT and general secure computation, establishing the strength of even the passive-security target. | 2021: Maji and Wang prove limitations on optimal fair coin tossing from black-box PKE or key agreement; this is further evidence about restricted constructions, not an unrestricted separation. | 2023: Li, Zhang, and Lin construct OT from rerandomizable PKE, replacing oblivious sampling with a public ciphertext-rerandomization requirement. | 2026-03-01: The journal version of Tanishita and coauthors’ work derives OT from updatable encryption with additional sampling properties. It does not remove all extra assumptions on the starting primitive.
working_summary: Oblivious transfer lets a receiver obtain one of two secret messages while hiding which message it chose. At the same time, the receiver must remain unable to learn the unchosen message. This project asks whether ordinary public-key encryption alone is enough to construct such a protocol in the classical plain model. The specified target already restricts corruption to semi-honest parties, yet privacy must hold on both sides. A general implication would connect basic encryption to a central primitive for secure computation without assuming extra algebraic structure or setup.

title: Does one-wayness suffice for collision-resistant hashing?
importance_reason: A central unresolved implication among cryptographic primitives, with consequences for authentication, data commitments and succinct verification.
formal: In the ordinary classical computational model, does the existence of a polynomial-time computable one-way function secure against all polynomial-size circuit families imply the existence of a publicly keyed collision-resistant hash family H_k:{0,1}^{2λ}→{0,1}^λ secure against all polynomial-size circuit families?
definitions: A one-way function is a deterministic uniformly polynomial-time computable map f on finite binary strings, with output length bounded by a polynomial in the input length, such that for every family of possibly randomized Boolean circuits A_n of size polynomial in n, Pr[f(A_n(1^n,f(X)))=f(X) and |A_n(1^n,f(X))|=n] is negligible in n, where X is uniform on {0,1}^n. The same invocation of A_n supplies the candidate preimage in both parts of this event. A function μ is negligible if for every c>0 there is N_c such that μ(n)≤n^{-c} for all n≥N_c. A hash family consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time key generator Gen(1^λ) producing a polynomial-length public key k, and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluator H(1^λ,k,x). For every key in the generator’s support, H_k maps every 2λ-bit input to a λ-bit output. Collision resistance means that for every polynomial-size possibly randomized circuit family B_λ, the probability that B_λ(1^λ,k) outputs distinct x,x′∈{0,1}^{2λ} with H_k(x)=H_k(x′) is negligible in λ, over k←Gen(1^λ) and the attacker’s coins. Both messages may be chosen after the attacker sees k. Circuit descriptions may depend on the security parameter, but not on the freshly sampled key. The implication permits arbitrary use of the description of f and arbitrary proof techniques; no random oracle, additional setup assumption, quantum resource, trapdoor, or stronger quantitative hardness assumption is supplied.
answer_criterion: Establish the stated existence implication without additional assumptions, or refute it in the ordinary unrelativized model. A positive result may use non-black-box techniques. An oracle world where one-way functions exist but collision-resistant hashing fails proves only a relativizing barrier. Failure of a particular construction, even for a specific one-way function, is also insufficient to refute the existence implication. Producing only target-collision resistance, noncompressing injective functions, or a construction from stronger product-hardness assumptions does not settle the proposition.
context:
A collision-resistant hash compresses its input while making it computationally difficult to find two distinct messages with the same digest. Collisions must exist by the pigeonhole principle: there are 2^{2λ} possible inputs and only 2^λ outputs. Security is therefore not a claim that collisions never occur, or that a digest uniquely identifies a message. It is a claim about what an efficient adversary can construct after learning the hash key.

A one-way function poses a different challenge. The attacker receives the image of a random input and must find any preimage. An injective one-way function can have no collisions at all, yet it is not a compressing hash. Conversely, a compressing map may have easily found collisions even if some inversion tasks look difficult. The question asks whether the minimal assumption of computationally hard inversion can always supply the more structured difficulty of finding collisions.

The public key matters to the asymptotic definition. If a single compressing function were fixed at each security parameter and security were required against nonuniform circuits, an attacker could hard-code one collision for each parameter. A fresh polynomial-length key prevents that pair from being selected in advance for the actual function used. The key is not secret: the adversary sees it before choosing either colliding message.

Target-collision resistance changes the order of moves. An attacker first commits to one message, then sees a random key and seeks a second message colliding with its committed target. Rompel constructs universal one-way hash functions of this kind from arbitrary one-way functions, as part of the route to secure signatures. That theorem does not give the present game, where both messages are chosen after the key is known. The order difference is small syntactically but central to the unresolved assumption gap.

Simon constructs an oracle setting with one-way permutations but no collision-resistant hash functions in the relevant relativized sense. It rules out building and proving the desired primitive by treating the assumed function purely as an oracle in the separated framework. The theorem does not rule out exploiting a function’s implementation or a proof that fails to relativize. The ordinary mathematical implication in this card therefore remains stronger than the black-box construction question already answered negatively.

Holmgren and Lombardi give a positive route under stronger assumptions about simultaneously inverting independent challenges. Their one-way product functions require quantitative batch hardness beyond ordinary one-wayness. They construct collision-resistant hashing from suitable such functions and connect the missing assumption to unusually strong parallel repetition. This identifies a concrete intermediate target without showing that every ordinary one-way function possesses the required batch security.

The separation also connects hashing to total search problems. Given a circuit for a compressing map, a collision is guaranteed to exist and can be checked efficiently. Folwarczný and coauthors study whether one-way functions can establish hardness for total NP search more generally, extending limitations for a class of single-query reductions. These are restrictions on reductions, not an unconditional proof that collision-resistant families cannot follow from one-wayness by any method.

Applications can sometimes avoid the full primitive. Rothblum’s July 2026 work constructs efficient interactive arguments for bounded-space computations from one-way functions. Communication depends on the space bound times a polynomial in log T and the security parameter, and the security loss depends polynomially on the computation time T. This weakens assumptions for that interactive application; it does not construct a publicly evaluable compressing hash that withstands arbitrary key-dependent collision attempts.

A resolution would clarify the foundations of many protocols that use short commitments to large data. It would either place full collision resistance on the same assumption level as ordinary one-wayness, or demonstrate a separation that survives beyond black-box barriers. The card asks for polynomial security only; requiring near-optimal exponential security or resistance to quantum attacks would introduce additional questions.
why: Determines whether a fundamental compressing cryptographic primitive needs assumptions beyond ordinary one-wayness, while exposing the gap between known black-box barriers and unrestricted constructions.
status_note: No unrestricted implication or refutation was found in the primary literature checked through 11 September 2026. Existing black-box separations do not settle this ordinary-model existence statement. The definitions explicitly use uniform honest algorithms, nonuniform classical adversaries, public fresh keys and factor-two compression.
progress: 1990: Rompel obtains universal one-way hashing and secure signatures from arbitrary one-way functions; this uses the weaker target-before-key collision game. | 1998: Simon proves an oracle separation from one-way permutations, establishing the classical black-box obstacle. | 2018: Holmgren–Lombardi construct collision-resistant hashing from quantitatively strong one-way product functions, an additional assumption. | 2023-06-16: Folwarczný and coauthors extend related barriers to single-query reductions for total search. | 2026-07-02: Rothblum constructs bounded-space interactive arguments from one-way functions, without resolving the hashing implication.
working_summary: Collision-resistant hashing compresses a message while making it difficult to find two different messages with the same hash value. The selected problem asks whether the existence of one-way functions alone guarantees a publicly keyed family with this security property. Collisions necessarily exist because the output space is smaller, so the issue is computational difficulty after the hash key is revealed. Inverting a random function output and deliberately constructing a colliding pair are different challenges. Resolving their relationship would identify whether collision resistance is an additional cryptographic assumption or a consequence of basic one-wayness.

title: One-way permutations from one-way functions
importance_reason: A longstanding question about the structure obtainable from minimal cryptographic assumptions, with strong construction barriers and a recent full-domain breakthrough under additional assumptions.
formal: Does the existence of classical one-way functions secure against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries imply the existence of a classical, efficiently generated family of full-domain one-way permutations with the same security convention?
definitions: A one-way function is a uniformly polynomial-time computable family f_n:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1}^{ℓ(n)}, for a polynomially bounded, computable output length ℓ, such that for every randomized polynomial-size circuit family A_n, Pr[f_n(A_n(1ⁿ,f_n(X)))=f_n(X)] is negligible in n for uniform X∈{0,1}ⁿ; outputs outside {0,1}ⁿ fail. A function μ is negligible if for every c>0, μ(n)≤n^{-c} for all sufficiently large n. A permutation family consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time key generator Gen(1ⁿ) and deterministic polynomial-time evaluation Eval(1ⁿ,pk,x), with a fixed polynomially bounded, polynomial-time computable integer m(n)≥n. For every pk in the support of Gen(1ⁿ), Eval defines a bijection π_pk:{0,1}^{m(n)}→{0,1}^{m(n)}. For every randomized polynomial-size adversary A_n, Pr[π_pk(A_n(1ⁿ,pk,π_pk(X)))=π_pk(X)] must be negligible, with pk←Gen(1ⁿ), independent uniform X and independent adversary coins. Malformed outputs fail. The public key is available to the attacker; no trapdoor is required or given. All security is classical. “Full-domain” fixes the input set to the whole Boolean cube; the valid public-key set need not be all bit strings of its length. The implication is an ordinary existence implication, without restrictions to black-box constructions and without extra assumptions such as obfuscation or subexponential security.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence implication, allowing any mathematical construction or proof technique, or refute that implication in the ordinary computational model. Proving that one-way functions do not exist would make the implication vacuously true. An oracle separation or a theorem excluding a restricted class of reductions is a construction barrier, not a refutation of the unrestricted implication. A permutation family on special sparse domains does not meet the full-domain convention fixed here; an additional trapdoor property would be a stronger positive result.
context:
A one-way function is easy to evaluate but hard to invert on a random input. It may identify many different inputs and need not cover its output space. A one-way permutation has exactly one preimage for every output in its domain. The extra requirement is structural: nothing is lost mathematically, yet efficiently recovering the uniquely determined input must remain infeasible.

This card fixes the full-domain, public-key family version because the original phrase “one-way permutation” leaves several conventions unspecified. A public key chooses a permutation of an entire Boolean cube; all input strings of that length are valid. A stronger unkeyed formulation asks for a single length-preserving permutation on all bit strings. A more permissive formulation allows key-dependent sparse domains. Results in those settings must be compared with their domain and sampling requirements visible.

Making a computation reversible is not enough. The map (x,z)↦(x,z XOR f(x)) is a bijection for any efficiently computable length-compatible f, but its inverse is obtained by applying exactly the same map. Likewise, simply attaching x to f(x) makes the output injective while revealing the desired preimage. The construction has to preserve computational difficulty while removing collisions and covering the domain, without publishing the information needed for inversion.

Many other forms of cryptographic structure can be derived from bare one-wayness. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby show that every one-way function yields a pseudorandom generator. That success does not enforce bijectivity. The permutation question tests whether computational hardness can always be reorganized into a particularly rigid, uniquely invertible mathematical object.

Rudich’s 1988 thesis developed the oracle-separation approach and gave a barrier for this implication conditional on a combinatorial conjecture. The thesis abstract states that qualification explicitly. It is misleading to describe the original thesis alone as an unconditional separation of the ordinary existence assumptions. An oracle world changes what algorithms can access, so it diagnoses limitations of proof techniques rather than settling the actual implication.

Matsuda and Matsuura subsequently prove a fully black-box barrier even when the starting function is injective, increases length by only one bit, and satisfies their stronger adaptive one-wayness condition. Thus an apparently tiny departure from a permutation already defeats a broad class of generic constructions. Their result concerns constructions that treat the supplied primitive and adversary through specified interfaces; it does not exclude exploiting the code or other structure of a concrete function.

Asharov and Segev address another subtlety: earlier negative arguments could fail when the construction’s domains depended on the underlying primitives. They exclude black-box constructions from one-way functions even without that domain-invariance requirement. They also give a separate barrier for constructions using oracle-aided indistinguishability obfuscation, under domain-invariance conditions. The two statements have different assumptions and should not be merged into an unrestricted impossibility theorem.

There is significant progress with stronger assumptions. Shmueli and Zhandry’s July 2025 paper constructs full-domain trapdoor one-way permutations assuming subexponentially secure indistinguishability obfuscation and subexponentially secure one-way functions. It uses a new kind of pseudorandom permutation that supports controlled permutation of its outputs. The trapdoor guarantee is stronger than this card requests, but both the extra primitive and the stronger hardness assumptions prevent this from proving the target implication.

The same paper explains why its full-domain result is compatible with the earlier obfuscation barrier. Its input domain is the whole cube, but its public keys are obfuscated programs. The valid-key domain therefore depends on the building blocks. The older formal domain-invariance condition constrains both input and key domains. Keeping these two notions separate prevents an erroneous claim that a published barrier has been contradicted.

A positive answer would show that unique, length-preserving inversion hardness is available whenever basic cryptographic hardness exists. A negative answer would reveal a structural separation inside foundational cryptographic assumptions. Existing barriers make the problem especially informative: a successful construction from ordinary one-way functions would need to escape the established generic approaches, rather than merely improve their efficiency.
why: Determine whether basic average-case inversion hardness necessarily supports efficient bijections, a rigid primitive at the foundation of cryptographic constructions.
status_note: No derivation from ordinary one-way functions alone, or refutation of the unrestricted existence implication, was found through 11 September 2026. The 2025 full-domain trapdoor construction requires subexponential iO and OWF assumptions. Existing oracle and black-box barriers do not settle the unrestricted question. This card explicitly fixes the full-domain keyed convention.
progress: 1988: Rudich develops oracle barriers; the thesis’s one-way-function-to-permutation argument is conditional on a combinatorial conjecture. | 1999: Håstad–Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby establish pseudorandom generators from arbitrary one-way functions, without obtaining a permutation guarantee. | 2011: Matsuda–Matsuura exclude fully black-box constructions from even one-bit-expanding injective one-way functions with adaptive one-wayness. | 2015–2018: Asharov–Segev handle domains depending on the primitives in their OWF-only barrier, and separately study domain-invariant constructions using obfuscation. | 2025-07-16: Shmueli–Zhandry obtain full-domain trapdoor permutations from subexponentially secure iO and OWFs; Section 1.4 distinguishes input-domain from key-domain invariance.
working_summary: A one-way permutation is an efficiently computable bijection that remains hard to invert on a random input. Unlike a general one-way function, it loses no information and gives each output exactly one preimage. This project asks whether arbitrary one-way functions imply an efficiently generated family of such permutations on full Boolean domains. The domain and security conventions matter because restricted-domain or differently keyed variants can express different requirements. A general construction would show that the unique-preimage structure comes for free from one-wayness rather than requiring a stronger assumption.

title: Chosen-ciphertext security from ordinary public-key encryption
importance_reason: A central question about the minimal assumptions for robust public-key encryption, connecting encryption, proof systems, trapdoor structure and generic security transformations.
formal: Does the existence of IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption imply the existence of IND-CCA2-secure public-key encryption in the plain model, with classical security against all nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries and no additional computational assumption?
definitions: A public-key encryption scheme has uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms Gen(1ⁿ)→(pk,sk) and Enc(pk,m)→c and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm Dec(sk,c)→m or ⊥. It supports bit-string messages of any polynomially bounded length. For every polynomial p, the maximum decryption-error probability over messages |m|≤p(n) is negligible in n, with probability over key generation and honest encryption. In the IND-CPA game an adversary receives pk, chooses equal-length messages m₀,m₁ and state, receives c*=Enc(pk,m_b) for an independent uniform bit b, and guesses b. Its advantage is |Pr[guess=b]−1/2|. In the IND-CCA2 game it also has adaptive access to Dec(sk,·), both before and after choosing the challenge messages and receiving c*. After the challenge, the oracle rejects the exact bit string c*; all other ciphertext queries are allowed. Security requires negligible advantage for every nonuniform probabilistic polynomial-time adversary, allowing any polynomial number of oracle queries. Negligible means eventually smaller than n^{-a} for every a>0. Each adversary has its own polynomial resource bound, but the scheme is fixed independently of that bound. The plain model has no ideal random oracle, externally supplied common reference string, hardware or trusted setup beyond the recipient generating its own key pair. This is an unrestricted existence implication, not a requirement that a compiler treat the original scheme as a black box.
answer_criterion: Prove that an IND-CCA2 scheme with these guarantees exists whenever an IND-CPA scheme exists, or refute that implication in the ordinary computational model. A conversion assuming additional trapdoor functions, suitable proof systems, special pseudorandom generators or ideal random oracles does not by itself suffice. A theorem excluding a restricted class of black-box conversions is a barrier, not a negative answer to the unrestricted implication. Fixed-query bounded CCA2, pre-challenge-only CCA1 and non-malleability without adaptive decryption access are weaker targets.
context:
Public-key encryption already allows anyone, including the attacker, to create ciphertexts. Ordinary chosen-plaintext security protects the contents of an honestly generated challenge ciphertext. Chosen-ciphertext security additionally protects it while the attacker submits other ciphertexts for decryption and uses the responses to decide what to ask next. The only forbidden query is the challenge itself, because returning its plaintext would make confidentiality impossible by definition.

A simple modification illustrates the gap between definitions. Start with a secure ordinary scheme, append an unused bit to every ciphertext, and make decryption ignore that bit. The modification preserves chosen-plaintext security. A chosen-ciphertext attacker flips the challenge’s unused bit and submits the resulting different string to the oracle, which returns the challenge plaintext. This proves that a particular CPA scheme need not itself be CCA-secure; it does not rule out building another scheme from its existence.

This is why the question concerns a construction or existence implication. A successful transformation may change the ciphertext format, use many public keys, encode messages, and inspect the original algorithms’ descriptions. It must arrange that responses to every other ciphertext remain harmless. A proof faces the corresponding simulation problem: how can it answer decryption queries while relying only on a challenge from the weaker security game?

The source proposal points to Trevisan’s cryptography project list, which explicitly asks whether CCA security can be derived from CPA security by black-box techniques or by any techniques. Its bibliography juxtaposes partial negative results with positive results for non-malleability. That distinction remains important: an advance for one attack model should not silently be reported as a solution for another.

Gertner, Malkin and Myers give a black-box separation for constructions whose new decryption algorithm never calls the original encryption algorithm. This covers a substantial class of natural attempts. It still leaves constructions that re-encrypt during decryption, and does not cover arbitrary use of the source code. The scope of that restriction is central to the theorem, rather than a technical detail that can be omitted.

Choi, Dachman-Soled, Malkin and Wee construct non-malleable encryption from any semantically secure scheme and extend their approach to bounded chosen-ciphertext attacks. In the bounded version, the permitted number q of decryption queries is fixed before constructing the scheme. Full CCA2 instead asks for one scheme that withstands every polynomial-time attacker, whose query polynomial can be larger than any particular bound built into that scheme.

Another productive route adds a primitive that helps enforce ciphertext validity. Hohenberger, Koppula and Waters prove in CRYPTO 2020 that injective trapdoor functions suffice for CCA-secure public-key encryption, without requiring lossiness or correlated-product security. This removes significant earlier restrictions. An arbitrary encryption scheme is not automatically such a trapdoor function: its decryption need only recover the message, not a unique full input including encryption randomness.

Koppula and Waters obtain generic upgrades using a hinting pseudorandom generator, whose security survives a special kind of auxiliary information. Ordinary pseudorandomness does not state that guarantee. Their construction offers another way to organize the decryption proof, but applying it to arbitrary public-key encryption still requires establishing the additional hinting property from the original assumption.

Matsuda’s PKC 2025 work shows that a publicly verifiable noninteractive batch argument for NP can supply the additional ingredient. The May 2025 revision weakens the required proof-length savings: they need not be strong enough for currently known constructions of noninteractive zero knowledge. This is progress in reducing the extra structure needed for the upgrade. The paper still assumes the batch argument; it does not construct it from arbitrary CPA encryption.

A PKC 2026 paper by Brzuska, Klooß and Woo gives CPA-to-CCA transformations for threshold encryption, where several parties jointly decrypt. Its generic transform from arbitrary CPA-secure threshold encryption uses a random oracle. Its other route has additional requirements, including a stronger semi-malicious CPA notion. The July 2026 revision therefore does not establish the plain-model implication in this card.

Resolving the implication would clarify whether protection against active ciphertext manipulation is an additional foundational assumption or a consequence of ordinary public-key confidentiality. It would also explain why existing general approaches repeatedly need structure beyond the weak starting primitive. The target is a foundational security theorem; it does not ask that the resulting construction be practical or preserve the original scheme’s efficiency.
why: Determine whether public-key confidentiality alone can always be strengthened to resist adaptive decryption attacks, without importing another cryptographic assumption.
status_note: No construction from ordinary CPA-secure public-key encryption alone in the plain model, or refutation of that unrestricted implication, was found through 11 September 2026. Bounded-CCA results and constructions with injective trapdoor functions, hinting PRGs, batch arguments or random oracles leave this target open.
progress: 2007: Gertner–Malkin–Myers exclude a class of black-box conversions whose decryption algorithm does not call the underlying encryption algorithm. | 2008: Choi–Dachman-Soled–Malkin–Wee construct non-malleable encryption from CPA encryption and obtain a bounded-CCA extension. | 2019: Koppula–Waters use a hinting PRG as an extra ingredient for generic chosen-ciphertext security transformations. | 2020: Hohenberger–Koppula–Waters derive CCA-secure encryption from arbitrary injective trapdoor functions. | 2025-05-12: Matsuda’s revised PKC paper weakens the batch-argument succinctness required to upgrade CPA encryption. | 2026-07-17: The revised threshold-encryption work retains additional-model or stronger-security requirements in its CPA-to-CCA transformations.
working_summary: Chosen-plaintext security protects an encrypted message even when an attacker can generate other encryptions. Chosen-ciphertext security additionally permits the attacker to obtain decryptions of adaptively chosen ciphertexts other than the challenge itself. This project asks whether any ordinary secure public-key encryption scheme can be upgraded to this stronger guarantee in the plain model. The upgrade must introduce no new computational assumption and may use techniques beyond black-box access to the original scheme. Establishing it would show that resistance to active decryption attacks is a general consequence of public-key encryption rather than a separate structural resource.

title: Noninteractive zero knowledge from one-way functions
importance_reason: A fundamental boundary between interactive and noninteractive zero knowledge, with implications for the assumptions behind privacy-preserving proof systems and cryptographic transformations.
formal: Does the existence of classical one-way functions imply reusable, adaptively secure noninteractive zero-knowledge arguments for circuit satisfiability in the honestly generated common-reference-string model, with computational soundness and computational zero knowledge against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries?
definitions: A one-way function is a uniformly polynomial-time computable family f_n on uniform n-bit inputs with polynomial-length outputs, such that every nonuniform randomized polynomial-size adversary given 1ⁿ and f_n(X) finds any n-bit preimage with negligible probability. Circuit satisfiability has statements x encoding Boolean circuits and witnesses w assigning their inputs, with R(x,w)=1 exactly when the circuit outputs 1. A proposed argument consists of uniform algorithms Setup(1^λ,1^B)→crs, Prove(crs,x,w)→π, and Verify(crs,x,π)→{0,1}; their time and output length are polynomial in λ+B, where B bounds statement and witness lengths. Setup is independent of the later statements; its private coins are not published. For every polynomial B=B(λ), completeness error is negligible uniformly over valid (x,w) of length at most B. Adaptive computational soundness means that every nonuniform polynomial-time adversary given crs has negligible probability of outputting an unsatisfiable x and an accepted π. Reusable computational zero knowledge means there exist uniform polynomial-time SimSetup and SimProve such that no nonuniform polynomial-time distinguisher separates these experiments: (i) it receives honest crs and can adaptively request Prove(crs,x,w) for polynomially many valid pairs; (ii) it receives simulated crs from SimSetup, and each valid query is answered by SimProve using the simulation trapdoor and x, without receiving w. Both experiments reject invalid queries, and the distinguisher retains arbitrary polynomial-size auxiliary information. All negligible bounds are in λ: for each a>0 the error is eventually below λ^{-a}. Only crs is public in the real system, and one proof message is sent for each statement. No random oracle, extra cryptographic assumption, online verifier challenge, proof of knowledge or succinctness requirement is included. Circuit satisfiability covers every NP language through witness-preserving polynomial reductions.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence implication, or refute it in the ordinary computational model. The result may use the code of the one-way function and need not be black-box. A construction adding LWE, an appropriate batch argument, trapdoor hashing, or strong extra complexity assumptions does not suffice unless those ingredients are themselves derived from the same ordinary OWF premise. An interactive proof, a witness-indistinguishable argument, or a single-theorem result without a justified reusable upgrade is not the specified conclusion.
context:
An NP witness can be easy to check and sensitive to reveal. For circuit satisfiability, publishing a satisfying assignment gives a verifier complete evidence, but also exposes every bit of that assignment. Zero knowledge asks for convincing evidence whose visible distribution can instead be simulated without the assignment. It formalizes the requirement that verification disclose no additional information beyond the statement’s truth.

The common reference string is an explicit resource. An honest setup algorithm produces public parameters before any statements are selected. After that setup, a prover sends one message that anyone can verify. The setup may retain randomness while generating the string, but that randomness is not handed to users. The simulation trapdoor exists only in the security experiment. This model differs from asking for a noninteractive system with no setup at all.

The card allows computational soundness: a computationally unbounded attacker might find a false accepted proof, but efficient attackers must not. Such a system is called an argument. It also asks for a reusable reference string, with statements chosen after seeing the string and earlier proofs. These choices make the target precise without requiring short proofs or a way to extract a witness from a successful prover.

The classical Goldreich–Micali–Wigderson theorem already supplies interactive zero-knowledge proofs for NP from one-way functions. Interaction gives the verifier a role in challenging what the prover has prepared. The inherited Damgård–Nielsen survey explicitly asks whether one-way functions suffice in the noninteractive setting. That survey discusses a proof-system version with stronger soundness; the argument target here asks for protection only against efficient cheating.

Known positive constructions use more structure. Peikert and Shiehian construct NIZK for NP from ordinary LWE in 2019. Their method builds hash families whose correlation-intractability property supports a sound Fiat–Shamir transformation. The point is a proved property of a specially constructed family, not simply substituting an arbitrary hash function for a verifier’s random challenge. LWE is a sufficient assumption, but it has not thereby been derived from arbitrary one-way functions.

Bradley, Waters and Wu show that an adaptively sound noninteractive batch argument for NP, together with a one-way function, yields NIZK. Their TCC 2024 result also studies how to obtain the needed adaptive soundness from other batch-argument guarantees. The title “Batch Arguments to NIZKs from One-Way Functions” must be read with its starting resource intact: the batch argument is an additional primitive, rather than something their theorem constructs from a bare one-way function.

Branco and coauthors develop a vector-trapdoor-hash approach, with an updated version in March 2026. Their constructions use either LWE or a combination of DDH and LPN assumptions. The initial black-box constructions provide single-theorem zero knowledge, and their multi-theorem upgrade uses cryptography in a non-black-box way. This distinction is compatible with the target here, which allows any construction technique but requires the OWF-only assumption and reusable security.

Chen, Rothblum and Tell pursue a different route through derandomization and strong computational hardness. Their construction combines a subexponentially secure one-way function with an additional complexity assumption and obtains computational soundness against uniform adversaries. It is progress toward avoiding highly structured cryptographic primitives, but the extra hardness and the adversary convention both differ from this card.

Recent results in the reverse direction should not be read as a construction. Chakraborty, Hulett, Khurana and Tomer show in February 2026 that nontrivial NIZK arguments imply one-way functions under the hypothesis that NP is not contained in ioP/poly, even in a broad high-error regime. Their amplification consequences improve existing weak NIZK systems. Neither direction starts with an ordinary OWF alone and produces the desired NIZK system.

Another 2026 result gives succinct zero-knowledge proofs using one-way functions as black boxes. Florentz–Konopnicki and Rothblum’s protocol is interactive: its theorem explicitly bounds a number of public-coin rounds that depends on the relation’s parameters. Its noninteractive commitment component does not make the whole protocol noninteractive. A resolution of this card would isolate exactly how much cryptographic structure is needed to remove that interaction after a single reusable setup.
why: Determine whether the minimal assumption supporting basic cryptography is sufficient for reusable, publicly verifiable proofs that reveal no witness and require no online interaction.
status_note: No construction of reusable adaptive NIZK arguments from ordinary OWFs alone, or refutation of that unrestricted implication, was found through 11 September 2026. The cited BARG, trapdoor-hash and derandomization constructions retain extra assumptions; recent OWF-only succinct proofs are interactive, and high-error characterizations run in the reverse direction.
progress: 1986: Goldreich–Micali–Wigderson establish interactive zero knowledge for NP from one-way functions; the inherited survey distinguishes the noninteractive open question. | 2019: Peikert–Shiehian construct NIZK for NP from plain LWE using correlation-intractable hashing. | 2024-09-20: The revised Bradley–Waters–Wu work derives NIZK from adaptively sound BARGs plus OWFs, retaining the extra batch-argument premise. | 2025-04-03: Chen–Rothblum–Tell’s revised work gives NIZK with uniform soundness from subexponential OWFs and additional strong complexity assumptions. | 2026-02-19: Chakraborty–Hulett–Khurana–Tomer extend conditional implications from nontrivial NIZK to OWFs and error amplification; this is not OWF-to-NIZK. | 2026-03-30: Updated vector-trapdoor-hash constructions distinguish black-box single-theorem NIZK from a non-black-box multi-theorem upgrade under stronger assumptions. | 2026-08-11: Florentz–Konopnicki–Rothblum’s CRYPTO 2026 chapter appears online; its succinct OWF-based zero-knowledge proof remains interactive.
working_summary: Noninteractive zero knowledge lets a prover demonstrate an NP statement with one message without revealing its witness. This project asks whether one-way functions suffice for reusable, adaptively secure arguments of this kind after an honest common-reference-string setup. Reusability means that the same public parameters must remain suitable as many statements are selected and proved. The target uses computational soundness and computational zero knowledge, so both guarantees are formulated against efficient adversaries. A construction would show that the setup model can support powerful noninteractive privacy guarantees from the basic assumption underlying symmetric cryptography.

title: Does perfect zero knowledge equal statistical zero knowledge?
importance_reason: A foundational comparison between two information-theoretic privacy notions, posed in a standard cryptography textbook, supported by a nontrivial oracle separation and explicitly retained in recent work on perfect zero knowledge.
formal: Does PZK=SZK for classical single-prover interactive proofs of promise problems, with polynomial-time verifiers and simulators, negligible proof error, and zero knowledge against every polynomial-time verifier?
definitions: A promise problem is a pair (Y,N) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings. An interactive proof consists of a computationally unbounded prover P and a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V exchanging polynomially many bits on common input x. There is a negligible function ε such that on x∈Y the honest interaction accepts with probability at least 1−ε(|x|), and on x∈N every prover strategy is accepted with probability at most ε(|x|). Negligible means smaller than |x|^{−d} for every fixed d>0 at all sufficiently large lengths. No condition is imposed outside Y∪N. The view of a verifier consists of its random bits and exchanged messages. SZK requires that for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V* there is a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulator S* which, on x alone, produces a distribution within negligible total variation distance of the view of (P,V*)(x), for every x∈Y. Total variation distance is one half of the sum of absolute probability differences over possible views. PZK instead permits S* to output a failure symbol ⊥ with probability at most 1/2; conditioned on nonfailure, its output distribution must equal that view exactly. Every runtime bound is a strict polynomial bound over all random outcomes, with a polynomial allowed to depend on the fixed verifier or simulator. This is the ordinary input-only simulation convention of the cited definitions, without a shared random string, an oracle, a setup assumption, or a restriction to honest verifiers.
answer_criterion: Prove that every promise problem admitting the stated statistical proof also admits a perfect one in this model, or exhibit a promise problem in SZK and prove that it has no PZK proof. The protocol may change completely in a positive result. An oracle separation, a failure of one proposed compiler, a perfect-zero-knowledge PCP, or an honest-verifier-only theorem does not resolve this unrelativized class equality.
context:
Zero knowledge formalizes the idea that a verifier can reproduce what it sees without receiving help from the prover. Statistical simulation permits a negligible discrepancy between distributions. Perfect simulation requires exact agreement after the allowed failure event. Goldreich’s textbook asks whether this difference changes which statements can be proved.

The failure convention is part of the model. A strict polynomial-time perfect simulator that never fails is a different requirement, often called super-perfect zero knowledge. Allowing an expected polynomial runtime is also a separate definitional issue discussed in the source. Neither convention is silently substituted here.

PZK is contained in SZK: repeat the bounded-failure perfect simulator polynomially many times until it succeeds, and use an arbitrary output if every attempt fails. The remaining probability of failure is negligible, while successful outputs retain the exact distribution. The open direction asks whether negligible simulation error can always be eliminated by some proof system.

Bouland, Chen, Holden, Thaler and Vasudevan construct an oracle relative to which SZK is not contained in PZK. This supplies evidence against equality and rules out a proof that relativizes in the corresponding way. It does not separate the classes in the ordinary model specified here.

Gur, O’Connor and Spooner explicitly retain PZK versus SZK as open in their 2024 paper. Their perfect-zero-knowledge construction is for probabilistically checkable proofs, where a verifier queries a proof oracle. That achievement concerns a different access model from ordinary interactive proofs and leaves this equality unresolved.

title: Does worst-case Nearest Codeword hardness imply low-noise LPN hardness?
importance_reason: Would connect worst-case coding hardness to a central average-case cryptographic assumption in a concrete low-noise regime.
formal: Does the following implication hold? If binary Nearest Codeword is not in BPP, then no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D has advantage at least $n^{-c}$, for any fixed $c>0$ and all sufficiently large square n, between $(A,As+e)$ and $(A,u)$. Here $A\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2\times n}$, $s\in\mathbb F_2^n$, and $u\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2}$ are independent uniform random variables, and the coordinates of e are independent Bernoulli variables with rate $1/\sqrt n$. Advantage is the absolute difference of D’s acceptance probabilities in the two experiments.
definitions: Binary Nearest Codeword receives a binary matrix G, a binary target y with the same number of rows, and an integer t, and asks whether $\min_z\operatorname{wt}(Gz-y)\le t$, with arithmetic over F_2 and Hamming weight wt. BPP means a uniform randomized polynomial-time decider correct with probability at least 2/3 on every instance. The LPN side here is a decision problem with n-squared samples, random secret, and inverse-square-root noise. Restricting n to squares makes the noise parameter an exact rational; this is an explicit specialization of the source’s broader low-noise direction.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed complexity-theoretic implication, for example by a reduction turning such an LPN distinguisher into a BPP algorithm for Nearest Codeword, or prove that the implication is false. Invoking simultaneous hardness of an additional problem on the dual code does not establish this implication.
context:
LWE has strong connections to worst-case lattice problems. Establishing comparable foundations for LPN at cryptographically useful noise rates is more difficult.

Without noise, enough independent parity equations reveal the secret by linear algebra. Flipping some answers breaks that direct procedure: the learner must cope with equations whose right-hand sides may be wrong. At a low noise rate, most equations remain correct, which makes the precise source of hardness especially important.

A worst-case-to-average-case reduction would start with an arbitrary hard coding instance and turn it into the random samples used by LPN. It must preserve a usable noise regime and show how an LPN solver would solve the original task. Requiring two different coding tasks to be hard simultaneously is a stronger premise than deriving the guarantee from one standard worst-case problem.
why: A basic security assumption would obtain an explanation through independently studied hardness. The extra assumption in the new reduction makes the remaining target concrete.
status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
progress: 2026-09-08: The revision gives a reduction for $\eta=n^{-\alpha}$, any constant $\alpha<1$, from simultaneous worst-case hardness of two tasks on a code and its dual. This advances beyond earlier near-half-noise reductions; the single-assumption target remains stronger.
working_summary: Learning parity with noise asks for information about hidden binary linear equations when some answers have been flipped. This project asks whether worst-case hardness of the binary nearest-codeword problem implies average-case hardness for a specified low-noise LPN distribution. The chosen regime uses quadratically many samples and a noise rate inversely proportional to the square root of the secret dimension. A reduction must produce that particular random-instance distribution rather than merely another hard coding problem or a different noise level. Such a connection would strengthen the theoretical foundation of low-noise LPN in the way worst-case reductions support lattice-based assumptions.

title: Quantum PCP: a constant promise gap for local Hamiltonians
importance_reason: A defining quantum-complexity conjecture connecting robust verification, approximation hardness, and the structure of many-body Hamiltonians.
focus_reason: A defining quantum-complexity conjecture connecting robust verification, approximation hardness, and the structure of many-body Hamiltonians.
formal: Do there exist integers k,d≥1 and a rational constant ε∈(0,1) such that the following promise problem is QMA-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Input is a list of m≤(n+1)^d k-local Hermitian terms H_i on n≥1 qubits and rational a<b in [0,1], with 0⪯H_i⪯I and b−a≥ε. For H=(1/m)Σ_i H_i, distinguish λ_min(H)≤a from λ_min(H)≥b.
definitions: Here 1≤m; each term is specified by at most k distinct qubit indices and the complete matrix on those qubits, with rational real and imaginary parts encoded by signed binary numerators and positive denominators. It is tensored with identity on the other qubits. n is written in unary, thresholds in binary rational notation; N counts every supplied bit. λ_min is the smallest eigenvalue. M⪯N means that N−M is positive semidefinite, equivalently z*(N−M)z≥0 for every complex vector z. Inputs violating the matrix promises or with a<λ_min(H)<b are outside the promise. QMA consists of disjoint pairs (Y,N₀) of sets of binary strings with a polynomial-time uniform quantum verifier: on x it uses polynomially many qubits and gates over {H,T,CNOT}, an arbitrary polynomial-qubit witness, and auxiliary qubits initialized to |0⟩. H=2^(−1/2)((1,1),(1,−1)) is the Hadamard matrix, T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)), and CNOT flips its target when its control is 1. A designated final qubit is measured. For x∈Y some witness gives acceptance probability ≥2/3; for x∈N₀ every witness gives probability ≤1/3. A deterministic machine produces the verifier circuit from x in polynomial time. QMA-hard means that for every such pair there is a deterministic polynomial-time map sending Y into the low-energy case and N₀ into the high-energy case, always producing legal instances on promised inputs. Constants k,d,ε are shared by the target problem; reduction polynomials may depend on the source promise problem.

context:
The classical PCP theorem replaces full verification by inspecting a small part of a proof with a constant gap. Entanglement and local indistinguishability obstruct a direct quantum analogue.

Normalization makes the target meaningful. Multiplying a Hamiltonian by a large number could enlarge its energy gap, but would also violate the bound on individual terms. The conjecture asks for a constant gap in average local energy while every constraint retains bounded strength.

A useful way to read the two cases is that one input admits a low-energy global state, while in the other every state has appreciably higher average energy. The challenge is to preserve computational hardness at that coarse resolution. Checking a few local terms can detect a constant average discrepancy, but constructing a reduction with that discrepancy is the unresolved step.
why: This asks whether approximating a quantum system’s energy captures the full difficulty of quantum witness verification. It connects complexity, quantum codes, and local testing.
