title: Can randomness always be removed from polynomial-time decision algorithms?
importance_reason: The main general derandomization question for polynomial-time decision algorithms, with broad consequences for the role of randomness and for hardness-versus-randomness techniques.
focus_reason: The main general derandomization question for polynomial-time decision algorithms, with broad consequences for the role of randomness and for hardness-versus-randomness techniques.
formal: Does P=BPP? Precisely, for every language L for which a randomized Turing machine R runs in polynomial time on every input and every random tape, and satisfies $\Pr[R(x)=1_L(x)]\ge2/3$ for every binary string x, does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine deciding L correctly on every x? The polynomial time bound of the deterministic machine may depend on R.
definitions: Input length is n=|x|. A polynomial-time bound means C(n+1)^k steps for fixed constants C,k, independent of x and of the random bits. R uses independent unbiased random bits, at most one fresh bit per computation step, and outputs a single bit. Its error may be on either yes or no inputs, but is bounded separately on each input. P consists of deterministic polynomial-time decision languages and BPP of languages meeting the randomized guarantee above. These are total decision problems, with no excluded promise inputs. No advice, oracle, quantum operations, or input distribution is allowed. The requested deterministic simulation may use a different algorithm; it need not reproduce R's random choices, preserve its precise exponent, or be generated by an effective compiler from R.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Randomized decision algorithms may use randomness to avoid exceptional choices or to test a property through a small sample. Their guarantee is pointwise: even the worst input must receive the correct answer with high probability. Repeating an algorithm reduces its error but leaves it randomized. The question asks whether every such use of randomness can ultimately be replaced by a deterministic polynomial computation.

Exhaustive majority evaluation over all random tapes has a time cost exponential in their length. That is correct, but takes exponential time when the tape has polynomial length. A suitable pseudorandom generator would reduce the search to a polynomial-size set of tapes, constructed efficiently. The hard part is ensuring that this small set fools the computation on every input.

A nonuniform version of this idea already works: after error amplification, an averaging argument supplies one polynomial-length advice string that works for every input of a given length. This proves BPP is contained in P/poly. The string can depend on the input length without an efficient procedure to find it, which is exactly why that inclusion does not answer the uniform question.

Strong circuit hardness provides a conditional route to full derandomization. Impagliazzo and Wigderson show that an exponentially circuit-hard function computable in exponential time suffices. The condition is substantially more specific than merely P≠NP. Current work also studies the amount of slowdown and the structure of the randomized algorithm, producing finer conditional results without an unconditional equality proof.

This card concerns computing one correct decision bit. Sampling a distribution, producing one of many valid witnesses, or deciding only inputs with a promise leads to related but different formulations. Keeping these tasks separate prevents a derandomization theorem for one setting from being silently substituted for another.
why: This determines whether random bits add power to efficient total decision computation. It is a central organizing question for pseudorandom generators, explicit constructions, and the connection between circuit lower bounds and algorithm design.

A July 2026 revision of a preprint claims separation; this review has not established its correctness or independent validation. The card is not marked resolved. title: Optimal explicit pseudorandom generators for read-once branching programs
importance_reason: A central constructive route to L=BPL, with optimal nonconstructive seed length known and a persistent gap for uniform space-efficient generators despite advances in restricted and weighted models.
focus_reason: A central constructive route to L=BPL, with optimal nonconstructive seed length known and a persistent gap for uniform space-efficient generators despite advances in restricted and weighted models.
formal: Do there exist absolute constants C,D and a uniform family of generators G_{n,w,p}:{0,1}^s→{0,1}^n, for all integers n,w≥2 and p≥1, with s≤C(log_2 n+log_2 w+p), such that |Pr_{u uniform in {0,1}^s}[B(G_{n,w,p}(u))=1]−Pr_{z uniform in {0,1}^n}[B(z)=1]|≤2^(−p) for every length-n, width-at-most-w ordered read-once branching program B? Require a single deterministic algorithm that, given n,w,p,u and an output position i, computes G_{n,w,p}(u)_i using at most D(log_2 n+log_2 w+p) work bits and time (nw·2^p)^D.
definitions: An ordered read-once branching program has layers V_0,…,V_n, each containing at most w states, a designated initial state in V_0, and an accepting subset of V_n. For each layer i−1, each state has one outgoing edge labeled 0 and one labeled 1 to V_i. On input z, the program follows the edge labeled z_i at step i and accepts exactly when the final state is accepting. Different edges may merge; neither regularity nor permutation transitions are required. The order is the fixed order z_1,…,z_n. Programs may be arbitrary nonuniform objects, but the generator cannot inspect their descriptions. The parameters and seed are read-only inputs to the generator algorithm, and the output bit is written separately; all work space, counters and intermediate storage are counted. Seed length is a computable function of the parameters within the stated resources. Uniform seeds induce an ordinary probability distribution, without signed or externally assigned weights. Set ε=2^(−p); this dyadic formulation gives the usual O(log(nw/ε)) target for arbitrary positive error by rounding down to a smaller dyadic tolerance.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The program processes a long stream while remembering only its current state. Width w corresponds to about log_2 w bits of memory; length n is the number of random bits it can inspect. A pseudorandom generator replaces that long random stream with the deterministic expansion of a much shorter genuinely random seed. The requirement is simultaneous: the same generated distribution must fool every permitted program, even though their transition tables may be entirely different.

There is no information-theoretic obstacle to the seed-length target. After padding to w states, the number of programs is at most w·2^w·w^(2nw). Choose a list of independent uniform n-bit strings and use a uniformly chosen list position as the seed. A concentration bound and union bound show that a list of O(ε^(−2)(nw log w+w)) strings suffices to approximate every acceptance probability. Indexing that list takes O(log n+log w+log(1/ε)) bits. The argument does not tell us how to generate its entries in the tiny workspace required here.

The computational payoff is direct. Fix an input to a bounded-error logarithmic-space randomized machine and view its evolution on random bits as a polynomial-length, polynomial-width branching program. A logarithmic seed permits enumeration of all seeds, regeneration of individual pseudorandom bits and counting accepting runs within logarithmic space. With constant error small enough to preserve the acceptance gap, this would prove L=BPL. The card asks for a uniform generator, which is a particular strong route to that complexity-class equality.

Nisan’s construction gives seed length O(log n·log(nw/ε)). For polynomial width and constant error this is O(log²n), so reaching the target would remove an entire logarithmic factor. The difficulty is generating a universally useful sample space in little space, rather than merely showing that some sample space exists. Even considerable improvements for simpler transition structures need not survive arbitrary merging of states.

Weighted pseudorandom generators relax the distribution requirement. They approximate acceptance by a weighted sum of program evaluations, with weights that may be negative. Hoza’s RANDOM 2021 construction attains seed length O(log²n+log(1/ε)) for width-n, length-n programs, improving the dependence on small error. Such weighted estimates can support deterministic simulation, but negative mass cannot be sampled as an ordinary probability distribution over the generated strings.

Cheng and Wu’s SODA 2026 work improves weighted generators across width and error regimes. Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma’s May 2026 revision improves error reduction and the dependence on the input alphabet. It still constructs a weighted object. title: Does deterministic logarithmic space equal bounded-error randomized logarithmic space?
importance_reason: A central derandomization question with a resource regime and known techniques distinct from P=BPP. Specialist work on space-bounded pseudorandomness, including 2026 weighted-generator results, documents continuing interest. The class equality merits a full card even alongside a more specific generator-construction target.
formal: Is L=BPL? Equivalently, for every language S⊆{0,1}* decided with two-sided error at most 1/3 by a uniform randomized Turing machine using O(log(n+2)) work space and polynomial time on inputs of length n, is there a uniform deterministic Turing machine deciding S with O(log(n+2)) work space?
definitions: The machines have a finite description, a read-only two-way input tape, and a fixed finite number of work tapes over a fixed finite alphabet. Space counts all visited work-tape cells; the input tape is excluded. A randomized machine receives independent fair coin outcomes one at a time, without a freely rereadable random tape: an outcome must be stored in counted work space to be remembered. It halts with ACCEPT or REJECT on every input and every random tape within K(n+2)^c steps and uses at most K log_2(n+2) work cells, for some constants K,c depending only on the machine. For each input x, acceptance probability is at least 2/3 if x∈S and at most 1/3 if x∉S. This is a language problem with no promise excluding intermediate-probability inputs. A deterministic decider must halt and give the correct answer on every input; any halting deterministic logarithmic-space decider has polynomially many configurations and hence polynomial running time. Both classes are uniform and have no advice. The deterministic machine and its space constant may depend on S. The equality does not demand a computable compiler transforming arbitrary machine descriptions, nor a particular pseudorandom-generator construction.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.
context:
A logarithmic-space computation can maintain indices and counters while remembering only a small part of the input. Randomness lets it explore many possible choices without storing all of them. The equality asks whether this apparent extra power disappears when the required output is only a bounded-error decision about the input.

The memory convention is central. Fresh random outcomes can be read once; a machine cannot revisit an arbitrarily long random string without paying for its storage or reconstructing it. Conversely, the deterministic simulator is allowed a different constant in its logarithmic-space bound. The question concerns equality of language classes, not identical execution traces.

Saks and Zhou gave a deterministic simulation using O(log^(3/2) n) space. Hoza improved the bound to O(log^(3/2) n / sqrt(log log n)), with the expression understood asymptotically. These bounds are substantially below squared logarithmic space but remain above a constant multiple of log n.

The 2026 work of Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma improves error reduction for weighted pseudorandom generators. Its revised account distinguishes weighted generators from ordinary generators and attributes the relevant arity/error connection to Cheng and Hoza. Those parameter improvements do not establish the equality of classes asked here.

The catalogue separately contains a concrete optimal-generator problem for read-once branching programs. Such a construction can have consequences for logarithmic-space derandomization, but the language-class equality does not prescribe that particular construction. This completed card retains the original TCS-0026 identity and Wigderson reference while making the computation and error models explicit.
why: Determine whether randomness increases decision power when only logarithmic work space is available.

title: Optimal deterministic restricted-isometry matrices
importance_reason: An optimal derandomization problem connecting compressed sensing, pseudorandomness, additive combinatorics and explicit geometric constructions.
formal: Do there exist universal constants C,B,b>0 and a deterministic algorithm which, for every pair of integers N≥2 and 2≤s≤N, outputs in at most B N^b bit operations a rational m×N matrix A, with m≤C s ln(eN/s), such that (2/3)‖x‖₂²≤‖Ax‖₂²≤(4/3)‖x‖₂² for every real vector x∈ℝ^N with at most s nonzero coordinates?
definitions: The input consists of N and s in binary. The output is an explicit list of all entries of A, each encoded as a signed integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary. Its total encoding length must also be at most B N^b. Time is ordinary deterministic Turing-machine bit complexity, polynomial in N; randomness, advice and unit-cost exact real arithmetic are unavailable. The row count m is a positive integer chosen by the algorithm. The same constants and algorithm work for all allowed pairs N,s. The norm is Euclidean, and the displayed inequalities concern squared norms. They define restricted isometry of order s and distortion δ=1/3. The condition must hold simultaneously for every support of size at most s and every real choice of coefficients on that support. No probability over supports or signals is permitted. The natural logarithm and the factor e ensure a nonzero expression when s is close to N. The omitted case s=1 is trivial and can be handled by a single row of ones.
answer_criterion: Give a deterministic algorithm satisfying all the uniform dimension, encoding, time and restricted-isometry requirements, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A negative result conditional on a complexity assumption must state it. An existence proof, a construction using random bits, success for most sparse signals, or a deterministic construction with a larger asymptotic row count does not settle the stated question.
context:
Suppose an unknown vector has N coordinates but only s of them matter. A measurement matrix replaces the vector by m linear measurements. Sparsity allows m to be much smaller than N, but the matrix must preserve every possible sparse direction if the measuring device is to work uniformly. The question asks whether a short, guaranteed measurement design can be computed without random choices.

The restricted-isometry requirement has a concrete spectral interpretation. For every set S of at most s column indices, all eigenvalues of A_SᵀA_S must lie between 2/3 and 4/3. Thus columns must behave almost orthogonally in every small group. Checking only individual column lengths, only pairs of columns, or a large collection of sampled test vectors leaves many of these simultaneous constraints untested.

This condition supports stable sparse recovery. If a matrix has restricted isometry of order 2t with distortion 1/3, then two different t-sparse signals cannot have identical measurements: their difference has at most 2t nonzero coordinates. Standard recovery theorems also give robust reconstruction by ℓ₁ minimization. The distinction between order t and order 2t is necessary; injectivity for t-sparse differences alone would not compare arbitrary t-sparse signals.

Random independent Bernoulli or Gaussian matrices attain m=O(s log(eN/s)) for fixed distortion, and matching row lower bounds make this the optimal order for s≥2. Rao’s paper summarizes this benchmark and improves the amount of randomness needed to attain it. The unresolved resource in the card is therefore deterministic construction time, rather than whether matrices with the desired geometric property exist.

Requiring rational output does not destroy the random benchmark. For example, choose the number of rows to be a perfect square t² within a constant factor of a sufficiently large target value, and use independent entries ±1/t. This keeps the usual normalized Bernoulli construction while giving an exact, short binary description of every entry. The real difficulty is choosing all the signs deterministically with a proof that every sparse direction is preserved.

One basic deterministic analysis bounds the coherence μ, the largest absolute inner product between two unit columns. Gershgorin’s theorem then gives restricted-isometry constant at most (s−1)μ. When μ is about 1/√m, this argument certifies only s on the order of √m. This is a limitation of that sufficient-condition analysis, commonly called the square-root bottleneck, rather than an impossibility theorem for deterministic matrices.

Bourgain, Dilworth, Ford, Konyagin and Kutzarova broke that bottleneck in a restricted parameter regime. Their explicit construction uses additive-combinatorial and exponential-sum estimates to control interactions beyond pairwise coherence. It is a major proof that deterministic analysis can go further, but its small exponent improvement does not reach the optimal s log(eN/s) row count uniformly in N and s.

Rao’s construction achieves the optimal row order with O(s log(N/s) log s) random bits in the sparse parameter regime discussed in the paper. Its proof extends the Hanson–Wright inequality to biased distributions. Reducing the seed length makes progress toward explicit construction, but enumerating all seeds can still take far more than polynomial time, and recognizing a successful seed is a separate issue.

The inherited 2025 paper of Fickus and Lake studies highly symmetric equiangular tight frames, which minimize coherence. It analyzes their minimal dependent column sets through regular simplices and designs. Such structure is informative in both directions: a dependent set of r columns immediately prevents restricted isometry of order r with distortion less than one. Optimal pairwise geometry alone does not guarantee the higher-order property.

For a simple illustration, the m+1 unit vertices of a regular simplex in ℝ^m have small and equal pairwise inner products, yet their sum is zero. Their coefficient vector of all ones is therefore a nonzero sparse kernel vector. The example explains why an attractive frame construction must be accompanied by control over all relevant column subsets, not just a calculation of coherence.

The all-parameter formulation also matters. The identity matrix handles s comparable to N, while many explicit algebraic constructions work only along particular dimension sequences or for specified sparsity ranges. A resolution must cover the intermediate sparse regimes with one polynomial-time procedure. Likewise, statistical recovery guarantees and ℓ₁-norm versions of restricted isometry answer different geometric questions.
why: A central gap between random existence and efficient explicit construction, with direct consequences for uniform sparse recovery and for how pseudorandomness controls exponentially many spectral constraints.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No polynomial-time deterministic construction with the required uniform optimal row bound was found in the checked sources. Optimal randomized row counts, restricted parameter regimes and coherence guarantees are recorded as partial progress.
progress: 2010–2011: Bourgain and coauthors give explicit RIP matrices beyond the coherence-based square-root bottleneck in a restricted parameter range. | 2013: Bandeira–Fickus–Mixon–Wong compare deterministic verification methods and formulate frame-based routes toward stronger constructions. | 2023–2025: Rao obtains optimal row counts with fewer random bits; the December 2024 revision appeared in Information Processing Letters 189 (2025), article 106553. | July–December 2025: Fickus–Lake’s revised and published frame results describe minimal dependencies in doubly transitive equiangular tight frames; their introduction still identifies optimal deterministic RIP construction as open.
working_summary: A restricted-isometry matrix approximately preserves the Euclidean length of every sparse vector. The reviewed question asks for deterministic polynomial-time construction with O(s log(eN/s)) rows and fixed distortion. Random matrices achieve this row order, but a usable deterministic construction must control every sparse support simultaneously. Optimal explicit matrices would provide guaranteed measurement designs for compressed sensing without random setup choices. The saved review identifies the limitations of pairwise coherence analyses and notes that reduced randomness or success on typical signals does not establish the requested all-signal guarantee.

title: Is k-Clique fixed-parameter tractable, equivalently FPT=W[1]?
importance_reason: The defining unresolved tractability separation of parameterized complexity, with Clique as a precise and widely used complete problem.
focus_reason: The defining unresolved tractability separation of parameterized complexity, with Clique as a precise and widely used complete problem.
formal: Do there exist a total computable function f:ℕ→ℕ, a constant c, and one deterministic algorithm that decides whether an n-vertex graph contains a k-clique in time at most f(k)(n+2)ᶜ on every input? Equivalently, is FPT=W[1]?
definitions: An instance is a finite simple undirected graph G on [n], encoded by its adjacency matrix, and an integer k with 0≤k≤n, encoded in binary. A k-clique is a set of k distinct vertices for which every pair is an edge; k=0 is a yes-instance. Inputs with k>n are rejected immediately, and other malformed inputs are rejected. The parameter is k, not treewidth, degree, or the size of a supplied decomposition. Running time counts deterministic Turing-machine steps on the full input. Constants and the function f may be arbitrary but must be fixed independently of n; the exponent c must also be independent of k. FPT comprises parameterized decision problems solvable in f(k)Nᶜ time, where N is their input encoding length. One equivalent definition of W[1] is the class of parameterized problems reducible to k-Clique by a deterministic f(k)Nᶜ-time many-one reduction whose output parameter is bounded by a computable function of k alone. This is the standard parameterized reduction convention under which Clique is W[1]-complete. No randomness, advice, or promise about G is allowed.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, 2^{2^k}n³ meets the requested form, while n^{k/10} does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If P=NP then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus FPT≠W[1] is a stronger separation conjecture than P≠NP in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every W[1] problem in FPT time. This is why a W[1]-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out f(k)n^{o(k)} algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is W[1]-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove FPT≠W[1].
why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.
status_note: Explicitly presented as the central open conjecture in Bottesch’s primary paper and the parameterized-algorithms textbook. Research through 10 September 2026 located no proof of equality or separation. Conditional lower bounds and improved fixed-k algorithms are recorded with their distinct quantifiers.

title: Does deterministic 3-SAT have a positive optimal exponential rate?
importance_reason: A foundational quantitative hardness hypothesis underlying exact, parameterized, graph, and geometric algorithm lower bounds.
focus_reason: A foundational quantitative hardness hypothesis underlying exact, parameterized, graph, and geometric algorithm lower bounds.
formal: Is there a constant c>0 such that, for every deterministic algorithm A that correctly decides every 3-CNF satisfiability instance, and every constant d≥0, A does not have worst-case running time O(2^{cn}L^d)? Here n is the number of variables and L is the full binary input length. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH).
definitions: A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of explicitly listed clauses, each containing at most three literals xᵢ or ¬xᵢ. Satisfiability means existence of a Boolean assignment satisfying all clauses. Variables are relabeled consecutively; n counts the distinct variables actually present, and L includes all literal indices, signs, delimiters, and repetitions. An empty clause is unsatisfiable and an empty conjunction is satisfiable. Algorithms are uniform deterministic Turing machines with no advice or oracles; they must halt and answer exactly on all inputs, with no promise about density, solution count, or distribution. Define s₃=inf{α≥0 : some such algorithm runs in O(2^{αn}L^d) for a fixed d}. ETH asserts s₃>0. The excluded exponent c is a single constant independent of the algorithm. The polynomial exponent and hidden constant may depend on the algorithm, but not the instance. Polynomial input factors allow the complete formula to be read even if clauses are repeated many times. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
NP-completeness describes the possibility of polynomial-time algorithms and does not itself impose a positive exponential rate. Even if P differs from NP, a running time such as 2^{√n} remains possible for 3-SAT. ETH asks for a stronger obstruction: some fixed amount of exponential work must remain unavoidable when complexity is measured by the number of Boolean choices.

That parameter must be preserved carefully by a reduction. An ordinary polynomial-time reduction may turn an n-variable formula into an instance of size n³, which can destroy a claimed exponential lower bound in the new parameter. Sparsification supplies a controlled disjunction of bounded-density formulas, allowing variables and clauses to be related without an arbitrary polynomial blowup. This is a main reason ETH can support sharp bounds across many problems.

The infimum over all algorithms matters. Excluding one 2^{o(n)} algorithm is the common informal wording, but the textbook explicitly keeps the stronger positive-infimum statement because the converse is unclear. ETH would be false if arbitrarily small constant exponents were attainable, even if the known algorithms depended on the desired exponent. A card that omitted this distinction would change the quantified question.

There are substantial deterministic improvements over trying all 2ⁿ assignments. Liu combines branching with derandomized local search to obtain a 1.32793ⁿ bound for 3-SAT, up to polynomial factors. Such an algorithm decreases an upper bound on s₃ while leaving it positive. Empirical solver success, promises of many solutions, and bounded-occurrence restrictions do not address worst-case unrestricted formulas.

ETH is weaker than SETH, whose optimal rates approach one as the fixed clause width grows. It also differs from randomized ETH and from Gap-ETH, which asks for hardness of distinguishing fully satisfiable formulas from formulas with a constant unsatisfied fraction. Recent lattice reductions illustrate the value of tracking these distinctions: some approximation hardness can be obtained from deterministic ETH, while other results use randomized ETH. They extend the consequences of assumptions without proving the assumptions.
why: ETH is the central hypothesis for ruling out subexponential exact algorithms and many fixed-parameter speedups. It turns the qualitative P versus NP question into a quantitative claim that can be transferred through carefully sized reductions.
status_note: The cited foundational and 2026 conference sources treat ETH as an open hypothesis. Checked through 10 September 2026. This formulation is uniform, deterministic, and a positive-infimum assertion; randomized, nonuniform, gap, and stronger all-width hypotheses are distinct.

title: Can general weighted TSP be solved in O*((2−ε)^n) time?
importance_reason: A central exact-algorithm question with a sixty-year base-two barrier and a modern improvement that carefully distinguishes prefactor from exponent. It is separate from metric TSP approximation and from Hamiltonian-cycle detection.
formal: Do there exist constants ε∈(0,1), c≥1 and a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every complete undirected graph on n≥3 labelled vertices with nonnegative binary-encoded integer edge weights of total encoding length L, outputs a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle with probability at least 2/3 in worst-case time O((2−ε)^n(n+L)^c)?
definitions: Each unordered pair of distinct vertices has one explicitly listed weight. A Hamiltonian cycle visits each vertex exactly once before returning to its first vertex, and its weight is the sum of its n edge weights. Output the cyclic list of vertex labels. The input has no metric, bounded-weight, planarity or sparsity promise. Use a random-access word RAM with w=B⌈n+log₂(L+2)⌉ bits per word for one fixed sufficiently large integer B; unit-cost operations are reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo 2^w and integer division by nonzero words. Integers occupying several words incur the cost of all word operations. This word size permits addressing exponential-space subset tables; its polynomial bit-operation overhead is already permitted by the polynomial factor in n+L. The running-time bound includes reading weights, preprocessing, random bits and output and holds on every execution. Only independent private fair random bits are allowed; there is no quantum access, advice or oracle. The constants ε,c,B and the implicit multiplicative constant are independent of n,L and the weights. A deterministic algorithm also qualifies. Dependence polynomial in the numerical maximum weight, rather than its binary length, does not qualify.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
context:
The exact travelling salesman problem asks for a cheapest tour through all vertices. In the general weighted setting, discovering a Hamiltonian cycle is not enough: the input is complete, so tours certainly exist, but their costs can vary greatly. The computational target is the minimum among them.

The classical subset dynamic program has a base-two dependence on the number of vertices. Stoian’s 2024 algorithm improves the familiar O(2^n n²) time by a factor 2^{Ω(√log n)}. Its bound retains the exponential base two and does not yield O*((2−ε)^n) for any fixed positive ε.

This distinction is substantial even though both bounds are exponential. A fixed base reduction saves an exponential factor on increasingly large instances, whereas savings in the polynomial or subexponential prefactor do not. The card asks about unrestricted classical algorithms, not about the optimality of the original dynamic-programming recurrence.

Weight encoding separates this target from several related exact questions. A method whose time is polynomial in the maximum integer weight can be very expensive when a large weight has a short binary representation. Likewise, faster algorithms for unweighted Hamiltonicity or for special weighted graph classes do not establish the general weighted guarantee.

No asserted reduction from SETH is built into the question. The desired algorithmic existence is itself the target; a conditional lower bound must state its assumption separately. The Parameterized and exact algorithms bucket is appropriate because the defining issue is the exponential dependence on n, rather than polynomial-time approximation of a tour.
why: Locate the fundamental exponential-time cost of exact weighted routing beyond the long-standing subset barrier.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No fixed classical exponential-base improvement for general binary-weighted TSP was found; polynomial-factor improvements and quantum algorithms are different guarantees.

title: Constant-factor approximation for Densest k-Subgraph
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A flagship approximation problem with a simple objective, a large algorithmic gap, strong conditional and relaxation barriers, and consequences for several other optimization problems.
focus_reason: A flagship approximation problem with a simple objective, a large algorithmic gap, strong conditional and relaxation barriers, and consequences for several other optimization problems.
formal: Do there exist a universal constant C≥1 and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm A such that, for every finite simple undirected unweighted graph G=(V,E) and every integer 1≤k≤|V|, A(G,k) outputs a set S⊆V with |S|=k and |E(G[S])|≥OPT(G,k)/C, where OPT(G,k)=max_{T⊆V, |T|=k}|E(G[T])|?
definitions: G is explicitly represented by its vertices and edges, and k is supplied in binary as part of the input. G[S] contains all edges of G with both endpoints in S; loops and parallel edges are absent. The running time is polynomial in the full input length with a fixed exponent independent of k. The same finite C must work for all graphs, all graph sizes and all choices of k; it cannot increase with n=|V| or with k. The output must be a vertex set, not only an estimate of the optimum. When OPT=0, every k-set meets the requirement. Because all feasible sets have the same cardinality, maximizing edge count, average degree 2|E(G[S])|/k, or edges per selected vertex gives the same approximation objective. No promise of a clique, graph expansion, metric edge weights or a random input distribution is supplied. This card fixes deterministic algorithms; a randomized constant-factor guarantee would be major progress but has a distinct derandomization requirement. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The task asks for a fixed-size collection of vertices containing as many internal interactions as possible. The cardinality restriction is what turns an otherwise tractable density objective into a central approximation problem. Without a prescribed size, maximizing edges per vertex can be solved in polynomial time. Allowing at least k vertices also changes which solutions compete: a large moderately dense region may be a valid answer even when no comparably useful k-vertex portion can be extracted.

Exact optimization contains CLIQUE: a graph has a k-clique precisely when OPT(G,k)=k(k−1)/2. This observation alone gives almost no multiplicative approximation gap. A k-set missing only one possible edge is nearly optimal as k grows, even though it is not a clique. To rule out a constant-factor algorithm, a reduction must create a substantial separation between the best densities of its YES and NO instances, not merely a one-edge difference.

Bhaskara, Charikar, Chlamtac, Feige and Vijayaraghavan achieve O(n^(1/4+ε)) approximation in n^O(1/ε) time for every fixed ε>0. Their method uses small tree patterns and a hierarchy of conditioned information to identify a dense region. The O(n^(1/4)) phrase in the paper’s title needs care: attaining that endpoint in their analysis takes quasipolynomial n^O(log n) time. Neither rate is a constant approximation.

There is substantial evidence against the target. Manurangsi proves that ETH rules out even approximation within n^(1/(log log n)^a), for a universal constant a>0. ETH asserts that 3SAT has no 2^o(N)-time algorithm on N variables. This is a stronger assumption than P≠NP; the result therefore already excludes every fixed constant under ETH, while leaving the weaker-assumption hardness problem unresolved. Its YES instances can contain a k-clique, a property called perfect completeness.

Semidefinite-programming lower bounds supply a different kind of evidence. Bhaskara, Charikar, Guruswami, Vijayaraghavan and Zhou construct polynomial integrality gaps for strong hierarchies of relaxations. A relaxation can assign a large fractional or vector-valued objective even when no genuine k-set has comparable density. Such a gap limits approximation guarantees obtained from that relaxation, but it is not a theorem excluding every polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm.

Chuzhoy, Dalirrooyfard, Grinberg and Tan propose a 2-CSP hardness conjecture that would imply NP-hardness of approximating Densest k-Subgraph within 2^((log n)^ε) for some ε>0. Their paper also connects its approximability to graph partitioning, dense coloring and bounded-crossing subgraphs. Some connections use quasipolynomial reductions, so they should not be read as constant-factor polynomial-time equivalences. The conjectural premise remains a real part of the hardness claim.

Laekhanukit, Manurangsi and Trabelsi’s May 2026 paper still reports that no NP-hardness of approximation is known for Densest k-Subgraph even at factor 1.001. They show that the absence of any constant-factor DkS algorithm implies a (3/2−ε) barrier for the at-least-k density problem. This transfers a hypothetical negative answer to a neighboring objective; the neighboring problem’s known 2-approximation does not answer this card.

An AAAI 2026 result by Liu, Liu, Ma and Konar gives an exact continuous penalization reformulation and an efficient nonconvex proximal-gradient method. Exactness concerns the relationship between optima of the formulations. It does not mean the method finds a global optimum, or even a fixed approximation ratio, on every graph in polynomial time. The distinction explains how useful practical progress can coexist with the unresolved worst-case guarantee.
why: Densest k-Subgraph is a basic test of how well algorithms can identify a concentrated combinatorial structure. Its unresolved approximation landscape influences many reductions and separates strong evidence of difficulty from the hardness consequences currently obtainable from P≠NP.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The constant-factor algorithm is already ruled out assuming ETH, which remains unproved. The May 2026 primary source explicitly notes the absence of NP-hardness of approximation even at factor 1.001. This card asks about a deterministic constant-factor algorithm on all unweighted graphs, and preserves the distinction between conditional evidence and an unconditional resolution.

The target is a polynomial-time algorithm whose edge count stays within one universal constant of optimum. Fixing the number of vertices prevents using a larger, moderately dense region as a substitute. Such a guarantee would clarify a central gap in approximation theory and influence several related network problems. The saved review describes strong conditional hardness under ETH, while distinguishing this evidence from hardness based only on P≠NP.

title: Unique Games: is near-satisfiability NP-hard to distinguish from low value?
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: An organizing conjecture for approximation thresholds, with consequences for whole families of constraint satisfaction problems and strong connections to SDP algorithms, PCPs, and analysis.
focus_reason: An organizing conjecture for approximation thresholds, with consequences for whole families of constraint satisfaction problems and strong connections to SDP algorithms, PCPs, and analysis.
formal: For every pair of rational constants ε,δ>0 with ε+δ<1, does there exist an integer q≥2 such that it is NP-hard to distinguish Unique Games instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\varepsilon$ from instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\le\delta$? Here q is the alphabet size, fixed independently of the input graph, and val(G) is the largest fraction of constraints simultaneously satisfied by any labeling.
definitions: An instance has finitely many vertices and a nonempty explicit list E of directed edges between distinct vertices; repeated edges are allowed and counted separately. Every vertex receives a label in [q]={1,…,q}. An edge e=(u,v) carries an explicitly given permutation π_e:[q]→[q] and is satisfied exactly when π_e(ℓ(u))=ℓ(v). Thus val(G)=max_ℓ |{e satisfied by ℓ}|/|E|. There are no graph expansion or degree promises. NP-hardness means a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3SAT mapping every satisfiable formula into the ≥1−ε case and every unsatisfiable formula into the ≤δ case. The reduction, its running-time exponent, and q may depend on ε,δ. Inputs with value strictly between the thresholds are outside the promise. The question is the NP-hardness proposition itself; P≠NP is needed when drawing the usual conclusion that no polynomial-time distinguishing algorithm exists. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Each constraint is locally simple: fixing either endpoint label determines exactly one compatible label at the other endpoint. Exact satisfiability of all constraints is decidable in polynomial time. Allowing a small fraction of constraints to fail changes the question sharply.

The conjecture says that an instance admitting an almost perfect assignment can nevertheless be hard to distinguish from one where every assignment fails almost everywhere. These are two promised regimes, rather than a request to compute the exact optimum. The alphabet is allowed to grow as the desired gap becomes more demanding. Indeed, a uniformly random labeling satisfies a 1/q fraction in expectation, so a soundness threshold below 1/q is impossible.

Raghavendra’s theorem connects such reductions to a general semidefinite-programming framework: under UGC, that framework achieves the approximation thresholds of fixed finite-domain constraint satisfaction problems, to arbitrary constant accuracy.

The strongest relevant hardness milestone must be read with its completeness parameter. The 2-to-2 Games Theorem implies hardness for Unique Games with value at least one half versus arbitrarily small value. It does not make the yes instances almost perfectly satisfiable. Raising completeness from one half to arbitrarily close to one is precisely a remaining gap relevant to this card.

Algorithmic progress also matters even when it is slower than polynomial time. Subexponential algorithms exploit spectral decompositions of the constraint graph, limiting what quantitative hardness reductions could establish. Because a polynomial reduction can enlarge the instance by a parameter-dependent power, these algorithms coexist with the NP-hardness conjecture.
why: UGC would turn many conditional approximation thresholds into NP-hardness theorems and explain the optimality of a general SDP framework. Its very simple permutation constraints isolate a fundamental boundary between exact consistency, approximate consistency, and hardness amplification.
status_note: The 2025 journal account distinguishes the proved 2-to-2 theorem from full UGC. No resolution of the quantified near-one-completeness statement was located in the primary-source search through 10 September 2026.

Under UGC, its achievable thresholds are optimal up to any fixed accuracy, unless P=NP. | 2010: Arora, Barak, and Steurer give, for an absolute α>0, an exp(q n^(ε^α))-time algorithm finding a (1−ε^α)-satisfying labeling in a (1−ε)-satisfiable q-label instance on n vertices. title: A polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation for Directed Steiner Tree
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A central approximation problem encompassing covering and rooted network design, with a persistent gap between polynomial and quasipolynomial algorithms.
formal: Do there exist constants a≥1 and C≥1 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every feasible Directed Steiner Tree instance with k terminals, outputs a feasible subgraph of cost at most a(log₂(k+2))^C times optimum with probability at least 2/3?
definitions: An instance consists of a finite directed graph G=(V,E), a root r∈V, a nonempty terminal set T⊆V∖{r} with k=|T|, and nonnegative rational arc costs c_e given exactly in binary. Every terminal is promised reachable from r; this can also be checked in polynomial time, with infeasibility reported otherwise. A feasible solution is an arc subset F⊆E such that (V,F) contains a directed path from r to every t∈T. Its cost is Σ_{e∈F}c_e, counting an arc once even if many paths use it. OPT is the minimum such cost. The algorithm must output a feasible subset on every execution and satisfy the approximation guarantee on every instance with probability at least 2/3 over its internal randomness. Its bit running time on every execution is bounded by one fixed polynomial in the entire input encoding length, including cost bits. The constants a,C and the polynomial are independent of n=|V|, k and the costs. If OPT=0, the successful output must also have zero cost. Local computation is ordinary uniform classical computation without advice or free optimization oracles. There is no planarity, acyclicity, bounded depth, bounded treewidth, metric, or supplied fractional-solution promise. The word tree refers to the optimization problem: any feasible subgraph may be returned, and redundant edges can be removed.
answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm and fixed constants satisfying these bounds, or prove that no such randomized polynomial-time algorithm exists. An O(k^ε)-approximation for every separately fixed ε>0, a polylogarithmic approximation taking quasipolynomial time, or a guarantee on a restricted graph class is partial progress. A gap for a particular LP relaxation limits that relaxation, not every algorithm. A hardness result ruling out only some smaller powers of log k does not exclude all fixed powers and therefore does not refute this proposition.
context:
The problem asks how cheaply a root can reach many destinations through one shared directed network. Buying a common initial segment can save cost across many root-to-terminal paths, but the directions restrict which branching structures are usable. With one terminal the problem is shortest path. With many terminals, selecting where the paths should share infrastructure becomes the central optimization challenge.

A simple reduction explains why ordinary reachability is insufficient. For a set-cover instance, create a vertex for each set and each element, an arc of cost one from the root to every set vertex, and zero-cost arcs from each set to its elements. Make all element vertices terminals. A feasible network must buy a collection of set arcs covering all elements, and its cost equals the number of chosen sets. The directed graph can thus encode a nontrivial covering problem even with only two layers after the root.

The familiar polynomial-time approximation frontier is O(k^ε) for every fixed ε>0, from the classical directed Steiner algorithms. The running-time exponent depends on the chosen accuracy parameter. Setting ε to a quantity that shrinks with k is not a free improvement: it changes that dependence and can produce quasipolynomial time. A power of k, however small and fixed, eventually exceeds every fixed power of log k.

Grandoni, Laekhanukit and Li obtain an O(log² k/log log k)-approximation in quasipolynomial time. Their techniques combine a structured reduction with a hierarchy of strengthened linear relaxations and dependent rounding. This establishes that a good approximation exists at a slower time scale. The requested advance is to achieve some polylogarithmic factor with a fixed polynomial running-time exponent; matching the sharper quasipolynomial factor is not required.

The same work gives near-matching quasipolynomial-time hardness under additional complexity assumptions, including the Projection Games Conjecture. This does not show that every polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation is impossible: a larger fixed logarithmic power is allowed in this card. The issue is a gap between what can currently be computed in polynomial time and what is known with more time, rather than the already settled hardness of exact optimization.

A natural flow relaxation buys a fractional capacity x_e for each arc and, separately for each terminal, sends a unit flow from the root using at most x_e on that arc. Different terminals may reuse the same purchased capacity because a network edge is bought once. In general graphs this relaxation has polynomial-size integrality gaps, including Ω(√k) examples. Those examples explain why a straightforward LP-rounding strategy cannot guarantee a polylogarithmic factor against that relaxation on every instance. They do not rule out stronger relaxations or a different algorithm.

The inherited Laekhanukit reference requires careful version tracking. Its December 2024 general claim was withdrawn in version 2. Version 3, submitted in October 2025, presents itself as a rectification restricted to a relatively integral fractional solution: each terminal flow on an edge is either zero or the entire purchased capacity. The record still displays the earlier withdrawal comment about a reachability-proof error. This card treats the later restricted statement as a reported claim, not an established general approximation; finding an appropriate fractional solution is an additional requirement.

Planarity changes the picture substantially. Friggstad and Mousavi give a polynomial-time O(log k)-approximation for planar directed graphs, using shortest-path separators. Later work extends the structural approach to other rooted planar network-design problems and bounds a natural planar LP gap by O(log² k). These theorems show that directedness alone does not preclude the requested factor, but their separator arguments do not apply to arbitrary directed graphs.

Chekuri and Jain’s July 2026 work extends planar results to length-constrained network design. Its guarantees are bicriteria: they approximate cost while allowing an O(log k) multiplicative violation of the path-length constraint. The paper explicitly retains the general Directed Steiner Tree approximation question as open. Removing a length constraint or changing the objective does not remove the planarity hypothesis needed by those algorithms.
why: A defining gap in directed network-design approximation: determine whether a shared directed connection network can be approximated within a polylogarithmic factor using only polynomial time.
status_note: The July 2026 primary literature explicitly leaves this general-graph question open. The inherited 2024 claim was withdrawn, and its October 2025 replacement is restricted to a special supplied fractional solution; that claim is not counted as an established general result. Planar and quasipolynomial algorithms do not satisfy this card. Checked through 11 September 2026.

working_summary: Directed Steiner Tree seeks a minimum-cost directed network connecting one root to every required terminal. The question asks for randomized polynomial-time approximation within a fixed power of the logarithm of the terminal count. Sharing arcs between routes can save substantially, but directionality complicates selecting useful branching structures. A positive result would close a major gap between polynomial-time algorithms and stronger guarantees obtainable in quasipolynomial time. The saved review warns that choosing a shrinking parameter in existing power-factor algorithms can destroy their polynomial running time.

title: The 4/3 conjecture for the metric TSP subtour relaxation
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A defining integrality-gap conjecture in combinatorial optimization with consequences for LP rounding and the limits of metric TSP approximation methods.
formal: Let Γ=sup_{n≥3,c} OPT_TSP(c)/OPT_LP(c), where c ranges over all metrics on n labeled points and OPT_LP is the subtour relaxation defined below. Is Γ=4/3?
definitions: For V={1,…,n} and E={{u,v}:u≠v}, a metric has c_uu=0, c_uv=c_vu>0 for u≠v, and c_uv≤c_uw+c_wv. Costs are arbitrary real numbers; no Euclidean embedding is assumed. OPT_TSP is the minimum sum of edge costs on a Hamiltonian cycle of the complete undirected graph. For S⊆V, δ(S) contains edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and x(F)=Σ_{e∈F}x_e. Define OPT_LP=min Σ_e c_e x_e subject to x(δ({v}))=2 for every v, x(δ(S))≥2 for every nonempty proper S⊊V, and 0≤x_e≤1 for every e. The LP is feasible and has positive optimum. The supremum ranges over every finite size, not one fixed n. This is the symmetric metric subtour-LP integrality gap, not an approximation ratio measured only against OPT_TSP, an asymmetric TSP relaxation, or a restricted geometric metric.
answer_criterion: Known constructions establish Γ≥4/3. Thus an affirmative resolution proves OPT_TSP(c)≤(4/3)OPT_LP(c) for every finite metric instance. A negative resolution gives an instance with ratio strictly greater than 4/3, or proves such an instance exists. A supremum need not be attained to make the question meaningful. Improving an algorithm’s upper bound while it remains above 4/3 is progress, not a resolution.
context:
The relaxation allows fractional edge purchases while retaining two elementary properties of every tour: each vertex has degree two, and every nontrivial cut is crossed at least twice. It therefore knows much more than a disconnected cycle-cover relaxation, but its feasible points need not be convex combinations of Hamiltonian cycles. The conjecture asks for the exact worst loss caused by that remaining freedom.

For example, a feasible fractional vector may put positive weight on several alternative connections at one vertex without choosing a single predecessor and successor. The cut inequalities ensure aggregate connectivity, yet they do not force these local choices to assemble into one integral cycle. The proposed factor 4/3 says that, in a metric, repairing all such inconsistencies never costs more than one third of the fractional optimum.

The metric assumption is what makes shortcutting possible. If a connected Eulerian multigraph visits a vertex several times, replacing a detour by the direct edge between its endpoints does not increase cost. One can consequently search for a suitably cheap Eulerian structure rather than construct a Hamiltonian cycle at every intermediate step. This observation explains why spanning trees and parity correction recur in approximation algorithms for the problem.

A minimum spanning tree followed by a minimum-cost matching on its odd-degree vertices yields the classical 3/2 guarantee. Wolsey’s analysis measures both components against the LP: the tree costs at most the fractional optimum, and the matching at most half that value. The inherited July 2026 paper recalls this argument before studying a particular randomized refinement.

An algorithmic ratio and an integrality-gap ratio must use the correct denominator. A guarantee cost≤α·OPT_TSP does not establish OPT_TSP≤α·OPT_LP, since the fractional optimum can be smaller. Karlin–Klein–Oveis Gharan’s FOCS 2022 result explicitly supplies an LP-relative guarantee below 3/2, extending the earlier approximation breakthrough. It is this later theorem that directly improves the general gap bound.

The modern approach samples a spanning tree from a distribution constrained by fractional edge marginals, then corrects its parity. Tree cost and parity-repair cost interact, so treating the two separately can lose the desired saving. Gurvits–Klein–Leake strengthen probability estimates using capacities of real stable polynomials. Their Lemma 4.5 is explicitly LP-relative and yields the certified bound Γ≤3/2−2.18·10^{−34}. The small constant reflects a worst-case proof, not a claim that practical tours are that close to 3/2.

A class can have a better integrality gap than the worst ratio of a particular algorithm on it. Jin–Klein–Williamson prove the 4/3 bound for half-integral cycle-cut instances using a specialized construction. Half-integral means that nonzero fractional coordinates are 1/2 or 1, with an additional restriction on the hierarchy of tight cuts. This result does not cover every half-integral instance, still less every subtour solution.

Their July 2026 paper, which supplied the inherited reference, proves a 10/7 guarantee for the maximum-entropy algorithm on that same restricted class. Since 10/7 exceeds 4/3, it improves understanding of the chosen algorithm rather than improving the already-known class gap. The authors also identify examples giving a lower bound of 11/8 on the algorithm’s performance. Such an algorithm-specific obstruction cannot refute the conjecture about the cheapest possible tour.

Two complementary approaches restrict the fractional solution in other ways. Villa–Vercesi–Barta–Mastrolilli prove the 4/3 bound when an optimal solution has at most n+6 nonzero components, combining structural reasoning and computation. This is a support-size condition, not a theorem for every instance on at most n+6 vertices. Larger support remains outside its stated guarantee.

Cook–Hougardy–Petrich’s September 8, 2026 revision reports exact verification for all metric instances through n=16 and for half-integral extreme points through n=18. It also repairs omissions in earlier extreme-point lists. This is stronger evidence than sampling finitely many random metrics, because the computation organizes the relevant polyhedral cases. It still leaves unbounded n, and the catalogue has not rerun that enumeration.

A September 2 preprint by Zhao Song claims a larger universal saving, ε★>2.05522·10^{−30}, through a refined maximum-entropy analysis. Its main theorem is explicitly relative to OPT_LP. The statement was checked, but the lengthy proof and numerical certificate were not independently verified here, so the value is recorded as a recent claim rather than silently replacing the established bound. Even if confirmed, it would remain far above the requested ratio 4/3.

title: Can metric k-Median reach the 1+2/e threshold?
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A major optimization problem with a substantial remaining algorithm–hardness gap and connections to coverage, facility location, LP rounding and parameterized approximation.
formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), does a randomized polynomial-time (1+2/e+ε)-approximation algorithm exist for general metric k-Median that always opens at most k facilities?
definitions: An input consists of a finite set V, a full table of nonnegative rational distances d on V encoded in binary, nonempty subsets C,F⊆V of clients and allowable facilities with C∪F=V, and an integer 1≤k≤|F|. The table is promised to satisfy d(u,v)=d(v,u), d(u,v)=0 exactly when u=v, and the triangle inequality. Each client has unit demand. For nonempty S⊆F define cost(S)=Σ_{c∈C}min_{s∈S}d(c,s), and OPT=min{cost(S):S⊆F,1≤|S|≤k}. L is the total bit length of the input. For each fixed ε the target is one uniform classical randomized algorithm A_ε, with constants K_ε,d_ε such that every execution takes at most K_ε L^{d_ε} bit operations. It always returns an explicit nonempty S⊆F with |S|≤k, and on each input Pr[cost(S)≤(1+2/e+ε)OPT]≥2/3. Here e is the base of the natural logarithm. The constants may depend on ε but not on k, |C|, |F| or distance precision. No Euclidean, low-dimensional, stability, capacity or input-distribution promise is made. Candidate facilities are part of the input and cannot be enlarged. The guarantee also covers OPT=0.
answer_criterion: Give the stated algorithms for every fixed ε>0, or rule them out for at least one fixed ε, explicitly identifying any complexity assumption used. This card fixes the yes/no question of approaching the known hardness threshold; it does not additionally require finding a different exact threshold after a negative answer. An algorithm opening k facilities only in expectation, one allowing k+o(k) facilities, or an FPT algorithm with unrestricted dependence on k does not prove the claim.
context:
Metric k-Median selects a limited number of service locations and minimizes total distance to the nearest selected location. The number of clients and the number of candidate facilities may differ, and the distance table need not come from a Euclidean embedding. The same formulation models representative selection for clustering and placement of facilities. Its simplicity makes the unresolved approximation threshold a central benchmark for algorithm design.

The two endpoint numbers are approximately 1.73576 and 2. The lower endpoint is the classical hardness threshold 1+2/e; the best general feasible guarantee in the checked literature is 2+ε. The inherited STOC 2025 paper explicitly asks for a tight approximation result after obtaining that upper bound. Asking for 1+2/e+ε for every fixed ε avoids requiring that an infimum approximation ratio be achieved exactly.

The coverage origin of the lower endpoint can be seen directly. Represent each set as a candidate facility and each universe element as a client. Give a client–facility pair distance one when the set contains the element and distance three otherwise, and give distinct pairs on the same side distance two. These distances satisfy the triangle inequality. A collection of k sets covering a fraction p of the elements then has clustering cost (3−2p) times the universe size.

Feige’s Max k-Cover gap distinguishes complete coverage from coverage of at most 1−1/e+η, for any fixed η>0. Under the preceding metric construction this becomes a gap between cost one per client and cost at least 1+2/e−2η per client. This is why the constant is not an arbitrary numerical target. A randomized algorithm beating that gap on every input would yield randomized algorithms for the underlying NP-hard decision problem; the appropriate exclusion is NP≠RP for this card’s success convention.

Jain–Mahdian–Saberi’s 2002 paper gives the classical metric k-Median lower bound through a reduction to approximating Set Cover. Its historical statement uses the then-known slightly-superpolynomial-time assumption for Set Cover hardness. The coverage reduction above explains the stronger ordinary NP-hardness formulation without silently changing the assumption in the original theorem. Neither lower-bound route excludes approximation from just above 1+2/e.

The 2025 algorithm combines two components. One permits a logarithmic number of extra centers while retaining a 2+ε cost bound; another handles instances where deleting one optimal center increases the optimum substantially. Combining them returns a feasible solution opening at most k centers. The full paper’s May 2026 revision retains this result. It is therefore incorrect to describe the headline 2+ε theorem as only a bicriteria approximation.

The usual linear relaxation has a separate barrier near two. It uses fractional openings y_s, assignments x_{c,s}≤y_s, unit total assignment for each client, and Σ_s y_s≤k. For a star with q≥3 leaves, all vertices available as facilities, clients at the leaves and k=q−1, every integral optimum has cost two. Set the central opening to 1/(q−1), each leaf opening to (q−2)/(q−1), and assign each client’s remaining fraction to the center. This feasible LP solution costs q/(q−1), giving an integrality gap approaching two.

That explicit example limits a guarantee measured against this relaxation, not every polynomial algorithm measured against OPT. A sharper algorithm might use additional constraints, a different relaxation, or another method. Likewise, a lower bound for one rounding framework is not a computational impossibility theorem for the original optimization problem. The card’s target is deliberately stated using the true integral optimum.

There is already a matching-threshold algorithm in a different runtime regime. Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li’s ICALP 2019 work achieves 1+2/e+ε in fixed-parameter time with respect to k. The potentially large dependence on the number of opened facilities is permitted there. This does not supply a polynomial-time algorithm when k grows as part of the input, but it shows that the target ratio has meaningful algorithmic support.

A 2026 development concerns geometric input. Cohen-Addad and coauthors improve approximation-scheme runtimes in low-dimensional Euclidean spaces, where additional structure is available. Such a scheme does not apply to arbitrary distance tables.

Anand and coauthors’ July 2026 spectral dual-fitting paper improves k-Means guarantees, including in general metrics. That objective sums squared distances; squaring changes both the analysis and the hardness constants. It does not establish the stated k-Median ratio.

Resolving this question would determine whether the coverage obstruction captures the full cost of efficient metric clustering. A positive answer would bridge the remaining gap beyond the familiar LP benchmark. A stronger hardness threshold would reveal an obstruction not expressed by coverage alone. The exact facility budget is essential to either conclusion: averaging an excessive number of facilities over random choices changes the feasible problem.
why: A central unresolved approximation threshold for metric clustering, separating known coverage hardness from the best algorithms with a strict facility budget.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The checked general-metric result remains 2+ε with a strict budget, while the classical hardness threshold is 1+2/e. The FPT algorithm, Euclidean schemes and 2026 k-Means results do not settle the polynomial-time target here.

The target is polynomial-time approximation arbitrarily close to 1+2/e from above while respecting the facility limit. title: Can an acyclic subgraph preserve a constant fraction of the optimal reachable pairs?
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A clean graph-optimization direction connecting acyclicity with preservation of global reachability. The constant-factor target captures a fundamental guarantee missing from the cited heuristic work, though its literature is narrower than core shortest-path and dynamic-graph frontiers.
formal: For a finite directed graph G=(V,E), let $R(D)=|\{(u,v)\in V^2:u\ne v,\text{ a directed path from }u\text{ to }v\text{ exists in }D\}|$ and $\mathrm{OPT}(G)=\max\{R((V,F)):F\subseteq E,\ (V,F)\text{ is acyclic}\}$. Do there exist a constant alpha>0 and a deterministic algorithm running in time polynomial in |V|+|E| that, for every G, outputs F subset E with (V,F) acyclic and R((V,F)) >= alpha OPT(G)? The constant and polynomial exponent must be independent of G. This card selects constant-factor approximation as a precise target within the source’s broader optimization question.
definitions: The input is an adjacency-list representation of an unweighted directed graph with labeled vertices 1,...,n, no self-loops, and at most one edge for each ordered pair. Oppositely directed edges may both be present. The algorithm may delete edges but may not add edges, reverse edges, identify vertices, or remove vertices. Reachability uses paths of positive length and counts ordered pairs of distinct vertices, not paths or retained edges. An acyclic graph has no directed cycle. Output is the list of retained edges. Polynomial time is measured in ordinary bit operations on the finite input; no oracle for reachability or optimization is free. When OPT(G)=0, any acyclic output satisfies the value requirement.
answer_criterion: Give a polynomial-time algorithm and prove one universal positive approximation ratio, or prove that no algorithm with the quantified guarantee exists. A conditional impossibility result must identify its complexity assumption. Guarantees on the number or weight of deleted edges, or empirical similarity to a reference hierarchy, do not establish the required guarantee on reachable pairs.
context:
A directed edge can represent a declared relation between two concepts, while a path represents an implied relation. Removing one edge can therefore erase many implications even if almost every input edge remains. The objective counts the implications preserved after all cycles have been removed. The optimum in the denominator already obeys acyclicity, so the algorithm is not asked to retain mutually contradictory reachability in both directions.

For example, a directed path on n vertices has only n-1 edges but n(n-1)/2 reachable ordered pairs. Deleting a middle edge destroys roughly a quarter of all n^2 ordered pairs. Conversely, adding a shortcut between vertices that are already connected by a path increases the edge count without adding a new reachable pair. These examples explain why edge-count approximation guarantees cannot simply be reused for this objective.

Ajwani’s 2016 question asks for an acyclic edge subgraph whose transitive closure has maximum size, motivated by cleaning taxonomies assembled from multiple contributors. The source explicitly welcomes approximation algorithms and scalable heuristics but specifies no approximation threshold. The constant alpha target here is an editorial specialization, rather than an approximation conjecture quoted from the seminar.

The 2017 follow-up on noisy hierarchies develops practical cycle-removal heuristics and evaluates recovery of inserted noisy edges. It identifies deviation in transitive closure as a possible further measure. Those experiments do not provide a worst-case ratio for R(D). A 2026 ranking paper likewise uses reachability to make edge reinsertion cycle-safe, but optimizes edge-weight disagreement; that use of reachability does not turn its objective into this one.
