title: The deterministic k-server conjecture
importance_reason: A foundational conjecture about online decision-making, with an optimal lower bound, one broadly applicable candidate algorithm, and a persistent gap on general metrics despite many resolved special cases.
focus_reason: A foundational conjecture about online decision-making, with an optimal lower bound, one broadly applicable candidate algorithm, and a persistent gap on general metrics despite many resolved special cases.
formal: For every integer k≥1, every metric space (M,d) with at least k+1 points, and every initial placement C_0 of k servers, does there exist a deterministic online serving rule A and a finite constant β≥0 such that cost_A(σ;C_0)≤k·OPT(σ;C_0)+β for every finite request sequence σ∈M*? The rule and β may depend on M,d,k,C_0, but neither may depend on future requests or on the length of the request sequence.
definitions: The metric is symmetric, has finite real distances, is zero exactly on equal points, and satisfies the triangle inequality; the space may be finite or infinite and is known to the online rule. There are exactly k interchangeable, unweighted servers, whose current positions form a multiset. A request r_t must be served before r_{t+1} is revealed. If a server is already at r_t, no movement is needed; otherwise the rule chooses one of the k servers and moves it to r_t, paying the metric distance. Restriction to these lazy moves loses no competitive power. A deterministic online rule is a function of the known metric, initial placement and revealed request prefix, with arbitrary memory and no access to future requests; this card imposes no running-time bound. OPT is the minimum total movement cost of an offline rule serving the same finite sequence from C_0 with the same k servers and advance knowledge of the sequence. The additive β must be fixed before requests arrive and cannot grow with the number or cost of requests. Randomization, advice about future requests, and extra servers are not supplied.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The problem isolates the price of making placement decisions without seeing future demand. Servers can represent cache slots, mobile resources or copies of data; a movement pays for changing which demand locations are covered. On a uniform metric, where every distinct pair has distance one, serving a request is precisely the paging problem. The online rule and the offline optimum have the same number of servers. Their difference is information about the future, not available capacity.

The proposed factor k is a sharp target, already forced by paging lower bounds. The classical work of Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator establishes the lower-bound framework and settles the two-server case on general metrics. An additive constant is included so that a fixed initial placement does not distort asymptotic performance. Allowing that constant to depend on the request sequence would make the definition vacuous, which is why its quantifiers are explicit.

Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou prove that the work-function algorithm is (2k−1)-competitive on every metric space. Its work function records the minimum offline cost of serving the already revealed prefix and ending in each possible server configuration. The algorithm uses these values to weigh movement against how well a configuration fits the past. This provides a single general strategy and leaves a factor approaching two between the known guarantee and the conjectured optimum.

It is widely conjectured that the same algorithm is actually k-competitive. Proving that stronger statement would settle this card, but the card permits a completely different algorithm. Similarly, failure of one proposed potential function only identifies a gap in that proof method. A potential proof typically compares changes in a quantity assigned to the current work function with the online and offline costs, so that the inequalities telescope over an arbitrarily long request sequence.

Several geometric settings attain the target. Chrobak and Larmore give k-competitive algorithms on tree metrics, covering line-like settings as well. Trees have unique connecting paths, which support movement rules unavailable in arbitrary metrics. This is substantial positive evidence, but arbitrary metric spaces can contain cycles and distance patterns that do not admit the same analysis.

Huang and Zhang prove that the work-function algorithm is 3-competitive on a circle, with distance measured along the shorter circular arc. Their result first appeared in a 2022 preprint and was published in Theoretical Computer Science in 2024. They also give computer-assisted evidence excluding their defined canonical family of potential functions for the general three-server case. The geometric theorem and the limitation of that proof family are different conclusions.

Bubeck, Coester and Rabani’s STOC 2023 theorem disproves the randomized O(log k) conjecture by constructing metrics with randomized competitive ratio Ω(log²k). It does not refute the deterministic target k: these are different claimed rates, and log²k is asymptotically smaller than k. The deterministic lower bound and the (2k−1) upper bound remain the relevant endpoints here.

Brilliantov, Bamas and Abbé’s April 2026 benchmark studies automated searches for potentials, particularly for four servers on a circle. A violated checked inequality refutes a candidate under the chosen formulation, while passing the finite checks is not a proof for every metric configuration and request sequence. Their experiments leave the open case unresolved. This offers concrete research tooling without changing the status of the conjecture.
why: A central problem in competitive analysis that asks whether the number of available servers exactly captures the worst-case price of future uncertainty. Its techniques and limitations inform caching, online movement and broader metric optimization problems.

title: A constant improvement over factor 2 for unrelated-machine makespan
importance_reason: A decades-old central scheduling problem with a large hardness gap, robust LP barriers and formal consequences for fair allocation.
focus_reason: A decades-old central scheduling problem with a large hardness gap, robust LP barriers and formal consequences for fair allocation.
formal: Does there exist a constant ε with 0<ε<1 and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm which, for every unrelated-machine scheduling instance, assigns all jobs to machines with makespan at most (2−ε)OPT?
definitions: An instance consists of m≥1 machines, n≥0 independent jobs, and an explicitly given m×n matrix of processing times pᵢⱼ in the nonnegative rationals or ∞. Rational numerators and denominators are binary encoded; ∞ forbids an assignment. Every job has at least one finite processing time. A schedule is a function σ:{1,…,n}→{1,…,m} with p_{σ(j),j}<∞. Its makespan is Cmax(σ)=maxᵢ Σ_{j:σ(j)=i} pᵢⱼ, and OPT is the minimum of this quantity over all feasible schedules. Jobs are available at time zero, indivisible and processed without interruption on one machine; there are no precedence constraints or communication costs. Jobs assigned to one machine can run consecutively in any order. The algorithm must output σ, not merely an estimate of OPT. Its bit running time is polynomial in the entire input length. ε and the polynomial are independent of m, n and all processing times; no predictions or promises on matrix structure are supplied. Empty or zero-optimum instances require makespan zero. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Each job can have a completely different processing time on each machine. There need not be a single ranking from fastest to slowest machines, as in the related-machine model. The challenge is to balance total load while respecting which assignments are expensive or forbidden. Even when every job has an individually attractive machine, sending all jobs to their favorite machines can create a severe bottleneck.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos obtain a polynomial-time factor-2 approximation by rounding a fractional assignment. For a candidate makespan T, assignments with pᵢⱼ>T are forbidden; the relaxation divides each job fractionally among the remaining machines while bounding each machine’s fractional load by T. Their rounding can charge the overload to at most one additional job per machine. Since every eligible job fits individually within T, the resulting schedule has load at most 2T.

The same foundational work establishes NP-hardness of approximation below 3/2. This leaves a genuine gap: the known hardness is compatible with an algorithm of ratio 1.9, 1.75 or 1.5. Moreover, Shchepin and Vakhania improve the general guarantee to 2−1/m. That is strictly less than two for each finite number of machines, but it approaches two as m grows. The ε in this question must be one fixed positive constant, so this refinement is not a resolution.

A stronger relaxation uses configurations: a variable represents an entire subset of jobs that fits on one machine within T. This remembers much more local packing structure than individual fractional assignments. Nevertheless, Verschae and Wiese construct an integrality gap approaching two even when each job is eligible on at most two machines. Thus rounding this relaxation solely against its own optimum cannot prove a universal constant improvement. This is a limitation of the relaxation, not a hardness theorem for all algorithms.

Restricted assignment is a special case in which job j has one processing time pⱼ on all eligible machines. It is substantially more structured than arbitrary unrelated processing times. Bamas and coauthors obtain a polynomial-time (1.75+δ)-approximation for the further restriction to two finite job sizes. Their general two-value unrelated-machine result instead gives 2−1/nᵟ for fixed δ>0, whose improvement still depends on instance size. Neither guarantee extends to the full target here.

The same SODA 2024 paper gives a formal connection to the Santa Claus allocation problem, where indivisible resources must be distributed to maximize the least satisfied player’s additive value. A (2−1/α)-approximation for makespan, for constant α≥2, would yield an (α+δ)-approximation for general Santa Claus for any fixed δ>0. Thus even a small fixed improvement here would also resolve a major constant-factor approximation question in fair allocation.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint studies predictions of assignments for heavy jobs. For accurate predictions their algorithm approaches factor one, while its worst-case guarantee with arbitrary prediction error remains two. This identifies valuable information that helps scheduling, but the classical question supplies no such information. A worst-case proof cannot assume that a learned assignment resembles an optimal schedule.

The fundamental issue is whether indivisibility forces an approximation barrier at two, or whether a stronger global argument can control the interactions that fractional rounding loses. Progress would clarify both the power of optimization relaxations and the complexity of balancing heterogeneous resources.
why: A defining unresolved approximation barrier in scheduling. Beating two by any fixed constant would also imply a constant approximation for general Santa Claus allocation, while known relaxation gaps rule out a large family of straightforward proofs.

title: Breaking factor two for precedence-constrained makespan
importance_reason: A central long-standing approximation question in scheduling, connecting greedy critical-path analysis, global dependency structure and conditional hardness.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant ε∈(0,1) and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every instance of P|prec|Cmax with an input number m of identical parallel machines, produces a feasible nonpreemptive schedule of makespan at most (2−ε)OPT?
definitions: An input specifies n≥1 jobs, a positive integer processing time p_j for each job, a directed acyclic graph of precedence constraints, and a positive integer machine count m. All numbers are encoded in binary and the graph is given explicitly. The machine count is not fixed in advance; one may cap it at n because additional machines cannot help. A feasible schedule chooses a machine a_j∈{1,…,m} and a nonnegative start time s_j for every job. Job j occupies that machine continuously during [s_j,s_j+p_j), without preemption or migration. Intervals assigned to the same machine must be disjoint. For every precedence edge i→j, require s_j≥s_i+p_i. Every job can run on every machine and its processing time is independent of the chosen machine. There are no release dates, deadlines, communication delays, setup costs or extra resource constraints. The makespan is Cmax=max_j(s_j+p_j); OPT is the minimum over feasible schedules using the same m unit-speed machines. With integer processing times, an optimal schedule with integer start times exists, so the algorithm can output binary-encoded integer starts. Polynomial time is measured in the full input bit length, not in Σ_j p_j. The same fixed ε must apply for all n, all m, all processing times and all precedence DAGs. The algorithm receives the whole instance before constructing the schedule.
answer_criterion: Give one such fixed ε and prove a polynomial-time (2−ε) guarantee for all inputs, or rule out every fixed improvement below two with any complexity assumptions explicitly stated. A bound 2−1/m does not supply a universal ε. Guarantees for fixed m, unit jobs only, special precedence orders, quasipolynomial running time, extra machines or faster processors do not prove the requested statement. A conditional hardness result based on a stronger conjecture must remain labelled conditional.
context:
Two basic obstructions limit how quickly dependent jobs can finish. Total work W=Σ_j p_j needs at least W/m time across m machines. A precedence chain must execute sequentially, so the length L of a longest weighted path is another lower bound. A schedule must manage both parallel throughput and the timely completion of jobs that unlock later work. Even with identical machines and no communication costs, these priorities can conflict.

Graham’s list scheduling follows a fixed priority order and starts available jobs whenever machines become free. A job is available once all its predecessors have finished. Its analysis gives Cmax≤W/m+(1−1/m)L, and hence Cmax≤(2−1/m)OPT. The bound approaches two as the machine count grows. Therefore the fact that each individual instance has a guarantee strictly below two does not resolve the constant improvement in this question.

A simple example shows why choosing priorities matters. Take m(m−1) independent unit jobs and one independent job of length m. If the long job comes last in the list, the units occupy all machines for m−1 time, and the final job finishes at 2m−1. An optimal schedule starts the long job immediately and runs the unit jobs on the other m−1 machines, finishing at time m. This proves a limitation of that list order, not hardness for every algorithm: the example has no precedence edges.

Classical NP-hardness excludes approximation factors below 4/3 unless P=NP, leaving room between that barrier and two. Svensson’s STOC 2010 work, published in 2011, connects the missing hardness to a different scheduling objective: minimizing total weighted completion time on one machine with precedences. Sufficiently strong hardness near factor two for that problem transfers to makespan on identical parallel machines, even with unit processing times.

Combined with Bansal and Khot’s hypothesis, the reduction gives hardness for every fixed factor below two. The hypothesis is a particular Unique Games variant with additional structure: near-perfect satisfiability on large subsets in the yes case and an expansion requirement in the no case. Svensson explicitly describes it as possibly stronger than the usual Unique Games conjecture. Thus this is substantial conditional evidence, but it should not be presented as a theorem following solely from P≠NP.

There has been strong progress when the number of machines is a fixed constant and jobs have unit length. Levey–Rothvoss initiate a line of approximation schemes based on hierarchy relaxations, followed by faster bounds. Das and Wiese provide a simpler quasipolynomial scheme by guessing selected jobs and time intervals and filling the remaining positions greedily. Their paper was published at ESA 2022, despite being uploaded to arXiv in January 2025. Its fixed-machine and running-time restrictions are essential.

Nederlof, Swennenhuis and Węgrzycki advance exact algorithms for unit jobs. Their bound (1+n/m)^{O(√(nm))} is subexponential when m=o(n), and they also give an exponential improvement when m is proportional to n. The work appeared at SODA 2025 and was published online in ACM Transactions on Algorithms in January 2026. Exactness is stronger than approximation, but these running times are not polynomial and the processing-time promise remains narrower than this card’s model.

Guruswami, Ren and Tang’s July 2026 preprint proves that even unit-length jobs can be hard to approximate within any constant when each job has one predetermined eligible machine. That extra restriction prevents the scheduler from freely distributing ready jobs. It is a different model, called unique-machine precedence scheduling, and its hardness transfers to certain communication-delay models. It does not contradict the factor-two guarantee available when every job may use any identical machine.

A fixed improvement below two would show that global information about the precedence graph can reliably overcome the worst interactions between chain length and machine utilization. A matching hardness theorem under a standard assumption would explain why a very old greedy guarantee remains near the limit of efficient scheduling. The question isolates that issue without combining it with heterogeneous machines, strategic reports, or communication delays.

title: Constant additive error for one-dimensional bin packing
importance_reason: A longstanding central problem in approximation algorithms, with connections to configuration LPs, discrepancy and the computational effect of input encoding.
formal: Do a universal integer C≥0 and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist that pack every explicitly listed one-dimensional bin-packing instance into at most OPT+C unit-capacity bins with probability at least 2/3?
definitions: The input is a list of n≥1 rational item sizes s₁,…,s_n∈(0,1], each encoded as a binary numerator and positive binary denominator; L is the total encoding length. A feasible packing is a map b:[n]→[k] with Σ_{i:b(i)=j}s_i≤1 for every bin j. OPT is the minimum feasible integer k. The algorithm is uniform and classical, has access to the entire input before assigning items, and must output an explicit feasible packing. For absolute constants K,d, every execution must take at most KL^d bit operations. Its output is always feasible, and on each fixed input it uses at most OPT+C bins with probability at least 2/3 over its private random bits. C,K,d are independent of n, the number of distinct sizes, OPT and coefficient precision. No capacity augmentation, splitting of items, cardinality constraint or promise on the input distribution is allowed. Repeated items are explicitly listed rather than represented by binary multiplicities. Randomization is expressly allowed; a deterministic algorithm would also resolve the question. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The objective is to minimize the number of identical containers needed to hold indivisible items. Each bin has a single numerical capacity constraint, so the model contains no geometric placement issue. Nevertheless, many different combinations of small and large items can fit exactly or almost exactly, and choices that look locally efficient can leave unusable capacity elsewhere. The inherited invited survey explicitly asks for an OPT+O(1) guarantee.

Additive and multiplicative errors behave differently as the optimum grows. A one-percent excess can mean thousands of unnecessary bins on a large instance; an additive constant remains fixed. Conversely, this card allows any universal constant, even a very large one. It does not ask for an additive-one algorithm or for exact optimization on small instances.

The elementary hardness example is distinguishing instances needing two bins from those needing three, through Partition. This rules out exact polynomial optimization under the usual complexity assumptions, but it does not settle constant additive approximation. With allowance C=1, a valid three-bin answer is permitted in both cases. A stronger hardness argument would need a gap that survives the particular additive allowance.

Asymptotic approximation schemes achieve a ratio approaching one, with additional losses depending on their accuracy parameter. This does not automatically give OPT+C. Choosing ε on the order of 1/OPT makes ε·OPT small, but the additive term and the running time may worsen as ε shrinks. The dependence on every parameter must be controlled simultaneously; the existence of a scheme alone does not establish the desired fixed loss.

Several published bounds use the Gilmore–Gomory configuration LP. A configuration specifies a multiset of item types that fits in one bin. The LP permits fractional numbers of such bins while covering all required items. Its optimum OPT_f is a lower bound on the integral optimum. Karmarkar–Karp obtain a polynomial-time packing with O(log² OPT) additive loss by combining approximate LP optimization with repeated rounding.

Hoberg–Rothvoss improve the guarantee to OPT_f+O(log OPT_f), and hence OPT+O(log OPT). Their Theorem 2 gives randomized expected polynomial time in the number of explicitly represented items, with the usual accounting for encoded numerical data. Packing first into intermediate containers, and then into bins, improves how rounding errors accumulate. This is the logarithmic-additive general algorithmic benchmark found in the checked literature.

A constant additive LP integrality gap is a related mathematical conjecture, but it is not identical to this card. An efficiently constructible packing within a constant of OPT_f would suffice. A nonconstructive proof of a small gap would still need an algorithmic rounding step. Conversely, an unbounded gap for this LP would not rule out a different algorithm whose guarantee is measured against the true integral optimum.

Discrepancy results explain why several familiar approaches encounter barriers. Eisenbrand–Pálvölgyi–Rothvoß connect a restricted bin-packing relaxation to discrepancy of three permutations. Their revised paper also proves limitations for a class of algorithms based on rounding item sizes upward. Those limitations concern specified techniques, rather than all algorithms for the original packing problem.

Newman–Nikolov disprove the conjecture that three permutations always have constant discrepancy, constructing examples requiring Ω(log n). This eliminates one proposed route to a constant additive bound. It does not itself provide numerical item sizes with a growing bin-packing integrality gap, and it does not show that every polynomial-time packing algorithm must lose logarithmically many bins.

Recent work also settles nearby structural questions. Jansen–Pirotton–Tutas’s ESA 2025 paper constructs bin-packing instances requiring exponentially many distinct configurations as a function of the number of item types. Its discussion records an OPT+1 algorithm whose runtime depends heavily on that parameter. Exponential support in the number of types does not contradict a polynomial algorithm in an explicit list of all items, and a parameter-dependent additive-one algorithm is not uniformly polynomial as the number of types grows.

The ICALP 2026 work of Jansen–Ohnesorge–Pirotton proves a tight ETH-based lower bound for the dependence on the number of types in a high-multiplicity exact algorithmic regime. Binary multiplicities can encode far more items than the input length. Both the compressed input model and exact optimization differ from the constant-additive, explicitly listed target here. The result should therefore not be reported as a negative answer to this question.

This problem isolates how close efficient approximation can come to an integral packing optimum. A constant-additive algorithm would show that all unavoidable combinatorial inefficiency can be confined to a bounded number of extra bins, regardless of instance size. A general impossibility theorem would establish a meaningful approximation barrier beyond the standard two-versus-three-bin hardness example.

status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No universal constant-additive polynomial-time algorithm or general impossibility result was found in the checked primary sources. The logarithmic-additive guarantee and recent high-multiplicity/support results do not settle this explicitly listed, randomized formulation.

title: Planted clique: can polynomial time detect a clique below the square-root scale?
importance_reason: A canonical computational threshold with broad consequences in average-case complexity, statistical inference, and the study of algorithmic lower-bound frameworks.
focus_reason: A canonical computational threshold with broad consequences in average-case complexity, statistical inference, and the study of algorithmic lower-bound frameworks.
formal: Is the following hardness statement true? For every fixed ε∈(0,1/2), there is no uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm A whose success probability in the experiment below is at least 2/3 for every sufficiently large n, with k=⌊n^(1/2−ε)⌋.
definitions: Set [n]={1,…,n}. The null distribution N_n draws a simple undirected labeled graph by including each unordered pair independently with probability 1/2. The planted distribution P_(n,k) first chooses S uniformly among all k-element subsets of [n], includes all edges inside S, and includes every other edge independently with probability 1/2. Draw b uniformly from {0,1}; draw G from N_n if b=0 and P_(n,k) if b=1. Give A the binary integers n,k and the full adjacency matrix of G, but neither b nor S. It outputs a bit b̂. Success means Pr[b̂=b], averaged over b, the graph, S when present, and A’s independent random bits. Equivalently success is (Pr_N[A=0]+Pr_P[A=1])/2. Polynomial time means at most C(n+1)^c bit operations for every input and random tape, with fixed C,c; they and A may depend on the fixed ε. The forbidden guarantee is ∃A,C,c,N ∀n≥N, success≥2/3. This is a one-graph detection problem; A may generate its own random graphs at its own computational cost. The size of S is exactly k, not an independent per-vertex planting probability. No advice, quantum computation, oracle, side information, or algorithm-family restriction is allowed.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
This asks whether a planted structure can be statistically obvious yet computationally inaccessible. In the specified regime, k grows as a positive power of n, while an unplanted graph has no clique of size r=⌈3 log_2 n⌉ with probability tending to one: a union bound is at most n^r·2^(−r(r−1)/2), which tends to zero. Enumerating all r-subsets therefore distinguishes the two distributions with success tending to one in quasipolynomial time n^O(log n). The obstacle is reducing that computation to polynomial time, not a lack of information in the graph.

The classical spectral algorithm of Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov recovers the hidden vertex set for every fixed positive constant times √n, with a polynomial whose exponent can depend on that constant. Recovery immediately yields detection here by checking that the reported set is a sufficiently large clique. Letting the constant shrink as n^(−ε) does not keep that analysis polynomial with a fixed exponent.

Substantial evidence comes from provable failures of general algorithmic frameworks. Barak and coauthors show that low-degree sum-of-squares relaxations assign a random graph an implausibly large clique value near √n, despite its true largest clique having only logarithmic size. This is an unconditional limitation of that relaxation. It does not rule out every algorithm allowed in this card.

Recent positive work also illustrates why an algorithmic barrier must state its model. Gheissari, Jagannath, and Xu permit local optimization to pass through vertex sets that are not cliques, penalizing missing edges. Starting from the whole graph, their procedure reaches the planted clique at a sufficiently large constant times √n. Restrictions to moves among actual cliques can fail even in easier regimes; those failures do not establish the unrestricted conjecture.

Nagda and Raghavendra obtain sharp bounds on efficient distinguishing advantage assuming planted-clique hardness. Their paper uses independent vertex planting, so the planted size fluctuates around its mean, and uses a different normalization of advantage. It strengthens consequences of a hypothesis in that related model. It is not an unconditional lower bound for the fixed-size experiment here.

The question isolates detection from stronger output requirements such as recovering every planted vertex. It also fixes the random background: arbitrary base graphs, geometric random graphs, and adversarially modified edges describe different experiments. Work on robust recovery of overlapping planted cliques in random intersection graphs continued in COLT 2026, but its distribution and signal regime do not settle this question.
why: A foundational average-case hardness hypothesis and a central test case for statistical–computational gaps. It asks for a clean separation between the presence of information and efficient extraction of that information; reductions transfer related assumptions to sparse estimation and latent-structure learning. Proving this formulation would in particular imply P≠NP, since a polynomial algorithm for maximum clique would distinguish the distributions.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026; no unrestricted polynomial-time solution below n^(1/2−ε) or unconditional hardness proof was identified. The exact formulation fixes constant-success detection and exactly k planted vertices. Low-degree and sum-of-squares bounds remain scoped to their models; the optimal-advantage result is conditional.

This is a restricted-model lower bound. | 2023–2025: Gheissari, Jagannath, and Xu show that an appropriate discrete gradient descent and low-temperature local chain recover at the √n scale from the full-graph initialization; the final preprint version is dated 15 May 2025. | 2025-07-19: Nagda and Raghavendra derive optimal efficient distinguishing advantages conditional on a planted-clique hypothesis, in the independent-vertex planting model. | 2026: Göbel, Ruff, and Schiller give robust sum-of-squares algorithms for multiple overlapping cliques in random intersection graphs when clique size is much larger than √(n log n). This is progress in a related model, not below the threshold fixed here.
working_summary: Planted clique detection distinguishes a random graph from one with a uniformly chosen clique inserted into it. The conjecture rules out polynomial-time classical randomized detection when the planted size is n^(1/2−epsilon) for fixed positive epsilon. The graph statistically contains a signal, but the challenge is finding a computationally accessible feature that reveals it below the square-root scale. focus_reason: One of the central missing implications in complexity theory, connecting worst-case lower bounds to feasible instance generation and the limits of algorithms on typical inputs.
formal: Is the implication $\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\Longrightarrow(\mathrm{NP},\mathrm{PSamp})\nsubseteq\mathrm{AvgP}$ true? That is, assuming P≠NP, must there exist a language L∈NP and a polynomial-time samplable distribution ensemble D={Dₙ} such that no deterministic exact decider for L runs in average polynomial time under D, in the moment-based sense defined below?
definitions: A sampler is one randomized Turing machine S which, given 1ⁿ, halts within q(n) steps on every random tape for a fixed polynomial q. Its output distribution Dₙ is over finite binary strings x; |x|≤q(n), and n is the ensemble parameter, not necessarily |x|. Sampling is exact with independent unbiased coin flips, and S has no advice or oracle. An exact decider A receives (1ⁿ,x), halts, and returns the membership bit of L correctly for every n and x. Write T_A(1ⁿ,x) for its running time. The pair (L,D) belongs to AvgP if there exist such an A, ε>0, C>0, and integer k≥1 with $\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}[T_A(1^n,x)^\varepsilon]\le C(n+1)^k$ for every n≥1. The constants and A may depend on L and S but not on n. This moment definition is the robust Levin notion, not the requirement that the first moment itself be polynomial. The algorithm is deterministic and never gives a wrong answer; difficult inputs may take a long time. NP uses ordinary polynomially bounded certificates and deterministic polynomial-time verification. Both the hard language and its sampler must be fixed across all input lengths.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Worst-case hardness says that an algorithm has difficult inputs. It does not say that a feasible instance generator produces them with enough probability to obstruct average efficiency. The sampler is therefore part of the mathematical problem. It may depend on the language, but it cannot contain an uncomputable table selecting a hard input at every length.

A padding example shows why a fixed familiar distribution is insufficient. Encode a formula x as 0 followed by |x|²−1 further zeros, a separator 1, and x. Satisfiability of these padded strings remains NP-complete under polynomial reductions. Under the uniform distribution on strings of a fixed length, valid encodings are so rare that checking the format and brute-forcing the rare valid formulas has polynomial average cost. An easy uniform distribution does not remove worst-case hardness.

Levin’s moment condition makes average efficiency stable under polynomial slowdowns. If a machine is simulated with its running time raised to a fixed power, a correspondingly smaller positive moment still suffices. This prevents the answer from depending on an incidental choice of machine representation. Exact computation with this runtime guarantee differs from a heuristic allowed to give incorrect answers on a small fraction of inputs.

Distributional completeness is already available: Impagliazzo and Levin extend the theory to polynomial-time samplable ensembles. Completeness identifies a common average-case target; it does not prove that this target is hard from P≠NP.

There are barriers for nonadaptive oracle reductions from worst-case NP hardness to average-case NP hardness: the relevant reductions would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such a barrier leaves other proof mechanisms open. Recent reductions for specific time-bounded Kolmogorov problems use additional assumptions or specific forms of hardness, so they do not supply the implication on this card.
why: This asks whether worst-case intractability necessarily survives on inputs generated by a feasible process. It is the basic bridge between the standard theory of NP-completeness and distributional complexity, and a prerequisite issue in attempts to derive useful cryptographic hardness from P≠NP alone.
status_note: The original question is explicitly open in Wigderson’s book and the revised average-case survey. Current primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no resolution from P≠NP alone was located. The card fixes deterministic exact AvgP and strict polynomial-time sampling, rather than conflating them with randomized heuristic hardness.
progress: 1986–1990: Levin develops robust average-time definitions and distributional completeness; Impagliazzo and Levin extend completeness to samplable ensembles. The survey develops the moment definition and this completeness theory. | 2003: Bogdanov and Trevisan show limitations of nonadaptive worst-case-to-average-case oracle reductions for NP. Their result is a conditional obstruction to a reduction method, not a disproof of the unrestricted implication. | 2018 / revised survey 2021: Wigderson’s Open Problem 4.5 and the revised Bogdanov–Trevisan survey explicitly ask whether P≠NP implies average-case NP hardness. | 2026-01: Liu and Pass obtain a worst-case-to-average-case reduction for an exact time-bounded Kolmogorov problem under an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. The extra hypothesis is stronger and more specific than P≠NP.

working_summary: Worst-case NP hardness means that some efficiently verifiable problem resists polynomial-time solution on all inputs. The question asks whether P unequal to NP forces such a problem to remain hard on average under an efficiently samplable distribution. The hard instances must occur often enough in a distribution that can itself be generated feasibly. A positive implication would connect worst-case complexity with the distributional hardness needed in many algorithmic and cryptographic settings. The reviewed target uses deterministic exact decisions and Levin's moment-based average-time definition, which differs from allowing errors on rare inputs or requiring only a polynomial first moment.

title: The computational threshold for dense tensor PCA
importance_reason: A central average-case inference problem linking tensor algorithms, statistical thresholds, low-degree methods and computational hardness.
formal: For every fixed integer k≥3, rational ε with 0<ε<(k−2)/4, and rational c∈(0,1), is the following impossibility statement true? No uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm, given the finite-precision observation of Y=n^{k/4−ε}v^{⊗k}+Z specified below, achieves |⟨u,v⟩|≥c with probability at least 2/3 for every sufficiently large dimension n, where v is uniform on the unit sphere in R^n and the n^k ordered entries of Z are independent N(0,1) variables.
definitions: The experiment draws v, Z and the algorithm’s random bits independently. For an ordered tuple (i₁,…,i_k)∈{1,…,n}^k, the signal entry is n^{k/4−ε}v_{i₁}⋯v_{i_k}. Noise is not pre-symmetrized and each entry has variance one. To give polynomial time a precise bit-model meaning, for n≥2 set b=⌈10k log₂n⌉ and Q_b(x)=2^{−b}⌊2^b max(−2^b,min(x,2^b))⌋. The input consists of n and all entries Q_b(Y_{i₁,…,i_k}), represented as signed dyadic rationals with O(log n) bits each. This fixed rounding convention is an explicit finite-precision version of the usual Gaussian-model question. An algorithm may depend on the fixed constants k, ε and c, but is one probabilistic Turing machine for all n, with worst-case running time polynomial in n on every input and random tape. For fixed k this is polynomial in the input size. It outputs a nonzero rational vector w, interpreted as the unit vector u=w/‖w‖₂; zero or invalid outputs fail. Success is the event |⟨w,v⟩|≥c‖w‖₂. The algorithm receives no side information about v, informative initial vector, or additional independent observations. The probability averages over the spike, noise and internal randomness. Absolute correlation makes the target invariant under the unavoidable sign ambiguity when k is even.
answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed (k,ε,c) in the stated ranges, each such polynomial-time algorithm has success probability below 2/3 for arbitrarily large n; or refute this by giving one fixed triple and one algorithm that succeeds with probability at least 2/3 for all sufficiently large n. Proving failure only for low-degree polynomials, a chosen iterative method, or a different spike prior does not prove the full assertion. An improvement by logarithmic factors at n^{k/4} does not supply the fixed power saving n^ε requested here.
context:
Ordinary principal component analysis looks for a hidden direction in a noisy matrix. Tensor PCA asks the analogous question when observations have three or more indices. Here the clean signal has rank one: every entry is a product of coordinates of the same hidden unit vector. Gaussian noise obscures those products. The goal is only a constant correlation with the direction, much weaker than estimating every coordinate accurately.

For fixed tensor order, information-theoretic recovery in the standard Gaussian model becomes possible at a signal scale of order √n. Montanari and Richard established the basic statistical-versus-computational distinction while studying tensor unfolding, power iteration and message-passing methods. Their noise normalization differs from the variance-one convention used in this card; their constant statistical threshold corresponds to order √n here.

Known polynomial-time methods reach signal strength around n^{k/4}, up to factors that do not change this leading exponent. Wu and Zhou’s 2024 introduction records both this algorithmic scale and the conjectured gap from √n. The interval for ε deliberately places our target strictly between them: λ/√n=n^{(k−2)/4−ε} grows without bound. There is therefore ample statistical signal in the usual model, while efficient recovery remains unproved.

For example, at order four and ε=1/8, the observation contains n^4 noisy numbers and signal strength n^{7/8}. The statistical scale is n^{1/2}, and the conjectured efficient scale is n. A polynomial-time algorithm below that latter scale would have to exploit structure that current threshold evidence misses. Merely reading all n^4 entries is allowed: the question concerns computation polynomial in the complete input, not a sublinear-access restriction.

Low-degree polynomial estimators provide one rigorous way to test proposed computational barriers. Kunisky, Moore and Wein establish the predicted degree-versus-signal tradeoff for detection with a spherical spike and derive a matching reconstruction lower bound for odd tensor orders. Their reconstruction theorem is specifically for odd orders; they explain that even orders require a sign-invariant estimand such as vvᵀ and additional work. Detection and recovery are separate tasks, and a detection lower bound should not silently be relabelled as their reconstruction theorem.

Fu and Sohn’s May 2026 preprint advances low-degree estimation bounds for tensor PCA with independent, mean-zero, variance-one spike coordinates and bounded moments. Its general-prior theorem controls estimation of fixed products of coordinates and obtains the predicted signal-versus-degree scaling within a stated degree range. Independent-coordinate priors are different from a vector conditioned to have unit norm. The result strengthens evidence for the computational gap without establishing an unrestricted polynomial-time lower bound for this card’s spherical prior.

Some recent algorithmic improvements resolve narrower conjectures. Wu and Zhou lower the threshold for randomly initialized power iteration by a polylogarithmic factor. Ding, Gu, Liu and Fang obtain improved guarantees for an overparameterized stochastic-gradient method using multiple independent observations. For even order, their stated sample-signal condition reaches the familiar n^{k/4} scale after averaging the observations. Neither result supplies the fixed-power improvement below that scale demanded here.

The rounding convention prevents an ambiguity about algorithms operating on exact Gaussian real numbers. Each coordinate is given with logarithmically many bits. Outside the clipping event, the total rounding error in Euclidean norm across the tensor is at most n^{k/2}2^{−b}, an extremely small inverse power of n; clipping has vanishing probability. This is a specified computational model, rather than an assertion that every exact-real algorithm automatically transfers to it. Likewise, polynomial-estimator theorems for unrounded observations do not by themselves cover arbitrary algorithms that process rounded entries.

A resolution would clarify whether a simple, highly symmetric random model can hide statistically recoverable information from every efficient algorithm. A successful method would challenge a widely used picture of algorithmic thresholds. A full impossibility proof would require a complexity argument beyond the restricted algorithm families currently understood. Both outcomes would inform how computational hardness assumptions are formulated for inference problems.
why: Determine whether the canonical statistical–computational gap for a dense Gaussian tensor persists against all polynomial-time recovery algorithms.
status_note: The May 2026 low-degree paper retains the conjectured gap for unrestricted algorithms and distinguishes spherical from independent-coordinate priors. The 2024 power-iteration and October 2025 stochastic-gradient improvements concern particular methods and do not provide a fixed-power improvement below n^{k/4}. No full resolution found through 11 September 2026. The card explicitly fixes a finite-precision bit model; restricted lower bounds in the standard unrounded model are evidence, not a proof for all algorithms here.
progress: 2014: Montanari–Richard introduce and analyze the spiked tensor model, exhibiting a gap between information-theoretic recovery and the analyzed polynomial-time methods. | 2024: Kunisky–Moore–Wein prove spherical-prior low-degree detection thresholds and odd-order reconstruction lower bounds with the predicted dependence on degree. | 2024-06: Wu–Zhou sharpen the analysis and stopping rule for randomly initialized power iteration; its threshold improves by a polylogarithmic factor. | 2025-10-16: Ding–Gu–Liu–Fang improve stochastic-gradient guarantees in a multiple-observation model; the even-order bound reaches the familiar conjectured computational scale. | 2026-05-28: Fu–Sohn establish low-degree estimation bounds for independent-coordinate priors, with the predicted degree–signal dependence and an additional technical restriction on degree.
working_summary: Dense tensor PCA observes a hidden rank-one tensor corrupted by independent Gaussian noise. The conjecture says that below a specified signal scale, no polynomial-time algorithm can recover a vector with constant correlation to the hidden direction. It asks about unrestricted computation rather than the performance of a particular spectral, gradient, or low-degree method. Resolving the threshold would clarify a prominent proposed gap between statistical recoverability and computational feasibility. The saved formulation fixes finite precision, unit-sphere normalization, one observation, and independent ordered noise entries, so results using different normalizations or extra samples require careful conversion.

title: The computational Kesten–Stigum threshold for sparse community recovery
importance_reason: A central, sharply parameterized computational-versus-statistical gap linking sparse random graphs, inference, message passing and average-case complexity.
formal: Do there exist a fixed integer q≥5, fixed rational constants a>b>0 satisfying (a−b)²<q(a+(q−1)b), a constant δ>0, and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm A such that, for every sufficiently large n, A weakly recovers the communities of the symmetric stochastic block model SBM(n,q,a,b), with expected overlap at least 1/q+δ?
definitions: Generate the hidden labels σ₁,…,σₙ independently and uniformly from [q]={1,…,q}. Conditional on these labels, each unordered pair of distinct vertices is independently an edge with probability a/n if its labels agree and b/n otherwise. Thus the graph is simple and undirected; take n≥a. Equal prior probabilities make communities asymptotically balanced, but their sizes are not conditioned to equal n/q. The algorithm receives this one graph and knows q,a,b; it receives no planted labels or auxiliary samples. It outputs a label vector σ̂∈[q]ⁿ. Define overlap(σ̂,σ)=max over permutations π of [q] of n⁻¹Σᵢ 1{σ̂ᵢ=π(σᵢ)}. The expectation in the question is over labels, graph edges and the algorithm’s random bits. Weak recovery means a fixed positive advantage over the limiting chance baseline 1/q. Running time is worst-case polynomial in n on a standard bit model, for every graph and random tape; the algorithm and polynomial exponent may depend on the fixed parameters but not on n. Put d=(a+(q−1)b)/q and θ=(a−b)/(a+(q−1)b). The strict inequality is dθ²<1, below the Kesten–Stigum threshold. All three model parameters remain constant as n grows.
answer_criterion: A positive answer must exhibit one fixed parameter choice below the threshold and prove the stated polynomial running time and nonvanishing expected overlap for all sufficiently large n. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm at every fixed parameter choice in the formulation. Recovery with unlimited computation does not answer the question. An algorithm with q growing with n, a result only above the threshold, or a lower bound conditional on an unproved computational hypothesis is partial progress. The question does not impose an extra promise of information-theoretic recoverability: any positive algorithmic example automatically has that property.
context:
Community detection asks whether the edges of a network reveal an underlying partition. Here every vertex has the same expected degree, regardless of its group. Consequently, sorting vertices by degree cannot directly identify their communities. The signal is in the pattern of connections between vertices, and each vertex has only a constant expected number of observations even as the network grows.

The target is deliberately much weaker than recovering every label. A constant-degree graph has many isolated vertices, whose memberships cannot be inferred from their incident edges. Weak recovery asks only for a fixed improvement over random guessing on average. Permuting all community names must be allowed: renaming the hidden groups changes neither the graph distribution nor the quality of an inferred partition.

The quantity dθ² compares the growth in the number of observed neighbours with the decay of label information along an edge. In a local tree approximation, d describes branching and θ describes how much a child’s label remembers its parent’s label. This explains why the value one is a natural boundary for algorithms based on propagation of small correlations. It does not by itself prove an impossibility result for algorithms that use the whole graph.

Abbe and Sandon prove efficient recovery above this boundary for every fixed number of communities. Their method uses an acyclic form of belief propagation and addresses the effect of cycles in the finite graph. This supplies the algorithmic side of the proposed threshold. The question asks whether a qualitatively different method can succeed strictly below it in the assortative case a>b.

There really are parameters for which the graph contains useful information below the Kesten–Stigum threshold. Banks, Moore, Neeman and Netrapalli establish such regimes for at least eleven groups in the assortative model. Their recovery argument permits exponential computation, searching over sufficiently plausible partitions. Their five-group statement concerns the disassortative case, where between-group edges are more likely; that is a different parameter range from this card.

This produces a concrete computational-versus-statistical puzzle. The missing labels are not intrinsically unidentifiable everywhere below the boundary, yet known efficient methods do not recover them throughout the information-theoretically possible region. An affirmative answer to this card would refute the universal fixed-community barrier with a single parameter example. A negative answer would establish that the obstruction is computational wherever recovery is statistically possible.

Ding, Hua, Slot and Steurer give conditional evidence in 2025. In their parameterized symmetric model, a low-degree conjecture implies a strong computational lower bound for recovery below the threshold by a fixed margin. Their recovery definition uses correlation with the centred membership matrix. The result is a reduction from a conjecture about testing to recovery hardness, not an unconditional exclusion of polynomial-time algorithms. Its model and hypothesis restrictions matter when applying it to a particular choice of a,b.

The precise conjecture in that paper also matters. Its bounded test functions must have expectation bounded below under the planted distribution. The authors explain that a broader earlier version was refuted using rare events. Thus citing a generic “low-degree conjecture” without stating that a hypothesis remains unproved would erase both the conditional nature of the result and an actual correction in the underlying evidence.

A 2026 revision of work by Chin, Mossel, Sohn and Wein gives efficient recovery below the usual boundary when the number of communities grows sufficiently quickly, in particular in a regime above √n. This is an important warning against treating the threshold as universal over every block model. Here q is fixed before n tends to infinity. Even a very large fixed q eventually lies below √n, so the growing-community algorithm does not supply the fixed-parameter example requested.

Settling this problem would test whether a threshold suggested by local propagation describes all efficient global algorithms in a basic random graph model. A new algorithm would identify exploitable structure missed by the familiar threshold calculation. A rigorous barrier would give a particularly clean example in which unlimited inference and efficient inference have different capabilities, with the data distribution specified by only three constants.
why: Determine whether the canonical local signal threshold is a true barrier for every efficient algorithm in a basic model of network inference.
status_note: Efficient recovery above the threshold and information-theoretic recovery below it in suitable fixed-q assortative regimes are proved. The checked fixed-community computational lower bound remains conditional on an unproved low-degree conjecture. Growing-community algorithms in the August 2026 revision concern a different quantifier regime. No unconditional settlement of this precise fixed-q question found through 11 September 2026.
progress: 2015–2018: Abbe–Sandon prove efficient recovery above the Kesten–Stigum threshold for all fixed community counts; preprint 2015, revised 2016, journal publication 2018. | 2016: Banks–Moore–Neeman–Netrapalli prove information-theoretic recovery below the threshold in suitable assortative regimes with q≥11, using a potentially exponential algorithm. | 2025-04-28: Ding–Hua–Slot–Steurer’s revised paper derives recovery lower bounds under its explicitly restricted low-degree conjecture; Theorem A.1 allows a fixed gap below the threshold. | 2026-08-23: Chin–Mossel–Sohn–Wein revise their many-community analysis, correcting the proof of Theorem 1.2. Their below-threshold algorithms require a growing community count and do not settle the fixed-q question.
working_summary: The symmetric stochastic block model generates a sparse graph with higher edge probability within hidden communities than between them. The question asks whether some fixed parameters below the Kesten–Stigum threshold permit polynomial-time weak recovery. Weak recovery means a constant improvement over chance after relabeling the output communities optimally. A positive example would cross a proposed computational threshold in a setting where information can persist beyond simple spectral methods. The reviewed model keeps the number of communities and edge parameters fixed, so results with growing community counts or only restricted-algorithm lower bounds do not settle it.

title: Can random 3-SAT at constant density be refuted in polynomial time?
importance_reason: A foundational average-case refutation problem with documented connections to proof complexity, learning and approximation. It supplies a different average-case task from planted recovery or detection. The exact-satisfiability variant is recorded without importing consequences of stronger gap hypotheses.
formal: Do there exist an integer C≥6 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm A such that A never outputs UNSAT on any satisfiable 3-CNF formula, and Pr[A(F)=UNSAT]→1 as n→∞ for F drawn from R_3(n,Cn)? The probability is over both the formula and A’s independent random bits.
definitions: For n≥3, R_3(n,m) is the distribution on ordered lists of m clauses obtained independently with replacement. Each clause selects a uniformly random three-element subset of {1,…,n} and independently negates each of its three variables with probability 1/2. Each clause is their disjunction; the formula is the conjunction of the list, with duplicate clauses permitted. On every input A outputs UNSAT or UNKNOWN. Soundness is exact: for every satisfiable formula and every random tape A returns UNKNOWN. Its time is bounded by a fixed polynomial in the explicit binary input length on every input and every random tape, including adversarial formulas; variable names are binary integers and n is part of the encoding. A may use only fresh independent fair random bits and has no advice or external oracle. The constant C, the machine, and the time polynomial are chosen before n. The probability limit means that for every η>0 there is n0 such that the probability is at least 1−η for all n≥n0. There is no requirement to use a specified refutation proof system: a sound decision procedure certifying unsatisfiability suffices. Restricting the existential choice to integers C≥6 loses no larger constant-density regime, since an algorithm at a smaller density can run on the corresponding prefix of the random clause list.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.
context:
At a sufficiently large fixed clause density, a random 3-CNF formula is unsatisfiable with probability approaching one. That fact alone does not give a sound algorithm for a particular input: a procedure that always announces unsatisfiability would incorrectly reject satisfiable adversarial formulas. The question is whether an efficient algorithm can recognize almost all random instances while retaining exact soundness on every satisfiable instance.

The random distribution and the algorithmic quantifiers have different roles. A is constrained on all inputs, but its success guarantee applies to the stated distribution. C is an absolute constant, so success only at a density growing with n does not meet the target. Likewise, proving that short certificates exist does not automatically yield an algorithm that finds them.

Allen, O’Donnell and Witmer define refutation as a sound UNSAT-or-fail procedure and develop refutation algorithms for random constraint satisfaction problems. They distinguish this task from planted-instance detection and from strong refutation, which certifies that every assignment violates a positive fraction of constraints. These distinctions determine which hardness assumptions and consequences apply.

Feige’s random-3-SAT hypothesis is often presented in a stronger gap formulation. For example, Barak’s formulation requires soundness even on nearly satisfiable formulas. This card records the exact-satisfiability, constant-density refutation question requested in the proposal; it does not identify that formulation with every version called Feige’s hypothesis. The gap formulation is documented as related context.

Chan, d’Orsi and Xu’s 2026 work generalizes density, sum-of-squares degree and refutation-strength tradeoffs for random CSPs. Its broader predicate model is not a polynomial-time, constant-density solution of this random-3-SAT target. The question remains a distinct counterpart to the catalogue’s planted-clique detection problem.
why: Separate the typical absence of satisfying assignments from the computational ability to certify that absence soundly.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No sound polynomial-time refuter meeting the stated constant-density success guarantee was found. The exact-satisfiability variant must be distinguished from the stronger near-satisfiability formulations in the cited Feige-hypothesis literature.
progress: 2012: Barak records a gap formulation of Feige’s hypothesis, requiring soundness on nearly satisfiable instances. | 2015: Allen–O’Donnell–Witmer give general random-CSP refutation algorithms and distinguish weak and strong refutation. | 2026-04-30: Chan–d’Orsi–Xu extend random-CSP refutation tradeoffs to predicates without uniformly random literals; the constant-density 3-SAT target is not established.

title: Does average-case NP hardness imply infinitely-often one-way functions?
importance_reason: Links average-case NP hardness to the existence of a basic cryptographic primitive; resolving it would clarify the foundations of complexity-based cryptography.
formal: Does $\mathrm{DistNP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{HeurBPP}$ imply the existence of a polynomial-time computable function f with the following property? For every probabilistic polynomial-time inverter I and every constant c>0, infinitely many lengths n satisfy $\Pr[|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)]<n^{-c}$, where $x\sim U(\{0,1\}^n)$ and $z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x))$. The probability includes inverter randomness. This card fixes the infinitely-often security convention used by the cited characterization.
definitions: DistNP consists of pairs (L,D) with L in NP and D_n a polynomial-time samplable distribution on n-bit inputs. Such a pair is in HeurBPP if a single randomized algorithm A runs in time polynomial in n and 1/delta and, for every n and $0<\delta<1$, at least a $1-\delta$ fraction of x drawn from D_n have $\Pr[A(x,\delta)=L(x)]\ge2/3$. The output is a decision bit. Infinitely-often security is weaker than requiring negligible inversion probability at all sufficiently large lengths; the latter is a distinct stronger target.
answer_criterion: Prove the implication under the two explicit distributional and security definitions, or prove that average-case NP hardness can hold while every polynomial-time function fails that infinitely-often inversion guarantee. A result only about an oracle world does not settle the unrelativized implication.
context:
Hardness of deciding typical instances and hardness of finding preimages are different requirements. The assumption P ≠ NP alone is weaker and belongs to a separate existing question.

An average-case decision problem asks an algorithm to classify instances drawn from a specified distribution. A one-way function creates a different experiment: sample an input, reveal its efficiently computed image, and ask an adversary to find any valid preimage. The sampling process and the form of the required answer both matter.

A reduction has to turn the first kind of difficulty into the second while preserving efficient generation and a meaningful success probability. It cannot simply use a hard yes/no question as a function and assume its inverse is hard. The question is whether some average-case hardness can exist without yielding the basic inversion obstacle on which one-way-function cryptography is built.
why: It asks whether distributional hardness alone suffices for basic cryptography: a central connection between average-case complexity and cryptographic constructions.
status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
progress: 2026-06-23: The revised paper characterizes the remaining obstruction by the gap between approximation factors $\ell^{1-o(1)}$ and $O(\ell)$ for minimum-description-length agnostic learning. Here $\ell$ is advice complexity of sampling. The original April version states a different quantitative claim.
working_summary: Average-case NP hardness says that some efficiently sampled verification problem defeats the specified randomized heuristic schemes. The question asks whether this implies a polynomial-time function that is hard to invert at infinitely many input lengths. Such a result would connect distributional decision hardness with a basic cryptographic form of computational asymmetry. The security target quantifies separately over every polynomial-time inverter and every inverse-polynomial success threshold. The saved formulation deliberately uses infinitely-often security, so a claim of hardness at all sufficiently large lengths would be stronger than the implication being asked about.

title: Polynomial smoothed complexity of FLIP for Max-Cut
importance_reason: A flagship unresolved explanation of why a canonical PLS local-search algorithm works efficiently on perturbed inputs.
formal: For every graph, after independent edge-weight perturbations with densities bounded by phi on a bounded interval, is every improving single-vertex-flip path of polynomial expected length in n and phi?
context:
Known polynomial bounds for complete or logarithmic-degree graphs do not cover arbitrary graphs.

This short research proposal states the target identified in the September 2026 fundamental-problem search. The references give the source models and related results. A full self-contained formulation and detailed progress review remain to be written.
why: A flagship unresolved explanation of why a canonical PLS local-search algorithm works efficiently on perturbed inputs.
status_note: Retained in the source-based research proposal dated 10 September 2026. No full resolution was found in that search; this is not a completed independent open-status review.
working_summary: FLIP improves a weighted cut by moving one vertex whenever that move increases the cut value. The question asks whether every improving path has polynomial expected length after independently perturbing edge weights with bounded densities. Smoothed analysis allows an adversarial graph while using small randomness in numerical data to prevent persistent worst-case degeneracies. A universal bound would explain why this simple local-search rule can behave efficiently beyond specially structured graphs. The saved proposal notes that complete-graph and low-degree results do not cover arbitrary graphs, and the expectation must control every improving path rather than a favorable pivot rule alone.

title: Does the expected redundancy of optimal alphabetic trees with random weights converge?
importance_reason: A precise average-case structural question connecting optimal search trees and information theory. Convergence is a focused first target within the broader expected-cost problem, rather than a general data-structure complexity barrier.
formal: For each n >= 2, let $D=(D_1,\ldots,D_n)$ be uniform on the probability simplex, equivalently Dirichlet(1,...,1). Let $C_n(D)=\min_T\sum_{i=1}^n D_i d_T(i)$, where T ranges over full ordered binary trees with leaves 1,...,n in that left-to-right order and d_T(i) is the depth of leaf i, with root depth zero. Define $H(D)=-\sum_iD_i\log_2D_i$ and $r_n=\mathbb E_D[C_n(D)-H(D)]$. Does the real sequence r_n converge to a finite limit as n tends to infinity? This is a precise limit-existence target within the source’s broader request to determine the expected optimal cost.
definitions: A full binary tree has exactly two children at every internal node. An ordered tree distinguishes left from right, and the fixed leaf order is the alphabetic constraint. Following left and right edges as bits gives an alphabetic prefix code: no leaf codeword is a prefix of another, and lexicographic codeword order agrees with symbol order. The tree is optimized separately after the probabilities D are realized; the expectation is taken afterward. To sample D, draw n-1 independent uniform points in (0,1), sort them, append endpoints 0 and 1, and take the n successive interval lengths. The weights are positive almost surely. For a fixed D, the cost is the expected number of binary decisions to find a leaf drawn with probabilities D; no random-tree distribution is assumed.
answer_criterion: Prove that for every epsilon > 0 there exists N0 such that |r_n-r_m| < epsilon for all n,m >= N0, or prove that this Cauchy property fails. A negative answer can be established by separated subsequential limits. Identifying the numerical value of a limit, if it exists, is useful further progress but is not required for the stated yes/no question. Bounded redundancy or finite Monte Carlo estimates alone do not settle convergence.
context:
An alphabetic tree preserves the order of the symbols, so a search can branch according to comparisons with boundaries in that order. This constraint is useful for searching and ordered merging, but can prevent the tree from using exactly the codeword lengths it would choose if the symbols were freely permutable. Redundancy measures the extra expected decisions beyond the entropy lower bound.

There are two levels of averaging. Once the weights are fixed, the weighted leaf depths describe the cost of queries to one optimized tree. The question then averages that optimum over a random probability vector. Optimizing a tree for the mean weight vector would be a different operation: it would choose a tree before seeing which symbols are common in the realized distribution.

The standard alphabetic coding bound gives 0 <= C_n(D)-H(D) < 2, so r_n is bounded. Boundedness does not imply convergence. Integer codeword lengths make it especially important not to assume that a constant correction term exists without proof. The present target isolates that issue before asking for the complete expected-cost formula.

Wild’s source question concerns the expected cost under exactly these random spacings, motivated both by alphabetic compression and by comparison-efficient partitioning in Quicksort. Its broad formulation asks to compute or approximate the expectation. This card extracts the specific convergence question explicitly; it does not attribute a conjectured limit or a claimed asymptotic formula to the source.
why: This asks whether the cost of optimal ordered searching has a stable average overhead beyond entropy under a canonical random-input model. It connects discrete codeword constraints with probabilistic analysis and separates a constant-order question from the much easier leading logarithmic growth.
status_note: Editorial specialization of the source’s expected-redundancy problem. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate a proof or disproof of convergence for this distribution; the author’s original question remains unanswered on the cited page. This is not a claim that a particular limiting value is known.

The expected redundancy is left unresolved.

The saved question asks whether that expected redundancy converges as the number of symbols grows. A stable limit would identify the average constant overhead imposed by ordered searching, while boundedness alone does not rule out persistent oscillation.

title: Rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics with Δ+2 colours
area_label: Sampling, Markov chains and mixing times

focus_reason: A longstanding general-graph conjecture linking local algorithms, approximate counting and spin systems; recent near-threshold results still require structural restrictions.
formal: Do absolute constants C,c>0 exist such that, for every finite simple n-vertex graph G with maximum degree Δ and every integer q≥Δ+2, the single-vertex heat-bath Glauber chain on proper q-colourings has total-variation mixing time t_mix(1/4)≤Cn^c?
definitions: Let n≥1 and Ω={σ:V(G)→[q] : σ(u)≠σ(v) for every edge uv}. Colours are labelled; unused colours are allowed. At each discrete step choose v uniformly from V(G), then choose a colour uniformly from [q]\{σ(u):u∈N(v)} and assign it to v, leaving all other vertices unchanged. The current colour is among the available choices. Let P be this transition matrix and π the uniform distribution on Ω. Define t_mix(1/4)=min{t∈Z_{≥0}: max_{σ∈Ω} (1/2)Σ_{τ∈Ω}|P^t(σ,τ)−π(τ)|≤1/4}. This counts individual vertex updates, not sweeps or bit operations. The constants C,c must be independent of n, Δ, q and G. The initial proper colouring is arbitrary, and the graph has no girth, treewidth or randomness promise. This card fixes a uniform polynomial bound across degrees, rather than leaving the exponent’s parameter dependence implicit.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A proper colouring is easy to construct greedily with this many colours. Sampling one nearly uniformly is a different task: a deterministic rule can strongly favour a small part of the solution space. Glauber dynamics is an appealing candidate because every update uses only a vertex and its neighbours, yet repeated local changes must reproduce the global distribution. The inherited paper states the conjecture and proves it for particular graph classes.

The threshold Δ+2 has a concrete role. On a clique with Δ+1 vertices and exactly Δ+1 colours, every vertex sees all other colours in its neighbourhood. No vertex can change colour, so each proper colouring is a separate absorbing state. With at least Δ+2 colours, the single-vertex chain is irreducible on every graph and converges to the uniform distribution. The unresolved issue is how long this convergence takes.

Connectivity of the recolouring graph is insufficient to control that time. A walk may need to cross a narrow passage between two large collections of colourings. Even short paths between every pair do not show that a random walk finds the appropriate passages often enough. The card therefore asks for a distributional guarantee from the worst starting colouring, rather than a bound on the number of recolourings in an intelligently chosen path.

The update convention matters when comparing sources. A second standard version proposes a colour uniformly from the entire palette and rejects it if a neighbour uses it. This is the Metropolis version used in several cited papers. Its off-diagonal transition probabilities and the heat-bath probabilities differ by a factor between 1 and q/(q−Δ). That factor is at most 1+Δ/2 in the present range, so the distinction is relevant to sharp runtime statements but does not create an exponential gap between their polynomial-mixing questions.

The early general-graph milestones were Jerrum’s q>2Δ regime and Vigoda’s improvement to roughly 11Δ/6. The latter used a flip chain that interchanges two colours on a small connected bichromatic component, followed by a comparison with single-vertex dynamics. Chen and coauthors subsequently crossed the 11/6 threshold by a small constant improvement. The 2026 ICALP paper retains Δ+2 as a conjecture, including its Glauber-dynamics version.

Carlson–Vigoda’s October 2024 revision gives a substantial further improvement. Theorem 1.1 assumes Δ≥125 and q≥1.809Δ and proves O(n log n) mixing for the flip chain. Comparison gives polynomial mixing for Glauber dynamics in that regime. Their optimal O(n log n) Glauber corollary has a constant depending on Δ and q; it is stated for fixed parameters. The headline coefficient should therefore not be read as an unrestricted optimal-time theorem for all degrees.

Graph structure can bring the colour threshold much closer to the target. Heinrich proves n^{O(tw(G)^3)} mixing with q≥Δ+2, so bounded treewidth is covered even when maximum degree is unbounded. For chordal graphs, the proved regime instead uses q≥(1+ε)(Δ+1) for a fixed positive ε. Letting treewidth grow with n, or substituting ε that shrinks with Δ, does not give the uniform statement in this card.

There was further progress during 2026. Jain–Mizgerd–Vigoda prove O_δ(n log n) mixing for the Metropolis chain when q≥(1+δ)Δ, Δ is sufficiently large in terms of fixed δ>0, and the graph has sufficiently large girth. Their August 27 revision improves the required girth from eleven to seven. This is stronger than the original April abstract, but still excludes general graphs and does not establish additive slack of only two colours.

Chen–Liu’s August 26 preprint reaches girth at least five in the same fixed-relative-slack regime for heat-bath dynamics. Its Theorem 1 proves spectral gap Ω_δ(1/n) and mixing time O_δ(n² log q+n log(1/ε)); the sharper O_δ(n log n) consequence requires degree bounded in terms of δ. Both the girth restriction and the dependence on δ matter. Taking δ=2/Δ is not justified by a theorem that first fixes δ and then requires sufficiently large Δ.

The other inherited 2026 source studies an additional constraint: prescribed colour-class sizes. Such a condition changes the sample space, and a single-vertex update generally cannot preserve it. Its algorithms for equitable or mildly skewed colourings therefore address a separate sampling problem. They provide useful context for why global constraints complicate local sampling, while explicitly leaving the unconstrained Δ+2 conjecture open.

This is fundamental because it tests whether the basic local sampler remains efficient throughout the universally ergodic range. A proof would connect a simple combinatorial availability condition with global probabilistic convergence. A negative answer would identify an obstruction to efficient local sampling that survives despite spare colours at every vertex and connectivity of the entire state space.
