context:
A minimum spanning tree connects a graph as cheaply as possible without redundant cycles. It is among the basic examples where a local greedy rule produces a global optimum, and it appears in network design and clustering. The optimization objective is well understood; the unsettled issue is how much computation is fundamentally needed to identify the right n−1 edges when the input already contains m edge records.

Sorting every edge is sufficient for Kruskal’s algorithm, but sorting is a stronger task than the required output. On a graph that is itself a tree, every edge belongs to the answer regardless of their relative weights. On a triangle, only the identity of a largest-weight edge is needed: discard it. Thus the familiar comparison lower bound for sorting all keys does not automatically become a lower bound for finding an MST. A faster algorithm must exploit the graph’s structure to avoid unnecessary ordering information.

The cut and cycle rules make this possible. A lightest edge across a cut can be selected safely, and a strictly heaviest edge on a cycle can be discarded. Equal weights can be handled consistently by comparing pairs consisting of the weight and the edge identifier. These rules avoid numerical arithmetic on weights, so the problem is meaningful for arbitrary real keys even though the objective is expressed as a sum.

Karger, Klein and Tarjan combine random sampling with linear-time MST verification to obtain a Las Vegas algorithm with expected O(m+n) running time. It always returns a correct tree; randomness controls the work spent on recursive filtering. The target here is a deterministic guarantee for every input, so fixing an arbitrary random seed does not inherit the expected-time theorem.

Chazelle’s deterministic algorithm achieves O(mα(m,n)) time, where α is a slowly growing inverse-Ackermann function. Its soft-heap machinery deliberately permits a controlled set of key increases inside an auxiliary data structure while the surrounding algorithm preserves the exact MST answer. The extra factor is tiny for practical input sizes, yet unbounded asymptotically. Removing it asks for an exact structural understanding of the problem’s complexity, not merely an implementation improvement.

Pettie and Ramachandran establish a different kind of optimality: total algorithmic running time can match, within a constant factor, the optimal worst-case number of edge comparisons for MST. Their algorithm is uniform; it constructs the small optimal decision trees it needs within the time analysis. But the asymptotic size of that optimum is itself unknown. Consequently a proof that linear-size comparison decision trees always suffice would settle the algorithmic question through their theorem.

The graph family also matters. Eisenstat and coauthors show that it is enough to solve graphs with at most 3n/2 edges, and separately relate the general problem to graphs with any fixed lower bound on girth, the length of a shortest cycle. Their available high-girth algorithm requires a lower bound that grows with n. That difference between a fixed girth threshold and a slowly growing threshold leaves the general deterministic question open.

Changing the access model can remove the obstacle. Fredman and Willard give a deterministic linear-time algorithm using integer-word operations on the weights. That theorem can exploit their binary representation, which the real-key comparison model deliberately withholds. Similarly, an algorithm that is fast for a random graph topology has an average-instance guarantee, even if the algorithm itself is deterministic; it does not bound the work on every graph.

The remaining challenge can therefore be stated without ambiguity: retain exactness, arbitrary real-key weights and all graph topologies, and make every part of the computation linear without random choices. A negative answer would be equally significant, by establishing an intrinsic cost for deterministic comparison-based optimization that expected-time random sampling avoids.
why: A central unresolved boundary between deterministic and randomized algorithms for a classical graph optimization problem, and a rare case where a provably optimal algorithm exists before its exact asymptotic complexity is understood.
status_note: The deterministic linear-time comparison problem remains open in the primary-author material checked through 11 September 2026. Integer-word algorithms, high-girth results and the optimal-decision-tree theorem do not settle this formulation.
progress: 1994: Fredman–Willard obtain deterministic linear time in a stronger integer-word model. | 1995: Karger–Klein–Tarjan obtain randomized linear time for arbitrary comparison weights. | 2000: Chazelle achieves deterministic O(mα(m,n)) comparison-based time. | 2002: Pettie–Ramachandran match the optimal decision-tree complexity with a uniform deterministic algorithm, without determining that complexity. | 2008: Pettie–Ramachandran develop alternative randomized MST algorithms using far fewer random bits; complete deterministic linear time remains unresolved.
working_summary: A minimum spanning tree connects every vertex while minimizing the total weight of its edges. This project asks whether arbitrary real comparison weights admit a deterministic algorithm whose worst-case time is linear in the graph size. Randomized linear expected time and nearly linear deterministic bounds provide contrasting benchmarks. Integer operations on weight representations answer a different model-specific question. A resolution would explain whether the remaining cost comes from essential deterministic comparison work or from limitations of existing graph filtering methods.

title: The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture for every forbidden induced graph
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A major unifying conjecture for hereditary graph classes, with a sharp qualitative gap between general bounds and the target and substantial recent progress on special cases.
formal: For every finite undirected simple graph H with at least two vertices, does there exist a real constant c(H)>0 such that every n-vertex undirected simple graph G with n≥1 and no induced copy of H satisfies max{α(G),ω(G)}≥n^{c(H)}?
definitions: An induced copy of H is an injective map f:V(H)→V(G) such that distinct u,v are adjacent in H if and only if f(u),f(v) are adjacent in G. Thus both edges and nonedges must match. α(G) is the maximum size of a set of pairwise nonadjacent vertices, and ω(G) is the maximum size of a set of pairwise adjacent vertices. The constant c(H) may depend arbitrarily on the entire fixed graph H, but not on G or n. No density, degree, dimension or algorithmic promise is imposed on G. The claim concerns existence of a clique or independent set, without requiring a polynomial-time construction. A hereditary graph class is one closed under taking induced subgraphs; the class of H-free graphs is hereditary.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Ramsey’s theorem guarantees a clique or independent set of logarithmic size in every sufficiently large graph, and random graphs show that this order of magnitude is unavoidable without further restrictions. Erdős–Hajnal predicts a dramatic change after forbidding even one fixed induced pattern: the guaranteed set should grow as a positive power of the number of vertices. The conjecture therefore asks how much global organization a single local structural exclusion forces.

For a simple example, a graph with no induced three-vertex path is a disjoint union of cliques. If it has t components, choosing one vertex from each gives an independent set of size t, while the largest component has at least n/t vertices and is a clique. One of these sets has size at least √n. This proves the conjecture for that forbidden graph and illustrates the desired polynomial gain through a structural decomposition.

The general theorem of Erdős and Hajnal gives a lower bound exp(c_H√log n). Bucić, Nguyen, Scott and Seymour improve it to exp(c_H√(log n·log log n)) for a positive constant depending on H. Their 2024 journal paper is the first improvement of this general bound. It is still smaller than nᵟ for every fixed δ>0 as n grows, so the extra logarithmic factor does not reach the conjectured scale.

Closure under complementation and vertex substitution lets proofs for a few building blocks settle many further forbidden graphs. Substitution replaces one vertex by a graph whose vertices all have the same neighbors outside the replacement. The remaining five-vertex building blocks were the bull, the five-cycle and the five-vertex path, together with its complement. Nguyen, Scott and Seymour’s proof for the path, published in March 2026, completes all forbidden graphs on at most five vertices.

For longer fixed paths, their separate all-path theorem gives homogeneous sets of size 2^{(log n)^{1−o(1)}}. This is close to the polynomial scale in its exponent but still does not assert n^c for any fixed positive c. In particular, the five-vertex result should not be described as resolving the conjecture for paths of arbitrary length.

Huang, Ju and Zhou’s August 2026 revision proves two additional six-vertex cases using an extension of iterative sparsification. The E-graph is a five-vertex path with a new leaf attached to its middle vertex. The Bird starts from a triangle with leaves attached to two different triangle vertices, then extends one of those leaves by one more edge. Both contain an induced five-vertex path, so excluding either permits a larger class than excluding the path itself.

A 28 August 2026 preprint by Tran and Nguyen reports another six-vertex case, specified without a drawing by vertex set {a,b,c,d,e,f} and edge set {ab,bc,cd,de,af,bf,df}. It develops the comb and sparsification framework further. This is an individual new forbidden pattern, rather than a proof for every six-vertex graph.

Another strand connects the conjecture with finding large nearly empty or nearly complete induced subgraphs. Bucić, Fox and Pham prove equivalence with polynomial quantitative versions of the Rödl and Nikiforov statements. This makes the problem relevant to structural decompositions and induced-pattern density, beyond locating a single clique or independent set.

There are also stronger quantitative results under additional hypotheses. Sun, Wang and Zeng’s July 2026 preprint gives exponent at least (Cd)⁻ᵈ for graphs of neighborhood VC-dimension at most d. This dimension bounds the size of a vertex set on which neighborhoods realize every possible subset. Such a restriction controls neighborhood complexity; arbitrary H-free graphs are not assumed to satisfy a fixed VC-dimension bound.
why: A foundational prediction that forbidding any fixed induced pattern forces polynomial-size order inside a graph. Its links to hereditary classes, neighborhood complexity and sparse/dense decompositions make it a central structural question with connections to algorithmic graph theory.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The 2026 primary literature explicitly retains the full conjecture as open. Sági’s historical revised claim is recorded separately and is not treated as a verified solution; the withdrawal of its earlier version does not itself refute the revision. New six-vertex and bounded-VC-dimension results have restricted scope.
progress: 1989: Erdős–Hajnal’s Ramsey-type theorems establish exp(c_H√log n) and pose the polynomial target. | 2023–2024: Bucić–Nguyen–Scott–Seymour improve the general bound by a √log log n factor in the exponent. | 2024: Bucić–Fox–Pham prove equivalence with polynomial Rödl and Nikiforov formulations. | 2026-03-23: The five-vertex-path theorem is published, completing the property for all forbidden graphs with at most five vertices; the preprint first appeared in December 2023. | 2026-07-10: Sun–Wang–Zeng sharpen the exponent for graphs of bounded VC-dimension, an additional restriction on the input graphs. | 2026-08-28: Tran–Nguyen post a proof for the six-vertex graph with edge set {ab,bc,cd,de,af,bf,df}. | 2026-08-31: Huang–Ju–Zhou revise their E-graph and Bird proofs and unified sparsification framework.
references: https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~asuk/erdos_hajnal.pdf | https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.10147 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.15333 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15032 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06258 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28551 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.08303 | https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09049 | https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.3876
working_summary: Forbidding one fixed induced graph excludes both its edge pattern and its nonedge pattern. The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture predicts that every graph with this restriction has a clique or independent set of polynomial size. The exponent may depend on the forbidden graph but must stay positive as the host graph grows. This would show that every proper hereditary restriction forces much stronger homogeneous structure than arbitrary graphs guarantee. The saved review records special-case advances and unvalidated full-solution claims separately, and a near-polynomial bound with a vanishing exponent does not establish the required fixed exponent.

title: Reed’s χ–ω–Δ conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A defining universal conjecture linking three basic graph parameters, with sharp examples and broad influence on colouring theory and its algorithmic methods.
formal: Does every nonempty finite simple undirected graph G satisfy χ(G)≤⌈(Δ(G)+1+ω(G))/2⌉?
definitions: A graph is simple when it has neither loops nor parallel edges. A proper k-colouring is a map from V(G) to {1,…,k} assigning different colours to endpoints of every edge; χ(G) is the minimum such k. The degree of a vertex is its number of neighbours, and Δ(G) is the maximum degree. A clique is a vertex set whose distinct vertices are all adjacent, and ω(G) is its largest possible size. The ceiling ⌈x⌉ is the least integer at least x. The statement concerns all such graphs, including disconnected graphs and graphs with isolated vertices. For an edgeless nonempty graph, χ=ω=1 and Δ=0. The empty graph can be included with χ=ω=Δ=0, without changing the question. There are no restrictions on graph size, maximum degree, forbidden subgraphs or the method used to obtain a colouring.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated inequality for every finite simple graph, or give a finite graph and a proof that its chromatic number exceeds the displayed ceiling. The target is an existence theorem, so a polynomial-time colouring algorithm is not required. An asymptotic bound with an additive error, a convex combination with clique coefficient less than 1/2, or a theorem restricted to sufficiently large maximum degree is partial progress unless the remaining cases are also covered.
context:
Two elementary bounds frame graph colouring. A clique needs a distinct colour for every vertex, so χ≥ω. On the other hand, greedily colouring vertices in any order uses at most Δ+1 colours: at most Δ colours are forbidden by already coloured neighbours. Reed asks whether an upper bound halfway between these two numbers always suffices, after rounding up. This would sharply connect a local obstruction, the size of a clique, to the global task of partitioning all vertices into independent sets.

The rounding is essential even for a five-cycle. It has maximum degree two and clique number two, but it needs three colours because an odd cycle is not bipartite. The unrounded average is 5/2. Complete graphs also meet the proposed upper bound exactly. These examples show that the question is about a precise universal inequality, rather than merely reducing the leading constant in a loose estimate.

There is also a useful family explaining the coefficient 1/2. Replace each vertex of a five-cycle by a clique of size t, joining every vertex of two replacement cliques whenever their cycle vertices were adjacent. The resulting graph has 5t vertices, maximum degree 3t−1 and clique number 2t. An independent set contains at most two vertices, so at least ⌈5t/2⌉ colours are necessary. A universal bound ⌈(1−ε)(Δ+1)+εω⌉ with ε>1/2 would give fewer colours for large t. Thus the conjectured interpolation coefficient cannot be increased.

Reed established a weaker universal interpolation with some fixed positive coefficient ε in place of 1/2. This already gives a saving proportional to the gap between maximum degree and clique number. Proving such a saving is difficult because high degree need not mean that a neighbourhood resembles a clique, and local savings must coexist across many overlapping neighbourhoods.

Hurley, de Joannis de Verclos and Kang report ε=0.119 for sufficiently large maximum degree, using a refined random colouring procedure and local sparsity estimates. Their published paper explicitly records a dependency: the 0.119 calculation uses a then-unreviewed result of Delcourt and Postle. Remark 3.1 gives ε=0.113 using an alternative published ingredient. The September 2026 digraph paper continues to cite the 0.119 bound. Both constants remain far below the conjectured 1/2.

A different advance handles graphs with much smaller cliques. Bonamy, Kelly, Nelson and Postle bound the chromatic number by O(Δ√(log ω/log Δ)), with related list and correspondence colouring results. For suitable relations between ω and Δ this is much stronger than a small fixed improvement on the greedy bound. It does not prove the desired average bound across the full range of clique sizes.

Recent related work also changes the task. The 2025 recolouring paper studies whether proper colourings can be connected by Kempe changes: swap two colours on a connected component induced by those colours. Its general conjectured interpolation coefficient is 1/3 because reconfiguration has obstructions beyond the existence of one colouring. Its positive results on odd-hole-free graphs therefore need to be read in that separate model.

Kawarabayashi and Picasarri-Arrieta extend the framework to directed graphs, where each colour class must induce an acyclic digraph. Their SODA 2025 work, revised in September 2026, proves a positive-ε interpolation and proposes the exact half-average analogue. Replacing each undirected edge by arcs in both directions recovers ordinary colouring, so the proposed directed statement would imply Reed’s conjecture. The directed partial theorem does not supply the missing coefficient.
why: A central structural colouring problem with an exact, best-possible target. It asks how much the absence of a large clique must reduce the number of colours, and guides probabilistic, structural and algorithmic approaches to colouring.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The September 8 primary revision explicitly retains the exact undirected inequality as open. Small-clique estimates, sufficiently-large-degree interpolation bounds, and the recolouring and directed variants do not settle the full statement. The published 0.119 bound’s stated dependency is preserved in the context.
progress: 1998: Reed proposes the half-average bound and proves an interpolation with some universal ε>0. | 2018–2022: Bonamy–Kelly–Nelson–Postle give stronger bounds in regimes with comparatively small clique number. | 2020–2022: Hurley–de Joannis de Verclos–Kang report ε=0.119 for large Δ; Remark 3.1 records the dependency and an ε=0.113 alternative. | 2025-02-14: De Meyer and coauthors develop a distinct Kempe-recolouring analogue with additional reconfiguration obstructions. | 2026-09-08: The revised digraph analogue retains the undirected exact inequality as Conjecture 1.1 and proves only a positive-ε generalization.
working_summary: Reed's conjecture bounds chromatic number by the rounded average of maximum degree plus one and clique number. It combines a local upper-bound scale from degree with the unavoidable coloring demand imposed by a largest clique. The question asks whether every finite simple graph admits a coloring at this intermediate threshold. A positive answer would give a unified quantitative relationship among three fundamental graph parameters. The saved formulation concerns ordinary vertex coloring on unrestricted graphs, so fractional, list, directed, or recoloring variants require separate interpretation and do not automatically settle the inequality.

title: Is graph isomorphism solvable in polynomial time?
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A canonical unresolved problem at the intersection of algorithms, permutation groups and complexity theory, with a precise best-known general upper bound.
formal: Does there exist one deterministic classical algorithm that, for every pair of finite simple undirected graphs G and H given by explicit adjacency matrices, decides whether G and H are isomorphic in time polynomial in the total input length?
definitions: Two graphs on equally many vertices are isomorphic if a bijection of their vertex sets preserves adjacency in both directions. The input contains the complete graph descriptions; unequal vertex counts are rejected immediately. The algorithm must be uniform, deterministic and correct on every graph pair, with no promise of bounded degree, rigidity, expansion, or random input. Polynomial time is measured in the binary input length, so the Θ(n²) adjacency data may be read in full. The question concerns ordinary vertex-permutation isomorphism, not quantum isomorphism, graph canonization under a different output requirement, or isomorphism of groups or tensors. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Graph isomorphism asks whether two finite graphs differ only by a relabelling of their vertices. A proposed relabelling is easy to verify, so the problem lies in NP, but ruling out all relabellings can be difficult for highly symmetric graphs.

Many special cases have polynomial-time algorithms, including bounded-degree graphs and several classes with strong structural restrictions. These results do not automatically combine into an algorithm for arbitrary graphs, whose automorphism groups can have a much richer structure.

Babai’s breakthrough gives a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm, with running time exp((log n)^{O(1)}), improving the earlier subexponential bound. Quasipolynomial time is still asymptotically larger than every fixed polynomial, so the final gap to P remains exactly the question on this card.

Graph canonization is closely related: producing a canonical labelled representative is at least as demanding as deciding isomorphism in many standard reductions, but a theorem about one output formulation must preserve the required runtime and uniformity before it answers the decision problem. Quantum graph-isomorphism relations and BQP algorithms likewise concern different computational problems.

No general polynomial-time algorithm or unconditional lower bound excluding one was found in the checked literature through 11 September 2026. The problem remains a clean benchmark for the boundary between efficiently verifiable symmetry and efficient recognition of symmetry.
why: Tests whether the central equivalence problem for finite combinatorial structures can be recognized in deterministic polynomial time after the quasipolynomial barrier was broken.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Babai’s deterministic quasipolynomial algorithm remains the best general worst-case bound located; no polynomial-time algorithm or unconditional exclusion of one was found.
progress: 2015–2017: Babai announces and corrects a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm for general graph isomorphism. | 2018: Babai’s survey records quasipolynomial isomorphism testing as the general frontier after the breakthrough. | 2026: Recent surveys and status checks continue to list polynomial-time general GI as unresolved; improvements remain parameterized or restricted to special graph classes.

title: Almost-linear-time exact maximum matching in general graphs
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A core combinatorial optimization primitive with a large gap between general graphs and the fast bipartite case, connecting augmenting paths, polyhedral methods and algebraic algorithms.
formal: Is there one randomized sequential algorithm that, on every explicitly represented finite simple undirected graph G with n vertices and m edges, outputs an exact maximum-cardinality matching with probability at least 2/3 and has expected running time (n+m+2)^{1+o(1)} in the word-RAM model below?
definitions: A matching M⊆E(G) is a set of edges no two of which share an endpoint. Its size is |M|, and ν(G)=max{|M|:M is a matching in G}. The algorithm must output valid edge identifiers forming a matching on every terminating execution, and |M|=ν(G) with probability at least 2/3 on each input. It must terminate with probability one. Vertices are labelled 1,…,n and the input is an adjacency-list or edge-list representation of size O(n+m); isolated vertices are included in n. Put N=n+m+2. Use a random-access machine with Θ(log N)-bit words, supporting constant-cost reads, writes, comparisons, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts on words, and fresh uniform random words. Intermediate larger integers require multiple words and their processing is charged. Preprocessing and output writing are included. The program is uniform, with no advice or free precomputed tables. The time statement means that this same algorithm satisfies: for every real ε>0 there are constants Cε and Nε such that for every input with N≥Nε, its expected number of operations is at most Cε N^{1+ε}. The expectation is over its own random choices, not a distribution on graph inputs. No edge weights, degree restriction, bipartiteness promise, approximation slack or auxiliary communication model is assumed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Maximum matching is a basic model of pairing compatible objects while using each object at most once. General graphs allow compatibility patterns that cannot be separated into two sides. Edmonds’ blossom method established that this optimization is polynomial-time solvable. The remaining question is how close its exact computational cost can come to the size of the graph that must be read.

Maximum and maximal have different meanings. A maximal matching merely cannot be extended by adding a single edge. On a four-vertex path, the middle edge alone is maximal, while the two outside edges form a maximum matching of size two. A greedy linear-time procedure can therefore solve maximal matching and still fail the exact task on a tiny input. The card requires the global optimum, with no allowed loss of even one matched pair.

Alternating paths explain how a nonmaximum matching can improve. Such a path alternates edges outside and inside the matching and starts and ends at unmatched vertices. Flipping its edge membership increases the matching size by one. In general graphs, odd cycles complicate the search for shortest augmenting paths; contracted structures called blossoms keep track of these possibilities. Micali and Vazirani’s classical algorithm achieves O(m√n) time, with later work developing its proof and presentation.

Bipartite graphs have a particularly effective flow formulation. Direct each edge from the left side to the right, join a source to left vertices and right vertices to a sink, and give every edge capacity one. Integral maximum flow gives a maximum matching. Almost-linear exact flow algorithms therefore solve bipartite matching within the desired time scale. There is no supplied bipartition in the present question, and the same construction does not automatically encode odd-cycle constraints.

A triangle illustrates the polyhedral obstacle without requiring a large example. If a fractional variable of one half is placed on each edge, every vertex has total incident value one, but the total value is 3/2 while an integral matching has size at most one. For any odd vertex set S, an integral matching uses at most (|S|−1)/2 edges entirely inside S. Handling these additional odd-set restrictions efficiently is part of what distinguishes general matching from its bipartite counterpart.

Algebraic algorithms offer another route. Mucha and Sankowski use Gaussian elimination to construct maximum matchings in randomized time governed by matrix multiplication, conventionally written O(n^ω) for an available exponent ω>2. This is a major improvement over combinatorial bounds on dense graphs. It still does not yield input-size almost-linear time on all sparse graphs, where a dense n-by-n matrix representation can itself exceed the input size by a large factor.

Approximation also behaves differently. Duan, Pettie and Su obtain a (1−δ)-approximation for maximum weight matching in O(mδ⁻¹ log δ⁻¹) time, hence linear time for fixed δ; unit weights cover cardinality. To force exact cardinality purely by rounding this guarantee, one would need δ small enough that the possible loss is below one edge. When the optimum is Θ(n), that requires δ=O(1/n), so substituting it into the approximation running time loses the desired almost-linear bound.

Ansaripour, Danaei and Mehlhorn’s 2024 implementation study is useful for interpreting experiments: the observed behaviour on random graphs can be close to linear, while specially constructed inputs expose substantial differences between algorithms. Empirical speed and average graph behaviour therefore cannot establish the bound quantified over every input here. Their paper also keeps the distinction between the faster bipartite results and general matching explicit.

A June 2026 revision by Chakraborty and coauthors places construction of a general maximum matching in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. This model permits a large auxiliary tape with arbitrary initial contents, provided those contents are restored. It is progress on space and reversible use of auxiliary memory. The polynomial-time statement is not an almost-linear running-time theorem, so it does not resolve this card.
why: A major remaining exact graph-optimization problem beyond the almost-linear flow framework. It asks whether odd-cycle and blossom structure impose a real asymptotic cost, even when randomization is allowed.
status_note: No almost-linear exact general-graph algorithm was found in the primary literature checked through 11 September 2026. Bipartite flow algorithms, approximation schemes and the 2026 catalytic-space result do not meet the stated target. This card explicitly permits bounded-error randomization and expected running time.
progress: 1980: Micali–Vazirani obtain the classical O(m√n) algorithm; later correctness work refines its alternating-path theory. | 2004: Mucha–Sankowski construct maximum matchings using fast algebraic operations. | 2011: Duan–Pettie–Su obtain linear-time approximation for each fixed accuracy parameter in general weighted graphs. | 2022: Chen and coauthors achieve almost-linear exact flow algorithms, giving the corresponding bipartite matching consequence. | 2024-09-23: Ansaripour–Danaei–Mehlhorn publish a detailed implementation and experimental study of Gabow’s general matching algorithm. | 2026-06-01: The catalytic-logspace revision constructs general maximum matchings with a polynomial-time bound, a different resource guarantee.
working_summary: Maximum matching chooses as many mutually vertex-disjoint edges as possible in an undirected graph. The target is an exact randomized algorithm with expected running time almost linear in the explicit input size. General graphs introduce odd cycles and the blossom structures needed to manage them. A fast maximal matching or an approximation does not guarantee the same answer. Progress would clarify whether finding the globally best pairing can approach the cost of simply reading all vertices and edges.

title: The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A central organizing conjecture for hereditary graph colouring and forbidden induced subgraphs, defining the proposed forest boundary for χ-boundedness.
formal: For every finite nonempty tree T and every integer r≥1, does there exist a finite integer B(T,r) such that every finite simple undirected graph G with clique number at most r and no induced subgraph isomorphic to T has chromatic number at most B(T,r)?
definitions: A tree is a connected graph with no cycle. All graphs here are finite, simple and undirected. The clique number ω(G) is the largest number of pairwise adjacent vertices, and the chromatic number χ(G) is the least number of colours in a proper vertex colouring, in which adjacent vertices receive distinct colours. Both parameters are zero for the empty graph. For S⊆V(G), the induced graph G[S] retains all edges of G with both endpoints in S. Saying that G contains an induced T means there is an injective map φ:V(T)→V(G) such that xy is an edge of T if and only if φ(x)φ(y) is an edge of G. Extra edges between image vertices are forbidden. The quantifier order is ∀T ∀r ∃B ∀G: the integer B may depend arbitrarily on T and r, but not on |V(G)|, maximum degree or any additional parameter of G. Equivalently, for each T there is a function f_T:N→N with χ(G)≤f_T(ω(G)) for every induced-T-free graph G. No prescribed polynomial growth, computability requirement for f_T, or efficient colouring algorithm is part of the target. The statement concerns ordinary chromatic number, not fractional, list, oriented or domatic colouring parameters.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated bound for all finite trees and all fixed clique bounds, or exhibit one fixed tree T and one fixed integer r together with induced-T-free graphs G_k satisfying ω(G_k)≤r and χ(G_k)→∞. A single finite graph can disprove a proposed numerical bound but cannot refute the existence of some larger bound. A bound that still grows with |V(G)|, or a theorem with a different excluded object or extra host-graph promise, is not a full resolution.
context:
A clique explains one elementary reason for needing many colours: its vertices must all receive different colours. But graphs can require arbitrarily many colours even when every clique has size at most two. The conjecture proposes that forbidding any one fixed induced tree eliminates this unbounded gap. Once the tree and clique bound are fixed, the same finite palette should suffice no matter how many vertices the graph has.

The induced condition is essential. A copy of a tree as an ordinary subgraph can ignore unwanted edges between its vertices. An induced copy must reproduce both adjacency and nonadjacency. Complete graphs contain every sufficiently small tree as an ordinary subgraph, while most of those trees do not occur as induced subgraphs. The difficult step in building the desired tree is therefore arranging its branches without creating extra edges among them.

Trees are the natural boundary for this kind of one-forbidden-pattern statement. High-girth graphs can have arbitrarily large chromatic number while containing no short cycles. If a fixed forbidden graph contains a cycle, choosing larger girth avoids that graph while retaining an unbounded chromatic number and a bounded clique number. The corresponding obstruction is absent for forests. This is why the conjecture is a proposed classification, rather than an arbitrary choice of forbidden shape.

There are substantial positive cases. Kierstead and Penrice proved the conjecture for every tree of radius at most two: some central vertex is within distance two of every other vertex. Paths and further tree families are also known. Scott and Seymour subsequently strengthen the radius-two result under exclusion of a fixed complete multipartite subgraph, with polynomial bounds in its part size. Such results exploit restrictions on how branches can interact.

Nguyen, Scott and Seymour’s 2023 preprint, published in 2024, obtains a copy of any fixed rooted tree under the conjecture’s high-chromatic-number hypotheses, with every path from the root induced. This controls unwanted edges along ancestor–descendant paths. It still permits edges between different branches, and those edges may prevent the whole vertex set from inducing a tree. The distinction isolates one of the remaining obstacles.

Their later work on near-linear stable sets applies to every fixed excluded forest and fixed clique bound. It proves an independent set of size n^{1−o(1)}, and consequently a chromatic bound n^{o(1)}, where n is the number of vertices. Thus every fixed positive power n^ε eventually exceeds the available upper bound. Nevertheless, a function such as log n is also n^{o(1)} and is unbounded, so subpolynomial growth does not establish the constant B(T,r) sought here.

That work also proves a bounded fractional chromatic number for multibrooms, formed by identifying the roots of several paths that have additional leaves at their far ends. Fractional colouring covers vertices by weighted independent sets and minimizes the total weight. Ordinary colouring requires an actual partition into colour classes. The paper retains the full conjecture for general multibrooms despite its stronger fractional conclusion.

Davies and Yuditsky establish the conjecture, with a polynomial bound in the clique number, for intersection graphs of axis-aligned boxes in every fixed dimension d. Their result first appeared in 2024 and was published in April 2026. Both the excluded forest and dimension are fixed parameters. Allowing the dimension to grow with the input would let the bound vary with an extra parameter, so the theorem does not cover arbitrary graphs with the uniform bound required here.

For algorithms, this conjecture identifies a structural source of bounded colouring complexity and large independent sets. It does not itself promise that a suitable colouring can be found efficiently. A proof with an effective construction would offer additional algorithmic information; a counterexample would reveal a family of sparse-clique graphs whose chromatic obstruction survives exclusion of one fixed induced tree. The size-independent existence statement is already fundamental.
why: Determine whether every fixed induced tree is an unavoidable pattern in graphs whose chromatic number grows while their clique number stays bounded.
status_note: The 2025 near-linear-stable-set paper and April 2026 bounded-boxicity paper explicitly retain the general conjecture. The former yields n^{o(1)} rather than a size-independent bound; the latter restricts the host class. September 2026 results on tournament analogues concern directed parameters. No resolution of this ordinary undirected statement found through 11 September 2026.
progress: 1994: Kierstead–Penrice establish χ-boundedness when the excluded tree has radius at most two. | 2022–2023: Scott–Seymour strengthen radius-two results under complete multipartite subgraph exclusions; checked preprint revised 10 January 2023. | 2023–2024: Nguyen–Scott–Seymour force path-induced rooted copies of arbitrary trees, while permitting extra edges between branches. | 2024–2025: Nguyen–Scott–Seymour prove near-linear independent sets and subpolynomial chromatic bounds for every fixed forest and clique bound; journal publication 25 September 2025. | 2026-04-02: Davies–Yuditsky’s journal publication proves polynomial χ-boundedness under the additional promise of boxicity bounded by a fixed dimension.
working_summary: The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture considers graphs excluding a fixed tree as an induced subgraph. It asks whether bounding clique number then also bounds chromatic number, independently of graph size. The proposed principle says that high coloring complexity with no large clique must eventually force every prescribed induced tree. This would organize a large collection of hereditary coloring classes through one structural mechanism. The saved review distinguishes genuinely induced trees from weaker path-induced copies and ordinary coloring from fractional results, while allowing an arbitrary bound rather than demanding polynomial growth.

title: The optimal quantitative Excluded Grid Theorem
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A central quantitative problem in graph minor theory with direct implications for structural decompositions, routing, packing and parameterized algorithms.
formal: For each integer r≥2, let f(r) be the least nonnegative integer t such that every finite simple undirected graph of treewidth at least t contains the r×r square grid as a minor. Determine the asymptotic order of f(r) up to universal constant factors, including the correct logarithmic dependence.
definitions: The r×r grid has vertex set {1,…,r}², with an edge between (i,j) and (i′,j′) exactly when |i−i′|+|j−j′|=1. It has r² vertices; r denotes side length. A graph H is a minor of G if H can be obtained by deleting vertices, deleting edges and contracting edges, after removing loops and merging parallel edges. Equivalently, a model of H consists of one nonempty connected vertex set in G for each vertex of H, all pairwise disjoint, with an edge of G joining the corresponding sets for every edge of H. Additional edges are permitted. A tree decomposition of G is a tree T with bags B_t⊆V(G), such that every vertex belongs to some bag, the endpoints of every edge belong together to some bag, and the bags containing any given vertex form a connected subtree of T. Its width is max_t |B_t|−1; treewidth tw(G) is the minimum such width. Robertson–Seymour’s Grid-Minor Theorem guarantees that f(r) is finite. The quantifier over G includes graphs of arbitrary size, degree and genus. This is an extremal existence threshold; no efficiency requirement for finding the grid model is imposed. Polylogarithmic factors mean (log r)^c for a fixed constant c, and matching bounds here must resolve such factors rather than suppress them.
answer_criterion: Identify an explicit asymptotic function h(r) and universal constants a,b>0 such that a h(r)≤f(r)≤b h(r) for all sufficiently large r. The upper bound must force a grid minor in every graph above the stated threshold; the lower bound must give graphs of comparable treewidth that exclude it. In particular, this determines whether f(r)=O(r²(log r)^c) for some fixed c. Merely improving a nonmatching polynomial exponent, solving the planar-host case, or replacing minors by a different containment relation is progress rather than a complete answer.
context:
Treewidth measures how large the interacting pieces of a graph must be when organized along a tree. Many algorithms work by dynamic programming across the bags of a tree decomposition, with a strong dependence on bag size. A grid provides a canonical obstruction to small treewidth: its rows and columns create many overlapping connections that cannot be separated into very small bags. The Excluded Grid Theorem states that every graph of sufficiently large treewidth contains such an obstruction as a minor.

The unknown quantity is how much treewidth must be spent to force a grid of a given side length. The qualitative theorem only says that some finite threshold exists. A sharp quantitative bound would explain how efficiently general tangled connectivity can be organized into a planar grid. This is not a statement that the graph itself is planar, or that a grid must appear as an induced subgraph.

A vertex-count example already rules out a linear threshold. The complete graph on r²−1 vertices has treewidth r²−2, but cannot contain an r×r grid minor because taking a minor cannot increase the number of vertices. Thus f(r)≥r²−1. Its many edges cannot replace the need for r² disjoint nonempty branch sets in a minor model. This is why the fact that the r×r grid itself has treewidth r does not imply a linear bound for arbitrary host graphs.

The known lower bound is stronger: f(r)=Ω(r² log r). Robertson, Seymour and Thomas obtain it using bounded-degree expanders of logarithmic girth. Such graphs have treewidth proportional to their number of vertices, while every cycle is long. A large grid contains quadratically many vertex-disjoint small cycles; lifting those cycles through a minor model requires quadratically many disjoint long cycles in the host. This consumes a logarithmic factor of additional vertices.

Chekuri and Chuzhoy obtain the first polynomial upper bound, replacing an enormous quantitative gap by a polynomial relationship between treewidth and grid size. Their proof is constructive: a randomized polynomial-time algorithm finds a grid model at the scale established by their theorem. This makes the result useful both as a structural guarantee and as a subroutine, although this card asks only for the optimal existence threshold.

Chuzhoy and Tan improve the general upper bound to O(r⁹(log r)^c) for an absolute constant c. Their SODA 2019 paper, published in journal form in 2021, builds on well-linked sets and paths of connected clusters. Well-linkedness supplies many disjoint connections; the challenge is arranging them into the grid’s particular pattern without losing too much width at successive stages. The lower and upper bounds still differ by a large power of r.

The same paper records competing predictions: Robertson–Seymour–Thomas conjectured that the r² log r lower bound is tight, while Demaine and coauthors proposed a cubic threshold. Consequently, the catalogue target is the actual asymptotic order. A near-quadratic upper bound would be a major result, but should not be described as the only conjectured answer. Even r² times an unspecified power of log r would leave part of the present target unresolved.

The 2025 paper The Grid-Minor Theorem Revisited strengthens the structural description of graphs excluding a fixed planar minor. It represents them inside clique blow-ups of graphs whose treewidth is controlled by the excluded graph’s treedepth. The blow-up size is an unspecified function of the excluded graph. This gives useful product structure and colouring applications, while leaving the optimal numerical threshold f(r) undetermined.

Catching Rats in H-minor-free Graphs, presented at SODA 2026, makes another substantial refinement under an extra host-graph restriction. For a fixed excluded graph H with t vertices and Euler genus g, a graph excluding both H and the r×r grid has treewidth O(gr+t^{2304}), hence O(t²r+t^{2304}). This is linear in r when H is fixed. General graphs in our question need not exclude any fixed H, so that additional parameter cannot be treated as a universal constant.

The threshold influences the quantitative strength of grid-based routing arguments, packing-versus-covering theorems and parameterized algorithms. Better bounds can improve how a large-treewidth case yields useful structure, or how a no-grid case bounds the state space for dynamic programming. A matching lower bound would be equally informative: it would identify an unavoidable loss in converting unrestricted graph connectivity into a planar obstruction.
why: Determine the exact asymptotic loss when converting large treewidth into a square-grid minor, a foundational link between graph structure and algorithms.
status_note: The checked general bounds remain Ω(r² log r) and O(r⁹ polylog r). The November 2025 product-structure result and SODA 2026 fixed-minor result refine different aspects and do not determine the all-graphs threshold. No matching asymptotic bounds found through 11 September 2026. The problem does not assume that either the near-quadratic or cubic conjecture is correct.
progress: 1986: Robertson–Seymour prove that sufficiently large treewidth forces any fixed planar graph, including every square grid, as a minor. | 1994: Robertson–Seymour–Thomas strengthen quantitative bounds; logarithmic-girth expanders give the Ω(r² log r) obstruction. | 2013–2016: Chekuri–Chuzhoy obtain the first polynomial relationship, with a randomized algorithm finding a grid model; STOC 2014 and JACM 2016. | 2019–2021: Chuzhoy–Tan prove the general O(r⁹ polylog r) upper bound; SODA 2019, Journal of Combinatorial Theory B 2021. | 2025-11-07: The Grid-Minor Theorem Revisited gives a qualitative product-structure strengthening, with an unspecified blow-up factor depending on the excluded planar graph. | 2026-01: Catching Rats in H-minor-free Graphs gives bounds linear in grid side length and polynomial in |V(H)| under additional exclusion of H; SODA 2026.
working_summary: The Excluded Grid Theorem guarantees a large grid minor when a graph has sufficiently large treewidth. The question asks for the optimal treewidth threshold forcing an r-by-r grid, including the correct logarithmic factors. Treewidth measures how difficult the graph is to decompose into small overlapping bags, while a grid supplies a concrete witness of large-scale complexity. Sharp bounds would quantify this foundational connection used throughout structural and algorithmic graph theory. The reviewed target concerns all graphs and grid side length, so bounds for an additional excluded-minor promise or suppressed polylogarithmic factors do not finish it.

title: Almost-linear triangle detection
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A fundamental graph primitive and fine-grained hardness assumption with consequences for dynamic data structures, joins and string matching.
formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph with n vertices and m edges given by adjacency lists, decides whether a triangle exists with success probability at least 2/3 and worst-case running time (n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}?
definitions: A triangle is a set of three distinct vertices u,v,w for which all three unordered edges {u,v},{v,w},{w,u} are present. The input gives labelled vertices 1,…,n and explicit adjacency lists; it is promised to describe a simple undirected graph, and can be disconnected or contain isolated vertices. The RAM has words of w=⌈4 log₂(n+2)⌉ bits, random-access memory, and unit-cost word reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2ʷ, and integer division by a nonzero word. Independent random words may be generated at unit cost. Input reading and all preprocessing count toward time. The running-time bound holds for every graph and every random tape, while correctness probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness. The o(1) is a function tending to zero as n+m tends to infinity, for this one fixed algorithm; equivalently, for every ε>0 the same algorithm eventually uses at most (n+m+2)^{1+ε} operations. There is no promise on density, degree, arboricity or triangle count. Matrix multiplication and other algebraic techniques are allowed if their implementation fits this machine model. Only one yes/no answer is required.
answer_criterion: Construct and analyze an algorithm meeting the stated all-input time and probability guarantees, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A deterministic O(n+m) algorithm would be an even stronger positive answer. A fixed exponent above one, an O(n²) bound that is only input-linear on dense graphs, output-sensitive listing, or an algorithm restricted to bounded-arboricity graphs does not settle the question. The target fixes the original draft’s “linear or at least almost-linear” alternative at the precise almost-linear threshold.
context:
Triangle detection is among the smallest nontrivial pattern-finding tasks in a graph. The pattern has only three vertices, but a graph may contain an enormous number of possible triples. The question asks whether all the relevant combinations can be handled in essentially the time required to read the graph. It must also handle triangle-free instances, where an algorithm cannot stop upon finding a convenient local witness.

Detection is different from listing. A complete graph has Θ(n²) input edges and Θ(n³) triangles, so explicitly listing every triangle cannot take linear time in the input size. A yes/no answer has constant output size and faces no such output-size obstruction. Likewise, approximate counting or finding triangles in a distribution of random inputs does not supply an exact decision guarantee on every adversarial graph.

Chiba and Nishizeki give triangle listing in O(m·a(G)) time, apart from reading isolated vertices, where arboricity a(G) is the minimum number of forests needed to cover the graph’s edges. This gives linear time on any family of bounded arboricity, including planar graphs. General graphs can have arboricity of order √m, so this approach has a superlinear worst-case cost. A sparse graph can still contain a dense, difficult region.

Alon, Yuster and Zwick improve the general sparse-graph bound using a degree threshold. Handle triangles touching a low-degree vertex by local enumeration, and use matrix multiplication on the smaller set of high-degree vertices. For an available square matrix-multiplication exponent τ, the resulting standard bound is O(n+m^{2τ/(τ+1)}), roughly O(n+m^{1.407}) at familiar current exponents. The optimization balances the cost of the two parts.

Even setting the matrix-multiplication exponent to two in this particular reduction leaves exponent 4/3 in m. Thus faster dense multiplication alone, inserted into the same degree-splitting argument, would not make the sparse algorithm almost linear. This is an observation about the upper-bound method, not a proof that a different graph algorithm cannot do better.

Abboud and Vassilevska Williams formulate a no-almost-linear triangle hypothesis and use it to derive conditional lower bounds for dynamic problems. The conjecture concerns general algorithms on logarithmic-word RAMs. Their separate combinatorial Boolean-matrix-multiplication conjecture restricts the kinds of techniques used; it should not be substituted for the unrestricted question here. Reductions transfer assumed hardness, rather than establish an unconditional superlinear lower bound.

The distinction remains useful in current work. Kumabe and Uezato’s ICALP 2026 paper reduces triangle detection to matching certain fixed regular expressions with two backreference uses. Consequently, an almost-linear algorithm for that matching task would also give an almost-linear triangle algorithm. This illustrates why a small graph pattern can govern complexity in a seemingly unrelated setting.

Search results require source checks. Dumitrescu’s March 2024 claim of faster combinatorial triangle algorithms was withdrawn three days after posting; the author states that the algorithm may fail and identifies an invalid case analysis. It is not an established improvement.

I also checked the parent-edge rule in Vega’s August 2025 linear-time proposal. Consider the path 0–1–2–3–4–5–6 plus edges 0–3, 3–6 and 0–6. A legal DFS follows the whole path. Its unique triangle is {0,3,6}, consisting entirely of back edges. No test restricted to a DFS parent, its child and a common neighbour can find it. A local simulation and exhaustive triple check confirm this counterexample to the stated rule; this is not a test of later replacement implementations.

A separate September 2026 Aegypti revision claims O(n²) time via bucket reduction. That claimed bound is not almost linear for every sparse input, even if its correctness were established. I have not adjudicated its different proof. An all-density statement must keep both n and m visible: a dense-case breakthrough and an input-linear sparse algorithm are distinct achievements.

A resolution would identify whether a basic three-way adjacency condition inherently requires substantial work beyond scanning an explicit graph. A positive algorithm would affect graph-pattern routines and invalidate hardness assumptions used by many reductions. A negative result would provide a major unconditional lower bound for a simple polynomial-time graph problem on a strong, standard machine model.
why: Determine whether detecting the simplest cyclic graph pattern requires a superlinear amount of computation beyond reading the input.
status_note: No established almost-linear algorithm or unconditional impossibility theorem found through 11 September 2026. The 2024 combinatorial proposal is withdrawn. The stated parent-edge rule in the August 2025 linear proposal has the explicit counterexample described above. The separate September 2026 O(n²) claim does not meet the all-density target and is not treated as an established bound.
progress: 1985: Chiba–Nishizeki give O(m·a(G)) triangle listing, yielding linear time for bounded-arboricity families. | 1997: Alon–Yuster–Zwick combine degree splitting with fast matrix multiplication to improve sparse triangle detection. | 2014: Abboud–Vassilevska Williams formulate the no-almost-linear triangle hypothesis and derive conditional dynamic lower bounds. | 2024-03-05: Dumitrescu withdraws the claimed faster combinatorial algorithm because its case analysis is invalid. | 2026-07: Kumabe–Uezato use triangle hardness to exclude almost-linear matching for a restricted two-use backreference class, conditionally. | 2026-09-08: A separate Aegypti revision claims O(n²), which is not an almost-linear guarantee for all graph densities; correctness not adjudicated here.
working_summary: Triangle detection asks whether an undirected graph contains three pairwise adjacent vertices. The proposed randomized algorithm must decide this in almost linear time on every explicitly supplied graph. Only existence is requested, so graphs with many triangles do not impose a large-output obstacle. Sparse special classes offer useful successes without covering arbitrary inputs. The challenge is to avoid examining too many combinations of neighbors while still giving a reliable negative answer when no triangle exists anywhere.

title: Seese’s conjecture for MSO₁ and clique-width
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A foundational conjecture asking whether bounded clique-width is unavoidable whenever an entire graph class has decidable vertex-set monadic logic.
formal: For every isomorphism-closed class C of finite simple undirected graphs, does decidability of its MSO₁ satisfiability problem imply that some constant k bounds the clique-width of every graph in C?
definitions: An MSO₁ sentence is built from vertex equality, adjacency E(x,y), membership x∈X in vertex sets, Boolean connectives, and quantification over individual vertices and subsets of the vertex set. There is no built-in vertex order, edge-set quantification, parity predicate or other counting extension. For a fixed class C, Sat_MSO₁(C) consists of all finite encoded MSO₁ sentences φ for which some G∈C satisfies φ. Decidable means that one Turing machine, allowed to depend on C, halts and answers correctly for every input sentence. C itself is not an input to that machine; no complexity bound is required. By negating sentences this is equivalent to deciding the theory Th_MSO₁(C)={φ: every G∈C satisfies φ}. A k-expression builds a labeled graph from single vertices with labels in [k], disjoint union, relabeling every vertex of one label to another, and adding all edges between two distinct labels. The clique-width cw(G) is the smallest k permitting such an expression after labels are forgotten; set cw(∅)=0. The conclusion is ∃k∀G∈C cw(G)≤k, with k depending on C. No hereditary, minor-closed, bounded-degree or finite-forbidden-subgraph assumption is imposed.
answer_criterion: Prove the implication for every such graph class, or give one class of unbounded clique-width together with a correct terminating algorithm for its entire MSO₁ satisfiability problem. A single finite graph cannot refute a uniform width bound for a class. Model checking on a supplied graph, or decidability with a promise about sentence size, is not the premise. Results requiring parity predicates or restricted graph classes do not prove the full statement.
context:
An MSO₁ sentence can describe a graph property by quantifying over sets of vertices. Three-colorability, for example, can be expressed by choosing three sets that partition the vertices and requiring each set to be independent. Checking such a sentence on one finite graph is always decidable by exhaustive search. The premise here is much stronger: from a sentence alone, decide whether it holds in at least one member of an entire, potentially infinite graph class.

Clique-width measures how many vertex labels are needed to construct a graph using a small repertoire of operations. Labels identify groups of vertices that receive the same future edge additions. Dense graphs can have small clique-width: a complete graph can be built with two labels by inserting one vertex, joining it to all previous vertices, and merging its label. Thus the conjectured structural restriction is not a sparsity condition.

The classical treewidth theorem provides the motivation. Seese proves structural restrictions from decidability of monadic theories, and the version allowing quantification over edge sets forces bounded treewidth. Grid-minor machinery supports that argument. The MSO₁ conjecture replaces edge-set quantification by vertex-set quantification and asks for bounded clique-width instead. Transferring the proof requires a logical way of recovering the appropriate obstruction.

Bounded-width descriptions support decidability because graph properties can be translated into properties of construction trees. In particular, for each fixed k the full class of graphs of clique-width at most k has decidable MSO₁ satisfiability. But the conjecture is only a necessary-condition statement for an arbitrary class C. One cannot infer that every subclass of a bounded-width class has decidable theory.

For a simple reason, such a converse would be false. Choose an undecidable set S of positive integers, and let C contain exactly the edgeless graphs whose numbers of vertices belong to S. All those graphs have clique-width one. A sentence specifying exactly n vertices would decide whether n∈S if satisfiability over C were decidable. Restricting which sizes occur can encode undecidability even when each individual graph has trivial structure.

Courcelle–Oum prove the implication after extending MSO₁ with the predicate Even(X), saying that a vertex set has even cardinality. Their vertex-minor and isotropic-system machinery establishes bounded clique-width from decidability of this stronger logic. This strengthens the premise: a decision procedure for ordinary MSO₁ sentences need not handle parity sentences. Therefore their theorem supplies substantial progress while leaving the exact statement here open.

Hereditary classes, which are closed under taking induced subgraphs, are a useful focus even though the card quantifies over all classes. If satisfiability is decidable on C, it is also decidable on its hereditary closure: ask whether some vertex subset induces a graph satisfying the input sentence, using a relativized MSO₁ formula. Unbounded clique-width is preserved on passing to that larger class. Thus a proof covering all hereditary classes would suffice.

Dawar–Sankaran develop a stronger route through interpreting arbitrarily large grids. Their Theorem 3.2 reduces that stronger assertion to two settings: antichains of unbounded clique-width under induced-subgraph containment, and minimal hereditary classes of unbounded clique-width. They verify the grid interpretation for the known minimal families studied in their paper. This is a research program and collection of cases, not a completed classification of all such families.

The inherited ICALP 2025 paper by Mählmann settles a different boundary: on hereditary classes, bounded shrub-depth characterizes coincidence of first-order and monadic second-order expressive power. Its conclusion formulates a stronger conjectural relationship between clique-width and MSO dependence, explaining how parts of that conjecture would imply Seese’s. Shrub-depth and clique-width are distinct parameters, and a theorem about expressive power does not by itself decide satisfiability.

Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk’s July 2026 preprint proves that every hereditary 2-WQO class has bounded clique-width. Here 2-WQO means that every infinite sequence of graphs with two possible vertex labels contains an earlier graph embedding as a label-preserving induced subgraph of a later one. This resolves a related structural conjecture, but it starts from a well-quasi-ordering hypothesis. It does not turn an arbitrary MSO₁ decision procedure into such an ordering property.

The unresolved implication asks whether decidable graph theories always have bounded constructional complexity. A proof would show that broad logical decidability cannot arise from some entirely different mechanism on classes of unbounded clique-width. A counterexample would reveal precisely such a mechanism. Either outcome would change how structural graph theory explains the limits of automated reasoning over whole families of finite structures.
why: A major proposed structural necessity for logical decidability, connecting graph decompositions, finite model theory and algorithms over infinite families of finite inputs.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Seese’s MSO₁ decidability implication remains unresolved in the checked primary literature. The parity extension, the shrub-depth expressiveness characterization and the July 2026 2-WQO result have distinct hypotheses or conclusions.
progress: 1991: Seese establishes foundational connections between decidable monadic graph theories and bounded structural width, and formulates the conjectural MSO₁ boundary. | 2007: Courcelle–Oum prove that decidable MSO₁ with parity predicates implies bounded clique-width. | 2020–2025: Dawar–Sankaran develop the antichain/minimal-hereditary-class reduction for the stronger grid-interpretation conjecture; preprint 2020, CSL 2022, journal volume 2025. | 2025: Mählmann characterizes bounded shrub-depth through logical expressiveness and records a stronger MSO-dependence conjecture that would imply Seese’s. | 12–26 July 2026: Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk prove bounded clique-width for hereditary 2-WQO classes; the hypothesis differs from decidability of MSO₁ satisfiability.
working_summary: MSO1 permits quantification over vertices and vertex sets in a graph. Seese's conjecture asks whether decidability of this logic over a graph class forces bounded clique-width. The proposed implication connects an algorithmic property of the class's whole logical theory with a finite construction complexity for its graphs. A proof would identify a strong structural obstruction to decidable graph reasoning. The saved formulation imposes no hereditary assumption and excludes edge-set and counting extensions, so results for narrower classes or stronger logics cannot be substituted for the stated general MSO1 question.

title: Exact directed maximum flow in O((m+n) polylog n) time
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A central static graph optimization primitive with broad algorithmic consequences. The precise remaining overhead separates the established almost-linear breakthrough from the longstanding nearly linear target; this is a general problem rather than a refinement of one fixed algorithm.
formal: For every fixed integer a≥1, do there exist a constant k≥0 and a uniform classical randomized algorithm A_a that, on every directed graph with n≥2 vertices, m arcs, distinguished distinct vertices s,t and integer capacities in {0,…,n^a}, outputs an exact maximum s–t flow with probability at least 2/3 in worst-case time O((m+n)(log(n+2))^k)?
definitions: The graph is explicitly given by its labelled vertex set {1,…,n} and an arc list, with no loops and at most one arc per ordered vertex pair; opposite arcs are allowed. A flow assigns an integer f_e to each arc, with 0≤f_e≤u_e and equal incoming and outgoing sums at every vertex other than s,t. Its value is the outgoing sum at s minus the incoming sum at s; maximum refers to the largest such value. Output the m flow values, not only an approximate value. Use a word RAM with word length B_a⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ for a fixed integer B_a large enough to store capacities, total flow and memory addresses. Unit-cost operations are random-access word reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo 2^w and integer division of nonzero divisors. Multiword computations are charged for their component operations. Independent fair random bits are allowed, with each generated word charged. All preprocessing and output are included, and the time bound holds on every random execution. There are no oracles or input-dependent advice. A_a, k, B_a and the hidden constant may depend on a, but not on the graph. The m+n convention includes explicitly listed isolated vertices.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
context:
Maximum flow is a basic model for routing through capacity constraints. A feasible solution must obey conservation at intermediate vertices, and optimality measures the largest transferable amount between two terminals. Even a graph with small integer capacities can require globally coordinated changes to a feasible routing. The question asks whether finding the exact optimum can cost only a polylogarithmic factor more than reading the graph.

Almost-linear algorithms already represent a major qualitative advance. Chen and coauthors obtained exact maximum flow and minimum-cost flow in m^(1+o(1)) time for polynomially bounded integral data. Li and Wice’s August 2026 preprint obtains an almost-linear maximum-flow bound through a different framework. Neither stated asymptotic guarantee is O(m polylog n).

The distinction concerns the remaining overhead. For example, exp(√log n) is subpolynomial in n but exceeds every fixed power of log n. A running time containing that factor can be almost linear without satisfying this card. Removing the residual gap would identify a sharper computational cost for a central graph optimization primitive.

Exactness is also a substantive part of the target. A flow whose value is within a fixed relative error of optimum does not determine the optimum integer value when that value is large. Conversely, restricting capacities to polynomial magnitude means their binary encodings occupy logarithmically many bits each. The question is therefore not asking an algorithm to read arbitrarily long capacities in a graph-size-only time bound.

The primary topic is a static graph algorithm, so the current catalogue places the question in Structural graph theory and graph algorithms. Dynamic maintenance, parallel computation and strong polynomiality for unbounded-bit linear programming impose different requirements. No existing maximum-matching or dynamic-connectivity card represents this flow target.
why: Identify whether exact flow optimization with polynomially bounded capacities admits genuinely polylogarithmic overhead over graph input size.
status_note: Primary-source check through 11 September 2026 found almost-linear bounds, not the fixed-polylogarithmic overhead required here. New preprint proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2022: Exact maximum flow and minimum-cost flow achieve almost-linear time for polynomially bounded integral data. | 2026-08-18: Li–Wice state an m^(1+o(1)) maximum-flow algorithm, leaving the polylogarithmic-overhead target unestablished.

title: Cereceda's quadratic recolouring conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: The principal structural diameter conjecture in graph-colouring reconfiguration.
formal: For every fixed d, does the reconfiguration graph of proper (d+2)-colourings of every n-vertex d-degenerate graph have diameter O_d(n^2), where one step recolours one vertex?
context:
No matching Cereceda or general quadratic degenerate-recolouring question was found.

This short research proposal states the target identified in the September 2026 fundamental-problem search. The references give the source models and related results. A full self-contained formulation and detailed progress review remain to be written.
why: The principal structural diameter conjecture in graph-colouring reconfiguration.

title: Erdős girth conjecture: is the classical spanner size bound tight?
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Connects extremal graph density with the optimal size of sparse distance-preserving structures; consequences extend across graph theory and algorithms.
formal: For every fixed integer $k\ge 2$, do there exist a constant $c_k>0$ and arbitrarily large simple undirected graphs $G$ with $n$ vertices, at least $c_k n^{1+1/k}$ edges, and no cycle of length at most $2k$? Equivalently, can the $O_k(n^{1+1/k})$ extremal upper bound for girth greater than $2k$ be attained up to a constant factor for every $k$? The first unsettled value is $k=4$: girth at least nine and $\Omega(n^{5/4})$ edges.
definitions: The girth is the length of a shortest cycle, with infinite girth for a forest. A $t$-spanner is a spanning subgraph $H\subseteq G$ satisfying $d_G(u,v)\le d_H(u,v)\le t\,d_G(u,v)$ for every reachable pair. The parameter $k$ is fixed as $n$ grows, and constants may depend on $k$. The question asks for existence; an efficient explicit construction would be a stronger result.
answer_criterion: Prove the required graph families exist for every fixed k, or refute the universal claim for at least one fixed k. Proving the k=4 case alone would resolve the first unknown case but not the whole conjecture.
context:
High degree tries to make short cycles unavoidable. In a graph whose small neighborhoods contain no cycles, a breadth-first search keeps discovering new vertices rather than revisiting old ones. Sustaining large branching for several levels consumes the available vertices rapidly. This is the reason a ban on short cycles forces an upper bound on density; the conjecture asks whether graphs can pack edges as efficiently as that counting argument permits.

The algorithmic connection is direct. Suppose a unit-weight graph has girth greater than $2k$. If a subgraph omits an edge $uv$, every remaining $u$–$v$ path has at least $2k$ edges: a shorter path together with $uv$ would create a forbidden cycle. Thus any $(2k-1)$-spanner must keep every edge. A dense graph of this kind is a certificate that no smaller spanner can preserve the required distances.

For example, a triangle-free graph alone is not enough for the $k=2$ application: a four-cycle allows one edge to be replaced by a three-edge detour. Excluding both triangles and four-cycles makes every edge indispensable for stretch three. This example explains why the exact girth threshold appears in the conjecture.

The conjecture is not an established law of graph sparsification. The 2026 source records that only the parameters 1, 2, 3, and 5 are known and discusses reasons to question the general statement. Its new fault-tolerant lower bound bypasses the conjecture for that model; it does not construct the missing high-girth families.
why: This is a structural problem with a short, rigorous reduction to an algorithmic limit. I include it because many claims that a distance-preserving graph representation is optimal depend on precisely this unproved construction. A proof would establish those lower bounds; a counterexample would force a re-examination of the expected stretch–space tradeoff.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The general conjecture remains unresolved; several individual values of k are settled.
progress: 1993: Althöfer, Das, Dobkin, Joseph, and Soares give sparse multiplicative spanners: every weighted $n$-vertex graph admits stretch $2k-1$ with $O_k(n^{1+1/k})$ edges. High-girth graphs give the corresponding obstruction to improving size. | 2026: Bodwin and Lopez review the remaining girth conjecture in Section 1.1. Their degree-fault-tolerant spanner lower bound is unconditional, separating a new algorithmic result from the still-open underlying conjecture.
