title: Constant-factor edit-distance approximation in O(n polylog n) time
importance_reason: A central remaining precision–runtime boundary for edit distance, distinct from the established n^{1+ε} constant-factor algorithms and from exact-computation hardness.
focus_reason: A central remaining precision–runtime boundary for edit distance, distinct from the established n^{1+ε} constant-factor algorithms and from exact-computation hardness.
formal: Do absolute constants C≥1, K>0 and d≥0 and a uniform randomized classical algorithm exist that, for every two length-n strings x,y, output an integer D satisfying ED(x,y)≤D≤C·ED(x,y) with probability at least 2/3 in at most Kn(log₂(n+2))^d time?
definitions: Use the unit-cost Levenshtein distance: ED is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming x into y; matching equal symbols costs zero. The input consists of n≥1 and two explicitly stored arrays x,y∈{0,…,n²+1}ⁿ. This fixes an integer alphabet whose symbols fit in O(log n) bits and includes binary and fixed finite alphabets. Computation is on a word RAM with word length B⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ for an absolute constant B, using random access, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and word arithmetic at unit cost. The algorithm may draw independent random bits, but has no input-dependent advice, preprocessed database or oracle. All preprocessing counts toward the bound, which must hold on every execution. Success is required separately for every input pair. Output only the distance estimate; an edit script is not required. The constants C,K,d,B are fixed independently of n and the strings. There is no promise about the distance, repetitions or input distribution, and no additive error is allowed. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2^w, integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length w=Θ(log n) (or Θ(log N) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Insertions and deletions make alignment the central difficulty. If a symbol is inserted near the start of a string, many later positions shift, even when almost all symbols are unchanged. Comparing corresponding positions can therefore report many mismatches while a short edit sequence exists. The task is to estimate the best alignment cost without inspecting the full quadratic dynamic-programming table.

For example, deleting the first symbol of an alternating binary string and reinserting it at the end produces an equal-length string with almost every position changed, but edit distance at most two. A Hamming-distance estimate can be linear in the length on this pair. This illustrates why a simple positional comparison cannot provide a universal constant-factor approximation.

The multiplicative guarantee is deliberately strict at small distances. When x=y, success requires D=0. When the true distance is one, the returned value must remain bounded by the same universal C used on arbitrarily long strings. An additive error such as n^{0.9} can be acceptable for very distant strings while being arbitrarily poor on these nearby pairs. Reading both complete strings is allowed; this is not a sublinear-query problem.

Early algorithms already showed that one could gain substantial speed by allowing larger distortion. Andoni–Onak obtain a subpolynomial approximation factor 2^{Õ(√log n)} in n^{1+o(1)} time, with a STOC 2009 precursor and a later journal version. Both quantities improve substantially on older polynomial approximations, but the factor still grows with input length.

Koucký–Saks obtain a constant-factor result for sufficiently distant pairs, with an additive n^{1−ζ} term in the general guarantee. The exponent ζ and the multiplicative constant depend on the fixed runtime parameter. Their theorem makes the missing regime explicit: the additive term cannot be absorbed into a constant times the true distance on every pair.

Andoni–Nosatzki remove that distance promise. Their Theorem 1.1 gives, for every fixed ε>0, an O(n^{1+ε})-time randomized algorithm with approximation f(1/ε). The manuscript notes doubly exponential dependence on 1/ε. Its FOCS 2020 result was revised on arXiv in July 2022 and published in SIAM Journal on Computing in August 2026. The recent publication date does not change the quantified n^{1+ε} guarantee into n times a polylogarithm.

The order of these choices is decisive. A fixed ε=0.01 gives a fixed approximation factor, but n^{0.01} eventually exceeds every fixed power of log n. Choosing ε as a function of n to force the desired runtime also changes the approximation factor and the hidden constants. The theorem does not provide the single constant C required here. This is a quantitative gap within already very fast approximation algorithms, rather than a question about whether any strongly subquadratic constant approximation exists.

Mao–Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 work improves a different part of the tradeoff. For every fixed accuracy parameter η>0, it gives a randomized (1+η)-approximation in n²/2^{log^{Ω(1)}n} time. The approximation can be arbitrarily close to exact, but the displayed speedup is over the quadratic scale, not down to n polylog n. It does not resolve this card’s constant-factor, much-faster-runtime target.

Backurs–Indyk’s SETH-based barrier concerns exact computation in strongly subquadratic time. It should not be applied indiscriminately to approximation: the known constant-factor algorithms already run in that regime. An impossibility result for the present question would need to preserve a multiplicative gap of the appropriate size while respecting the randomized model and the very small runtime overhead.

The card concerns ordinary strings and numerical estimation. Tree edit distance, distances between languages, weighted edit operations and quantum algorithms each change the problem. Likewise, an efficient nearest-neighbour data structure with substantial preprocessing does not immediately yield the stated two-string algorithm. These distinctions keep the target useful as a precise benchmark for the algorithmic complexity of a basic sequence metric.

A positive resolution would show that constant distortion suffices to reduce this alignment problem to essentially the cost of reading its input, up to logarithmic factors. Even a large universal approximation constant would settle that structural issue. Reducing the constant, producing an alignment, and obtaining practical implementations would remain meaningful subsequent goals.

The separate card TCS-7220 asks whether every fixed ε>0 permits a (1+ε)-approximation in O(n^(2−δ_ε)) time for some fixed δ_ε>0. Its near-exact guarantee does not by itself provide this card’s O(n polylog n) runtime, while this card’s unspecified constant factor does not supply arbitrary 1+ε accuracy. The user explicitly approved retaining both targets on 11 September 2026.
why: Determines whether a universal constant loss in accuracy makes the basic string-alignment metric computable with only polylogarithmic overhead beyond input reading.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No O(n polylog n)-time, fixed-constant approximation for all input pairs was found in the checked primary sources. The August 2026 journal publication gives n^{1+ε} time, and the STOC 2026 approximation scheme targets a different runtime–accuracy regime.
progress: 2009–2012: Andoni–Onak give subpolynomial distortion in n^{1+o(1)} time. | 2015: Backurs–Indyk establish SETH-based hardness for strongly subquadratic exact edit distance; this does not rule out constant approximation. | 2019–2020: Koucký–Saks prove a constant-factor guarantee on sufficiently distant pairs, with an additive term on general inputs. | 2020–2022: Andoni–Nosatzki obtain constant approximation for arbitrary pairs in n^{1+ε} time for each fixed ε; July 2022 revision states the parameter dependence. | 2026-03-31: Mao–Rubinstein post their STOC 2026 approximation schemes, with near-exact accuracy and a quasipolynomial speedup over quadratic time. | 2026-08-17: The Andoni–Nosatzki journal article is published online; its runtime remains n^{1+ε}, rather than n polylog n.
working_summary: Edit distance counts the cheapest sequence of insertions, deletions, and substitutions transforming one string into another. The reviewed question asks for a randomized universal constant-factor approximation in near-linear time. Insertions can shift many positions, making direct coordinate comparisons misleading even when edit distance is tiny. The target would estimate global alignment cost without constructing the full quadratic dynamic-programming table. The guarantee is purely multiplicative, so identical strings must yield zero and nearby strings cannot be hidden behind a large additive error.

title: A (1+ε)-approximation for edit distance in n^(1+o(1)) time
importance_reason: A central accuracy–runtime frontier for sequence comparison, with recent work on each side of the tradeoff. It is a genuinely stronger near-exact runtime target than TCS-7220, retained under the user’s explicit acceptance of related edit-distance questions.
formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm A_ε that, on every pair of explicitly given strings of total length n≥2, outputs an integer D with ED(x,y)≤D≤(1+ε)ED(x,y) with probability at least 2/3, using worst-case time n^(1+o(1))?
definitions: ED(x,y) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming x into y, with unit cost per edit and zero cost for an equal-symbol match. String symbols are integers in {0,…,n²+1}, stored in arrays, so binary and other fixed alphabets are included. Use a word RAM with w=B_ε⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits for a fixed sufficiently large integer B_ε; unit-cost operations are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo 2^w and integer division by a nonzero word. Larger integers require multiple charged operations. Independent fair random bits are allowed. For each fixed ε there is one algorithm A_ε, and for every rational η>0 there are constants C_{ε,η},N_{ε,η} such that every execution on every pair of total length n≥N_{ε,η} uses at most C_{ε,η} n^(1+η) operations. A_ε halts on all inputs and has a finite worst-case bound at each smaller length as well. Constants may depend on ε and η; the algorithm may depend on ε but not on η. All preprocessing and output are charged; no advice, preprocessing oracle or input distribution is supplied. Success is required separately for every input pair. There is no additive error or promise that ED is large. Only a numerical estimate is required, not an edit script. No polynomial dependence on 1/ε or effective procedure generating A_ε from ε is required.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
context:
Edit distance captures alignment when one sequence may have inserted or deleted symbols. The near-linear target concerns every input pair and every fixed relative tolerance. It asks whether extremely accurate estimates can be computed with an exponent approaching one, rather than merely improving on the quadratic dynamic program.

The catalogue has two related but different targets. TCS-7220 asks for a (1+ε)-approximation in n^(2−δ_ε) time, with a fixed positive exponent saving for each accuracy. TCS-6624 asks for some fixed constant-factor approximation in O(n polylog n) time. The present target strengthens the running-time requirement of the former. Its n^(1+o(1)) guarantee does not itself promise the fixed polylogarithmic overhead of the latter.

The quantifier over runtime slack is important. For a fixed accuracy ε, one algorithm must meet n^(1+η) bounds for every fixed η>0 once n is large enough. A different algorithm for each η, with uncontrolled dependence on η, is not automatically such an algorithm. Conversely, this card does not demand a common running-time bound polynomial in inverse accuracy.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain constant-factor approximation in n^(1+η) time for each fixed η. Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 approximation scheme moves toward arbitrarily accurate approximation, but its stated runtime is quasi-strongly subquadratic. Those advances concern different points of the accuracy–time tradeoff and do not establish the present joint target.

Purely multiplicative error also controls almost identical strings. On equal strings the successful output must be zero; an additive error term increasing with n would violate the statement. This requirement separates the question from weaker large-distance guarantees. The three cards therefore record distinct accuracy–runtime requirements, with their implications stated separately.
why: Determine whether worst-case sequence alignment can simultaneously achieve arbitrarily small fixed relative error and a time exponent approaching one.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No algorithm meeting the combined arbitrary fixed relative accuracy and n^(1+o(1)) worst-case time target was found. Neither the 2026 scheme nor a family with fixed runtime slack is silently upgraded to that target.
progress: 2020–2022: Andoni–Nosatzki establish constant-factor approximation in n^(1+η) time for every fixed η>0. | 2026-03-31: Mao–Rubinstein give approximation schemes in quasi-strongly subquadratic time; this is not a near-linear bound.

title: A (1+ε)-approximation for edit distance in truly subquadratic time
importance_reason: A longstanding central accuracy–runtime question for edit distance, explicitly posed before the constant-factor breakthroughs and sharpened by the 2026 approximation scheme. Retained alongside TCS-6624 because one target asks for near-exact accuracy and the other for nearly linear overhead; their stated algorithmic guarantees do not imply one another.
formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), do there exist constants δ_ε∈(0,1), K_ε>0 and a uniform classical randomized algorithm A_ε such that, for every n≥1 and every pair of length-n strings x,y, A_ε runs in at most K_ε(n+2)^(2−δ_ε) time and outputs an integer D satisfying ED(x,y)≤D≤(1+ε)ED(x,y) with probability at least 2/3? ED is unit-cost Levenshtein distance in the model below.
definitions: ED(x,y) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions converting x to y; matching equal symbols costs zero. The input strings are explicitly stored arrays over {0,…,n²+1}, including binary and fixed finite alphabets. Symbols occupy O(log n) bits. Use a word RAM with word length B⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ for a fixed sufficiently large constant B, with random access, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and word arithmetic at unit cost. The algorithm may use independent random bits but no input-dependent advice, preprocessing oracle or preprocessed database. The runtime bound includes all preprocessing and holds on every execution; success is required separately on every input pair. Output a numerical distance estimate, with no additive error and no promise on the distance or input distribution. An edit script is not required. For each fixed ε the algorithm is uniform in n and the strings; its constants and exponent saving may depend on ε. No polynomial dependence on 1/ε, common positive saving for all ε, or efficient procedure generating A_ε is required. Rational ε suffice for every positive fixed accuracy by choosing a smaller rational parameter.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence statement for every fixed positive accuracy, or prove that for some fixed ε>0 no randomized algorithm achieves that multiplicative guarantee in O(n^(2−δ)) time for any fixed δ>0. A result for just one constant approximation factor does not establish the universal accuracy claim. A savings factor that is subpolynomial in n, an additive approximation, or a guarantee confined to special input distributions is insufficient. A deterministic algorithm would suffice for the positive direction, but a lower bound against deterministic algorithms alone would not settle the negative direction. Any conditional lower bound must retain its explicit assumption.
context:
Edit distance measures the cost of aligning two sequences when insertions and deletions can shift all later positions. The question asks whether a small fixed multiplicative loss permits a fixed polynomial improvement over the quadratic dynamic-programming scale on every input. Rubinstein explicitly posed this approximation-scheme question in 2018, separately from the search for a fast constant-factor approximation.

The two parameters play different roles. Choosing ε=0.01 fixes a one-percent approximation tolerance; the desired δ_ε must then remain positive as n grows. A runtime such as n²/logⁱ n, for fixed i, is n^(2−o(1)) and does not meet the target. The requirement permits the exponent improvement to become arbitrarily small as ε approaches zero. It therefore does not ask for an exact subquadratic algorithm.

Mao and Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 paper gives randomized (1+ε)-approximation for each constant ε in n²/2^{log^{Ω(1)} n} time. Theorem 6.1 supplies a multiplicative ED estimate with high probability. This is a substantial improvement beyond logarithmic shaving, but the established quasipolynomial speedup does not provide a fixed δ_ε>0. The remaining question is whether near-exact approximation can cross that fixed-exponent boundary.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain a different tradeoff: for each fixed η>0, a constant-factor approximation in n^(1+η) time. The approximation constant depends on η and is not guaranteed to be 1+ε for an arbitrarily prescribed ε. Thus a very fast coarse estimate and a slower near-exact estimate are distinct algorithmic achievements.

The existing card TCS-6624 asks for one fixed approximation factor in O(n polylog n) time. A positive answer here would not by itself yield that running time. Conversely, the guarantee requested in TCS-6624 does not give arbitrary 1+ε accuracy. Neither displayed guarantee alone implies the other, so both cards remain separate with the user’s explicit approval.

Backurs and Indyk establish a SETH-based barrier for exact strongly subquadratic edit distance. Such an exact-computation reduction does not automatically preserve a fixed multiplicative approximation gap. In particular, the parameter ε is fixed before the input length grows; choosing ε below 1/n to force exactness is outside any fixed-ε runtime guarantee.

Multiplicative accuracy also constrains close pairs. When ED=0 a successful estimate must be zero, and when ED=1 and ε<1 an integer successful estimate must be one. An additive term that grows with n cannot be ignored for such inputs. Weighted edits, tree edit distance and guarantees for random strings each change the problem; none is substituted for the worst-case unit-cost question here.

A resolution would locate a basic accuracy–runtime boundary for sequence comparison. It would either show that every fixed relative tolerance permits a polynomial exponent saving or identify a near-exact accuracy regime with an inherent computational obstruction. This is the scientific reason for retaining the question alongside the faster, coarser approximation target.
why: Determine whether arbitrarily accurate fixed-factor approximation can break the quadratic exponent for a central sequence-alignment problem. This tests a different computational boundary from constant-factor estimation with nearly linear overhead.
status_note: No resolution with a fixed positive exponent saving for every fixed ε was found in the primary-source check through 11 September 2026. The 2026 scheme improves quadratic time by a quasipolynomial factor and does not establish the target O(n^(2−δ_ε)) bound.
progress: 2015: Backurs–Indyk establish a conditional strongly subquadratic barrier for exact edit distance. | 2018-07-20: Rubinstein explicitly asks for (1+ε)-approximation in truly subquadratic time as Open question 2. | 2020–2022: Andoni–Nosatzki obtain constant-factor approximation in n^(1+η) time for each fixed η>0; the approximation constant is not arbitrarily close to one. | 2026-03-31: Mao–Rubinstein give a randomized near-exact approximation scheme with a quasipolynomial improvement over quadratic time, accepted to STOC 2026.
working_summary: Unit-cost edit distance counts the fewest single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to transform one string into another. The question asks whether every fixed positive ε permits a randomized (1+ε)-approximation in O(n^(2−δ_ε)) time for some fixed δ_ε>0 on every input pair. Mao and Rubinstein’s 2026 approximation scheme gives a quasipolynomial speedup over quadratic time without establishing that fixed exponent saving. The numerical estimate must have purely multiplicative error even for strings with very small distance, and all preprocessing is included in the runtime. This accuracy target remains separate from TCS-6624, which allows a fixed constant factor but requires O(n polylog n) time.

importance_reason: A principal approximation barrier for a core bioinformatics optimization problem, requiring a constant improvement independent of the number of sequences.
formal: Does some universal ε>0 admit a polynomial-time (2−ε)-approximation for minimum sum-of-pairs multiple sequence alignment with an arbitrary number of input strings and metric substitution/gap costs?
context:

title: Does the smallest grammar problem admit a constant-factor approximation?
importance_reason: Asks whether a basic measure of reusable string structure can be approximated within a constant, linking compression and approximation complexity.
formal: Do there exist an absolute constant C and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every explicit nonempty string s, outputs an acyclic context-free grammar generating exactly s whose size is at most $C g^*(s)$? There is one production per nonterminal, one designated start nonterminal, and every right-hand side is a nonempty string of terminals and nonterminals. The dependency graph on nonterminals must be acyclic. Grammar size is the sum of all right-hand-side lengths, and $g^*(s)$ is the minimum such size. The alphabet is part of the input, encoded by integer symbols in {1,...,|s|}.
definitions: Expanding a nonterminal means repeatedly replacing it by its unique right-hand side. Acyclicity guarantees termination, and the start expansion must equal the input string with no extra strings generated. Each terminal or nonterminal occurrence on a right-hand side contributes one unit to size. Runtime is measured in the ordinary binary encoding of the explicit input, not the compressed output length. Constant C cannot depend on the alphabet size, string length, or optimal grammar size. Arbitrarily long right-hand sides are permitted; the size convention is not just the number of productions.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of one polynomial-time algorithm with some fixed approximation constant valid for all strings, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A hardness theorem conditional on P != NP should be reported with that assumption. Exact optimization and ratios tending to one are stronger targets than the constant-factor question.
context:
A grammar can share repeated pieces of a string and then share larger pieces assembled from them. For example, a sequence of doubling rules represents an exponentially long run using only a linear number of rules. This makes grammar size a useful concrete measure of repetitive structure, with a finite optimum that can in principle be found by exhaustive search.

The problem is to choose the shared pieces. Two useful repeated substrings may overlap, and a locally attractive substitution can prevent a better organization at a larger scale. A method that compresses some families extremely well can therefore still have an unbounded ratio to the best grammar on other families. The proposed guarantee must cover every input, not only average compression performance.

Known approximation guarantees depend logarithmically on the ratio between the explicit string length and its optimal grammar size. Hardness rules out sufficiently accurate approximation under P != NP, but this does not exclude a coarser universal constant. The space between these two conclusions is the question on this card.

The size measure is essential. Counting productions, binary concatenations, or all right-hand-side symbols gives related but different optimization problems. Stating the measure explicitly also avoids confusing exact binary-alphabet hardness questions with the unrestricted constant-factor approximation target.
why: This is a fundamental compression-versus-optimization question: can an efficient procedure recover a representation within a fixed factor of the best hierarchical description? It also supplies a benchmark for compressed-data algorithms, whose costs often depend on grammar size rather than on the original string length.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026 using the primary approximation and fixed-alphabet papers, with a search for later results. No general constant-factor algorithm was located. Recent assembly-index work uses additional size conventions and is not treated as resolving this proposition.
progress: 2005: Charikar and coauthors give an O(1+log(|s|/g*(s))) approximation and rule out approximation ratios below 8569/8568 unless P = NP. | 2020-11 / 2021: Casel and coauthors establish hardness over fixed alphabets of size at least 17 and retain constant-factor approximation as Open Problem 2. The hardness result does not rule out every constant.
working_summary: A grammar can compress a string by naming repeated pieces and assembling them through acyclic production rules. The question asks for a deterministic polynomial-time approximation within a universal constant of the smallest such grammar. The size measure counts all symbols on right-hand sides, including references to other rules. Choosing repeated pieces is difficult because useful substrings can overlap and interact across scales. The saved review separates this constant-factor target from known logarithmic guarantees and emphasizes that alternative grammar-size conventions describe different optimization problems.

title: Can LZ77 random access use linear compressed space and logarithmic query time?
importance_reason: Random access is a basic interface for compressed computation. The linear-space target would remove a persistent overhead for a central repetitiveness measure.
formal: Given the greedy LZ77 parse with z phrases of a string $S[1..N]$ over an integer alphabet of size at most N, is there a deterministic word-RAM data structure using O(z) words in total that returns S[i] for any $1\le i\le N$ in worst-case O(log N) time? Words have $\Theta(\log N)$ bits. A phrase is a new literal or a longest prefix of the unparsed suffix having an occurrence starting earlier in S; overlapping copies are allowed. Space includes the stored parse and all query-support information. The uncompressed string is unavailable at query time.
definitions: All asymptotic constants are universal. The model permits standard arithmetic, multiplication, shifts, bitwise operations, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of words. A copied phrase beginning at b and referring to a<b is decoded sequentially, so self-overlap is well-defined. Preprocessing may take polynomial time in N; the target concerns final storage and query time, not construction in compressed time. Use 1+log N at the smallest lengths.
answer_criterion: Construct a uniform data structure meeting both bounds for every greedy LZ77 parse, or prove that no such structure exists in the stated model. Linear space measured by a larger grammar or an LZ-End parse does not meet the O(z) requirement.
context:
Lempel–Ziv compression replaces a repeated block by its earlier starting position and length. This can encode a long text with few phrases, but a position inside one copied phrase may lead to another copy, and then another. Random access asks for just one character without expanding the whole text.

The challenge is not that every deeply referenced string is hard. A long run of one repeated character can be accessed immediately once its simple structure is recognized. The target must work for arbitrary mixtures of copied material, where both the reference chains and the phrase lengths vary. Any shortcuts used to navigate those chains must fit in the compressed-space budget.

Converting the parse to a balanced grammar supplies a route to fast navigation, but the grammar can be larger than the original parse by a logarithmic factor. A space bound proportional to that grammar therefore need not be linear in z. Balancing a grammar already supplied as input is a different, solved representation problem.

The July 2026 LZ-End result is close in spirit: it obtains linear space and improved polylogarithmic access for a variant that restricts copy endpoints. Its parameter counts LZ-End phrases. Since the parsing rule and the number of phrases differ, those guarantees cannot be substituted directly for the classical LZ77 target.
why: I include this because compression is most useful when a small representation remains usable for selective queries. This question asks whether an extra logarithmic storage cost is an inherent price of navigating repeated data or a consequence of converting to a more convenient representation.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the July LZ-End result. The stated parse convention, space parameter, and deterministic query guarantee are explicit.
progress: 2019 / 2021: Ganardi, Jeż, and Lohrey show that a straight-line grammar can be balanced to logarithmic derivation depth with only constant-factor size growth. This settles the corresponding logarithmic-access target in terms of grammar size. | 2025-05: Gawrychowski explicitly asks for linear space in the Lempel–Ziv representation and logarithmic-time character access. | 2026-07: Boneh and Gawrychowski obtain deterministic O(z_end)-space random access in $O(1+\log^2(N/z_{\rm end}))$ time for LZ-End. Their introduction retains classical LZ77 random access as open and records $O(z\log(N/z))$-space solutions for it.
working_summary: An LZ77 parse represents repeated text through references to earlier occurrences, possibly allowing overlap. The reviewed question asks for random character access in logarithmic time using space linear in the number of phrases. The original uncompressed string is unavailable when queries arrive. A solution must navigate arbitrary chains of copied material while keeping every stored shortcut inside the compressed-space budget. The saved record distinguishes ordinary LZ77 from restricted parsing variants and notes that converting to a larger grammar does not automatically preserve the required linear space.

title: Can pattern matching run in linear time in the LZ77 input size?
importance_reason: Tests whether a fundamental string task can run at the size of its compressed input, including preprocessing; useful beyond one particular index implementation.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given a valid LZ77 representation of z phrases of a text T of length N and an explicit nonempty pattern P of length m, decides whether P occurs contiguously in T in O(z+m) worst-case time? Self-referencing copy phrases are allowed. Symbols are integers in $\{1,\ldots,(z+m)^c\}$ for a fixed constant c. Use a word RAM with word size $\Theta(\log(N+m+2))$, the operations specified below, and O(z+m) working words. The input is the compressed text and the explicit pattern; all preprocessing is included.
definitions: Each phrase is either one literal symbol or a pair (s,l) instructing the decoder to append l symbols copied sequentially from an earlier starting position s in the text. For a phrase beginning at p, require 1 <= s < p; the copied interval may overlap the phrase being produced. Phrase boundaries and references occupy O(1) words per phrase. No promise of a greedy parse is needed. title: Can grammar random access use O(g log g) bits with logarithmic query time?

formal: Is there a deterministic data structure that, for every binary straight-line program G with g rules generating a binary string T of length N, stores a representation in $O(g\log(g+2))$ bits and returns T[i] for any $1\le i\le N$ in $O(\log(N+2))$ worst-case time? The representation may replace G; it need only answer queries to T correctly.
definitions: A binary straight-line program has ordered variables X_1,...,X_g, one rule per variable, and start variable X_g. A rule is X_j -> 0, X_j -> 1, or X_j -> X_a X_b with a,b < j. All variables must be reachable from the start variable. Expansion is unique and finite; g counts rules, not expanded occurrences. The input specifies rule types and indices in O(g log(g+2)) bits. Machine words have $\Theta(\log(N+g+2))$ bits; random access, comparisons, word addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division, Boolean operations, and shifts cost one step. Arithmetic results are restricted to a word. Stored bits may be packed; charge the final partially filled word as well. Queries may use O(log(N+2)) temporary words, initially empty and discarded afterward; this workspace contains no persistent advice. Every input-dependent table retained between queries counts toward the representation budget.
answer_criterion: Construct a uniform representation, preprocessing algorithm, and query algorithm satisfying all bounds for every valid G, or prove that no such data structure exists. Space linear in g machine words is insufficient when log N is asymptotically larger than log g. A scheme whose preprocessing first expands an exponentially longer T does not meet the polynomial-in-g preprocessing requirement.
context:
A grammar rule stores references to smaller pieces, so its two references need only logarithmically many bits in the number of rules. A position in the expanded string can require many more bits. To locate a position inside a concatenation, the usual navigation step compares that position with the length of the left expansion. Storing an exact expanded length with every variable is straightforward, but can consume g log N bits. The target asks whether this information can be organized or recovered using a representation comparable in bits to the original grammar, while keeping logarithmic access time.

title: Can a supplied Karp–Rabin fingerprint be verified in near-linear time?
importance_reason: A concrete test of whether a widely used randomized string primitive can be certified at almost its construction cost; narrower than the general compressed-access barriers.
formal: Given a string $S\in\{0,\ldots,\sigma-1\}^{n}$ and a prime $q$, with $\sigma,q\le n^{O(1)}$, define $h_q(x_1\cdots x_\ell)=\sum_{t=1}^{\ell}x_t\sigma^{\ell-t}\bmod q$. Can one decide in $O(n\log n)$ time whether there exist equal-length substrings $A,B$ of $S$ such that $A\ne B$ but $h_q(A)=h_q(B)$? The modulus is part of the input and cannot be replaced. The deterministic decision problem is the precise target here; the source also permits randomized certification that never accepts a colliding modulus and rejects a collision-free one only with small probability.
definitions: Use a word RAM with word size $\Theta(\log n)$, enlarged by a fixed constant to hold the polynomially bounded alphabet symbols and modulus. Arithmetic on a constant number of words costs $O(1)$. Substrings may overlap. The quantified lengths range from $1$ through $n$. This is certification for a fixed string and fixed modulus, not a universal collision-free hash for all strings.
answer_criterion: Give a deterministic O(n log n)-time verifier for every supplied string and modulus, or prove that no such verifier exists in the stated word-RAM model. Certifying a replacement composite fingerprint does not answer this question.
context:
Rolling fingerprints turn a long substring into one machine-sized value. Prefix hashes let an algorithm obtain that value without reading the substring again. Unequal fingerprints certify unequal strings, but equal fingerprints only suggest equality. A verifier would determine whether that suggestion is reliable simultaneously for every substring length in the particular input.

For example, in the binary string 001110, the length-three substrings 001 and 110 represent the integers 1 and 6. Modulo 5 their fingerprints coincide, although the strings differ. Two occurrences of 001 would not be a collision: positions are allowed to differ, and it is the substring contents that matter.

For a fixed length there are only linearly many substrings, but repeating the check independently over all lengths creates quadratic work. The hoped-for improvement must share information between lengths. Checking only a predetermined pattern or only the substring comparisons actually made by one application supplies a weaker guarantee.

There is an important existing workaround: verify power-of-two lengths, then represent a general substring by a pair of overlapping power-of-two fingerprints. This changes the fingerprint being certified. It does not certify the single supplied polynomial residue at every length, so it does not settle this question.
why: I include this because it separates fast probabilistic equality tests from fast certification of the hash itself. Near-linear verification of a supplied modulus would make a common assumption in string data structures checkable at nearly the cost of reading the input, while clarifying which composite-fingerprint workarounds are actually necessary.

To make communication in bits precise, a public integer B≥1 bounds the binary lengths of the numerator and positive denominator of each value. This is a bound per value, not permission to transmit the exponential table. One uniform protocol must work for every n,m,B with at most P(n,m,B) communicated bits in the worst case, for one fixed polynomial P. Arbitrary interactive messages and demand queries are allowed; all query descriptions, replies, allocations and payments count toward communication. Local computation by bidders and auctioneer is unrestricted but must terminate. An outcome consists of pairwise disjoint bundles S_1,…,S_n and rational payments p_1,…,p_n; unallocated items are allowed. Utilities are quasilinear, u_i=v_i(S_i)−p_i. There are no private budgets or distributional assumptions. Universal truthfulness means the mechanism is a report-independent distribution over deterministic dominant-strategy truthful mechanisms: for every fixed random seed r, every i, every admissible true and alternative reported type v_i,v_i′, and every v_{−i}, v_i(S_i(v_i,v_{−i};r))−p_i(v_i,v_{−i};r)≥v_i(S_i(v_i′,v_{−i};r))−p_i(v_i′,v_{−i};r). A low-communication protocol implements this outcome and payment rule on the distributed reported types. OPT=max Σ_i v_i(T_i), where the maximum is over pairwise disjoint T_i⊆[m]. The expected welfare guarantee holds for every truthful valuation profile, with expectation only over the mechanism’s randomness; C is independent of n,m,B. No additional individual-rationality or transfer-sign restriction is imposed in this formulation.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A bidder may value several items as substitutes. For example, a coverage valuation assigns each item a set of useful features and values a bundle by the total weight of features covered at least once. Receiving an item has less marginal value when many of its features are already covered. Submodularity abstracts this diminishing-returns property without requiring the valuation to be supplied as an explicit coverage instance.

The auctioneer must allocate the items using information held by strategic bidders. Maximizing the sum of their values is the social-welfare objective; maximizing the auctioneer’s revenue would be a different problem. Payments influence what information bidders choose to provide, but are transfers and do not enter the welfare objective. Even a very poor revenue guarantee would be acceptable here if incentives and welfare met the stated requirements.

Two established results cover separate parts of the requirements. With complete reports and unrestricted resources, the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism obtains optimal welfare and truthful incentives. If incentives are omitted, submodular welfare admits constant-factor approximation from compact queries. The difficulty is combining the guarantees while avoiding communication of exponentially many bundle values. The 2026 graph-auctions paper describes this communication perspective explicitly.

Universal truthfulness is a strong use of randomization: each mechanism obtained after fixing the coins must itself make truthful reporting optimal. Truthfulness in expectation requires only that the average utility discourage lying. The distinction has mathematical force; Dobzinski and Dughmi separate the two notions in a restricted multi-unit setting. Their separation is useful background, but their multi-unit approximation scheme does not supply a mechanism for arbitrary heterogeneous submodular valuations.

A demand query offers item prices and asks a bidder to choose a bundle maximizing its value minus its total price. Sending that bundle requires only m membership bits, even when finding it takes enormous local computation. This is why allowing demand queries changes the problem substantially. The formulation deliberately measures communication: an algorithm that delegates difficult optimization to a bidder can qualify. It would need further work to become computationally efficient for that bidder.

Dobzinski’s impossibility theorem rules out universally truthful m^{1/2−ε}-approximation using polynomially many value queries, for every fixed ε>0. A value query reveals only one specified bundle’s value. The theorem is a genuine barrier in that access model, but it cannot be extended by simply treating a demand query as one more value query. A demand answer can encode the result of comparing exponentially many bundles.

Assadi and Singla reached an expected O((log log m)³) approximation using O(n) demand queries, at FOCS 2019. Assadi, Kesselheim and Singla subsequently improved the submodular guarantee to O((log log m)²), while obtaining O((log log m)³) for the broader subadditive class. These asymptotic factors grow with the number of items, despite growing very slowly.

The latter mechanism learns approximate item prices through random groups of bidders. A bidder participates in a single fixed-price auction, so its own report cannot manipulate the menu it faces. Some price-learning rounds can become the final allocation rather than merely gathering information; the analysis accounts for welfare earned in those rounds. This makes price discovery compatible with truthfulness, but leaves a loss between the learned allocation and optimal welfare.

Recent positive results for graph auctions restrict each item to a small set of eligible bidders. For example, the 2026 paper gives a truthful factor-two mechanism when each item has two eligible bidders and valuations are subadditive. This structural restriction supplies information absent in a general auction, so it does not settle the present question. A general constant-factor mechanism would show that exact incentive compatibility need not impose an unbounded welfare loss in this central communication model.
why: Determine whether exact truthful incentives inherently cause an unbounded loss of allocative efficiency, even when arbitrary compact communication and unlimited local optimization are available.
status_note: The checked primary literature retains a gap between constant nontruthful welfare approximation and the general universally truthful guarantee. Theorem 2 of the SODA 2021 paper supplies O((log log m)²) for submodular bidders. The 2026 graph-auction results impose eligibility restrictions. No general constant-factor resolution found through 11 September 2026. The public per-value precision parameter makes the inherited polynomial-communication question explicit in bits.

working_summary: A combinatorial auction allocates indivisible items among bidders whose bundle values satisfy diminishing returns. The reviewed question asks for a constant-factor welfare approximation using polynomial communication and universal truthfulness. Payments must make honest reporting optimal for every fixed random choice, while values may require exponentially large tables to describe completely. A mechanism would show that strategic incentives need not cause an unbounded welfare loss in this communication model. The saved review distinguishes demand queries from weaker value access and universal truthfulness from truthfulness only in expectation.

title: Existence of complete EFX allocations for additive valuations
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory and fair division
importance_reason: A central existence question for a strong and widely studied fairness guarantee for indivisible goods.
focus_reason: A central existence question for a strong and widely studied fairness guarantee for indivisible goods.
formal: For every integers n≥4 and m≥0 and every matrix of nonnegative real values (v_ig)_{i∈[n],g∈[m]}, is there a partition (A₁,…,A_n) of [m] such that, for every i,j∈[n] and every g∈A_j with v_ig>0, Σ_{h∈A_i}v_ih≥Σ_{h∈A_j∖{g}}v_ih?
definitions: There are n agents and m indivisible goods, with [0]=∅. Agent i values a bundle S by v_i(S)=Σ_{g∈S}v_ig; values are finite, nonnegative real numbers. A partition consists of pairwise disjoint bundles whose union is all goods; empty bundles are allowed. Every good must be allocated exactly once. There are no payments, chores, probabilistic allocations or discarded goods. The displayed condition is envy-freeness up to any positively valued good (EFX): the removed good is tested using the values of agent i, not those of agent j. If v_i is zero on all of A_j, there is no inequality to check for that pair. This fixes the EFX convention of Definition 5 and Open Problem 2 of the cited survey. No algorithm, runtime, or restriction to rational or strictly positive values is required.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context: Algorithms for strategic participants and scarce resources. Existence, incentives, fairness, and computational efficiency are separate requirements.
why: The significance of this particular question has not yet been individually assessed. The question asks for an object to exist or to be constructed efficiently. Bridging existence and explicit computation is often essential for using the structure.

working_summary: The problem asks whether every instance with at least four agents and nonnegative additive values admits a complete EFX allocation of indivisible goods. Complete means that each good is assigned to exactly one agent, with empty bundles allowed. For every potentially envious agent i and other bundle A_j, removing any good that i values positively must leave a bundle worth at most i’s own bundle. The statement permits zero values and fixes the positive-good EFX convention, without requiring payments or an efficient algorithm. Universal existence would establish this fairness guarantee despite the inability to divide individual goods.

title: A constant-factor approximation for general Santa Claus allocation
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
importance_reason: A major approximation barrier in fair allocation and scheduling, linked by reductions to beating two for unrelated makespan and by relaxation gaps to the limits of fractional methods.
formal: Is there a universal constant C≥1 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that allocates indivisible items with arbitrary nonnegative additive agent-specific values so that, with probability at least 2/3, every agent receives total value at least OPT/C, where OPT is the largest achievable minimum agent value?
definitions: An input consists of n≥1 agents, m≥1 items and an explicit n×m matrix (v_ij) of nonnegative rational values, encoded by binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Agent i values a bundle S⊆[m] at v_i(S)=Σ_{j∈S}v_ij. An allocation is a tuple of pairwise disjoint bundles (S_1,…,S_n); unallocated items are permitted. Its value is F(S_1,…,S_n)=min_{i∈[n]}v_i(S_i), and OPT is the maximum of F over all allocations. Let L be the total input bit length. There must be one algorithm, one C independent of n,m and all numerical values, and one polynomial P such that the algorithm always outputs a feasible allocation within P(L) bit operations, for every random tape, and Pr[F≥OPT/C]≥2/3 on every input. The probability refers only to the algorithm’s independent internal random bits and requires the guarantee for all agents simultaneously. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as a special case. Zero values and OPT=0 are allowed, and no positive lower bound on OPT is supplied. The input values are used as given: one may not rescale each agent separately without changing the optimization problem. No identical-valuation, restricted-assignment, bounded-number-of-agents, bounded-number-of-values or bounded-item-degree assumption is imposed. All values are available to a centralized algorithm; incentives, payments and valuation oracles are not part of this problem.
answer_criterion: Construct a polynomial-time algorithm achieving the stated guarantee for some fixed C, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Hardness results conditional on a complexity assumption must identify that assumption, including the distinction between deterministic and randomized algorithms. A factor depending on the number of items or agents, a quasi-polynomial-time constant approximation, an estimate without an allocation, or an expected-value guarantee separately for each agent does not meet the target.
context:
The objective protects the least satisfied participant. Suppose two agents value each of two items at one. Allocating one item to each gives minimum value one, whereas giving both items to either agent gives minimum value zero. A lottery that gives both items to a uniformly chosen agent gives each agent expected value one, but its minimum value is always zero. This illustrates why the guarantee must concern the quality of one simultaneous allocation.

Even additive values allow substantial heterogeneity: an item can be extremely valuable to one agent, moderately valuable to another, and worthless to a third. Maximizing total welfare would assign each item to an agent valuing it most, independently of the other items. Maximizing minimum welfare couples those decisions because every agent needs adequate value from resources that cannot be reused. The valuations are inputs to the optimization problem, without strategic reporting constraints.

The name Santa Claus is used differently across papers. Some reserve it for restricted assignment, where each item j has a single intrinsic value w_j and v_ij is either w_j or zero. This card uses the broader max-min allocation problem with arbitrary entries. The difference is decisive: constant-factor algorithms are known for restricted assignment, while the general constant-factor question remains open.

Chakrabarty, Chuzhoy and Khanna give an approximation within m^ε for every fixed ε>0, where m is the number of items in this card’s notation. Their approximation–time tradeoff also yields a polylogarithmic factor in quasi-polynomial time. Choosing a smaller fixed ε improves the approximation exponent but increases the polynomial running-time exponent. Letting ε depend on m to try to force a constant factor does not preserve the known polynomial-time guarantee.

Their work also highlights a limitation of a standard configuration relaxation. For a target T, a configuration for agent i is a bundle worth at least T; fractional variables select configurations while respecting item capacities in aggregate. Integral feasible configurations would give every agent enough value. In the general setting, however, the relaxation can overestimate the integral optimum by a factor of order √n. The algorithm uses the relaxation recursively on transformed instances, instead of relying on a constant-loss rounding of its original optimum.

Restricted assignment has stronger structure. Haxell and Szabó’s 2025 work improves its configuration-LP integrality-gap bound from 3.808 to 3.534 using topological criteria for independent transversals. This is a bound on the distance between fractional and integral optima in the restricted model. It does not assert a 3.534 algorithm for the arbitrary-value matrix, and an existence argument for a good integral solution must be distinguished from an efficient way to construct it.

There is a striking link with minimizing makespan on unrelated machines. Bamas, Lindermayr, Megow, Rohwedder and Schlöter show that a (2−1/α)-approximation for unrelated makespan, for fixed α≥2, would yield an (α+δ)-approximation for general Santa Claus for every fixed δ>0. Thus any fixed improvement below two in that scheduling problem would answer this question positively. Their general implication goes in this direction; equivalence is established for a specified two-value case.

Bamas, Morell and Rohwedder’s SODA 2025 result extends the m^ε and quasi-polynomial polylogarithmic guarantees to arbitrary monotone submodular valuations. It uses a recursively structured LP with exponentially many variables and constraints. This broadens the class of preferences that can be handled, while retaining a growing approximation factor even on the additive instances considered here.

More recent constant guarantees also require attention to their input promise. Boehmer’s April 2026 paper obtains value at least 0.4OPT for identical monotone submodular valuations. Identical preferences are a substantial restriction, even though submodularity is more general than additivity. The outstanding question concerns unrestricted disagreement about item values. Settling it would clarify whether balancing heterogeneous indivisible resources admits a constant loss at polynomial computational cost.
why: The central unresolved max-min allocation question: can all agents be protected to within a constant factor when indivisible resources have arbitrary heterogeneous additive values?
status_note: The SODA 2024 reduction paper and SODA 2025 submodular paper explicitly retain the general additive constant-approximation question. Later checked constant guarantees concern restricted assignment or identical valuations, not arbitrary additive matrices. No general resolution found through 11 September 2026. Randomization and simultaneous success for all agents are explicit in this formulation.
progress: 2009: Chakrabarty–Chuzhoy–Khanna achieve an arbitrarily small fixed power of the number of items in polynomial time, and a polylogarithmic approximation in quasi-polynomial time. | 2023–2024: Bamas and coauthors show that any fixed improvement below two for unrelated makespan implies a constant-factor approximation for general Santa Claus. | 2024–2025: Bamas–Morell–Rohwedder extend the additive problem’s approximation–time tradeoff to monotone submodular valuations; the work appears at SODA 2025. | 2025-03-27: Haxell–Szabó prove a 3.534 configuration-LP integrality-gap bound for restricted assignment; arbitrary agent-specific values are outside the result. | 2026-04-14: Boehmer obtains a 0.4 welfare guarantee for identical submodular valuations, a different restricted input class.
working_summary: Max-min allocation distributes indivisible items to agents with arbitrary nonnegative additive values. The question asks for a randomized polynomial-time constant-factor approximation to the best achievable minimum agent value. One simultaneous allocation must serve every agent adequately, so favorable expected values alone are insufficient. The difficulty is that agents compete for items whose value can differ substantially between recipients. The saved review separates this general model from restricted assignment, where each item has a common positive value whenever an agent can use it.

title: The power of randomization in truthful unrelated-machine scheduling
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: The central randomized counterpart of the resolved Nisan–Ronen conjecture, with a constant-versus-linear gap independent of computational restrictions.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as m→∞, the function R(m): the infimum worst-case expected-makespan approximation ratio achievable by truthful-in-expectation mechanisms with monetary payments for m unrelated machines and an arbitrary number of indivisible jobs. The infimum ranges over all mechanisms, without a computational or communication restriction. In particular, is R(m)=Θ(1)?
definitions: There are m≥2 machines and n≥1 jobs. Machine i privately knows a vector t_i∈R_{≥0}^n; processing a set S costs it Σ_{j∈S}t_{ij}. Every entry is finite. A direct-revelation mechanism maps reported vectors b=(b₁,…,b_m) to a distribution over assignments σ:{1,…,n}→{1,…,m} and payments to the machines. Jobs are indivisible and every job is assigned exactly once. Let x_{ij}(b)=Pr[σ(j)=i] and let p_i(b) be the finite expected payment to i. Risk-neutral utility is payment minus true processing cost. Truthfulness in expectation means that for every i, true t_i, alternative report b_i and fixed reports b_{−i}, p_i(t_i,b_{−i})−Σ_j t_{ij}x_{ij}(t_i,b_{−i})≥p_i(b_i,b_{−i})−Σ_j t_{ij}x_{ij}(b_i,b_{−i}). This is a dominant-strategy condition against arbitrary fixed reports, without a prior on types. The makespan is C(σ,t)=max_i Σ_{j:σ(j)=i}t_{ij}, and OPT(t)=min_σ C(σ,t). For each m, consider a family M=(M_{m,n})_{n≥1} satisfying this incentive condition for every n and report profile. Its ratio is sup_{n,t:OPT(t)>0} E[C(M_{m,n}(t),t)]/OPT(t), and it must also have expected makespan zero when OPT(t)=0. R(m) is the infimum of those ratios. Random assignments may be correlated across jobs. No budget balance, bound on transfers, individual-rationality constraint, anonymity, task independence or efficient representation is imposed. Since only expected utilities matter, payments can equivalently be deterministic amounts p_i(b).
answer_criterion: Give an explicit asymptotic scale f(m) and universal constants a,b>0 such that a f(m)≤R(m)≤b f(m) for all sufficiently large m, with matching incentive-theoretic lower bounds and mechanisms achieving the upper scale. A constant-factor mechanism for all numbers of machines and jobs would settle the target as Θ(1). Showing only that R(m) is unbounded would rule out that possibility but would not determine the requested asymptotic order without matching bounds. Restrictions on the mechanism class or input distributions must not be silently added.
context:
A machine has a reason to exaggerate how long jobs take: receiving fewer jobs reduces its work. Payments are intended to counteract that incentive while keeping the overall schedule short. The private information is a whole vector, since a machine may be fast on one job and slow on another. A single speed parameter would describe a different and substantially more structured scheduling model.

The optimization objective creates the difficulty. Minimizing total processing cost can be implemented truthfully by a VCG mechanism, which assigns each job to a cheapest machine. But total cost and makespan differ. The largest load is at most the total cost, while the total cost of an optimal makespan schedule is at most m times its makespan. Thus this familiar truthful rule gives an m-approximation. Without incentive constraints and with unlimited computation, one could simply choose an optimal assignment.

Christodoulou, Koutsoupias and Kovács prove that the factor m is unavoidable for deterministic truthful mechanisms, resolving the Nisan–Ronen conjecture. Their result appeared as a 2023 preprint and in the Journal of the ACM in February 2026. It is an unconditional incentive restriction, independent of computational hardness. The paper’s related-work discussion expressly separates the unresolved randomized setting from this deterministic conclusion.

There are two different ways to randomize truthfully. A universally truthful mechanism draws a deterministic truthful mechanism before seeing the reports. Truthfulness in expectation only asks that honest reporting maximize expected utility; individual random outcomes need not implement truthful rules on their own. Universal truthfulness implies the latter condition, but the definition in this card permits the larger class. Mu’alem and Schapira nevertheless prove a lower bound of 2−1/m even for that larger class.

Randomization already helps when there are two machines. Lu and Yu’s STACS 2008 mechanism is universally truthful and beats the deterministic factor two. Their later WINE 2008 paper gives a truthful-in-expectation mechanism with ratio (m+5)/2 for general m, using a fractional allocation and a suitable rounding procedure. The improvement is substantial in its leading constant, but the guarantee still grows linearly with the number of machines.

The WINE paper also proves a lower bound (m+1)/2 for its task-independent class. A mechanism in the full question may use all reported jobs together and correlate their assignments. Consequently, a lower bound that treats each job separately does not close the gap between the general constant lower bound and linear upper bound. Whether such global dependence can change the asymptotic answer is part of what makes this question interesting.

Expected makespan must be distinguished from the largest expected machine load. Consider m identical machines and m unit jobs. Assigning all jobs to one uniformly random machine gives expected load one on every machine, yet the makespan is always m. Assigning one job per machine has makespan one. Thus the same marginal load target can conceal a factor-m difference in the objective. A truthful fractional solution, or an argument that controls only marginal probabilities, needs a valid rounding analysis before it yields a guarantee for this card.

Fine numerical results for small cases illuminate mechanisms without settling the asymptotic problem. Kuryatnikova and Vera obtain almost matching bounds near 1.505996 for two machines and two jobs within a class of randomized monotone scale-free algorithms. Their paper does not identify the optimal ratio over every truthful-in-expectation mechanism, every job count and a growing number of machines. Both the input restriction and mechanism restriction matter when interpreting the result.

The final question is whether allowing random outcomes fundamentally reduces the price of truthful multidimensional cost reporting. A constant answer would permit useful load balancing despite unrestricted private processing times. A growing lower bound would show that even risk-neutral incentives and unrestricted payments cannot recover the efficiency available to a scheduler who knows the true costs. Matching bounds would quantify that loss as a function of system size.
why: Determine the asymptotic efficiency loss caused solely by truthful multidimensional incentives when randomization and payments are fully available.
status_note: The Nisan–Ronen proof, now published in JACM in February 2026, resolves only deterministic truthful mechanisms. Its randomized discussion records 2−1/m and (m+5)/2 bounds. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no matching unrestricted randomized bounds; results for task-independent mechanisms, fractional objectives, Bayesian types or no-payment models do not resolve this formulation.
progress: 2007: Mu’alem–Schapira establish the lower bound 2−1/m for randomized scheduling, including truthfulness in expectation; the full version gives the extended weak-monotonicity argument. | 2008: Lu–Yu give improved universally truthful two-machine mechanisms and a general truthful-in-expectation upper bound (m+5)/2; the linear lower bound in their WINE paper assumes task independence. | 2019–2020: Kuryatnikova–Vera sharpen bounds for a restricted scale-free mechanism class on two machines, including an almost tight two-job calculation; first published 30 May 2019. | 2023-01-27: Christodoulou–Koutsoupias–Kovács post the proof that deterministic truthful scheduling has optimal ratio m, while recording the distinct randomized bounds. | 2026-02-11: The deterministic Nisan–Ronen proof is published online in the Journal of the ACM; its theorem does not cover truthful-in-expectation randomization.
working_summary: Unrelated-machine scheduling assigns jobs to machines with privately known processing times for each job. The question asks for the optimal expected-makespan approximation achievable by truthful-in-expectation mechanisms as the number of machines grows. Random assignments can correlate decisions across jobs while payments discourage strategic misreporting. A constant ratio would show that randomization overcomes the large incentive cost known for deterministic mechanisms. The saved review emphasizes that maximum expected load is different from expected maximum load, and restricted task-independent lower bounds do not settle the unrestricted mechanism class.

title: Polynomial query complexity of exact envy-free cake cutting
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: The main worst-case complexity gap for exact envy-free cake cutting; recent single-exponential and average-case results sharpen the boundary without settling polynomial query complexity.
formal: Do absolute constants C,d>0 and a deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol exist that, for every n and every profile of n nonatomic additive cake valuations, use at most Cn^d queries to produce a complete exactly envy-free allocation, allowing disconnected pieces?
definitions: The cake is [0,1]. Agent i has an arbitrary nonatomic Borel probability measure μ_i: values are nonnegative, countably additive, μ_i([0,1])=1 and μ_i({x})=0 for every point x. No density formula, bounded-density promise or random valuation model is supplied. The protocol learns valuations only through exact queries: Eval(i,x,y) returns μ_i([x,y]); Cut(i,x,α), with 0≤α≤μ_i([x,1]), returns a point y≥x for which μ_i([x,y])=α. Endpoints used by the protocol are 0, 1 and previously returned cut marks; interval values can be combined by additivity. If several cut points satisfy a query, the protocol must remain correct for any valid response. Count each evaluation or cut query as one; finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-complexity bound. Output a partition (A₁,…,A_n) of the entire cake into finite unions of intervals with endpoints among the known marks. Assign cut endpoints arbitrarily, since every agent values them at zero. Require μ_i(A_i)≥μ_i(A_j) for every ordered pair i,j. There is no unallocated residue, approximation error, randomization, or connected-piece requirement. The bound Cn^d is uniform over all valuation profiles and valid query responses.
answer_criterion: Give a deterministic protocol with the stated worst-case polynomial query bound, or prove that every such protocol has superpolynomial worst-case query complexity as n grows. A lower bound on the number of queries used by one known protocol is not a general impossibility result. A finite bound depending arbitrarily on n, an average-case polynomial bound, or a polynomial protocol permitting positive envy or discarded cake leaves this question open.
context:
Envy-freeness asks each person to compare the allocated pieces using their own valuation. It does not require different people to agree on values or to receive pieces of equal geometric length. For two agents, cut-and-choose works: one divides the cake into two equally valued parts and the other selects a preferred part. Extending this idea while controlling every pairwise comparison becomes much harder as the number of agents grows.

Completeness prevents a trivial answer. If the protocol could discard everything, giving everyone an empty piece would create no envy. Allocating the full cake also makes envy-freeness imply proportionality: for each agent, the value of their own piece is at least the average value of the n allocated pieces, namely 1/n. The converse fails because receiving a fair share does not prevent preferring someone else’s larger-valued share.

Disconnected pieces are essential to the computational question being asked. Exact envy-free allocations with connected pieces cannot, in general, be obtained by finite Robertson–Webb protocols once there are at least three agents. That obstruction does not apply when an agent may receive several intervals. Likewise, a bound on the number of final cut locations alone is not a bound on the number of valuation questions needed to discover suitable locations.

Nonatomicity gives the cut oracle its power: an interval can be cut to achieve any intermediate value. It does not impose a simple shape on preferences. A valuation may put almost all its mass in a very small region or have intervals of zero value. Exact comparisons must remain valid on these profiles, so a fixed numerical mesh or a small positive tolerance cannot silently substitute for an exact protocol.

Procaccia’s general lower bound is Ω(n²) Robertson–Webb queries. This already separates envy-free division from the Θ(n log n) query complexity of proportional division, but it remains compatible with a polynomial protocol. A quadratic lower bound cannot justify describing the target as impossible or necessarily exponential.

Aziz–Mackenzie’s FOCS 2016 breakthrough establishes a bound depending only on n for every profile, resolving the earlier question of whether any bounded protocol exists. Their displayed upper bound is a tower of six copies of n. This is stronger than merely terminating on each profile: earlier finite procedures could require arbitrarily many queries while n stayed fixed. The existence of a bounded protocol leaves the growth rate of that bound open.

Sokolov’s June 2023 preprint revises parts of the protocol and sharpens the analysis to n^{8n²(1+o(1))}. That is a major quantitative reduction, equal to 2^{(8+o(1))n² log₂n}, although it remains far above polynomial. The inherited 2025/2026 average-case article still quotes the older tower benchmark; the progress account here therefore also checks subsequent and separately posted algorithmic work.

A very recent advance is Ye–Bai’s September 4, 2026 preprint. Its Theorem 1.1 states a deterministic protocol using n^{O(1)}2^n queries for complete envy-free allocation with arbitrary nonnegative additive nonatomic valuations. The proof replaces a very large family of partial allocations by a polynomial-sized collection and controls how their pieces can be reassigned without conflicts. This is the latest reported general upper bound found in the review, and is identified as a preprint.

The same paper distinguishes query complexity from local computation. title: Is the matrix multiplication exponent equal to two?
importance_reason: One of the main questions in algebraic algorithms, governing a widely used primitive and many dependent complexity bounds. Both faster constructions and a superquadratic lower bound would have broad consequences.

formal: Fix the field of complex numbers. Let s(n) be the minimum number of arithmetic gates in a circuit that computes all entries of AB exactly for arbitrary n-by-n matrices A,B. Is it true that $\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists C_\varepsilon>0\;\forall n\ge2:\ s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{2+\varepsilon}$? Equivalently, is $\omega=\inf\{\tau:s(n)=O(n^\tau)\}=2$?
definitions: The inputs are 2n² independent complex variables a_ij,b_ij. The required n² output polynomials are c_ij=sum_{k=1}^n a_ik b_kj. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with binary addition, subtraction, and multiplication gates; any complex constants and unrestricted reuse of intermediate values are allowed. Size counts arithmetic gates, including operations involving constants. Input nodes, constant nodes, and output designations are not gates. No division, order comparisons, branching, approximation, or randomization is permitted. A different circuit may be chosen for every n: this is the standard nonuniform arithmetic-complexity formulation over C. The cost of encoding a complex number in bits is outside this model. The elementary lower bound s(n)>=n² for n>=2 follows because the n² distinct non-input output polynomials require distinct gates.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The usual algorithm computes n² inner products of length n, spending cubic arithmetic work. That computation treats the outputs separately even though they share their input matrices. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent log₂7.

The question is whether one can keep reducing the extra exponent all the way to zero. Its quantifiers matter. An algorithm for each exponent 2+epsilon is enough, even when its constant depends badly on epsilon. Conversely, improving one decimal place in the current upper bound does not establish the conjecture. Fixing the field and counting exact scalar operations also separates this question from approximate numerical multiplication or hardware throughput.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

There are also lower bounds on what specific tensor methods can achieve. For example, Alman’s universal-method barrier for Coppersmith–Winograd tensors prevents that route from reaching exponent two. It is not a lower bound on all arithmetic circuits for matrix multiplication. The distinction leaves room for different starting tensors or mathematical constructions.
why: Matrix multiplication is a basic operation whose exponent enters many algorithms in linear algebra and graph theory. Determining whether its arithmetic cost can approach the quadratic scale would settle a central question about sharing computation among many related outputs.
status_note: The latest primary upper bound located through 10 September 2026 is the reported omega<2.371177 from August 2026. It leaves the omega=2 question open. The model is exact arithmetic over C; the catalogue has not independently reproduced the numerical certificate.
