title: Is rational solvability of polynomial equations decidable?
importance_reason: A central unsolved decidability problem for an elementary, pervasive constraint language. A resolution would locate the computability boundary for rational polynomial feasibility.
focus_reason: A central unsolved decidability problem for an elementary, pervasive constraint language. A resolution would locate the computability boundary for rational polynomial feasibility.
formal: Does there exist a Turing machine that, given any integer-coefficient polynomial f(X₁,…,Xₘ), always halts and correctly decides whether $\exists (q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m:f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0$? The number of variables and polynomial degree are unrestricted parts of the finite input.
definitions: Encode m≥1 and a finite list of monomials, each with a signed binary integer coefficient and an m-tuple of nonnegative binary exponents. Repeated monomials may be combined effectively; zero polynomials are allowed. A rational solution consists of exact fractions qᵢ=aᵢ/bᵢ, where aᵢ∈ℤ and bᵢ is a positive integer, with no prescribed bound on numerators or denominators. The required algorithm is one finite deterministic program, independent of m, degree, and coefficients. It must return yes exactly when a rational zero exists and no otherwise; it may use any finite amount of time and space on each input. Malformed encodings are rejected. The task supplies no oracle, height inequalities, integrality constraints on the unknowns, or promise of a solution. Rational coefficients would give an equivalent problem by clearing coefficient denominators. A finite system f₁=⋯=fᵣ=0 is equivalent over ℚ to the single equation f₁²+⋯+fᵣ²=0.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Rational tuples can be enumerated by increasing bounds on their numerators and denominators, and substitution into an integer polynomial is exact and computable. Thus yes-instances can already be recognized eventually. The difficulty is knowing when to stop searching and certify that no rational point exists. The question asks about computability itself, before any requirement of efficiency.

Hilbert’s original problem required integer solutions. Matiyasevich’s completion of the Davis–Putnam–Robinson program proves that version undecidable. Permitting fractions changes the problem: a polynomial can have a rational zero and no integer zero, so applying a rational solver directly to the same equation would not decide the integer problem. A reduction must encode the missing integrality restriction using only the allowed rational polynomial equations.

An existential definition of ℤ inside ℚ would provide such an encoding and imply undecidability. Koenigsmann instead gives a universal definition of the integers, which is a major advance in definability but uses a different quantifier form. The full first-order theory of ℚ is already undecidable; the unresolved target concerns its existential fragment. 

Recent results settle the analogous problem over the ring of integers of every number field. A ring of integers restricts denominators; it is not the whole number field. In particular the ring of integers of ℚ is ℤ, so this breakthrough does not decide the question on this card. Poonen’s July 2026 account explains how rank stability of abelian varieties yields the required Diophantine definitions for those rings.

Other nearby formulations add conditions comparing heights of rational coordinates. Garcia-Fritz, Pasten, and Vidaux prove an undecidability result with finitely many such conditions. Their formulation includes predicates absent here, and their paper explicitly retains ordinary Hilbert’s tenth problem over ℚ as open. This distinction matters when interpreting a result whose title refers to undecidable effectivity for rational points.
why: This is a fundamental boundary between algorithmic arithmetic and undecidability. It asks whether exact rational polynomial constraints admit any general terminating solver, connecting computation, logical definability, and the arithmetic geometry of rational points.
status_note: Explicitly open in the cited rational-solvability and local-global sources. Research through 10 September 2026 found no resolution over ℚ. The recent results for rings of integers and for additional height predicates do not answer this formulation.
progress: 1970: The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem settles the integer-solution problem negatively. The rational-solution analogue remains distinct. | 2010–2016: Koenigsmann gives a universal first-order definition of ℤ in ℚ and related low-quantifier undecidability results. This does not supply an existential definition. | 2023: Anscombe and coauthors survey local-global methods and explicitly identify Hilbert’s tenth problem over number fields, including ℚ, as open. | 2023–2025: Garcia-Fritz, Pasten, and Vidaux prove undecidability after adjoining finitely many height-comparison conditions. formal: Does there exist a constant C>0 and a classical randomized algorithm A running in polynomial time such that, for every rank-n rational lattice basis B, A outputs a nonzero integer vector z satisfying ∥Bz∥₂≤n^C λ₁(L(B)) with probability at least 2/3?
definitions: The input is an explicitly encoded matrix B∈ℚ^{d×n}, d≥n≥1, with linearly independent columns. Each rational entry is given by a binary numerator and positive binary denominator. L(B)={Bz:z∈ℤⁿ} is the lattice, and λ₁(L)=min{∥v∥₂:0≠v∈L} is the length of a shortest nonzero vector in the Euclidean norm ∥v∥₂=(Σᵢvᵢ²)^{1/2}. Rank n, rather than ambient dimension d or coefficient magnitude, controls the approximation factor. There must be one polynomial P such that every run halts in at most P(L) bit operations, where L is the input’s total bit length; output bits and random bits are counted. Randomness consists of independent fair bits. Require z to be a nonzero integer vector on every run, while the length guarantee may fail with probability at most 1/3. Both P and C are independent of all input parameters. There are no distributional, uniqueness, conditioning, ideal-lattice or basis-quality promises. A deterministic algorithm would also qualify. The one-dimensional case is exactly solvable by a basis vector. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A lattice basis can disguise very short vectors as cancellations between long columns. For example, b₁=(N,1) and b₂=(N+1,1) both have length about N, while b₂−b₁=(1,0) has length one. Simply selecting the shortest input column therefore has no dimension-only approximation guarantee. Basis reduction changes the representation without changing the lattice, aiming to expose short integer combinations.

The LLL algorithm solves a major version of this task in polynomial bit time: with the standard reduction parameter, it finds a nonzero vector within 2^{(n−1)/2} of the shortest length. The factor is exponential in rank, even though the running time is polynomial. This was enough to transform computational number theory and enable applications such as factoring rational polynomials, but it leaves the much stronger approximation asked for here open.

Block reduction improves the quality by solving shorter-vector problems in projected sublattices of limited rank. The best general polynomial-time guarantees summarized by Bennett have approximation factor 2^{O(n log log n/log n)}. That is smaller than the basic LLL factor but still grows faster than every fixed power of n. Larger blocks improve approximation at the cost of more expensive local computations; a polynomial number of calls to an expensive subroutine does not imply polynomial total time.

Known hardness results approach, but do not reach, the polynomial-factor regime. Haviv and Regev show that approximation within 2^{(log n)^{1−δ}}, for fixed δ>0, cannot be polynomial time unless NP has randomized quasipolynomial-time algorithms. Stronger assumptions give further nearly polynomial factors. Every such factor must be read with its quantifiers: hardness for a smaller approximation factor concerns a more demanding task and does not eliminate the possibility of a much looser nᶜ approximation.

Decision and search also need care. GapSVP distinguishes λ₁≤r from λ₁>γr, with no requirement on intermediate inputs. Aharonov and Regev place the decision problem with γ=O(√n) in NP∩coNP, using short certificates on both sides. This is strong evidence about its structural complexity and a barrier to certain NP-hardness proofs. It is not a polynomial-time search algorithm that finds a short lattice vector.

The intermediate approximation regime is central to lattice cryptography. Worst-case to average-case reductions relate particular polynomial-factor lattice problems to problems such as SIS and LWE at specified parameters. These implications have a direction: an efficient worst-case algorithm would invalidate the corresponding hardness premise, but the existence of a security reduction alone would not prove that every deployed cryptosystem is broken. The exponent, problem variant and cryptographic parameters all matter.

Sato and Yasuda’s May 2026 PotBKZ algorithm guarantees termination after a polynomial number of calls to its potential-reducing enumeration routine. This improves control of the reduction process, including a self-dual variant. It does not give a polynomial-time polynomial-factor approximation for arbitrary rank, because the cost and quality of the block enumeration must still be accounted for.

Hirahara and Ogitsuka’s August 2026 preprint improves the randomness properties of lattice hardness reductions. Under a stated exponential lower-bound assumption for nondeterministic circuits, they obtain deterministic NP-hardness reductions for every constant Euclidean approximation factor. Both qualifications matter: the derandomization is conditional, and the approximation factors are constants, rather than all polynomial factors. Their separate parameterized hardness results also use a different resource measure.

The question isolates the large gap between useful reduction algorithms and the approximation range used in fundamental hardness assumptions. Even an algorithm with a very large fixed exponent C would be a major qualitative advance; the target does not demand exact SVP or a small approximation constant.
why: A central algorithmic gap in lattice complexity: known polynomial-time methods give superpolynomial approximation factors, while key computational and cryptographic questions lie in the polynomial-factor regime.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No classical polynomial-time algorithm with any fixed polynomial approximation factor was found for unrestricted Euclidean search SVP. Recent termination guarantees count costly subroutine calls, and the August conditional hardness theorem concerns constant factors. The card explicitly allows bounded-error classical randomization.
progress: 1982: LLL gives polynomial-time lattice reduction with an exponential-in-rank approximation guarantee. | 2004–2005: Aharonov–Regev place O(√n)-GapSVP in NP∩coNP; the theorem concerns gap decision certificates. | 2007–2012: Haviv–Regev strengthen approximation hardness to nearly polynomial factors under randomized complexity assumptions. | 2023: Bennett’s survey documents the polynomial-time upper factor 2^{O(n log log n/log n)} and the unresolved polynomial-factor region. | 2026-05-11: Sato–Yasuda prove a polynomial bound on PotBKZ’s enumeration calls, without making unrestricted block enumeration polynomial time. | 2026-08-14: Hirahara–Ogitsuka obtain one-sided-error reductions and conditional deterministic constant-factor Euclidean NP-hardness.
working_summary: The shortest vector problem seeks a nonzero integer combination of lattice basis vectors with minimum Euclidean length. The reviewed question asks for polynomial-time approximation within some fixed polynomial in the lattice rank. Long basis vectors can cancel to form much shorter vectors, so the input representation hides the relevant geometry. Reaching polynomial factors would close a major gap between general reduction algorithms and fundamental lattice-hardness regimes. The saved review separates subexponential approximation factors, decision certificates, and constant-factor hardness from the requested polynomial-factor search guarantee.

title: Can a classical randomized algorithm factor every integer in polynomial time?
importance_reason: A defining open problem of computational number theory, with broad consequences for cryptography, arithmetic algorithms, and classical-versus-quantum computation.
formal: Do there exist constants C,c and a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, on every positive integer N given in binary, outputs its complete prime factorization with probability at least 2/3 and always halts within C(n+1)ᶜ bit operations, where n=⌊log₂N⌋+1?
definitions: For N≥2, the required output is the ordered list (p₁,e₁),…,(pᵣ,eᵣ), with distinct primes p₁<⋯<pᵣ, positive integer exponents eᵢ, and N=∏ᵢpᵢ^{eᵢ}. All output integers are encoded in binary. The factorization of N=1 is the empty list; zero and malformed encodings are outside the positive-integer domain and are rejected. The same finite probabilistic Turing machine must work for all N. Its random tape contains independent fair bits, and the success probability is over these bits separately for each fixed input. The polynomial time bound holds on every random tape. An incorrect output or a failure symbol counts as failure. There are no quantum operations, input-dependent advice, factoring or order-finding oracles, promises of a special form for N, or supplied factors of nearby integers. In particular n is the bit length of N, not its numerical value.
answer_criterion: Answer yes with a proved algorithm meeting the worst-case polynomial running time and per-input success guarantee. Answer no by proving that every uniform classical randomized algorithm fails one of these requirements for some inputs, regardless of its polynomial exponent. Deterministic factoring would suffice for yes, but a deterministic lower bound alone would not suffice for no. Experiments or algorithms for a restricted class of integers do not settle the statement.
context:
Multiplying the prime factors is easy, and the factors themselves fit in a polynomial-size output. Discovering them is the unresolved step. Trial division up to √N is polynomial in the number’s value but exponential in its binary input length. The distinction between N and log N is essential even when a newer algorithm improves the power of N substantially.

Primality testing and factorization are different tasks. The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena algorithm decides in deterministic polynomial time whether a number is prime, without necessarily exhibiting a divisor when the answer is composite. It also makes a proposed full factorization efficiently checkable: verify that every listed base is prime and that the product is N.

Because an output can be checked, a bounded-error polynomial-time factoring algorithm can be repeated until a valid factorization is obtained, giving an always-correct algorithm with polynomial expected time. Conversely, a polynomial expected-time always-correct algorithm can be truncated at a suitable constant multiple of its expected bound to obtain the formulation above. This equivalence concerns performance on every input; success on a sampled family of integers alone is weaker.

The general number field sieve has the familiar heuristic expected-time estimate exp(((64/9)^{1/3}+o(1))(ln N)^{1/3}(ln ln N)^{2/3}). This is subexponential but still superpolynomial in the bit length. Rigorous deterministic bounds of N^{1/5+o(1)} make a different tradeoff and remain exponential in that length. Neither bound is a proof that faster classical factoring is impossible.

Shor’s quantum algorithm factors in polynomial time, using quantum order finding. It provides an upper bound in a more powerful computational model; it does not establish a classical lower bound. A classical polynomial-time algorithm would undermine factoring-based cryptographic assumptions, but the absence of such an algorithm has not been proved from P≠NP or from the efficiency of multiplication.
why: Integer factorization is a basic inverse problem in arithmetic and a central test case for the potential power of quantum computation. Its classical complexity has direct consequences for factoring-based cryptography and for algorithms that currently require access to a factoring subroutine.
status_note: Explicitly identified as unknown in Harvey and Hittmeir’s June 2026 paper. Research through 10 September 2026 found no proved classical polynomial-time algorithm for all integers or impossibility theorem for the stated randomized model. Numerical scaling evidence and quantum algorithms do not establish either answer.
progress: 1980s–1990s: Sieve methods establish powerful subexponential classical approaches. The standard general number field sieve estimate remains a heuristic expected-time analysis, as summarized in the current large-order paper. | 1994–1997: Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for factorization and discrete logarithms. Quantum computation is outside the classical model fixed here. | 2002–2004: Agrawal, Kayal, and Saxena prove deterministic polynomial-time primality testing. The result does not give a polynomial-time factoring algorithm. | 2021–2022: Harvey and Hittmeir rigorously factor N in O(N^{1/5}(log N)^{16/5}/(log log N)^{3/5}) deterministic bit operations, improving the preceding exponent-one-fifth bound by a logarithmic factor. | 5 June 2026: Harvey and Hittmeir’s revised large-order algorithm removes earlier power-of-N lower restrictions on its target order parameter. Their introduction still explicitly identifies polynomial-time integer factorization as unknown; the improved subroutine does not provide such a factoring algorithm.
working_summary: Integer factorization recovers the prime factors and multiplicities whose product is a given positive integer. The reviewed question asks whether one classical randomized algorithm can do this in time polynomial in the input's bit length. Multiplication and verification are efficient, but discovering factors remains a different computational task from testing primality. A polynomial algorithm would transform computational number theory and undermine corresponding factoring-based hardness assumptions. The saved review distinguishes subexponential classical methods and polynomial-time quantum factoring from the requested worst-case classical guarantee on every input.

title: Are discrete logarithms in prime fields in randomized polynomial time?
importance_reason: One of the principal unresolved number-theoretic algorithmic problems, with direct connections to cryptography, index calculus, and quantum speedups.
formal: Is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every prime p, every generator g of the multiplicative group Fₚ*, and every h∈Fₚ*, returns the unique integer x∈{0,…,p−2} satisfying gˣ≡h (mod p), with probability at least 2/3 and worst-case running time polynomial in log₂p?
definitions: The input consists of ordinary binary integers (p,g,h), with p prime and 1≤g,h≤p−1, promised that g has multiplicative order p−1. Set n=⌈log₂(p+1)⌉; the total input length is Θ(n). A single probabilistic Turing machine must use at most C(n+1)^c bit operations on every random tape, for fixed constants C,c independent of p,g,h. It may output failure on unsuccessful runs. Success probability is over its own independent fair random bits and must be at least 2/3 separately on every promised input. Its only input is (p,g,h): no factorization of p−1, precomputed logarithm table, advice, special-form description of p, or oracle is supplied. Any preprocessing it performs counts in its runtime. The algorithm may exploit the ordinary integer encoding and all efficiently computable arithmetic modulo p; it is not restricted to generic group operations. The group is multiplication of nonzero residues, not an elliptic-curve group or the additive group. For p=2 the only logarithm is x=0.
answer_criterion: Give and prove a classical algorithm with the specified uniform polynomial worst-case time and per-instance success guarantee, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A generic-group lower bound, a fast algorithm for a restricted family of primes, a quantum algorithm, or a polynomial bound in p rather than log p does not settle the question.
context:
Computing gˣ mod p is efficient by repeated squaring, even when x is given in binary and is as large as p−2. The inverse problem asks which exponent produced a residue. A polynomial-time solution would remove the computational asymmetry used in finite-field discrete-logarithm cryptography. It would also solve the corresponding computational Diffie–Hellman problem by recovering an exponent, although hardness of discrete logarithms alone does not establish every stronger security assumption.

A proposed answer is easy to verify: check the exponent range and compute gˣ mod p. Consequently a bounded-error polynomial algorithm could be repeated until a verified answer is obtained, giving expected polynomial time with no incorrect output. Conversely, a verified expected-polynomial-time solver can be truncated and repeated to obtain constant success within a polynomial budget. This makes the fixed runtime convention compatible with the usual Las Vegas formulation.

The number field sieve exploits arithmetic structure that generic group algorithms cannot see. It gathers multiplicative relations among suitably smooth objects, solves a large linear system, and reduces an individual target to the resulting logarithms. Its usual large-characteristic complexity estimates have the heuristic subexponential form exp(O((ln p)^{1/3}(ln ln p)^{2/3})). This grows faster than every polynomial in the bit length.

Generic lower bounds do not settle the concrete prime-field problem. Shoup proves a square-root barrier in the size of the largest prime factor of a group’s order when elements are accessed through an abstract random encoding. The present algorithm receives actual residues and can use their number-theoretic structure, as the sieve already does. A proof against the oracle model cannot simply be transferred to this richer interface.

The field regime is crucial. Kleinjung and Wesolowski give a rigorous expected-time bound (p·d)^{2log₂d+O(1)} for discrete logarithms in F_{p^d}. For fixed p and growing extension degree d this is quasipolynomial in the input size. For prime fields d=1 and growing p, that expression is merely polynomial in p, which is exponential in its binary length. Their breakthrough therefore leaves this question open.

Later sieve work also studies how preprocessing can be shared across targets and across fields. The Discrete Logarithm Factory paper develops such improvements, especially for non-prime fields, and distinguishes the cost of a target logarithm from the cost of building reusable data. Here all preprocessing is charged to the algorithm on a single input, so a cheap online lookup after a very expensive table construction is insufficient.
why: A fundamental inversion problem in computational number theory and a central candidate for separating efficient classical from quantum computation. Its resolution would clarify which arithmetic structure can overcome generic group barriers and would reshape finite-field cryptographic assumptions.
status_note: Open in the cited computational-number-theory literature; checked through 10 September 2026. No uniform classical polynomial-in-log-p solver or unrestricted exclusion was found. The card keeps heuristic sieve analyses, fixed-characteristic extension fields, reusable preprocessing, and quantum algorithms separate.
progress: 1990s: Number-field-sieve methods give heuristic subexponential algorithms for prime-field discrete logarithms; their arithmetic relations go beyond the generic group model. | 1994–1997: Shor gives quantum polynomial-time algorithms for factoring and discrete logarithms. The classical requirement in this question is essential. | 1997: Shoup proves square-root lower bounds for generic group algorithms, parameterized by the largest prime factor of the group order. These are model-restricted lower bounds. | 2019–2022: Kleinjung and Wesolowski prove quasipolynomial expected time for fixed-characteristic finite fields. Their theorem does not give polynomial time in log p for the prime-field family. | 2024: Al Aswad, Thomé, and Pierrot develop the Discrete Logarithm Factory approach to sharing sieve computations, while continuing to describe NFS variants as the leading methods outside small characteristic.
working_summary: A discrete logarithm in a prime field asks which exponent of a supplied generator produces a target nonzero residue. The question seeks a classical randomized algorithm with running time polynomial in log p for every promised input. Exponentiation is efficient, but reversing it requires identifying one exponent among p−1 possibilities. A solution would remove a foundational computational asymmetry used in finite-field cryptography. The saved review distinguishes prime fields from fixed-characteristic extension fields and explains why generic-group lower bounds do not rule out algorithms exploiting the concrete arithmetic of residues.

title: Can a quantum algorithm approximate Euclidean SVP within a polynomial factor in polynomial time?
importance_reason: A foundational quantum-algorithm question with broad relevance to lattice complexity and computational cryptography. The model and accuracy combination is distinct from both existing classical approximation and quantum exact-search cards.
formal: Do there exist a constant C>0 and a uniform quantum algorithm A with polynomial running time such that, for every rational matrix B∈Q^(d×n) with d≥n≥1 and linearly independent columns, A outputs a nonzero z∈Z^n satisfying ∥Bz∥₂≤n^C λ₁(L(B)) with probability at least 2/3?
definitions: The full matrix, dimensions and every rational entry are given classically; rationals use signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Let N be the total encoding length. L(B)={Bz:z∈Z^n}, λ₁(L)=min{∥v∥₂:0≠v∈L}, and ∥v∥₂=(Σ_i v_i²)^(1/2). Approximation depends on rank n rather than the ambient dimension d or N. Use a uniform quantum circuit computation with classical polynomial-time control, polynomially many qubits initially in computational basis states, gates H=2^(−1/2)[[1,1],[1,−1]], T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)) and CNOT, and computational-basis measurements with classical feed-forward. The classical input bits may be copied into input qubits. One polynomial p(N) bounds total classical bit operations, gate applications, measurements and output bits on every branch. Classical control and circuit generation are uniform in the input length and use no advice or oracle; a unit-cost quantum random-access oracle for the input is not supplied. The output is a binary-encoded integer coefficient vector, required to be nonzero on every branch; the norm guarantee may fail with probability at most 1/3. The constants C and p are independent of all inputs. There is no uniqueness, average-case, ideal-lattice, modular or conditioning promise.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
context:
A short lattice vector may be hidden by cancellation among much longer basis columns. The task is to find an integer combination with length bounded relative to the shortest possible nonzero combination. Allowing a factor n^C is a substantial relaxation of exact shortest-vector search, yet remains far stronger than the guarantees of basic polynomial-time lattice reduction.

The existing TCS-6667 asks the same approximate search question for a classical randomized algorithm. TCS-7169 instead asks about a quantum algorithm for exact SVP. This card distinguishes the missing intermediate combination: quantum computation with a polynomial approximation factor. A classical solution of the matching approximation target would qualify here, but a quantum solution would not automatically give a classical one.

Regev’s worst-case to average-case reduction connects specified GapSVP and SIVP tasks to Learning With Errors. Its consequence has a direction: a suitable efficient LWE solver yields quantum algorithms for the lattice tasks in the theorem. It does not establish an unrestricted equivalence between arbitrary polynomial-factor search SVP and every LWE parameter family.

The distinction matters for interpretation of a breakthrough. An algorithm satisfying this card would substantially change our understanding of quantum lattice reduction. Its effect on a particular cryptographic assumption would still depend on the approximation exponent, the exact lattice problem and the reduction parameters. Merely naming LWE is insufficient to infer that every parameter choice has been broken.

Rank and bit length are separate variables. Increasing coefficients must not be mistaken for increasing the allowed approximation factor, and a polynomial algorithm must include the cost of reading and manipulating their binary representations. The specified gate model permits ordinary quantum computation while excluding an additional oracle resource hidden in a data-access convention.
why: Isolate the potential power of quantum computation in the central polynomial-factor regime of worst-case lattice approximation.
status_note: No general quantum polynomial-time algorithm with a fixed polynomial approximation factor was found through 11 September 2026. This status is about the specified worst-case search target, not a claim about all LWE formulations.
progress: 2005–2009: Regev establishes a quantum worst-case-to-average-case reduction involving GapSVP, SIVP and LWE at specified parameters. | 2023: Bennett’s survey documents the large unresolved polynomial-factor region in general SVP complexity. | 2024-01-08: The posted Regev version preserves the earlier theorem, with a proof correction, rather than announcing a new lattice algorithm.

title: Exact Euclidean SVP in single-exponential time and polynomial space
importance_reason: A longstanding resource boundary for exact lattice algorithms, central to enumeration versus sieving and increasingly relevant to lattice time-space hardness assumptions.
formal: Do absolute constants C,d>0 and a randomized classical algorithm exist that, given any rational rank-n lattice basis B of bit length L, find a shortest nonzero Euclidean lattice vector with probability at least 2/3 using at most 2^{Cn}L^d bit operations and L^d bits of working space?
definitions: The input is B∈Q^{m×n}, with m≥n≥1 and linearly independent columns; each rational entry is encoded by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. L includes the matrix dimensions and all entry encodings. The lattice is Λ(B)={Bz:z∈Zⁿ}, and λ₁(Λ)=min_{z∈Zⁿ\{0}}‖Bz‖₂, with the ordinary Euclidean norm in R^m. Output a nonzero integer coordinate vector z satisfying ‖Bz‖₂=λ₁(Λ); any minimizer is acceptable. The algorithm is a uniform probabilistic Turing machine with read-only input, write-only output and a stream of independent random bits. Every stored bit, including retained randomness and intermediate lattice vectors, counts toward space; external writable storage and preprocessing oracles are unavailable. The time and space limits must hold on every execution, and the success probability must hold separately for every valid input. The exponent n is lattice rank, not ambient dimension or coefficient precision. All preprocessing and precision management count. There is no promise of a unique shortest vector, a random lattice, a reduced input basis or approximation slack.
answer_criterion: An affirmative answer gives an algorithm satisfying both bounds simultaneously with a proof of exact success on every lattice. A negative answer proves that every randomized polynomial-space algorithm fails some single-exponential-time requirement, or establishes an appropriate time-space lower bound excluding the stated constants. An example defeating one enumeration or sieving method is not enough. Exponential-space algorithms and polynomial-space algorithms taking 2^{Θ(n log n)} time leave the question open.
context:
The familiar exact algorithms offer two different resource profiles. Enumeration explores candidate lattice vectors while retaining a relatively small search state, but its proved worst-case time is n^{O(n)}. Sieving and Voronoi methods achieve 2^{O(n)} time by retaining exponentially many vectors or geometric constraints. The question asks whether one can obtain the faster asymptotic time without the exponential memory.

These time scales differ by more than a constant in the exponent: n^{cn}=2^{cn log₂n}. For any fixed C, the factor log₂n eventually makes n^{cn} exceed 2^{Cn}. Conversely, this card permits a large constant C. A polynomial-memory algorithm with time 2^{100n} would resolve the existence question affirmatively even if it were unusable in practice and slower than current exponential-memory algorithms at moderate ranks.

The output is exact, and the zero vector is excluded. Returning a vector whose length is within a fixed or polynomial factor of optimum solves a different task. Ties create no ambiguity: if several shortest vectors exist, any one is valid. Rational input also allows exact comparison of squared lengths, so the definition does not rely on floating-point tolerance or an unspecified geometric oracle.

The standard basis illustrates why practical performance alone says little about the general bound. For B=I, a shortest vector is immediately visible. A basis with long, strongly correlated columns may describe a lattice with much shorter integer combinations. Preprocessing can improve the basis substantially, but its own running time and memory must be charged. Supplying an already ideal basis would remove part of the problem.

Kannan’s enumeration method uses recursive preprocessing to control the search region. Hanrot–Stehlé’s analysis gives the more precise n^{n/(2e)+o(n)} time benchmark, up to polynomial input-size factors, and later work reduces preprocessing overhead. This refines the constant multiplying n log n; it does not change that scale to O(n). The bound is about the method, not an unconditional lower bound on every polynomial-space algorithm.

The inherited Micciancio–Voulgaris paper proves a different landmark: deterministic single-exponential algorithms using Voronoi-cell computations. Its March 2012 revision improves the bound to roughly 2^{2n} time and 2^n space, suppressing polynomial factors. The paper explicitly leaves single-exponential time with polynomial space as an open direction. Reading only the phrase deterministic single exponential in its title would miss the resource that remains unresolved.

Exponential memory can encode reusable relationships among many short vectors. Recomputing a discarded value may save space, but repeated recomputation can increase the running time beyond the allowed bound. A valid positive solution must control this global cost as well as the size of each local calculation. Streaming a large list through a small buffer is not sufficient if later steps require repeatedly reconstructing most of the list.

Theoretical and heuristic guarantees also need separation. Pruning an enumeration tree or keeping a smaller sieve pool may work well on tested lattices. A proof for the present question must additionally show that the retained search process reaches an exact minimizer with probability at least 2/3 on every input within the stated time. Successful benchmark instances cannot supply that universal guarantee.

A January 2026 paper by Koyuncu–Linker–Ozel proposes a sheaf-based sieving framework and discusses polynomial memory under coarse graining. Its §4 initially gives storage O((M+K)n) for M initial vectors and K iterations, then suggests reducing memory when most new vectors replace old ones. It does not provide a uniform proof that this replacement regime retains the exact-success guarantee and a 2^{O(n)} iteration bound on every lattice. It is therefore recorded as a related proposal rather than a resolution of this precise question.

The resource gap is also used in current cryptographic research. Albrecht–Lai–Postlethwaite’s CRYPTO 2026 work derives consequences from hypothetical algorithms for hinted inhomogeneous short-integer solutions, connecting them to single-exponential algorithms with polynomial memory for broader worst-case lattice tasks. Its hardness conclusions rely on a time-space assumption; they do not prove that such algorithms are impossible.

The importance of the problem is that it isolates memory as a potential source of exponential speedups in exact geometry. A solution could change the theoretical basis for choosing between enumeration and large-pool methods. Its cryptographic consequences would still have to be assessed through the relevant reductions and concrete parameters; the existence of some 2^{Cn}-time exact solver is not itself a polynomial-time attack.
why: A canonical time-space tradeoff question in exact algorithms: can the single-exponential speed of lattice sieving and Voronoi methods be achieved with only polynomial memory?
status_note: Open for exact Euclidean SVP with the simultaneous worst-case time and space bounds stated here, following primary literature checked through 11 September 2026. The 2026 sheaf-based proposal discusses a memory-saving regime but does not establish the required uniform exact-success and runtime theorem. Cryptographic time-space hardness is an assumption, not an unconditional negative resolution.
progress: 1983–1987: Kannan obtains exact lattice algorithms using n^{O(n)} time and polynomial space. | 2001: Ajtai–Kumar–Sivakumar obtain randomized single-exponential-time SVP with exponential space, as described in the inherited paper. | 2007: Hanrot–Stehlé sharpen the enumeration analysis to n^{n/(2e)+o(n)} for SVP, retaining polynomial space. | 2010–2013: Micciancio–Voulgaris establish deterministic Voronoi-cell algorithms; the March 2012 revision gives roughly 2^{2n} time and 2^n space, followed by the SIAM journal publication. | 2015: Micciancio–Walter reduce enumeration preprocessing overhead while retaining the n^{O(n)} time scale. | 2026-01-06: Koyuncu–Linker–Ozel discuss a coarse-grained polynomial-memory sieving regime; a general exact-success and single-exponential-time guarantee for that regime is not established in the inspected analysis. | 2026: Albrecht–Lai–Postlethwaite connect hinted-ISIS algorithms to polynomial-memory single-exponential algorithms for broader lattice tasks, relying on rather than proving time-space hardness.
working_summary: Exact Euclidean SVP asks for a shortest nonzero vector in a lattice given by a rational basis. The question seeks single-exponential time in the rank together with polynomial working space. Known fast approaches retain exponentially much geometric information, while small-memory enumeration has a larger worst-case time scale. Combining both resources would clarify whether memory is essential to the strongest exact lattice algorithms. The saved review requires every stored bit and all recomputation to count, and does not treat heuristic memory reductions or unverified framework proposals as a proof of the universal guarantee.

title: Vinogradov's least quadratic nonresidue conjecture
importance_reason: A classical barrier in effective number theory governing the deterministic search for basic finite-field witnesses.
formal: For every epsilon>0, is the least positive quadratic nonresidue modulo an odd prime p bounded by p^epsilon for all sufficiently large p?
context:
No matching question about least quadratic nonresidues was found; placement uses the computational number-theory scope.

This short research proposal states the target identified in the September 2026 fundamental-problem search. The references give the source models and related results. A full self-contained formulation and detailed progress review remain to be written.
why: A classical barrier in effective number theory governing the deterministic search for basic finite-field witnesses.
status_note: Retained in the source-based research proposal dated 10 September 2026. No full resolution was found in that search; this is not a completed independent open-status review.
working_summary: A quadratic nonresidue modulo an odd prime is a nonzero residue that is not the square of another residue. Vinogradov's conjecture asks whether the least positive example is smaller than p^ε for every fixed positive ε at sufficiently large primes. The question asserts that a small witness of nonsquareness always appears very early among the integers. title: The exact capacity region of the two-user Gaussian interference channel
importance_reason: A foundational multi-user capacity frontier with a simple channel model, strong approximate results and unresolved exact tradeoffs. Recent disputed claims make the precise formulation and status record especially valuable.
focus_reason: A foundational multi-user capacity frontier with a simple channel model, strong approximate results and unresolved exact tradeoffs. Recent disputed claims make the precise formulation and status record especially valuable.
formal: Determine the capacity region C(a,b,P₁,P₂) of the memoryless real channel Y₁,t=X₁,t+aX₂,t+Z₁,t and Y₂,t=bX₁,t+X₂,t+Z₂,t for every fixed a,b∈ℝ and finite P₁,P₂≥0, with independent messages, average power constraints, no feedback or cooperation, and vanishing average decoding error. Equivalently, determine the exact function F(a,b,P₁,P₂,λ)=sup_{(R₁,R₂)∈C}[λR₁+(1−λ)R₂] for every λ∈[0,1], under the operational definitions below.
definitions: For a block of n uses, messages M_i are independent and uniform on {1,…,K_{i,n}}. Transmitter i applies a deterministic encoder f_{i,n}:{1,…,K_{i,n}}→ℝⁿ depending only on its own message. Its codebook satisfies (nK_{i,n})⁻¹∑_{m=1}^{K_{i,n}}∑_{t=1}ⁿ f_{i,n}(m)_t²≤P_i. All Z_{i,t} are mutually independent N(0,1) random variables independent of the messages. Receiver i applies a measurable decoder g_{i,n}:ℝⁿ→{1,…,K_{i,n}} to its own received vector. The probability that either decoded message is wrong is averaged over both messages and all noise. A nonnegative pair (R₁,R₂) is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes with this error tending to zero and liminf_{n→∞} n⁻¹ log₂ K_{i,n}≥R_i for i=1,2. C is the closure of achievable pairs, measured in bits per real channel use. Gains, powers and both codebooks are known to all terminals. Arbitrary encoding across time and predetermined time sharing with power allocation are permitted; transmitters have no messages in common, output feedback, or communication between them. C is compact, convex and downward closed, so the nonnegative supporting function F uniquely determines it.

context:
Two independent conversations share the same medium: each receiver sees its desired signal, a scaled version of the other sender’s signal, and Gaussian noise. With only one sender, Shannon’s formula gives the rate ½ log₂(1+P). With two senders, improving one link can make the other harder to decode. The mathematical object is therefore a two-dimensional region of feasible rate pairs. Knowing its largest total rate does not identify all tradeoffs between the users.

Han–Kobayashi coding splits each message into a part decoded by both receivers and a private part decoded only by its intended receiver. It includes treating interference as noise and decoding interference as special strategies. Time sharing can also allocate different powers to different phases while meeting the average constraints. Shang and Chen’s monograph organizes these inner bounds and the exact results in particular regimes, including the distinction between full regions and sum-rate capacity.

Strong interference is a solved benchmark. When |a|≥1 and |b|≥1, the capacity region consists of R₁≤½log₂(1+P₁), R₂≤½log₂(1+P₂), and R₁+R₂≤min{½log₂(1+P₁+a²P₂),½log₂(1+b²P₁+P₂)}. Both receivers can decode both messages. With a=b=0, the region is the rectangle given by the two individual bounds. These exact cases anchor the question but do not characterize arbitrary interference strengths.

Etkin, Tse and Wang show that a simple Han–Kobayashi strategy and new converse bounds locate the general region within a universal additive gap. Their celebrated one-bit theorem also gives high-signal-to-noise insights. A fixed gap can be extremely useful for system design while leaving the exact boundary unknown: it does not shrink merely because longer codes are allowed.

Recent work separates several different Gaussian-optimality questions. Nair and Zhao’s ISIT 2025 result identifies a substantial parameter range in the one-sided, or Z, channel where the optimized Gaussian-signaling region needs no multiplexing. This optimizes a particular achievable region; it does not prove that no other signaling distribution or coding strategy can do better.

Their January 2026 manuscript then shows that Gaussian distributions can be suboptimal within a single-phase Han–Kobayashi region when power control is disallowed. Its Conjecture 1 still asks whether Gaussian signaling with power control achieves full Z-channel capacity. Remark 2 reports difficulty verifying parts of an earlier Khandani proof claim. The counterexamples concern the restricted single-phase statement and do not disprove optimality after the allowed power allocation and time sharing.

Gohari, Nair and Zhao’s February 2026 work combines auxiliary-receiver and genie-aided converse techniques. Its Gaussian specialization captures known corner and sum-rate behavior, including associated changes in boundary slope. The theorem supplies an outer region rather than a general equality with an achievable region, so it advances the converse side without itself resolving the full target.

Khandani’s preprint, revised on 7 September 2026, makes a stronger claim: Gaussian Han–Kobayashi coding attains capacity throughout weak interference, with at most two time-sharing phases. This would settle a major part of the problem if established. The current revision has not been independently validated in this review. The earlier Nair–Zhao criticism predates it and cannot automatically be applied to every revised argument. This card therefore marks the present status as uncertain and records the claim explicitly.

The original short proposal cited a withdrawn paper by Huleihel and Merhav. Its claimed improvement using codewords with Gaussian memory was withdrawn in April 2018. Nair and Ng subsequently establish that temporally correlated Gaussian inputs do not enlarge the Gaussian Han–Kobayashi region once the comparison includes the appropriate scalar time sharing. The withdrawn result is retained only as a status correction, not as evidence of progress.
why: A defining problem in network information theory: even two interfering sender–receiver pairs expose limits of our ability to characterize optimal communication. An exact solution would distinguish which forms of message splitting, interference decoding and power allocation are fundamentally necessary.

Nair–Zhao’s January manuscript questions parts of an earlier version and disproves a restricted Gaussian-optimality statement without power control; that is not an adjudication of v12. This review has not established the correctness of the latest claim or a complete arbitrary-parameter characterization. Established partial results are separated from the claim. The original proposal’s arXiv:1508.05726 reference was withdrawn in 2018.

working_summary: Two independent senders share a Gaussian channel, so each receiver observes its intended signal mixed with interference and noise. The question asks for the exact region of jointly achievable communication rates for every pair of gains and power constraints. Splitting messages into common and private parts can let receivers decode some interference while treating the rest as noise. Determining the whole region would identify every tradeoff between the two users, beyond sum-rate or constant-gap guarantees. The saved review records an unverified 2026 weak-interference capacity claim and carefully separates restricted Gaussian-signaling results from full capacity.

title: The optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance tradeoff
importance_reason: A foundational coding-theory limit with a precise extremal target, a large gap between existence and converse bounds, and connections to combinatorics, information theory and quantum methods.
focus_reason: A foundational coding-theory limit with a precise extremal target, a large gap between existence and converse bounds, and connections to combinatorics, information theory and quantum methods.
formal: Determine R₂(δ)=limsupₙ→∞ (1/n)log₂ A₂(n,⌈δn⌉) for every fixed real δ∈(0,1/2), where A₂(n,d) is the largest size of a binary length-n code with minimum Hamming distance at least d.
definitions: A code C is any nonempty subset of {0,1}ⁿ; it need not be linear or efficiently encodable or decodable. The Hamming distance d_H(x,y) is the number of coordinates on which x and y differ. Require d_H(x,y)≥d for every pair of distinct codewords x,y∈C; a singleton satisfies this condition vacuously. A₂(n,d) is the maximum of |C| over all such subsets. A code has rate (log₂|C|)/n, measured in information bits per transmitted bit, and relative distance d/n. The ceiling fixes integer rounding. The limsup permits code families on a subsequence of blocklengths; existence of a full limit is not assumed. δ is fixed before n grows. All logarithms in this card are base two unless stated otherwise. The binary entropy function is h₂(t)=−t log₂t−(1−t)log₂(1−t), with 0 log₂0=0. The endpoint regimes are known: R₂(0)=1 and R₂(δ)=0 for 1/2≤δ≤1.

context:
A binary code represents messages by selected bit strings. Keeping codewords far apart lets a receiver distinguish them after errors, while selecting many codewords increases the amount of information carried by each transmitted block. The rate–distance function asks for the best possible compromise, allowing every conceivable code. It is therefore an information-theoretic limit that must be understood before asking how efficiently an optimal code can be built or decoded.

For a small example, the repetition code {000,111} has rate 1/3 and distance three, so it corrects one arbitrary flipped bit. The full set of eight three-bit strings has rate one and distance one, so it cannot correct even one arbitrary flip. Generally, disjoint Hamming balls of radius t around codewords are necessary and sufficient for unique correction of every pattern of at most t errors; this requires minimum distance at least 2t+1.

The Gilbert–Varshamov bound guarantees R₂(δ)≥1−h₂(δ). A maximal distance-d code covers the cube by balls of radius d−1, because otherwise another codeword could be inserted. Comparing the cube’s size with the volume of these balls gives the lower bound. In contrast, disjoint balls of radius roughly d/2 give the elementary Hamming upper bound 1−h₂(δ/2). The different radii create a genuine asymptotic gap.

McEliece, Rodemich, Rumsey and Welch’s 1977 linear-programming bounds greatly sharpen the converse. The first gives R₂(δ)≤h₂(1/2−√(δ(1−δ))); the second also uses constant-weight restrictions and is never weaker. The argument constrains a code’s distribution of pairwise distances through positivity relations, extracting information that a volume count loses. These were the long-standing general benchmarks, but they are no longer the strongest reported bounds after August 2026.

Alrabiah and Guruswami’s August 2026 preprint uses classical-input, quantum-output channels to prove stronger bounds for classical binary codes, including nonlinear codes. Mixed-qubit channels strictly improve the first MRRW bound, and a masked version strictly improves the second throughout 0<δ<1/2. Quantum states enter the converse proof as an analytical tool; the codes whose sizes are bounded still consist of ordinary bit strings. The result narrows the gap without matching the Gilbert–Varshamov lower curve.

Barg’s September 2026 note explains the relationship between this channel argument and a concurrent Delsarte-certificate proof. For the improvement of the first bound, he shows that the two variational expressions coincide. The geometric change is to associate a moving subspace, rather than a single vector, with each codeword, allowing a stronger packing argument. This provides a further derivation and interpretation of the new bound; it does not establish the exact rate function.

Lower-bound improvements require equally careful interpretation. Jiang and Vardy improve the finite-length Gilbert bound by a factor proportional to n in the fixed-distance regime they cover. Yuan and Zhu’s January 2026 preprint gives a concise probabilistic proof of a square-root-n improvement for linear codes and extends the method to quantum codes; the classical square-root factor had predecessors. After taking log₂ and dividing by n, any polynomial multiplicative factor contributes only O(log n/n). Such refinements do not increase the leading rate exponent.

Changing the error model also changes the answer. Capacity for independent random bit flips and capacity for list decoding are not the same quantity as the largest rate at a prescribed minimum distance. This card asks about worst-case pairwise separation with unrestricted binary codes. It also does not transfer improvements for sufficiently large alphabets directly to binary codes: changing alphabet and concatenating codes changes their rate and distance parameters.
why: The basic unresolved packing limit for reliable binary information. An exact answer would identify how much redundancy is intrinsically necessary for a prescribed worst-case separation, independently of algorithmic or algebraic restrictions on the code.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The August and September primary sources report genuine asymptotic upper-bound improvements beyond MRRW, but retain a gap above the binary GV lower curve. The exact function remains undetermined; polynomial multiplicative size improvements and results for other alphabets or coding models do not settle it.

title: The capacity region of a general two-receiver broadcast channel
importance_reason: A central multiuser capacity problem with a precisely defined rate region, decades of partial characterizations and recent challenges to the longstanding candidate inner bound.
formal: Determine the weighted capacity F(W,λ)=sup{λR₁+(1−λ)R₂:(R₁,R₂)∈C(W)} for every finite-alphabet discrete memoryless broadcast channel W(y,z|x) with rational transition probabilities and every rational λ∈[0,1]. C(W) is the capacity region for two independent private messages, vanishing average decoding error, and no feedback. Require a characterization admitting certified evaluation to arbitrary accuracy as specified below.
definitions: The nonempty finite alphabets X,Y,Z and the full table of nonnegative rational numbers W(y,z|x), summing to one for each x, are explicitly given. Over n uses, the conditional law is ∏_{t=1}^n W(y_t,z_t|x_t). Independent messages M₁ and M₂ are uniform on sets of sizes K₁ and K₂. One deterministic encoder, knowing both messages, sends xⁿ=f(M₁,M₂); receiver 1 observes only Yⁿ and estimates M₁, while receiver 2 observes only Zⁿ and estimates M₂. The average error is Pr[the first estimate is wrong or the second estimate is wrong], averaged over both messages and channel randomness. A rate pair is achievable if there are codes with block lengths tending to infinity, error tending to zero, and liminf (log₂Kᵢ)/n≥Rᵢ for i=1,2. C(W) is the closure of achievable nonnegative pairs. There is no common message, feedback, receiver communication, secrecy constraint, input-cost constraint or restriction on code complexity. Arbitrary dependence among a codeword’s symbols and time sharing are allowed. C(W) is compact, convex and downward closed; its support values for all rational λ determine it. Rational channel laws make the evaluation task a finite-input question.
answer_criterion: Give a matching achievability and converse characterization together with one terminating algorithm that, on input (W,λ,p), where p≥1 is an integer, outputs rational ℓ≤u with u−ℓ≤2⁻ᵖ and ℓ≤F(W,λ)≤u. No efficiency bound or single-letter restriction is imposed. A finite-dimensional formula with justified auxiliary-cardinality bounds, or a multiletter characterization with an effective certified convergence bound, would qualify. A bare limit over all block codes, an unevaluated regularization without an error bound, or numerically close inner and outer estimates does not. A proof that such uniform certified evaluation is impossible would instead settle the computability obstruction to this formulation.
context:
A broadcast channel has one transmitter that knows both messages and two receivers with different observations. This differs from an interference channel, whose transmitters know separate messages. The difficulty is to use one sequence of transmitted symbols for two purposes simultaneously: some structure can help both receivers, while other structure must carry information tailored to only one. A capacity region records all achievable tradeoffs, not just the best sum of rates.

The two point-to-point capacities alone do not determine this tradeoff. If a noiseless binary symbol X is delivered identically to both receivers, each receiver separately has capacity one, but independent private messages must satisfy R₁+R₂≤1. If X instead consists of two bits and each receiver gets its own bit, the region is the square 0≤R₁,R₂≤1. Both examples have the same individual capacities and different joint possibilities.

Marton’s coding method introduces auxiliary random variables describing private and shared layers and uses correlated codebooks to coordinate their information. Its inner region is achievable, so it gives a lower bound on capacity. For important structured channel classes it is exact, but neither efficient evaluation of that inner region nor optimality on those classes determines the general answer.

Gohari and Anantharam establish finite auxiliary-cardinality bounds for Marton’s region, turning the previously unrestricted optimization into a computable finite-dimensional problem. They also show that Marton’s inner region and the Nair–El Gamal outer region differ for some channels. A gap between an achievable region and an outer bound alone does not reveal which bound is loose; it is not evidence that an intermediate numerical value is capacity.

There is already an exact multiletter perspective: applying Marton’s construction to successively larger product channels and regularizing recovers the operational capacity region. Geng, Gohari, Nair and Yu develop this approach and establish new special cases. The obstacle in the present formulation is a certified finite answer: an asymptotic union without an effective convergence guarantee does not tell us how many channel uses must be examined for a requested accuracy.

Huang, Liu and Liu’s August 2026 preprint claims strict suboptimality of the full one-letter Marton region. It first finds a ternary-input example with a fixed-input-distribution advantage for two-letter coding, supported by interval-arithmetic bounds. A separate constraint-removal construction then produces a finite unconstrained channel with M(W⊗W)>2M(W), where M is Marton’s maximum private-message sum-rate. The unconstrained example has an enlarged alphabet; the result should not be stated as an unconstrained ternary-input counterexample.

That claimed inequality means a two-use code can beat the one-letter inner bound after normalizing rates per use. It does not compute capacity: further block lengths may improve the region again, and a matching converse is still needed. The paper explicitly retains the general capacity question as open. Its numerical certificates and auxiliary construction have not been independently rerun as part of this card.

On the converse side, Gohari, Liu and Nair’s ISIT 2026 work introduces two auxiliary receivers to strengthen outer bounds. These are hypothetical observers used in the proof, not additional terminals allowed in the communication model. Their reported bounds improve the sum-rate upper bound for examples such as the binary skew-symmetric broadcast channel, while still leaving an inner/outer gap.

Finding globally optimal numerical values is also separate from deriving the correct region. Dou and coauthors develop Blahut–Arimoto-style methods for evaluating inner and outer bounds, with convergence statements tied to the optimization’s structure. Such methods help explore examples, but convergence to a local optimum or to an optimum of an unproved bound is not a capacity theorem.
why: One of the smallest communication networks whose full capacity region is unknown. It asks for the basic law governing simultaneous transmission of independent information to different receivers, with consequences for coding methods and converse techniques throughout network information theory.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The general capacity question remains open in the checked primary literature, including the August 2026 paper. That paper’s narrower Marton-suboptimality claim is identified as a preprint result; accepting it would not solve the full characterization or certified-evaluation task.

working_summary: A broadcast channel sends one transmitter's input to two receivers with different noisy observations. The reviewed question seeks the exact private-message capacity region together with certified evaluation to arbitrary accuracy. One codeword must simultaneously carry information useful to each receiver, creating tradeoffs not determined by their individual capacities. A full characterization would resolve a fundamental multi-user communication problem beyond particular channel families. The saved review describes gaps between inner and outer bounds and an unverified 2026 claim that two-letter coding can outperform the full one-letter Marton region.

title: The Li–Li undirected multiple-unicast conjecture
importance_reason: A central capacity conjecture whose resolution would clarify the power of network coding and influence circuit and data-structure lower bounds.
formal: For every finite undirected network with positive rational edge capacities and independent unicast sessions, is the zero-error causal network-coding rate region, under the entropy-capacity convention below, equal to its fractional multicommodity-routing region?
definitions: Let G=(V,E) be a finite connected undirected graph, with capacities c_e>0, and let (s_i,t_i), i=1,…,k, be ordered pairs of distinct vertices. Different pairs may share endpoints. Source s_i initially knows its own message M_i, uniformly distributed over a finite alphabet; the messages are mutually independent. A finite deterministic code specifies in advance a finite sequence of directed edge uses. Each transmitted symbol is a function of messages initially at its sender and symbols previously received there. Every t_i must recover M_i for every message tuple. Local computation and storage are unrestricted; nonlinear functions are permitted. Let X_{u→v} be the whole tuple sent from u to v on edge {u,v}, and measure Shannon entropy H in bits. For a scale b>0, the code supports r∈R_{≥0}^k when H(M_i)≥b r_i for all i and H(X_{u→v})+H(X_{v→u})≤b c_{uv} for every edge. Define C(G) as the closure in R^k of all such supported rate vectors, over all finite alphabets, codes and scales. This explicitly fixes the entropy formulation used in the cited network-coding literature, with exact decoding and capacity shared between directions; it is not a definition using two independent full-capacity arcs. Define R(G) by nonnegative real path flows f_{i,P}, for simple s_i-to-t_i paths P, satisfying Σ_P f_{i,P}≥r_i and Σ_{i,P:e∈P} f_{i,P}≤c_e. The target is C(G)=R(G) for every G and session list. No multicast destinations, correlated sources, initial side information about other messages, or computation of functions in place of message recovery is supplied.
answer_criterion: Prove C(G)⊆R(G) for every specified network and session list; the reverse inclusion follows by routing and closure. Alternatively, exhibit a finite undirected instance with a coding-supported rate vector outside the closed routing polytope, together with a valid causal code and a proof of fractional-routing infeasibility. The latter can use a linear-programming dual certificate. Beating integral edge-disjoint paths, a particular routing algorithm, or a cut bound that is already larger than the routing optimum is insufficient. A multicast or directed-network advantage does not refute this unicast conjecture. A theorem about vanishing-error codes must be related explicitly to this zero-error entropy formulation.
context:
Routing treats each message as a separate commodity that consumes capacity along paths. Network coding lets an intermediate node combine messages before forwarding them. If a node knows bits x and y, it may send x⊕y; a receiver that already knows y can recover x. Whether the necessary side information can be supplied cheaply enough to improve total throughput depends on the entire network. The conjecture says that undirected edges always let fractional routing match the best coding rate for independent one-destination messages.

Fractional routing is essential to the comparison. A message may be split among many paths, and different commodities may share an edge up to its total capacity. This is more flexible than requiring one path per message or requiring edge-disjoint paths. The rate region is described by a linear program, so an apparent coding improvement over a greedy routing choice does not establish a gap. One must beat the optimum over all fractional routings.

The capacity convention also matters. An undirected edge of capacity one has one combined budget for both directions, rather than a separate budget of one in each direction. The formal statement follows the cited entropy-based definition: the entropy of each complete directional transcript is counted, and decoding is exact. Taking the closure permits limiting rates. This states precisely which capacity notion is being compared instead of assuming that all zero-error, fixed-length and vanishing-error conventions are interchangeable.

Cut constraints provide a necessary upper bound: information needed across a partition must cross its boundary. For multiple commodities, satisfying every cut constraint need not make the demands fractionally routable. Jain, Vazirani, Yeung and Yuval study the small K_{3,2} example with four same-side sessions. Its sparsity bound is one, while its maximum concurrent routing rate is 3/4; their entropy inequalities show that coding also cannot exceed 3/4. The gap between cuts and flows therefore does not by itself give a coding advantage.

Braverman, Garg and Schvartzman show that a counterexample would have consequences well beyond one small network. Any fixed coding advantage greater than one can be amplified into a family with a gap growing as a positive power of log |V|. A general logarithmic upper bound comes from multicommodity-flow and cut relationships. Thus even a modest strict separation would open the door to much larger asymptotic gains.

The conjecture is also connected to computation rather than communication alone. Afshani, Freksen, Kamma and Larsen show that it implies an Ω(n log n) lower bound for constant-degree Boolean circuits multiplying two n-bit integers. Their reduction turns a sufficiently small circuit into a forbidden network-coding advantage. This is a conditional circuit lower bound, not an already proved consequence of ordinary cut arguments.

Recent positive results remain sensitive to the session arrangement. Vamsi and Thakor’s ISIT 2025 work handles specified asymmetric demands in layered networks, including partition-symmetric demands in their Type-I bipartite family. It also studies gaps between routing constructions and information-theoretic bounds for three-layer cases. Such a gap is a reason to examine an instance more closely; it is not itself a demonstrated coding scheme outside the routing region.

An August 2026 preprint by Liu, Que, Li and Li reports new cases via graph metrics, including networks with at most five terminal locations and certain planar instances supported on at most three designated face boundaries. In the planar case, each session has both endpoints on one of those faces. Five terminal locations is not the same restriction as five sessions or five total graph vertices. The general conjecture remains explicitly open in that paper.

The strongest recent undirected separation located in this review changes the demand model. Braverman and He obtain a superconstant multicast coding advantage using locally decodable codes. Each source message there must reach a set of receivers, and the routing comparison is a Steiner-tree packing problem. Replacing those copies by independent unicast messages removes exactly the shared-message structure used by the construction, so the result does not disprove Li–Li.

title: The exact capacity of the binary deletion channel
importance_reason: The canonical capacity problem for synchronization errors, connecting coding, information theory, sequence reconstruction and the structure of optimal input processes.
formal: Determine the capacity function C(δ) of the binary independent deletion channel for every fixed δ∈[0,1], in bits per input bit, with matching achievability and converse results.
definitions: For input x=x₁⋯x_n∈{0,1}^n, retain each bit independently with probability 1−δ and output the retained subsequence in its original order. The receiver sees the subsequence and its length, but neither terminal sees the deletion locations; there are no erasure markers, substitutions, insertions, feedback or side channels. Both terminals know n and δ. A block code consists of deterministic maps Enc_n:[M_n]→{0,1}^n and Dec_n:⋃_{k=0}^n{0,1}^k→[M_n]. Its average error is Pr[Dec_n(Y)≠M], where M is uniform on [M_n] and Y is the channel output on Enc_n(M). A rate R is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes with liminf_{n→∞}(log₂ M_n)/n≥R and average error tending to zero. Define C(δ) as the supremum of achievable nonnegative rates. Encoding and decoding have no computational or storage restrictions. The parameter δ is fixed as n grows. Equivalently, Dobrushin’s coding theorem gives C(δ)=lim_{n→∞} C_n(δ), where C_n(δ)=(1/n) max_{P_X on {0,1}^n} I(X;Y), with base-two mutual information. These C_n are normalized per input bit; the random output length is not the normalization. The endpoints are C(0)=1 and C(1)=0.
answer_criterion: Give the exact capacity curve, with codes approaching the proposed rate from below and a converse showing that no higher rate has vanishing average error, for each fixed δ. The displayed multiletter limit already defines and characterizes the quantity; simply restating it is not a new determination of capacity. A capacity result at one interior parameter, a finite-block numerical interval, or a finite-order expansion near an endpoint is valuable partial progress rather than resolution of the whole curve.
context:
A deletion removes a bit and also hides where it belonged. For example, receiving 00 after sending three bits is compatible with several input strings and deletion patterns. The output length reveals how many symbols survived, but it does not reveal their positions. This uncertainty couples the interpretation of consecutive output symbols even though the deletion decisions themselves are independent.

If the receiver were additionally given the deletion locations, the channel would become the binary erasure channel with capacity 1−δ. Revealing information cannot make decoding harder, so C(δ)≤1−δ is an immediate upper bound. The challenge is to quantify the further loss caused by missing alignment. Counting surviving bits alone therefore does not determine the answer.

The basic coding theorem is known. Optimizing mutual information over distributions on n-bit inputs and letting n grow gives the operational capacity. Moreover, C_n(δ)−log₂(n+1)/n≤C(δ)≤C_n(δ). Thus the issue is not the absence of a definition or an approximation scheme in principle. The finite optimization has 2^n possible inputs, and its rapidly growing size obstructs useful evaluation at large block lengths.

The input bits should not automatically be assumed independent. Correlations can make runs of equal symbols easier to identify after deletions. Run-based constructions choose a distribution on run lengths and analyze how deleted runs disappear and neighboring surviving runs merge. Rubinstein and Con optimize such distributions to prove C(δ)>0.1221(1−δ) for every 0<δ<1. This establishes a positive constant fraction of the surviving-bit rate throughout the parameter range.

Near the noiseless endpoint, a much sharper asymptotic description is available. Kanoria and Montanari prove C(δ)=1+δ log₂ δ−A₁δ+A₂δ²+O(δ^{3−ε}) for every fixed ε>0 as δ tends to zero, with explicit constants A₁≈1.15416377 and A₂≈1.67814594. They also identify input distributions achieving this order. This determines several leading terms, but its remainder does not vanish identically at a fixed nonzero deletion probability.

Numerical converse bounds use finite channels in which the input and output lengths are bounded and the transition matrix is explicit. Blahut–Arimoto optimization can bound their capacities, which in turn upper-bound the unsegmented deletion channel. Pinto and Ribeiro’s 2026 implementation handles larger instances, including selected input lengths of 31, and reports C(δ)≤0.3578(1−δ) for δ≥0.64. These are computer-assisted bounds reported by the authors; this review has not rerun their large computations.

The half-deletion point illustrates the remaining gap. Rubinstein and Con report an achievable rate above 0.104075, while the 2026 upper-bound table gives 0.1896. A universal lower bound proportional to 1−δ is useful for the whole curve, but it can be weaker than a pointwise run-length optimization. These different types of statements should therefore not be collapsed into one purported best numerical bound for every parameter.

An August 2026 preprint by Chen claims a further half-deletion lower bound above 0.11032415, using joint information from several output runs and a rational certificate. Its asserted slightly sharper upper number is conditional on a precision assumption about a previously published table. This card records the new lower bound as a preprint claim whose certificate has not been independently reproduced here, and does not present the conditional upper number as a separately established converse. Even if the new lower bound is confirmed, a substantial gap remains.

This is a transmission problem: the sender may select a codebook designed for the channel. Trace reconstruction instead starts with an arbitrary unknown string and observes repeated independently deleted copies of that same string. Adversarial deletion codes also use a different error model. Progress in either neighboring subject can be informative without giving the exact Shannon capacity requested here.
why: The simplest channel with hidden synchronization errors still lacks an exact nontrivial capacity formula. Resolving it would establish how much information is fundamentally lost through missing alignment.
status_note: The 2026 primary sources retain a gap between achievable rates and converses. The August half-deletion improvement is recorded as an unreplicated preprint claim, not an exact-capacity solution. Checked through 11 September 2026.
