importance_reason: A classical foundational question of finite model theory and descriptive complexity, explicitly surveyed as an unresolved central spectrum problem. Its complement target is distinct from PTIME capture, query containment and ordinary finite satisfiability.
formal: For every first-order sentence φ over a finite relational vocabulary, does there exist a first-order sentence ψ over some finite relational vocabulary such that, for every positive integer n, ψ has a model with exactly n elements if and only if φ has no model with exactly n elements?
definitions: A vocabulary is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a specified positive integer arity; the list and the arities may vary with the sentence and are not bounded by a fixed global constant. Equality is allowed. Sentences use variables, relation atoms, equality, Boolean connectives and first-order quantification, with no free variables. A finite model has a nonempty domain A and interprets each k-ary relation as a subset of A^k, with equality interpreted as equality on A. The spectrum Spec(φ) is {n∈N:n≥1 and some finite model of φ has cardinality n}. The required equality is Spec(ψ)=N_{>0} minus Spec(φ). The vocabulary of ψ need not be the vocabulary of φ. No bound on the length of ψ and no effective transformation φ↦ψ are required. Restricting to relational vocabularies loses no ordinary first-order spectra: functions and constants can be represented by their graph relations with first-order axioms for totality and uniqueness. This is closure of the class of spectra, not a decision procedure for finite satisfiability.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
context:
A spectrum forgets the internal structure of a model and remembers only its possible finite sizes. A sentence can impose substantial combinatorial conditions on its relations, but the resulting object is just a subset of the positive integers. Asser’s question asks whether sizes excluded by one finite description can themselves be the allowed sizes of another finite description.

Negating the sentence does not solve the problem. If φ describes a graph consisting of disjoint edges covering all vertices, its spectrum contains the positive even numbers. An even-sized edgeless graph nevertheless satisfies ¬φ, so even numbers also belong to Spec(¬φ). Existence of a countermodel at a given size is different from absence of every model at that size.

The quantifier order is therefore essential. The target permits a new sentence ψ, chosen after φ but before n, which represents the entire complement simultaneously. It is not enough to provide a separate sentence for each excluded size. Allowing ψ a different vocabulary also prevents an arbitrary choice of representation from imposing an unintended extra restriction.

The spectrum problem helped shape finite model theory and descriptive complexity. The survey by Durand, Jones, Makowsky and More records Asser’s complement question as unresolved and connects the subject with bounded computational resources and structural restrictions on models. The importance here is the closure operation on the full expressive class, rather than one particular encoding of a graph family.

The existing logic-for-PTIME card asks for a logical characterization of efficient properties of individual finite structures. This card instead concerns the sets of cardinalities admitting some structure satisfying a sentence. It adds a different foundational question to the database and finite-model-theory bucket, even though both connect logic with computation.
why: Determine a basic closure property of finite first-order expressibility after taking possible model sizes.
status_note: No general resolution was found in the source and later-work searches through 11 September 2026. The principal detailed reference is the 2009/2012 survey; this is not a claim that every later paper on spectra was checked.
progress: 1950s: Asser formulates whether complements of spectra are spectra, as documented in the historical survey. | 2009–2012: The comprehensive survey retains the general complement question among its unresolved problems.

title: Decidability of conjunctive-query entailment in SROIQ
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: A longstanding foundational question connecting description logics, database queries and infinite-model reasoning, with sharply different outcomes for nearby restrictions.
formal: Does one total algorithm decide, for every finite SROIQ knowledge base K and every Boolean conjunctive query q, whether K⊨q under the standard semantics over all finite or infinite models?
definitions: Fix classical SROIQ without datatypes, using the syntax of Horrocks–Kutz–Sattler (2006), Definitions 1–6. Concept names denote subsets of a nonempty domain; nominal concept names denote singletons; individual names denote elements, without a unique-name assumption. Role names denote binary relations, inverse roles reverse their arguments, and U denotes the universal relation. Concepts are built from names, ⊤, ⊥, Boolean operations, ∃r.C and ∀r.C, qualified number restrictions ≥k s.C and ≤k s.C, and ∃s.Self. The last three require a simple role s. They mean, respectively, at least or at most k distinct s-successors satisfying C, and an s-edge from an element to itself. The nonnegative integer k is encoded in binary. K consists of concept inclusions C⊑D, individual assertions C(a), r(a,b), ¬r(a,b), a≠b, and a legal role box. Role inclusions have form w⊑R, with R a non-universal role name and w a nonempty string of non-universal roles, interpreted by relational composition. Regularity requires a strict partial order ≺ on roles satisfying S≺R iff Inv(S)≺R, such that each inclusion has w=RR, w=Inv(R), or w=S₁…Sₜ, RS₁…Sₜ, or S₁…SₜR with every Sᵢ≺R. Equivalent roles can first be identified. Transitivity and symmetry are represented by RR⊑R and Inv(R)⊑R. A role is non-simple if a composition of length at least two is included in it, or in one of its subroles, closing under inverse; all other roles are simple. Reflexivity assertions are allowed; irreflexivity, strict asymmetry and role-disjointness assertions require simple roles. U cannot occur in role-box assertions. These are the standard global regularity and simplicity restrictions, not unrestricted role-chain rules. The query is q=∃x₁…xₜ ∧ⱼαⱼ, where each atom is A(u) or r(u,v), A is a concept name, r is a role name, and terms are variables or individual names. Query roles may be non-simple. Query atoms have no negation, inequality or regular-path operators; variables may receive the same value. A model satisfies q when some assignment makes every atom true. K⊨q means every model of K satisfies q, including infinite models; an inconsistent K entails every query. Both K and q are input, and the sought algorithm must halt on every legal pair, with no prescribed complexity bound.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A knowledge base describes incomplete information about a world. Its assertions name some objects, while its general axioms can require additional unnamed objects in every possible world. A Boolean query asks whether a finite relational pattern must exist. The problem is to decide whether the pattern follows from the whole specification, rather than whether it can be found among explicitly stored facts.

For example, let K assert Person(a) and Person⊑∃knows.Person. Every model then contains a person who knows a person, so K entails ∃x∃y(Person(x)∧knows(x,y)∧Person(y)). No named witness for y is needed. The same individual may serve as both variables when the model permits it. More complicated queries reuse variables across several edges, requiring a single assignment that satisfies all joins simultaneously.

SROIQ combines concept negation, existential and universal restrictions, singleton concepts, inverse roles, counting and regular role chains. This expressive combination underlies the logical core of OWL 2 DL. The role restrictions in the definitions are substantive: removing regularity or allowing arbitrary counting over composite roles produces different logics. The original SROIQ paper supplies a decision procedure for consistency, but that alone does not answer arbitrary conjunctive queries.

The conjunction of K with ¬q is inconsistent exactly when K entails q, but the negation of an arbitrary joined relational pattern need not be expressible as a SROIQ knowledge base. Likewise, a finite graph built by a consistency tableau is usually a compact representation of models, not an ordinary database on which evaluating q automatically gives the right answer. Unfolding repeated nodes can change whether a query cycle exists.

Rudolph and Glimm resolved a major part of the surrounding question in 2010. They handle nominals, inverse roles and counting together, and obtain decidability for SROIQ when all binary query predicates are simple roles. Thus the mere presence of those three constructors is not the remaining obstacle. The full question on this card also allows the query to inspect roles affected by transitivity and more general role compositions.

A different positive frontier comes from Horn restrictions. Ortiz, Rudolph and Šimkus show decidability even for a stronger path-query language over Horn-SROIQ, with doubly exponential combined complexity. Horn knowledge bases exclude forms of disjunctive choice that full SROIQ permits. Their result is therefore highly relevant progress, while leaving the unrestricted combination of knowledge-base features and query joins unresolved.

The distinction between all models and finite models is particularly consequential. Rudolph proves undecidability of finite conjunctive-query entailment already in a fragment of SROIQ. This is not an undecidability proof for the semantics chosen here: the sets of countermodels differ, and the distinction can affect the answer even on a small example.

To see the difference directly, require every domain element to have exactly one r-successor and at most one r-predecessor, and require a named element a to have no predecessor. The role r can be simple. Such a knowledge base has an infinite model, the natural-number successor chain, but no finite model: on a finite set, an injective total successor function would be surjective. A fresh predicate A may be empty in the infinite model, so ∃x A(x) is not entailed over all models. Over finite models it is vacuously entailed, because there are none.

Steigmiller and Glimm’s 2019 absorption method addresses practical entailment checking in very expressive logics and is implemented in Konclude. Its termination argument depends on a bounded supply of newly generated nominals in the difficult feature combination. Useful empirical behavior and termination on substantial fragments do not establish a total procedure for every SROIQ input. This conditional termination is exactly why the inherited source continues to present full decidability as open.

There is relevant progress as recently as 2026, but on a different slice of the language. Ibáñez-García, Jung, Michielini and Murlak show that conjunctive-query entailment for S, which adds transitive roles to ALC, is 2ExpTime-complete; hardness already uses two transitive roles and a Boolean conjunctive query. Their May 2026 full version also treats restrictions giving smaller upper bounds. This settles a complexity question for S, not the decidability of full SROIQ.

A positive solution would establish that general finite query patterns can always be answered against this expressive ontology language in principle. A negative solution would identify a sharp gap between consistency checking and pattern entailment inside a standard logical framework. Either outcome would clarify which expressive features can be combined while retaining an algorithmic foundation for querying incomplete knowledge.
why: A basic decidability boundary for querying expressive ontologies: the logic has decidable consistency, but unrestricted conjunctive-query entailment still lacks a general resolution.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No general decision procedure or undecidability proof for Boolean CQ entailment over all SROIQ models was found in the checked sources. Simple-role queries, Horn fragments, finite-model undecidability and the 2026 complexity result for S concern distinct restricted problems.
progress: 2006: Horrocks–Kutz–Sattler define SROIQ and prove decidability of its standard consistency reasoning tasks. | 2010: Rudolph–Glimm establish query decidability with nominals, inverses and counting, including SROIQ queries restricted to simple roles. | 2011: Ortiz–Rudolph–Šimkus establish decidable path-query answering for Horn-SROIQ. | 2016: Rudolph proves finite-model conjunctive-query entailment undecidable in a SROIQ fragment; this uses finite semantics. | 2019: Steigmiller–Glimm present absorption-based checking, while explicitly retaining the full decidability question and a termination condition involving new nominals. | 8 May 2026: The revised full version of the AAAI 2026 paper proves 2ExpTime-completeness for S, including Boolean-query hardness with two transitive roles.
working_summary: An expressive ontology describes facts and rules that can require additional unnamed objects in every model. The reviewed question asks whether one terminating algorithm can decide all Boolean conjunctive queries against finite SROIQ knowledge bases. Such a query looks for a relational pattern, including joins that require several conditions to hold for the same objects. Consistency checking and known decidable fragments do not settle the unrestricted combination of query joins, counting, inverse roles, and role compositions. The chosen semantics includes infinite models, so the saved undecidability result for finite-model entailment addresses a different question.

title: Is containment of conjunctive queries under bag semantics decidable?
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: A longstanding central decidability question for the most basic duplicate-sensitive query language. It has broad consequences for query rewriting and connects finite-model counting with undecidability boundaries.
formal: Does a Turing machine exist that halts on every pair of finite conjunctive queries q_1 and q_2 with the same output arity and decides whether $q_1(D)(a)\le q_2(D)(a)$ for every finite bag database D over their common relational signature and every output tuple a? A query $q(x)\!:\!-A_1,\ldots,A_m$ is evaluated by $q(D)(a)=\sum_{h:h(x)=a}\prod_{j=1}^{m}D(A_j[h])$, where h ranges over assignments of its variables to the finite database domain and D(A_j[h]) is the nonnegative integer multiplicity of the instantiated tuple. Both input relations and query answers retain multiplicities.
definitions: A relational signature lists finitely many relation names and their arities. A finite bag database supplies a finite domain U and, for each relation symbol of arity r, a function U^r to the nonnegative integers. Zero means the tuple is absent. A query body is a finite list of positive relational atoms with variables or named constants as arguments; constants denote distinct fixed elements of U. Every variable, including every output variable, must occur in a body atom. Repeated occurrences of relation names, variables, or entire atoms are allowed and are interpreted by the displayed sum-product rule. Assignments fix constants. No disjunction, negation, inequality, comparison predicate, aggregation operator, or recursion is permitted. The output tuple lists the values of the head variables in order. Boolean queries have an empty head and return the multiplicity of the single empty tuple. The question is about deciding containment from the queries alone, with no database supplied and no size or multiplicity bound on databases.
answer_criterion: Construct a total algorithm deciding exactly this universal multiplicity inequality, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Enumerating counterexample databases only semidecides noncontainment. A procedure for set-valued databases, query equivalence, or a proper subclass of queries is insufficient; undecidability for unions, inequalities, or a modified numerical comparison is insufficient unless reduced to the stated plain-CQ problem.
context:
Containment asks whether one query can ever produce more of some answer than another. Under set semantics only presence matters. Under bag semantics, a join multiplies available copies and projection adds contributions from different witnesses. The multiplicities can therefore change even when the two queries return exactly the same set of answers.

For a minimal example, let q(x) have body R(x), and let r(x) have body R(x),R(x). If R(a) has multiplicity m, then q returns m copies of a and r returns m^2. Their answer sets always coincide, but the reverse bag-containment r contained in q fails as soon as m=2. This demonstrates why duplicate-insensitive rewrites need a different correctness argument.

For one fixed finite database, both values can be computed by enumerating assignments. The challenge is the quantifier over every database of every size and every choice of multiplicities. Noncontainment has a finite witness that can eventually be found by exhaustive enumeration. A decision procedure also needs to halt when no witness exists; a counterexample search by itself does not solve that side.

The 2025 seminar still identifies this as a longstanding unresolved boundary. Recent work establishes decidability for a restricted left-hand query in which existential variables do not participate in joins, while related work proves undecidability after extending the query language or numerical comparison. These results make the precise boundary especially significant: small changes around the basic formulation have known answers, but do not settle two unrestricted plain conjunctive queries.
why: Bag semantics captures duplicate-sensitive query behavior, and containment is a basic correctness test for query optimization. Its unknown decidability marks a fundamental gap between simple positive query syntax and unbounded counting over finite structures. The problem also connects database theory with homomorphism inequalities and arithmetic decision problems.
status_note: Open in the 2025 seminar, the June 2025 revised CQ-versus-UCQ paper, and the maintained problem list accessed 10 September 2026. No resolution was located in current searches. The problem includes bag input multiplicities and is not the separate bag-set variant.
progress: 1993: Chaudhuri and Vardi raise the bag-containment decidability question; the 2025 seminar traces the problem to their PODS paper. | 2024 / preprint posted 2025: Marcinkowski and Orda prove undecidability for nearby generalizations, including comparison after a supplied linear transformation of a Boolean query’s count. This is not the unmodified containment predicate. | 2025-03-21: Konstantinidis and Mogavero prove decidability when the left query is join-on-free and the right query is a general CQ. This extends the earlier projection-free decidable case. | 2025-06-01: The revised Marcinkowski–Ostropolski-Nalewaja paper develops techniques connecting CQ and UCQ containment, while explicitly leaving ordinary CQ-versus-CQ bag-containment decidability open. | 2026-09-10 check: Amarilli’s maintained question list continues to list bag-containment decidability. Current searches did not locate a resolution of the plain two-CQ formulation.
working_summary: Under bag semantics, database tuples and query answers have multiplicities rather than just presence or absence. The question asks whether containment of two conjunctive queries is decidable when their output multiplicities must be ordered on every finite bag database. Each query sums products of input multiplicities over satisfying assignments, so ordinary set-containment reasoning does not directly capture the comparison. A decision procedure would settle a basic semantic question relevant to duplicate-preserving query transformations. The saved review distinguishes progress for unions or restricted joins from the plain unrestricted conjunctive-query problem retained here.

title: Does naive evaluation over p-stable semirings converge in O((p+1)n) rounds?
area: Database theory and finite model theory
area_label: Database theory and finite model theory
original_area: Database theory and finite model theory
importance_reason: A foundational convergence question for semiring-valued recursion, with implications beyond one query language. Its historical significance is high, but a newly announced directly relevant paper makes current open status uncertain.
formal: Is there a universal constant C such that the following holds for every integer p>=0, every n>=1, every commutative p-stable semiring S, and every polynomial map F:S^n -> S^n with coefficients in S? Starting with x^(0)=(0,...,0), perform synchronous iteration x^(t+1)=F(x^(t)). There must exist an integer t<=C(p+1)n with x^(t+1)=x^(t). Here p-stability means $1\oplus a\oplus\cdots\oplus a^p=1\oplus a\oplus\cdots\oplus a^{p+1}$ for every a in S. The constant C is independent of the semiring, coefficients, number of monomials, and polynomial degrees. This is the grounded polynomial-system formulation of the source’s proposed linear convergence bound.
definitions: A commutative semiring has associative, commutative addition op-plus with identity 0 and associative, commutative multiplication op-times with identity 1. Multiplication distributes over addition, and 0 times a=0. No additive inverses are assumed. Powers use semiring multiplication and a^0=1. Every component of F is a finite sum of finite products of coefficients and variables; repeated variables and constant terms are allowed. S need not be finite. One round evaluates all components using only the previous vector, not partially updated coordinates. Equality means exact equality of semiring elements. The cost measure is the number of rounds, irrespective of the work needed to evaluate a component or represent an element. In a grounded Datalog program, coordinates represent individual derived facts and their values are annotations; using all n coordinates also includes any that remain zero.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal bound, or refute it by constructing systems whose first fixed-point time divided by (p+1)n is unbounded. A fixed example exceeding n rounds does not refute an unspecified constant C. A bound with a growing factor depending on degrees, coefficients, or n does not establish this target. A faster evaluation algorithm with a different update rule does not by itself bound the number of synchronous naive iterations.
context:
In ordinary Boolean Datalog, a derived fact switches from absent to present at most once. A nonstationary round must add a fact, so the number of possible facts bounds the number of rounds. Annotated recursion can improve the value attached to an already known fact many times. Counting how many coordinates exist therefore ceases to give an immediate termination bound.

The stability assumption controls repeated use of a single semiring element. It says that a sufficiently long truncated geometric sum absorbs the next power. The question asks whether a system of n interacting recurrences can multiply the resulting delay by only O(n), even when the equations are nonlinear. This is a structural claim about composition of recursive dependencies, not a bound on the time taken by one database join.

The examined Im–Moseley–Ngo–Pruhs preprint proves a polynomial convergence bound, with explicit dependence on sigma, the number of distinct coefficients referenced, and lambda, the maximum number of multiplicands. Its bound is O(sigma p n^2 (n^2 log(lambda+1)+log(sigma+1))) for positive p; the 0-stable case has a separate linear bound. Suppressing sigma and lambda would conceal part of the remaining challenge.

The 2025 seminar asks for O((p+1)n), matching the order of its stated lower bound. A newer paper titled Optimal Convergence of Iterative Methods for Datalogo is now listed by its authors. The inspected listings supply no theorem or accessible manuscript for that entry. This card therefore preserves the precise historical question with an uncertain current status; the title alone does not identify which convergence bound, iteration scheme, or semiring hypotheses it settles.
why: The problem asks whether local algebraic stability imposes a sharp global limit on recursive evaluation. A universal linear bound would explain why a broad class of annotated recursive computations needs only an output-scale number of rounds, while a separation would expose a fundamental cost of nonlinear interactions.
status_note: Open in the 2025 source. A directly relevant paper, Optimal Convergence of Iterative Methods for Datalogo, is announced on author pages accessed 10 September 2026. The inspected entry has no theorem text or manuscript link; the similarly placed arXiv link on the home page leads to a different paper on even-cycle listing. Do not treat this card as a verified currently open problem until the new result’s precise scope is checked.

The inspected arXiv v2 states the additional sigma and lambda dependencies explicitly. | 2025: Ngo records the gap between the polynomial upper bound and Omega((p+1)n), and proposes a matching linear upper bound. | 2026-09-10 check: Author publication pages list Optimal Convergence of Iterative Methods for Datalogo, with a forthcoming PODS 2027 label on Ngo’s page. No theorem text was obtained for that entry. Its relationship to this exact target requires verification.
working_summary: A polynomial system over a commutative semiring can be evaluated by repeatedly updating every coordinate from the previous vector. The question asks whether p-stability guarantees convergence after O((p+1)n) rounds from the zero vector. The proposed bound is linear in the number of coordinates and uniform across coefficients and polynomial degrees. It would sharpen convergence guarantees for grounded Datalog computations carrying semiring annotations. The saved formulation counts synchronous rounds rather than arithmetic time, so a bound on evaluation cost or a result for a different update schedule would address a separate resource question.
